snapshot.title: Riyadh airport hit again after deadly Houthi missile attack, Saudi authorities say
snapshot.evidenceText: Unidentified projectile strikes King Khalid airport as escalating attacks threaten to draw more countries into Yemen conflict Analysis: attack will force rethink of Trump strategy Unidentified projectile strikes King Khalid airport as escalating attacks threaten to draw more countries into Yemen conflict Analysis: attack will force rethink of Trump strategy A projectile hit a passenger terminal at the airport in Riyadh on Sunday, the day after a deadly missile attack on the facility carried out by Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthi rebel group killed 13 people. An unidentified projectile hit terminal 4 at King Khalid international airport, starting a fire and causing injuries, according to Saudi authorities. Air defences also intercepted a cruise missile in the vicinity of the airport. It was the latest of several attacks on the airport in the past week. The escalating attacks threatened to draw more countries into the Yemen conflict and further widen the regional fallout of the US-Iran war, which has already spread to Lebanon and Iraq. After Saturday’s strike on Riyadh airport, the US president, Donald Trump, said he was weighing whether to join the Saudi military campaign in Yemen, telling reporters: “We’re going to look into it.” The Iran-allied Houthis claimed to have launched several attacks on the airport, including the attack on Saturday, which killed 13 people and injured more than 300 – the deadliest attack on a Gulf country since the war with Iran started in March and an apparent escalation in the Houthis’ war with Saudi Arabia and the Yemeni government that Riyadh sponsors. In response to the attack, Saudi authorities extended the closure of the airport and said schools would be moved online until Thursday. The Houthis claimed that Saudi Arabia struck the airport in Yemen’s rebel-held capital, Sana’a, on Sunday, without providing more information on damage or casualties. Videos circulated on social media showing travellers walking through debris-strewn ground in the Riyadh airport as sirens blared. Four Saudi citizens, two Bangladeshi nationals, a Palestinian, a US citizen, an Egyptian, a Jordanian, a Syrian and a Sudanese were killed in the missile strike. On Sunday evening, Saudi authorities also confirmed King Fahd international airport in the eastern city of Dammam had been attacked, with the country’s civil aviation authority saying on X: “The assessment of the damage and verification of the safety of airport facilities were still under way, in coordination with the relevant authorities.” On Saturday night, the spokesperson for the Saudi-led coalition in Yemen, Maj Gen Turki al-Maliki, said the coalition would “respond firmly” to the attack, offering few other details. The Houthis said a Saudi airstrike on Sana’a on Sunday hit a home and killed a child, as well as injuring six others. The Houthis doubled down on their threats on Sunday, warning airlines, passengers and staff to stay away from Saudi airports. The group said “the worst is yet to come” if Saudi military action in Yemen continued. “We renew our warning to all airlines, experts, employees, workers and travellers against using Saudi airports and airspace, as they are vulnerable to attack and have become a theatre of operations for our forces,” the Houthis said on X. Trump said he would speak to the Saudi crown prince, Mohammed bin Salman, on Saturday night, after the previous attack on the airport. The US has already been assisting with intelligence cooperation and targeting, with about 200 US military advisers stationed in Saudi Arabia to help with the campaign. Until now, the US has not directly taken part in fighting against the Houthis. Direct US involvement could lead the group to resume its targeting of ships passing through the Bab al-Mandab strait, through which about 10% of global maritime goods transit. It would also further entangle the US in Middle East wars as the American public grows increasingly frustrated with the continuing Iran conflict. Trump faces the prospect of midterm elections in November with an unpopular war and soaring prices at home, threatening his party’s performance at the polls. Saudi Arabia is already carrying out airstrikes against the Houthis in Yemen. The Houthi government’s health ministry said coalition airstrikes over the last six weeks had killed 91 Yemenis and wounded 168, 60% of whom it said were women and children. Saudi-backed government forces in Yemen launched a campaign to push the Houthis back from the areas the group conquered over the last month. Despite claiming initial successes, the government forces have not been able to loosen the Houthis’ grip over areas closest to the Bab al-Mandab strait such as Perim Island. The Indian embassy in Saudi Arabia said one of its citizens died on Sunday after being wounded in the Riyadh airport attack a day earlier. The Egyptian woman killed in the attack on the airport was a flight attendant identified as Azza Ramzy, 28, who worked for the Saudi airline Flynas, according to Egyptian state-run TV. The Syrian woman was a widowed mother of four who had been living in Saudi Arabia for five years, a relative told the Associated Press. The Syrian embassy in Riyadh identified her as Buthaina Ahmad Oweida. Her niece, Nisreen Oweida, said her aunt was 56, from Syria’s northern Idlib province, and had left during the country’s civil war. She was living in Mecca and had been returning from a visit to her sister in Riyadh when she was killed, the niece said. The airport attack was met with a wave of international condemnation, including from the UN secretary general, António Guterres, and the president of the European Commission, Ursula von der Leyen. “Attacks by Iran’s proxies are pushing the region into a spiral of violence,” von der Leyen wrote on X. “They are destabilising crucial global transport and energy nodes.” The increasing intensity of Houthi attacks against Riyadh and its energy infrastructure has brought more foreign involvement in the Yemen war. Governments are facing pressure over oil prices, already high from the US-Iran war since March. On Monday, Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Turkey issued a joint statement saying they would move quickly to implement their mutual defence pact, including by speeding up the deployment of military forces in the kingdom. The UK said it would assist with defensive military support of Riyadh, providing refuelling for aircraft working to intercept Houthi missiles into Riyadh. Saudi Arabia has asked for further assistance from France, Egypt, the UK and Pakistan as its stock of interceptor missiles are running low. The Houthis launched a military campaign to take Yemen’s Red Sea coast in early September after months of escalating tensions with the Yemeni government and its Saudi patron. The campaign interrupted years of relative calm in the country after a 2022 UN-brokered ceasefire froze frontlines between the Houthis and the government. Despite the Saudi-supported counteroffensive, the group seems to have held on to its recent gains. It is unclear what further Saudi military action would look like against the Houthis, who resisted years of strikes by an international coalition, as well as by the US. Saudi Arabia led an international coalition that intervened against the Houthis in Yemen in 2015 after the group took over Sana’a and toppled the Yemeni government. Recent Houthi attacks against Saudi energy infrastructure, as well as Houthi military advances, have pulled Saudi Arabia back into the Yemen war.

snapshot.title: Saudi Arabia's Riyadh airport hit by second Houthi strike in two days
snapshot.evidenceText: An international airport in the Saudi capital Riyadh has been hit by a second strike in as many days, officials have said. A Saudi military spokesman said a projectile had hit King Khalid International Airport on Sunday, causing a fire in one of its passenger halls. Saudi Arabia's civil aviation authority said there had been injuries. It comes a day after a strike on the same airport killed 13 people and injured 308 others, following similar strikes earlier this week. The Houthis in Yemen said they were behind the attacks and warned airlines and passengers against using Saudi Arabian airports and airspace. The group said they had targeted the airport with a mix of ballistic and cruise missiles, as well as drones in the past 24 hours. They also attacked oil facilities and Dammam airport in eastern Saudi Arabia, their military spokesman Brig Gen Yahya Saree said. He vowed to continue the "escalating operations deep inside Saudi Arabia", warning that all Saudi airports were potential targets apart from those in the holy cities of Mecca and Medina. The Houthis have said they are targeting Saudi Arabia over its support for government forces in Yemen's civil war, as well as an air strike on the airport in Sanaa. On Sunday Maj Gen Turki al-Maliki, spokesman for the Saudi-led military coalition, said air defences had intercepted a missile near the airport in Riyadh, while authorities were dealing with the fire caused by an "unknown projectile" that hit Passenger Hall No 4. US President Donald Trump has said the US would "make a decision" and "move very quickly" on whether to strike the Houthis, while UK Defence Secretary Wes Streeting suggested the UK could "potentially" provide more support for Saudi Arabia. Saturday's strike was the deadliest single attack on a Gulf Arab country since the war between Israel, the US and Iran began in February. The Saudi-led coalition vowed to respond, calling it a "war crime". Four Saudi nationals, two people from Bangladesh and one person each from the US, Jordan, Palestine, Syria, Sudan and Egypt were among the dead, the Saudi civil aviation authority said. The Indian embassy in Saudi Arabia said on Sunday that an Indian man had succumbed to the injuries he sustained in the attack. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio condemned the attacks and confirmed that a US citizen was killed in the strikes. Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband said he was "appalled". The UK Foreign Office is advising against all travel to parts of Saudi Arabia, including areas within 10km (6.2 miles) of the border with Yemen, while other western embassies have warned their nationals about travel in the region. Houthi-run Al Masirah TV said "the Saudi enemy" had launched an air strike on Sanaa International Airport in Yemen's capital. Saudi Arabia has not confirmed the attack and the BBC has been unable to verify this claim. Abdullah Al-Alimi Bawazir, vice-president of Yemen's internationally recognised government, called for "decisive actions" from regional and international partners. Riyadh's airport was struck on Thursday, an attack that killed three Saudi nationals . The Houthis claimed responsibility and said they had used cruise missiles to target the airport. There were two other deadly attacks on Saudi airports in Abha and Riyadh in the two days prior to that. The latest uptick in violence comes after a temporary ceasefire between the Houthis and Saudi-led forces, brokered in 2022, collapsed in July. The conflict worsened after the Houthis seized strategically important stretches of the Red Sea coast in a rapid offensive, prompting Saudi strikes. Yemeni pro-government forces later said they had secured the regions. The Houthis currently control around a quarter of Yemeni territory and as much as 80% of the country's population. The Iran-backed armed group hopes to eventually seize complete control. Saudi Arabia fears this would lead to the establishment of an Iranian satellite state on its southern border. The boat was travelling from Djibouti to Yemen with 305 people on board, when it capsized near the port town of Obock on Thursday night. The Houthis have claimed responsibility for the attacks, which mark an escalation in the conflict. The families allege that men with links to the Saudi government helped those who carried out the 2001 attacks, something the country denies. The BBC reports from a school in Taiz, Yemen, where children are determined to keep learning despite the vicious civil war. Saudi-backed forces gave conflicting reports of whether they had also seized the port city of Mokha, near the Bab al-Mandab Strait.

snapshot.title: Saudi Arabia: Second strike hits Riyadh airport
snapshot.evidenceText: Sunday's strike came as the King Khalid International Airport remained closed after a deadly attack on Saturday, and after a warning from Houthi rebels in Yemen that "worse is yet to come." Dammam airport was also hit. King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia , was struck by an "unidentified projectile" for the second time in two days on Sunday, according to the Saudi-led coalition fighting Iran-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen . "King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh was subjected to a new attack on Sunday afternoon," the General Authority of Civil Aviation said in a statement, adding that it "resulted in injuries, and the assessment of the damage and verification of the safety of the facilities are still under way." Coalition spokesman Major General Turki al-Maliki also said that a cruise missile had been intercepted by air defense systems in the vicinity of the airport, but no further details were immediately available. The Houthis later claimed responsibility for the strikes, saying they had "carried out four qualitative operations in the past 24 hours using ballistic and cruise missiles and drones." A spokesman said the group targeted the Riyadh airport multiple times, as well as the Dammam airport in the east of the country and two facilities belonging to the Saudi state oil company Aramco. Later on Sunday evening, Saudi authorities also confirmed an attack on Dammam airport. Sunday's strikes came as Riyadh airport remained closed following an attack on Saturday which killed 12 people and injured over 300 more — the deadliest such strike on the kingdom in over a decade. On Sunday, the Indian embassy in Saudi Arabia confirmed that one of its citizens died after being wounded in Saturday's attack. "It is learnt that one Indian national injured in the Riyadh attack has unfortunately lost his life today," read a statement posted on social media. "We convey our heartfelt condolences to the family of the deceased." To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video The latest Houthi strikes also came just hours after the rebel group warned airlines and travelers to avoid Saudi airports. "We renew our warning to all airlines, experts, employees, workers and travelers against using Saudi airports and airspace, as they are vulnerable to attack and have become a theater of operations for our forces," read a statement released by the group on social media. It added that airports in the holy cities of Mecca and Medina would not be targeted. "We ‌urge everyone to take our warnings seriously," the statement continued, stating: "Saudi Arabia bears responsibility for any failed interceptions." To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video Saudi Arabia has stepped up its military involvement in Yemen in recent weeks, launching strikes against the Houthis and backing a Yemeni government counteroffensive after the rebels seized strategic territory along the Red Sea coast last month, including around the vital Bab el-Mandeb Strait. The Houthi-run health authority claimed this weekend that 91 Yemenis have been killed by the Saudi-led coalition in the last five weeks, 60% of them women and children. Earlier on Sunday, it said a child was killed and six people wounded in a suspected Saudi airstrike on a house in Sanaa. The Houthi-run Al Masirah TV also reported that Saudi Arabia had struck the international airport in Sanaa on Sunday afternoon. There was no immediate comment from Saudi authorities on the claims. "Unless the Saudi enemy stops its aggression and interference in Yemen, worse is yet to come, God willing," the Houthi-run Foreign Ministry said in statements carried by Al Masirah TV on Sunday, adding that its ​actions would be guided by the principle of reciprocity. The Saudi-led coalition, which supports the internationally recognized Yemeni government in its conflict against the Iran-backed Houthi rebels, vowed a tough response to the attack, which it labeled a "full-fledged war crime." The Houthi strikes on Riyadh come amid a surge in Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia this week, which have targeted other airports, military sites and oil infrastructure. The spike in attacks has followed a major military offensive by the Saudi-led coalition against the Houthis. The rebels, one of Tehran's regional proxies , have been fighting Yemen's government, which is recognized by the international community, since the outbreak of a civil war over a decade ago. While a truce in 2022 froze the conflict, it failed to secure a lasting peace deal. The US-Israeli war with Iran has seen fighting flare up again in Yemen, worsening an already severe humanitarian crisis . To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video US President Donald Trump on Saturday said he would be speaking to Saudi Arabia's de facto leader, Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, in the wake of the attack, which he said was "not acceptable." Trump also said that the US was "going to look" at potentially joining Saudi strikes against the rebels. On Sunday, European leaders expressed their "shock" at the attack on Riyadh airport. The president of the European Commission, Ursula von der Leyen, said the EU stands in "solidarity with Saudi Arabia" as she condemned the "dangerous escalation." "These attacks by Iran's proxies are pushing the region into a spiral of violence. They are destabilizing crucial global transport and energy nodes with shock waves sent through the world," von der Leyen said. German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul "firmly" condemned what he described as "a terrorist act against Saudi Arabia and civil aviation". "Our thoughts are with the victims and I send my sincere condolences to their loved ones," he said on X. UK Defense Secretary Wes Streeting slammed the attacks as "contemptible" and a "dangerous escalation," while the French Foreign Ministry condemned the "heinous attack" and stressed its "total solidarity" with Saudi Arabia. Russia, which is a strategic partner of Iran, also condemned the Houthis' attack and called for the hostilities to end "through political and diplomatic means." Australia, meanwhile, has urged its citizens in the Saudi capital to "shelter in place" amid the escalating attacks. snapshot.evidenceText: 5 October: King Abdullah bun Abdulaziz International Airport and Najran International Airport were targeted, according to the Saudi civil aviation authority, who said that no deaths were reported and three people were injured. A statement from Yemen's Houthi group that evening claimed the group had carried out attacks on different locations, including King Khalid Airport in Riyadh, Aramco facilities in Rabigh, and Abha Airport. 6-7 October: Two separate attacks took place over this period, one at King Khalid International Airport, resulting in one death and eight injuries, and another at Abha International Airport, killing two people and injuring 28. Houthi statements claimed responsibility for an attack on Abha International Airport and on King Khalid International Airport. 8 October: King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh was subject to two attacks that killed three Saudi Arabian nationals, according to Saudi's civil aviation authority, The Houthis said they had attacked the airport with ballistic missiles. 10 October: The same airport was targeted again yesterday, killing 12 people and injuring over 300, the Saudi civil aviation authority confirmed. A Houthi spokesman statement reiterated a "warning" to those using Saudi airports and airspace. 11 October: The Saudi-led coalition said further attacks had been launched on the airport, with an "unknown projectile" hitting a passenger hall and causing a fire. On Sunday, the Houthis said they had carried out three phases of attacks on the airport, starting on Friday evening which "resulted in the complete closure of the airport".

snapshot.evidenceText: Saudi authorities said Sunday that King Fahd International Airport in Dammam has been attacked, with few details. The city is on the Persian Gulf near Bahrain and Qatar. The statement came hours after authorities said the international airport in the capital, Riyadh, had been attacked once again. The Flightradar24 monitor noted at least one flight diverting from the airport in Dammam. Iran-backed Houthi rebels in neighboring Yemen have been claiming a series of attacks in the past week on Saudi airports and military and oil facilities. THIS IS A BREAKING NEWS UPDATE. Check back for updates. AP’s earlier story follows below. A projectile struck a passenger terminal at the international airport in Riyadh on Sunday, a day after a missile hit the same terminal and killed 12 people, the Saudi-led coalition fighting Iran-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen said. The Houthis claimed responsibility for those attacks and others. Saudi authorities said there were injuries in the latest attack on the King Khalid International Airport complex for terminals 3 and 4 for domestic flights. Saturday’s missile attack was the deadliest in a Gulf Arab nation since the Iran war began, with another 300 people wounded, some critically. The airport was still closed Sunday. The sharp escalation in the new front in the war threatens to draw in greater U.S. military involvement, as President Donald Trump has said he is weighing joining the fight against the Houthis. There was no immediate White House comment Sunday. India’s embassy in Saudi Arabia said one of its citizens died Sunday of injuries sustained in Saturday’s attack, which would bring the toll to 13. The latest strike in Riyadh came shortly after the Houthis said the airport in the rebel-held Yemeni capital of Sanaa had been struck again, and blamed the Saudis. At stake, again, in this escalation are global supplies and prices of oil as well as commercial shipping through a crucial alternative waterway to the Iran-threatened Strait of Hormuz — along with civilians and aviation throughout the region. Trump on Saturday also said he planned to speak with Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, who has been seeking assistance. A U.S. intervention could prompt the Houthis to halt shipping through the Bab el-Mandeb Strait at the southern end of the Red Sea off Yemen and further restrict the flow of oil out of the Persian Gulf. The rebels seized key areas along the strait last month and the Saudi-led coalition has been trying to seize them back. Saudi Arabia is running low on missile interceptors and has asked France, Britain, Pakistan and Egypt to deploy air defense support to the region, regional officials told The Associated Press last month, with one noting that the U.S. has seen its own stock dwindle during the war with Iran. Sunday’s attack occurred as the Saudis hosted a major international energy conference in Riyadh, with other high-profile events including an investment gathering on the horizon. Saudi Arabia under Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman has sought to open more to the world as a business and tourism destination, but the Houthi attacks threaten those efforts. “There is no way that somebody will break our back. We are like a phoenix, we come out of the ashes all the time,” the Saudi energy minister, Prince Abdulaziz bin Salman Al Saud, told the conference. He added that the kingdom is also working on pipelines in addition to the East-West one that was attacked and closed for days last month, with no details. Earlier Sunday, the Houthi-run health ministry said a child was killed and six people wounded in a suspected Saudi airstrike on a house in Sanaa. The ministry also said 91 Yemenis have been killed by the Saudi-led coalition in five weeks, 60% of them women and children. There was no immediate comment from Saudi authorities on the claims. On Sunday, the Houthis also claimed attacks on King Fahd Airport in the city of Damma, as well as oil and gas facilities in the kingdom’s east. They have targeted the Riyadh airport, which has no military facilities, every day since Wednesday. The rebels again warned “all airlines, experts, employees, workers and ​travelers against using Saudi airports and airspace, as they are vulnerable to attack and have become a theater of operations for our ​forces.” Several international airlines have suspended flights for varying periods. Saudi authorities said the dead in Saturday’s attack included four Saudi citizens, two Bangladeshi nationals, a Palestinian, a U.S. citizen, an Egyptian, a Jordanian, a Syrian and a Sudanese. The Egyptian woman was a flight attendant for Saudi airline Flynas identified as Azza Ramzy, according to Egyptian state-run TV. The Syrian woman was a widowed mother who had been living in Saudi Arabia, relative Nisreen Oweida told The Associated Press. The Syrian Embassy identified her as Buthaina Ahmad Oweida. Until recently, the Houthis had been largely on the Iran war’s sidelines, but they have developed their military capabilities in recent years to become one of Tehran’s most powerful allies. Now, they are helping Iran to pressure a key U.S. ally. The Saudis and the Houthis began fighting in 2015, when the kingdom entered Yemen’s civil war on behalf of the internationally recognized government. Relative calm after a 2022 ceasefire ended in July when the Houthis resumed attacks, saying the Saudis fired on the Sanaa airport as a plane from Iran was trying to land. The attack revived anger over the Saudi-led blockade that has largely isolated Houthi-run areas. The rebels say they have now imposed a blockade on Saudi Arabia. Fighting has escalated, with the Saudi-led coalition providing air support for Yemeni government forces attempting to reverse recent Houthi gains near the Bab el-Mandeb, a crucial alternative to the Strait of Hormuz, where Iran has attacked ships. Ahmed Nagi, the International Crisis Group’s senior analyst for Yemen, said the Houthi pressure tactics could backfire: “Rather than pushing Riyadh to step back, attacks on critical Saudi infrastructure could make the Saudis more determined to continue the campaign.” A previous version of this report has been corrected to show that the Egyptian killed was a woman, not a man. Frankel and Anna reported from Jerusalem. snapshot.title: Trump says he is 'going to look at' joining Saudi Arabia in the fight against Iran-backed Houthis after deadly airport strike
snapshot.evidenceText: President Donald Trump said he is considering joining Saudi Arabia in its retaliation against Tehran-backed Houthis in Yemen after a deadly attack on Riyadh's main airport, a move that could draw the U.S. further into a second front in the Iran war . "We may. We're going to look at it," Trump told reporters outside the White House on Saturday when asked if the U.S. would back Saudi Arabian strikes. "We just found out about the recent attack. So, we'll make a decision. We move very quickly." Two Saudi Arabian government officials told MS NOW that the kingdom is requesting "urgent defense support" from the U.S. following the attacks. The officials, including a senior member of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, did not want to be identified because of the matter's sensitivity. They added that the U.S. needs to intervene "as soon as possible" to help the Saudi-led coalition in Yemen fight the Houthis. The White House did not immediately respond to a CNBC request for comment. On Sunday, a projectile struck a passenger terminal at the Riyadh airport, one day after a missile struck the same terminal, the Associated Press reported. No immediate details were available about the latest strike on the King Khalid International Airport complex for terminals 3 and 4 for domestic flights, AP said. The Saudi General Authority of Civil Aviation said Saturday's attack on King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh killed 12 people and injured 309 others, the country's official Saudi Gazette media outlet reported . Colonel Turki Al-Maliki, the spokesman for the Saudi-led Coalition to Support Legitimacy in Yemen, which has been leading the fight against the Houthis, described the attack as a "war crime." "Therefore, the Joint Forces Command of the Coalition will respond decisively to this terrorist attack in accordance with the Customary International Humanitarian Law," Al-Maliki said in a post on X. It was the second deadly assault on Riyadh's airport in less than a week. Three Saudi nationals, including a pilot , were killed in attacks on the facility by Iran-backed Houthi militants on Thursday. Following Saturday's attack, the Houthis renewed their warning against using Saudi airports. "We renew our warning to all airlines, experts, employees, workers and travellers against using ⁠Saudi ‌airports and airspace, as they are vulnerable to attack and have become ⁠a theatre of operations for our forces, with the exception of the airports in (the holy cities of) Mecca and Medina," the Houthis said in a post on X. Saudi Arabia, a key U.S. ally in the Middle East, intervened in Yemen's civil war between the Houthis and its internationally recognized government after the group seized the Yemeni capital Sanaa in 2014. Last month, the Trump administration approved the potential $24.3 billion sale of nearly 50 F-35 warplanes to Saudi Arabia in what was seen as a major boost for the kingdom as it faces intensifying attacks from the Houthis. The sale is under congressional review. The Saudi energy ministry said a long-planned international energy conference will still take place in Riyadh on Sunday, Reuters reported. The five-day WPC Energy Congress ⁠is taking place at a convention center near King Khalid airport. State television told Reuters that more than 70 ministers, ⁠300 company executives and representatives of more than 25 international energy organizations have confirmed their attendance, though it was not clear ⁠whether the participants would attend in person or virtually. Reuters said a ministerial meeting of the International Energy Forum is also set to take place, with its plenary session to be held behind closed doors. In addition to attacks on civil aviation, the Houthis have also been trying to choke off oil tanker traffic through the Bab el Mandeb strait, a key entry point to the Red Sea, as Iran has effectively done in the Strait of Hormuz to the north of the Arabian Peninsula. Earlier this month, Yemeni government forces said they reclaimed the strategic port city of Mokha from the Houthis. Energy prices have soared since the start of the Iran war, which began with U.S. and Israeli airstrikes on Iranian targets on Feb. 28, putting pressure on consumers globally. The surge in domestic fuel prices has been a key issue for voters ahead of next month's U.S. midterm elections. But that support would be expensive militarily. "Potential U.S. involvement in the Saudi-Yemeni government air campaign to degrade Houthi ballistic missile capabilities would mark the first direct U.S. military action against the group since the conclusion of Operation Rough Rider in May 2025," according to the Critical Threats Project, part of the American Enterprise Institute think tank. The offensive aimed to suppress the Houthis' capabilities, but recent attacks show the group has regrouped. "After seven months of war, there are questions about the U.S. capacity to wage a sustained campaign against the Houthis, return to combat against Iran if necessary, and prepare for contingencies in other parts of the world, notably East Asia," Steven Cook, an expert on Arab and Turkish politics at the Council on Foreign Relations think tank, wrote last month. Meanwhile, the United Kingdom's defense secretary said his government is also examining how to support Saudi Arabia. "I've spoken to my Saudi counterpart [Khalid bin Salman] on a number of occasions in recent weeks to look at what more we can do to support Saudi Arabia, and I'm afraid last night explains precisely why we are providing that support," Wes Streeting said in an interview on BBC television on Sunday. Streeting said the U.K. is not getting involved in offensive operations "at this stage." "We've always been clear that there isn't a military solution to this conflict," Streeting added. representative.title: Saudi-led coalition vows to ‘respond decisively’ to deadly Riyadh airport attack | The National

snapshot.title: Saudi-led coalition vows to ‘respond decisively’ to deadly Riyadh airport attack | The National
snapshot.evidenceText: The Saudi-led coalition in Yemen has vowed to “respond decisively” to a Houthi attack on Riyadh that killed 12 people and wounded more than 300. Coalition spokesman Maj Gen Turki Al Malik condemned Saturday’s strike on King Khalid International Airport as “a full-fledged war crime according to the customary international humanitarian law”. “It is a heinous act that contradicts all principles, values, and ethics,” he said on Sunday morning, adding that the coalition would respond in accordance with international humanitarian law. The airport was closed as a precaution on Saturday. Authorities on Sunday extended the shutdown by 24 hours, until 1am local time on Monday, flight-tracking platform Flightradar24 said. Passengers were advised to check with their airlines for updates. US President Donald Trump said Washington could join Saudi Arabia in strikes against the Houthis, who are backed by Iran, following the attack , which killed an American citizen. Asked whether the US would participate in any Saudi action, Mr Trump said: “We may. We're going to look at it.” “We just found out about the recent attack, so we'll make a decision. We move very quickly,” he added. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio condemned the strike, saying it had taken “numerous innocent lives, including an American citizen”. “These reprehensible attacks demonstrate a blatant disregard for innocent civilian life. They must stop now,” Mr Rubio wrote on X. “We stand with the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia and its people and extend our condolences to the victims and their families.” UN Secretary General Antonio Guterres said he was “deeply shocked” by the attack and called for an immediate halt to strikes on civilians and civilian infrastructure, warning that such attacks violate international law. UN special envoy for Yemen Hans Grundberg described the latest series of attacks as a “grave escalation”, saying it threatened regional security, perpetuated violence and further complicated efforts to secure peace in Yemen. He urged the Houthis to cease the attacks and respect international humanitarian law. Governments in the region and beyond rallied behind Riyadh. Pakistani Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif called the attack “completely unacceptable”, reaffirming Islamabad’s “unwavering solidarity” with the kingdom and its commitment to Saudi Arabia’s sovereignty, territorial integrity and security. Qatar described the strike as a “grave violation” of Saudi sovereignty, stressing that the kingdom’s security was integral to its own and to that of Gulf Co-operation Council states. Jordan also condemned the attack, reporting that one Jordanian was was killed and four wounded. Kuwait condemned what it described as a “blatant assault” by the Houthis, according to the state-run Kuwait News Agency. It renewed its “absolute solidarity” with Saudi Arabia and called on the international community to take a firm position to protect civilian sites and hold those responsible to account. The Netherlands also condemned the attacks on Saudi Arabia, including strikes on multiple airports that caused casualties. Dutch Foreign Minister Tom Berendsen expressed condolences to victims’ families, saying the Netherlands stood in “full solidarity with the people of Saudi Arabia and our Gulf partners”. Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney called the attacks “abhorrent”, saying there could be no justification for attacking civilian infrastructure. US Democratic Senator Chris Murphy was among those to criticise Mr Trump, writing that the situation now represented “a full regional war” and the US President had started the conflict. "This is now a full regional war. Started by Donald Trump. For no good reason," he wrote on X. "It’s a civilian airport that should never, ever be a target. This campaign of terror by the Houthis must stop immediately," he added.

representative.title: Why Saudi airport attacks matter for Bangladesh | The Daily Star

snapshot.title: Why Saudi airport attacks matter for Bangladesh
snapshot.evidenceText: Copyright: Any unauthorized use or reproduction of The Daily Star content for commercial purposes is strictly prohibited and constitutes copyright infringement liable to legal action. The latest wave of attacks on Saudi airports has killed two Bangladeshis and forced Biman Bangladesh Airlines to suspend its Dhaka-Riyadh flight, bringing the escalating security threat closer to home for Bangladeshis travelling to the kingdom for work and pilgrimage. Saudi Arabian civil aviation authority said 12 people, including two Bangladeshis, were killed and 309 others injured in an attack on Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport on October 10. The identities of the two Bangladeshis could not be immediately established. Besides, four Bangladeshis are receiving treatment in the intensive care unit (ICU) of a hospital in Riyadh after the attack, State Minister for Foreign Affairs Shama Obaed Islam said today. This attack, the third on Riyadh airport within a week, damaged airport facilities and prompted a temporary suspension of operations, with flights cancelled or diverted. Biman announced on Saturday that its Dhaka-Riyadh-Dhaka flights BG339 and BG340 had been suspended until further notice, citing the suspension of inbound flights at the Riyadh airport. The disruption has also affected other airlines operating between Dhaka and Riyadh. According to CAAB figures reported by Prothom Alo, several flights operated by Saudia and Riyadh Air were cancelled by Sunday morning following the closure of the airport in Riyadh. A US-Bangla Airlines flight was also reported to have diverted on Saturday, arriving in Dhaka early Sunday. For Bangladesh, any prolonged disruption in such a major hub as Riyadh could have wide-ranging consequences. Saudi Arabia is a major destination for Bangladeshi migrant workers, while Jeddah and Madinah are key gateways for those travelling for Umrah and, during the Hajj season, the annual pilgrimage. The demand is reflected in figures cited by the Bangladesh Civil Aviation in August, when its chair said around 1.1 million Bangladeshis travelled to Saudi Arabia through indirect routes. The reference period for the figure was not specified. The two countries also agreed in August to increase direct passenger flights from 49 to 84 a week, reflecting efforts to expand capacity in this corridor. These are permitted flight frequencies, and not the number of flights actually operated. Nonetheless, it reflects the growing traffic on this vital route. Saudi Arabia was Bangladesh's largest source of remittance in the 2025-26 fiscal year, with inflows of $5.85 billion, up from $4.26 billion the previous year, according to Bangladesh Bank. Although remittances do not represent airline revenue, the figures are important as they underline the economic importance of maintaining connectivity between the two countries. Many of the journeys to Saudi Arabia are tied to employment commitments, visa conditions, and prepaid accommodation arrangements. Connectivity delays or flight cancellations could create additional difficulties for passengers with limited flexibility as regards their travel plans. The security threat has also expanded to eastern Saudi Arabia, where the Saudi-led coalition in Yemen reported that a projectile landed near King Fahd International Airport in Dammam late Saturday. Coalition spokesman Major General Turki Al-Maliki confirmed the incident. The development is significant for Bangladesh because Dammam is another destination served by Biman and used by travellers heading to Saudi Arabia's Eastern Province. The incident widens the geographical concern beyond Riyadh, where repeated attacks have already disrupted airport operations. On October 9, the European Union Aviation Safety Agency (EASA) expanded its warning for Saudi Arabia, advising airlines to avoid additional portions of Saudi airspace following the attacks on Riyadh. The revised advisory recommends that airlines avoid two designated areas, including an additional area in the northwest, while exercising caution elsewhere in the Jeddah Flight Information Region. Aviation safety organisation OPSGROUP has gone further, recommending that its members avoid Saudi airspace entirely, including the use of Saudi airports as alternate landing destinations. For airlines operating between Bangladesh and Saudi Arabia, these warnings would require strengthening contingency arrangements in case of unforeseen disruptions. Flight-tracking records reviewed by The Daily Star show that disruptions on Bangladesh-Saudi services had begun before Saturday's attack, although the reasons for individual incidents could not be independently established. Saudia's Dhaka-Riyadh flight SV805 was listed as cancelled on October 8. The same service experienced a delay of approximately six hours on October 6, while delays exceeding an hour were also recorded on October 3 and 4, before the latest wave of attacks began. A Biman flight from Dhaka to Jeddah was recorded by Flightradar24 as diverting to Madinah on October 6 before continuing to its destination. The reason could not be ascertained. On October 9, Saudia's Dhaka-Jeddah flight SV809 departed 42 minutes behind schedule, according to Flightradar24. The latest developments raise questions about how airlines operating between Bangladesh and Saudi Arabia would maintain services if attacks on airports or restrictions on surrounding airspace continue. The situation also draws attention to contingency arrangements, including alternative landing options, passenger rebooking, accommodation assistance and communication during sudden disruptions. Changes to routes can also affect fuel consumption, aircraft utilisation, crew duty hours and subsequent flight schedules. The latest casualties and confirmed flight suspension demonstrate that the escalating security situation now has direct consequences for Bangladesh. The concern is no longer confined to suspended flights to Riyadh. With security threats emerging near other Saudi airports, the risks extend to a travel corridor that supports Bangladesh's overseas workforce, pilgrimage traffic and wider economic ties with the kingdom. How airlines and aviation authorities on both sides maintain the connectivity amid an increasingly volatile security environment is now the larger challenge. representative.title: Saudi coalition vows retaliation after deadly Houthi attack on Riyadh airport | Saudi Arabia | The Guardian
representative.author: William Christou

snapshot.title: Riyadh airport hit again after deadly Houthi missile attack, Saudi authorities say
snapshot.evidenceText: Unidentified projectile strikes King Khalid airport as escalating attacks threaten to draw more countries into Yemen conflict Analysis: attack will force rethink of Trump strategy Unidentified projectile strikes King Khalid airport as escalating attacks threaten to draw more countries into Yemen conflict Analysis: attack will force rethink of Trump strategy A projectile hit a passenger terminal at the airport in Riyadh on Sunday, the day after a deadly missile attack on the facility carried out by Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthi rebel group killed 13 people. An unidentified projectile hit terminal 4 at King Khalid international airport, starting a fire and causing injuries, according to Saudi authorities. Air defences also intercepted a cruise missile in the vicinity of the airport. It was the latest of several attacks on the airport in the past week. The escalating attacks threatened to draw more countries into the Yemen conflict and further widen the regional fallout of the US-Iran war, which has already spread to Lebanon and Iraq. After Saturday’s strike on Riyadh airport, the US president, Donald Trump, said he was weighing whether to join the Saudi military campaign in Yemen, telling reporters: “We’re going to look into it.” The Iran-allied Houthis claimed to have launched several attacks on the airport, including the attack on Saturday, which killed 13 people and injured more than 300 – the deadliest attack on a Gulf country since the war with Iran started in March and an apparent escalation in the Houthis’ war with Saudi Arabia and the Yemeni government that Riyadh sponsors. In response to the attack, Saudi authorities extended the closure of the airport and said schools would be moved online until Thursday. The Houthis claimed that Saudi Arabia struck the airport in Yemen’s rebel-held capital, Sana’a, on Sunday, without providing more information on damage or casualties. Videos circulated on social media showing travellers walking through debris-strewn ground in the Riyadh airport as sirens blared. Four Saudi citizens, two Bangladeshi nationals, a Palestinian, a US citizen, an Egyptian, a Jordanian, a Syrian and a Sudanese were killed in the missile strike. On Sunday evening, Saudi authorities also confirmed King Fahd international airport in the eastern city of Dammam had been attacked, with the country’s civil aviation authority saying on X: “The assessment of the damage and verification of the safety of airport facilities were still under way, in coordination with the relevant authorities.” On Saturday night, the spokesperson for the Saudi-led coalition in Yemen, Maj Gen Turki al-Maliki, said the coalition would “respond firmly” to the attack, offering few other details. The Houthis said a Saudi airstrike on Sana’a on Sunday hit a home and killed a child, as well as injuring six others. The Houthis doubled down on their threats on Sunday, warning airlines, passengers and staff to stay away from Saudi airports. The group said “the worst is yet to come” if Saudi military action in Yemen continued. “We renew our warning to all airlines, experts, employees, workers and travellers against using Saudi airports and airspace, as they are vulnerable to attack and have become a theatre of operations for our forces,” the Houthis said on X. Trump said he would speak to the Saudi crown prince, Mohammed bin Salman, on Saturday night, after the previous attack on the airport. The US has already been assisting with intelligence cooperation and targeting, with about 200 US military advisers stationed in Saudi Arabia to help with the campaign. Until now, the US has not directly taken part in fighting against the Houthis. Direct US involvement could lead the group to resume its targeting of ships passing through the Bab al-Mandab strait, through which about 10% of global maritime goods transit. It would also further entangle the US in Middle East wars as the American public grows increasingly frustrated with the continuing Iran conflict. Trump faces the prospect of midterm elections in November with an unpopular war and soaring prices at home, threatening his party’s performance at the polls. Saudi Arabia is already carrying out airstrikes against the Houthis in Yemen. The Houthi government’s health ministry said coalition airstrikes over the last six weeks had killed 91 Yemenis and wounded 168, 60% of whom it said were women and children. Saudi-backed government forces in Yemen launched a campaign to push the Houthis back from the areas the group conquered over the last month. Despite claiming initial successes, the government forces have not been able to loosen the Houthis’ grip over areas closest to the Bab al-Mandab strait such as Perim Island. The Indian embassy in Saudi Arabia said one of its citizens died on Sunday after being wounded in the Riyadh airport attack a day earlier. The Egyptian woman killed in the attack on the airport was a flight attendant identified as Azza Ramzy, 28, who worked for the Saudi airline Flynas, according to Egyptian state-run TV. The Syrian woman was a widowed mother of four who had been living in Saudi Arabia for five years, a relative told the Associated Press. The Syrian embassy in Riyadh identified her as Buthaina Ahmad Oweida. Her niece, Nisreen Oweida, said her aunt was 56, from Syria’s northern Idlib province, and had left during the country’s civil war. She was living in Mecca and had been returning from a visit to her sister in Riyadh when she was killed, the niece said. The airport attack was met with a wave of international condemnation, including from the UN secretary general, António Guterres, and the president of the European Commission, Ursula von der Leyen. “Attacks by Iran’s proxies are pushing the region into a spiral of violence,” von der Leyen wrote on X. “They are destabilising crucial global transport and energy nodes.” The increasing intensity of Houthi attacks against Riyadh and its energy infrastructure has brought more foreign involvement in the Yemen war. Governments are facing pressure over oil prices, already high from the US-Iran war since March. On Monday, Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Turkey issued a joint statement saying they would move quickly to implement their mutual defence pact, including by speeding up the deployment of military forces in the kingdom. The UK said it would assist with defensive military support of Riyadh, providing refuelling for aircraft working to intercept Houthi missiles into Riyadh. Saudi Arabia has asked for further assistance from France, Egypt, the UK and Pakistan as its stock of interceptor missiles are running low. The Houthis launched a military campaign to take Yemen’s Red Sea coast in early September after months of escalating tensions with the Yemeni government and its Saudi patron. The campaign interrupted years of relative calm in the country after a 2022 UN-brokered ceasefire froze frontlines between the Houthis and the government. Despite the Saudi-supported counteroffensive, the group seems to have held on to its recent gains. It is unclear what further Saudi military action would look like against the Houthis, who resisted years of strikes by an international coalition, as well as by the US. Saudi Arabia led an international coalition that intervened against the Houthis in Yemen in 2015 after the group took over Sana’a and toppled the Yemeni government. Recent Houthi attacks against Saudi energy infrastructure, as well as Houthi military advances, have pulled Saudi Arabia back into the Yemen war.

representative.author: WORLD

snapshot.title: Syria declares ceasefire in parts of Aleppo after days of clashes
snapshot.evidenceText: The Syrian government announced a ceasefire in several neighborhoods of Aleppo early Friday after days of deadly clashes between Syrian forces and Kurdish-led Syrian Democratic Forces (SDF). In a statement, the Syrian Defense Ministry said the ceasefire was introduced “to prevent any slide towards a new military escalation within residential neighborhoods.” The truce took effect at 3:00 a.m. local time and covers the Sheikh Maqsoud, Ashrafieh, and Bani Zeid districts of northern Aleppo. The ministry emphasized that the decision is part of broader efforts to de-escalate tensions and stabilize the situation in the city. According to the announcement, internal security forces, working alongside the Syrian army, will oversee mechanisms for the withdrawal of armed groups from the affected neighborhoods toward northeastern Syria. Authorities said the move aims to restore calm, reestablish state authority, and prepare conditions for the return of civilian life and rule of law in the impacted areas, following several days of violence that heightened fears of renewed urban conflict in Aleppo. The clashes had raised regional concern due to Aleppo’s history as one of the most contested battlegrounds of Syria’s long-running conflict. Further details on implementation of the ceasefire and the timeline for withdrawals have yet to be released. representative.author: WORLD

snapshot.title: Bangladesh flood death toll rises to 44 as more than one million people affected
snapshot.evidenceText: Relentless monsoon rains, flash floods and landslides have left at least 44 people dead and affected more than one million people across seven districts in Bangladesh, authorities said on Sunday, as emergency responders continued relief operations amid warnings of further flooding. According to the Ministry of Disaster Management and Relief, more than 1.022 million people have been affected by the flooding, with 267,918 families remaining stranded by rising waters. At least 39 people have been injured since the severe weather began. The worst-hit districts include Khagrachhari, Rangamati, Bandarban, Cox's Bazar, Chattogram, Moulvibazar and Habiganj, where floodwaters have inundated 58 sub-districts (upazilas), damaging homes, roads, bridges and other critical infrastructure. Although rainfall eased over the past 24 hours in several parts of the country, flood risks remain elevated. The Flood Forecasting and Warning Centre (FFWC) warned that fresh short-term flooding could occur in Feni, Sylhet and northern districts, particularly along the Teesta River basin, due to continued upstream inflows and additional rainfall. The agency said water levels at seven monitoring stations on the Sangu, Matamuhuri, Kushiyara, Manu and Someswari rivers remained above danger levels, keeping low-lying communities at risk. Authorities have opened 1,131 emergency shelters, where 44,457 displaced people are currently staying after being evacuated from flood-affected areas. The Disaster Management Ministry said it had allocated 145 million taka ($1.2 million) and 2,650 metric tonnes of rice to the seven worst-hit districts to support relief efforts. Since July 7, district administrations across the country have also received 345 million taka and 6,900 metric tonnes of rice for emergency response operations. However, aid workers and local officials said many flood-affected families have yet to receive sufficient assistance as access to some remote communities remains difficult. Shortages of food, clean drinking water and essential medicines have been reported in several inundated areas, raising concerns over the risk of waterborne diseases. Health officials said pregnant women, young children and elderly residents remain among the most vulnerable groups as floodwaters continue to submerge homes and farmland. Bangladesh, one of the world's most climate-vulnerable countries, experiences severe monsoon flooding almost every year. Scientists say climate change is increasing the intensity of extreme rainfall events, contributing to more frequent floods and landslides across South Asia. Authorities said relief operations were continuing while closely monitoring river levels and weather forecasts, warning that additional rainfall could worsen conditions in low-lying areas over the coming days. snapshot.title: TASIS denies Abu Shandi strike, alleges Egyptian drone attack - The Sudan Times
snapshot.evidenceText: The Sudan Founding Alliance (TASIS) has denied responsibility for the deadly drone strike in Abu Shandi in Sudan’s Blue Nile region, alleging instead that an Egyptian military drone launched from an army-held area carried out the attack. The death toll from Friday’s strike near a displacement site in Abu Shandi, Wad al-Mahi locality, has risen to 41, according to Emergency Lawyers. The group blamed the Rapid Support Forces (RSF), a leading member of the TASIS alliance, and said eight children and numerous women were among those killed. TASIS rejected the accusation in a statement issued by its spokesman Ahmed Tugud Lisan, describing reports blaming its forces as an attempt to discredit the alliance following recent military advances in Blue Nile. The alliance alleged that the drone which struck civilians in Abu Shandi belonged to Egypt and had been launched from the police headquarters in Wad al-Mahi by Egyptian technicians. TASIS further alleged that a local figure identified as Mek Zaidan, whom it accused of working with the army-aligned Port Sudan authorities, travelled toward the traditional gold-mining area as the drone approached and withdrew shortly before the strike. The alliance claimed his movements demonstrated prior knowledge of the attack. TASIS said the accusations against its forces were intended to turn local communities against the alliance and encourage recruitment into Sudan’s military and allied Popular Resistance formations. The United Nations has condemned the attack but has not publicly attributed responsibility. UN officials initially reported that around 40 civilians had been killed, most of them women and children, after what the organisation described as a suspected drone strike near a displacement site close to the Sudan-Ethiopia border. The UN called for those responsible to be held accountable under international humanitarian law. The attack occurred amid intensified fighting in Blue Nile between Sudan’s military and the TASIS-aligned forces, including the RSF and Sudan People’s Liberation Movement-North. Abu Shandi lies in Wad al-Mahi, an increasingly contested area near the Ethiopian border where thousands of civilians have been displaced by the recent fighting.

It has forced more than 12.4 million to flee their homes, according to U.N. figures, creating what aid groups call the world’s largest humanitarian crisis. Across Sudan , 33.7 million people, including 17.3 million children, urgently need aid this year, and an estimated 825,000 children face severe acute malnutrition. representative.title: Ethiopia, Eritrea ramp up rhetoric: Are they inching towards war? | Explainer News | Al Jazeera

snapshot.title: Ethiopia, Eritrea ramp up rhetoric: Are they inching towards war?
snapshot.evidenceText: Allegations of Eritrean troop incursions into Tigray deepen the rift with Ethiopia, as fighting in northern Ethiopia rages on. Ethiopia and Eritrea have exchanged accusations of aggression at the United Nations, raising fears of a new conflict in the Horn of Africa region as fighting intensifies in Ethiopia’s northern Tigray region. The diplomatic spat comes as Ethiopian troops and allied armed groups advanced across Tigray, where forces from Asmara have allegedly crossed the border to support rebels fighting the government forces. The two neighbours, which fought a deadly border war between 1998 and 2000, were allies during Ethiopia’s devastating 2020-2022 Tigray war. However, they have since been at loggerheads over the 2022 peace agreement that ended a two-year civil war between the government in Addis Ababa and Tigray rebels, and over Ethiopia’s demands for access to the Red Sea. So, what did Eritrea and Ethiopia accuse each other of, and are they inching towards war? Eritrean troops had advanced as far as 60km (37 miles) into Tigray, Ethiopia told the UN Security Council on Friday, accusing its neighbour of violating its sovereignty. In a letter, Ethiopian Foreign Minister Gedion Timothewos described the alleged incursion as “a blatant act of aggression that engages Ethiopia’s inherent right to self-defence”. He invoked Article 51 of the UN Charter, which recognises a country’s right to self-defence, but did not specify what measures Ethiopia was taking. Eritrea, which won independence from Ethiopia in 1993, rejected the accusations of incursions into Ethiopia, calling them a pretext for an Addis Ababa offensive. Eritrean Foreign Minister Osman Saleh, in his own letter to the UN Security Council on Saturday, urged the body to condemn Ethiopia’s “deplorable declaration of war” and take “deterrent measures”. He warned that an Ethiopian offensive would cause “huge devastation to the peoples of both countries and destabilise the whole region”. The accusations come amid a broader dispute over access to the Red Sea. Landlocked Ethiopia has repeatedly argued that securing direct sea access is essential, while Eritrea fears Addis Ababa intends to seize its port of Assab. Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed reiterated on Monday that Ethiopia must have access to the Red Sea. Hossamaldeen Ibrahim, an analyst at Bloomsbury Intelligence and Security Institute (BISI), said the narratives of both countries contain “verifiable elements”. “The danger lies in the fact that each side now treats the other’s narrative as existential,” he told Al Jazeera. Eritrea and Ethiopia fought a deadly border war from 1998 to 2000. Relations improved after Abiy came to power in 2018, but have soured again in recent years. Professor Matthias Rompel from the Institute of Sociology at the Justus-Liebig-University Giessen in Germany, said that both sides have legitimate security concerns, but their accusations need to be distinguished from independently verified facts. “Ethiopia’s allegations of Eritrean military incursions into Tigray… and …the scale of Eritrean involvement, and particularly allegations that Asmara is orchestrating the rebellion against Addis Ababa, remain difficult to substantiate independently,” he told Al Jazeera. He added that the latest developments suggest that the confrontation is no longer merely about Tigray. “Ethiopia’s quest for Red Sea access, Eritrea’s concerns about sovereignty, and Egypt’s strategic rivalry with Ethiopia over the Nile are interconnected,” he said. “The conflict, therefore, has the potential to destabilise the wider Horn of Africa, with repercussions for Sudan, Somalia and Red Sea security.” Fighting escalated on September 23 when a rebel alliance, including the Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF), launched attacks against Ethiopian government forces across Tigray, Amhara and Afar regions. The rebels captured Tigray’s capital, Mekelle, and its airport before announcing their withdrawal on October 3. Government-allied forces subsequently entered the city. In the latest on the battlefront, government and allied forces took Idaga Hamus early Friday and Abiy-Adi, in the Tembien area, on Thursday afternoon, according to Ermiyas Ababu, a commander of the government-allied Tigray Peace Force. Residents, according to Reuters news agency, also reported the takeover of Idaga Hamus. Gebremedhin Kihishen, a business owner in Tembien, said government-allied forces controlled Abiy-Adi. It was unclear from those accounts who held the towns immediately before the reported government advance or whether Eritrean troops were involved in the fighting. Ermiyas previously reported Eritrean personnel entering Adigrat on Tuesday and Idaga Hamus on Wednesday, citing reports from his personnel. Al Jazeera was unable to independently verify the claims. The Armed Conflict Location and Event Data Project (ACLED), a United States-based conflict monitor, reported that Eritrean troops crossed into Ethiopia near Zalambessa and came under Ethiopian drone attack while advancing towards Idaga Hamus. Eritrea has yet to comment on the development. Addis Ababa accuses Asmara of financing, arming and directing armed groups, as well as deploying troops inside Tigray. Eritrea denies the allegations, which have not been independently verified. The renewed fighting threatens to unravel the 2022 peace agreement. That conflict began in November 2020 after months of tensions between Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed’s government and the TPLF, which had dominated Ethiopian politics for nearly three decades before Abiy took office in 2018. Eritrea fought alongside Ethiopian federal forces against the TPLF, its longtime adversary. The war killed hundreds of thousands of people and was marked by allegations of massacres, sexual violence and widespread hunger. The November 2022 Pretoria agreement ended major hostilities, but Eritrea was not a party to the deal. Relations between Addis Ababa and Asmara subsequently deteriorated. Multiple media reports say Ethiopian government troops and allied militias entered Adigrat, a strategic city roughly 30km (19 miles) from the Eritrean border, on Saturday. Three residents confirmed their presence to Reuters, while verified footage showed government-allied militia members walking through the city. Associated Press news agency footage also showed Ethiopian military vehicles entering Adigrat as some residents welcomed the troops. Government-allied forces have reported capturing Idaga Hamus and Abiy-Adi, while explosions and alleged drone strikes have been reported near Adigrat. Analysts warn that Ethiopia and Eritrea may already have moved beyond threats and into a dangerous phase of possible military confrontation. BISI’s Ibrahim said the two countries have moved beyond “inching” towards war, noting that “The situation has entered a high-risk phase of limited but direct military confrontation with a real possibility of rapid escalation into interstate war.” He warned that the severing of diplomatic ties removed the “last formal mechanism for crisis management”, while Ethiopian military advances towards the Eritrean border increased the risk of “miscalculation”. Tom Gardner, a correspondent for The Economist, said the current tensions should be understood in the context of decades of hostility between the neighbours. Their brief alliance during the 2020-2022 Tigray war was an exception and was driven by a shared hostility towards the TPLF, Gardner told Al Jazeera. “The Ethiopian government’s strategic goal number one is access to the Red Sea, but also removing Eritrea’s government from the picture,” he noted. “It’s very much looking like the most dangerous moment for the region since that 1998 to 2000 war.” Rompel from Justus-Liebig-University Giessen said that the current situation is evolving. “The danger of a wider interstate conflict is real, and the situation has already moved beyond a purely diplomatic confrontation,” he said. “The central danger is not necessarily that either government has decided to launch a full-scale war, but that military miscalculations, mutual distrust and domestic political pressures could trigger a further escalation neither side can easily control. “A wider conflict is not inevitable, but the space for diplomatic de-escalation is rapidly narrowing,” he said.

snapshot.title: Ethiopia, Eritrea Seek Rival UN Security Council Action
snapshot.evidenceText: Get the latest headlines, discounts for the military community, and guides to maximizing your benefits Ethiopia and Eritrea have taken their escalating border confrontation to the United Nations Security Council, each accusing the other of aggression and seeking international action. Eritrea appealed to the Council on October 10, a day after Ethiopia invoked its right to self-defence over an alleged Eritrean invasion of Tigray. The competing appeals came as Ethiopian forces entered the strategic border city of Adigrat and UN Secretary-General António Guterres called for an immediate end to hostilities. Ethiopian Foreign Minister Gedion Timothewos notified the Security Council on October 9 that Eritrean forces, including mechanised units, had advanced as far as 60 kilometres into northern Ethiopia. Addis Ababa invoked Article 51 of the UN Charter, which recognises a state’s inherent right of self-defence following an armed attack. Eritrea denied invading Ethiopian territory and accused its neighbour of using the allegations to justify military action. Eritrean Foreign Minister Osman Saleh responded by asking the Council to condemn Ethiopia and take deterrent measures under Chapter VII of the UN Charter. Asmara characterised Ethiopia’s accusations as preparation for a war of aggression. Reuters reviewed the letter, which did not specify what measures Eritrea wanted the Council to adopt. Chapter VII gives the Security Council authority to address threats to international peace and security, including through sanctions and, in certain circumstances, military action. Article 51, which forms part of the same chapter, separately recognises the right of individual or collective self-defence. Eritrea is seeking action by the Council, while Ethiopia is asserting its right to respond to an alleged armed attack. Neither government’s appeal establishes the legality of its military conduct or automatically triggers UN enforcement measures. The UN Secretary-General expressed grave concern about renewed fighting in Tigray, Amhara and Afar in a statement dated October 9 and published the following day. Guterres called for an immediate cessation of hostilities and a return to dialogue under the African Union-brokered Pretoria peace agreement of 2022. He also expressed concern about reports of Eritrean forces inside Ethiopia and urged regional governments to respect territorial integrity and refrain from actions that could intensify the conflict. The competing diplomatic appeals coincided with significant military developments. On October 10, Ethiopian government troops and allied Tigrayan militia entered Adigrat, approximately 30 kilometres from Eritrea’s border. Reuters verified footage showing pro-government militia members in the city, while three residents confirmed seeing Ethiopian soldiers and military vehicles. The agency did not independently establish complete government control. The Armed Conflict Location & Event Data Project (ACLED) reported that Eritrean forces crossed the border near Zelambesa on October 7 and subsequently withdrew from Adigrat. Ethiopian drone strikes reportedly targeted vehicles carrying Eritrean personnel and equipment during the withdrawal. Eritrea continues to deny that its forces invaded Ethiopia, and the full scale of the reported incursion remains independently unverified. The confrontation follows renewed fighting in northern Ethiopia that began on September 23. Ethiopian federal forces have since recaptured several major towns from a rebel alliance led by the Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF). Ethiopia and Eritrea fought together against the TPLF during the devastating 2020–2022 war but later became adversaries. Their relations have also deteriorated over Ethiopia’s pursuit of direct access to the Red Sea. Landlocked since Eritrea gained independence in 1993, Ethiopia regards maritime access as a strategic necessity, while Eritrea fears that Addis Ababa’s ambitions could threaten its sovereignty and coastline. The Security Council now faces competing requests from two neighbouring states whose forces have reportedly engaged in cross-border military operations. Guterres has offered UN assistance in resolving the crisis, but no binding Council response to the latest appeals has been established. Further troop movements, drone strikes and diplomatic initiatives will indicate whether the confrontation can be contained or develops into sustained interstate warfare. snapshot.evidenceText: Allegations of Eritrean troop incursions into Tigray deepen the rift with Ethiopia, as fighting in northern Ethiopia rages on. Ethiopia and Eritrea have exchanged accusations of aggression at the United Nations, raising fears of a new conflict in the Horn of Africa region as fighting intensifies in Ethiopia’s northern Tigray region. The diplomatic spat comes as Ethiopian troops and allied armed groups advanced across Tigray, where forces from Asmara have allegedly crossed the border to support rebels fighting the government forces. The two neighbours, which fought a deadly border war between 1998 and 2000, were allies during Ethiopia’s devastating 2020-2022 Tigray war. However, they have since been at loggerheads over the 2022 peace agreement that ended a two-year civil war between the government in Addis Ababa and Tigray rebels, and over Ethiopia’s demands for access to the Red Sea. So, what did Eritrea and Ethiopia accuse each other of, and are they inching towards war? Eritrean troops had advanced as far as 60km (37 miles) into Tigray, Ethiopia told the UN Security Council on Friday, accusing its neighbour of violating its sovereignty. In a letter, Ethiopian Foreign Minister Gedion Timothewos described the alleged incursion as “a blatant act of aggression that engages Ethiopia’s inherent right to self-defence”. He invoked Article 51 of the UN Charter, which recognises a country’s right to self-defence, but did not specify what measures Ethiopia was taking. Eritrea, which won independence from Ethiopia in 1993, rejected the accusations of incursions into Ethiopia, calling them a pretext for an Addis Ababa offensive. Eritrean Foreign Minister Osman Saleh, in his own letter to the UN Security Council on Saturday, urged the body to condemn Ethiopia’s “deplorable declaration of war” and take “deterrent measures”. He warned that an Ethiopian offensive would cause “huge devastation to the peoples of both countries and destabilise the whole region”. The accusations come amid a broader dispute over access to the Red Sea. Landlocked Ethiopia has repeatedly argued that securing direct sea access is essential, while Eritrea fears Addis Ababa intends to seize its port of Assab. Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed reiterated on Monday that Ethiopia must have access to the Red Sea. Hossamaldeen Ibrahim, an analyst at Bloomsbury Intelligence and Security Institute (BISI), said the narratives of both countries contain “verifiable elements”. “The danger lies in the fact that each side now treats the other’s narrative as existential,” he told Al Jazeera. Eritrea and Ethiopia fought a deadly border war from 1998 to 2000. Relations improved after Abiy came to power in 2018, but have soured again in recent years. Professor Matthias Rompel from the Institute of Sociology at the Justus-Liebig-University Giessen in Germany, said that both sides have legitimate security concerns, but their accusations need to be distinguished from independently verified facts. “Ethiopia’s allegations of Eritrean military incursions into Tigray… and …the scale of Eritrean involvement, and particularly allegations that Asmara is orchestrating the rebellion against Addis Ababa, remain difficult to substantiate independently,” he told Al Jazeera. He added that the latest developments suggest that the confrontation is no longer merely about Tigray. “Ethiopia’s quest for Red Sea access, Eritrea’s concerns about sovereignty, and Egypt’s strategic rivalry with Ethiopia over the Nile are interconnected,” he said. “The conflict, therefore, has the potential to destabilise the wider Horn of Africa, with repercussions for Sudan, Somalia and Red Sea security.” Fighting escalated on September 23 when a rebel alliance, including the Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF), launched attacks against Ethiopian government forces across Tigray, Amhara and Afar regions. The rebels captured Tigray’s capital, Mekelle, and its airport before announcing their withdrawal on October 3. Government-allied forces subsequently entered the city. In the latest on the battlefront, government and allied forces took Idaga Hamus early Friday and Abiy-Adi, in the Tembien area, on Thursday afternoon, according to Ermiyas Ababu, a commander of the government-allied Tigray Peace Force. Residents, according to Reuters news agency, also reported the takeover of Idaga Hamus. Gebremedhin Kihishen, a business owner in Tembien, said government-allied forces controlled Abiy-Adi. It was unclear from those accounts who held the towns immediately before the reported government advance or whether Eritrean troops were involved in the fighting. Ermiyas previously reported Eritrean personnel entering Adigrat on Tuesday and Idaga Hamus on Wednesday, citing reports from his personnel. Al Jazeera was unable to independently verify the claims. The Armed Conflict Location and Event Data Project (ACLED), a United States-based conflict monitor, reported that Eritrean troops crossed into Ethiopia near Zalambessa and came under Ethiopian drone attack while advancing towards Idaga Hamus. Eritrea has yet to comment on the development. Addis Ababa accuses Asmara of financing, arming and directing armed groups, as well as deploying troops inside Tigray. Eritrea denies the allegations, which have not been independently verified. The renewed fighting threatens to unravel the 2022 peace agreement. That conflict began in November 2020 after months of tensions between Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed’s government and the TPLF, which had dominated Ethiopian politics for nearly three decades before Abiy took office in 2018. Eritrea fought alongside Ethiopian federal forces against the TPLF, its longtime adversary. The war killed hundreds of thousands of people and was marked by allegations of massacres, sexual violence and widespread hunger. The November 2022 Pretoria agreement ended major hostilities, but Eritrea was not a party to the deal. Relations between Addis Ababa and Asmara subsequently deteriorated. Multiple media reports say Ethiopian government troops and allied militias entered Adigrat, a strategic city roughly 30km (19 miles) from the Eritrean border, on Saturday. Three residents confirmed their presence to Reuters, while verified footage showed government-allied militia members walking through the city. Associated Press news agency footage also showed Ethiopian military vehicles entering Adigrat as some residents welcomed the troops. Government-allied forces have reported capturing Idaga Hamus and Abiy-Adi, while explosions and alleged drone strikes have been reported near Adigrat. Analysts warn that Ethiopia and Eritrea may already have moved beyond threats and into a dangerous phase of possible military confrontation. BISI’s Ibrahim said the two countries have moved beyond “inching” towards war, noting that “The situation has entered a high-risk phase of limited but direct military confrontation with a real possibility of rapid escalation into interstate war.” He warned that the severing of diplomatic ties removed the “last formal mechanism for crisis management”, while Ethiopian military advances towards the Eritrean border increased the risk of “miscalculation”. Tom Gardner, a correspondent for The Economist, said the current tensions should be understood in the context of decades of hostility between the neighbours. Their brief alliance during the 2020-2022 Tigray war was an exception and was driven by a shared hostility towards the TPLF, Gardner told Al Jazeera. “The Ethiopian government’s strategic goal number one is access to the Red Sea, but also removing Eritrea’s government from the picture,” he noted. “It’s very much looking like the most dangerous moment for the region since that 1998 to 2000 war.” Rompel from Justus-Liebig-University Giessen said that the current situation is evolving. “The danger of a wider interstate conflict is real, and the situation has already moved beyond a purely diplomatic confrontation,” he said. “The central danger is not necessarily that either government has decided to launch a full-scale war, but that military miscalculations, mutual distrust and domestic political pressures could trigger a further escalation neither side can easily control. “A wider conflict is not inevitable, but the space for diplomatic de-escalation is rapidly narrowing,” he said.
