snapshot.title: Russian strike kills at least 33 in eastern Ukraine in deadliest single attack this year - Egypt Independent
snapshot.evidenceText: Kyiv, Ukraine — At least 33 people were killed on Thursday when a Russian strike caused two public buses to catch fire in eastern Ukraine, local authorities said, making it the deadliest single attack this year. Another 18 people were injured in the attack in Kramatorsk, a city in the Donetsk region, which prompted authorities there to shut down the public transport system and urge people to move to safer parts of the country. “The Russians are deliberately targeting civilians,” said Vadym Filashkin, the head of the Donetsk regional military administration. “For them, a bus full of passengers is an attractive target precisely because a single strike can kill as many people as possible.” The State Emergency Service of Ukraine (SES) said the Russian strike caused a fire on two buses and in the surrounding area. Police in Donetsk said Russian drones targeted officers who were helping victims of the strike. Police were still working to identify the victims of the strike, with some bodies having to be pieced together from fragments, they said in a statement. Footage they released of the rescue operation shows bodies strewn across the road. Drones can be seen near the scene of the strike as responders load the injured onto stretchers and into emergency vehicles. One emergency worker can be heard asking an injured woman for her name. The woman responds weakly, “Tanya…legs, legs.” Shots can be heard ringing out and the woman is put into an emergency vehicle. Filashkin said he had ordered the suspension of public transportation in the cities of Kramatorsk and Sloviansk in the wake of the attack and called on civilians to move to safer areas. “I urge everyone who remains in the Donetsk region to evacuate to safer regions of Ukraine,” he said. “Russia is bringing death to Ukrainian soil. It is striking our cities, killing our people, and multiplying its crimes every day,” added Filashkin as he offered his condolences to the families and loved ones of victims. CNN has reached out to Russia’s defense ministry for comment. Ukraine’s team heads to the US The deadly strike comes as Ukrainian negotiators are expected to visit the US for talks on Friday and Saturday. A source familiar with the matter told CNN US envoy Steve Witkoff and President Donald Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner would meet with Ukraine’s intelligence chief Rustem Umerov and Kyrylo Budanov, head of the Office of Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelensky. Zelensky said in his nightly address on Thursday that the talks would last two days and that Ukraine counted on its European allies to join in. He added Umerov and Budanov would also use the meeting to raise the issue of air defenses – a critical issue for Kyiv. Earlier on ⁠Thursday, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said that the war in Ukraine is at a dangerous stalemate and that Washington remains committed to finding a peaceful resolution to the conflict. “We’d love to see a negotiated settlement to this war ⁠that is permanent, enduring, and fair. And that’s what we’re committed to continuing to do,” Rubio said during a visit to ⁠Portugal. Reacting to his comments, Kremlin ‌spokesman Dmitry Peskov said Russia agreed with Rubio that ​the Ukraine conflict was at a stalemate. “Yes, we agree with him,” Russian state news agency RIA Novosti quoted Peskov as saying, adding it was up to diplomats to find ways of moving towards peace. “The art of diplomacy precisely involves finding some way out that would allow ‌moving onto ⁠a peaceful track,” Peskov was quoted as telling journalists in Turkmenistan, according to Reuters on Thursday. The past few months have been exceptionally deadly for Ukrainian civilians. Russia has been launching near daily mass aerial attacks against the country, taking advantage of Ukraine’s critical shortage of interceptors. A mass Russian missile attack on Kyiv in July killed 33 people across the city in a coordinated barrage. In August, 38 people were killed when a Russian drone strike on an ammunition depot near the capital triggered a large fire and multiple explosions that lasted hours in a residential area near Kyiv. Both Kramatorsk and Sloviansk are crucial industrial cities close to the front line. Together with nearby Kostiantynivka and Druzhkivka, they form the core of Ukraine’s remaining “fortress belt” in the Donetsk region. Kramatorsk has long served as a strategic rear point for the Ukrainian units serving along the eastern front – and as a place to which exhausted troops could retreat for a few days of rest before their next mission. But a press officer with Ukraine’s 93rd mechanized brigade told CNN last month that is no longer an option due to frequent shelling. The fortress belt has slowly eroded over the past four and a half years. Its southernmost anchor, Kostyantynivka, has now been effectively lost as a stronghold. CNN’s Ivana Kottasová and Jonny Hallam contributed to this report.

representative.title: Woman Killed, 8 Injured in Kharkiv Guided Bomb Strike
representative.author: Tymur Dubovyk

snapshot.title: Russian Guided Bomb Strike Kills Woman, Injures 10 in Kharkiv
snapshot.evidenceText: In brief: A Russian guided aerial bomb strike hit the Nemyshlianskyi district of Kharkiv on Sunday, Oct. 11, killing a 35-year-old woman and injuring ten civilians, including a seven-year-old boy. The bombardment destroyed two private homes, damaged 15 others, and set several vehicles ablaze near an auto repair facility, while emergency crews suppressed fires and treated the wounded. A Russian guided aerial bomb strike on the Nemyshlianskyi district of Kharkiv killed a 35-year-old woman and injured ten other civilians, including a child, on Sunday, Oct. 11, municipal and regional authorities reported. Kharkiv Mayor Ihor Terekhov and Kharkiv Regional Military Administration Head Oleh Syniehubov confirmed the attack on Telegram, stating that Russian tactical aviation launched guided aerial bombs (KABs) into the private residential sector of the district. Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official . Emergency medical teams attempted to resuscitate a 35-year-old woman extracted from the rubble of a destroyed house, but she succumbed to her injuries at the scene, Terekhov said . Syniehubov reported that four additional civilians sustained injuries in the strike: a seven-year-old boy, a 44-year-old woman, a 30-year-old man, and a 61-year-old man. All injured individuals received medical assistance from responding emergency crews. The aerial bomb impact ignited localized fires across the strike perimeter, engaging residential structures and parked vehicles. Terekhov stated that the munitions struck adjacent to an auto repair facility and direct hits completely leveled two private residences. An estimated 15 neighboring homes sustained structural damage from the supersonic blast wave, which shattered windows and collapsed roofing materials. Several passenger vehicles parked near the impact crater also caught fire. Rescue brigades from the State Emergency Service of Ukraine (SES) and municipal utility teams deployed to the neighborhood to suppress the fires, clear collapsed masonry, and assist displaced residents. Later, Siniehubov reported that the number of injured had risen to 8 people. Subsequently, Terekhov confirmed 10 injured people after Russian strike. According to him, 35 houses and 8 cars were damaged The attack in Kharkiv forms part of a wider wave of Russian standoff strikes targeting Ukrainian municipal settlements and emergency services on Sunday. Earlier on Sunday morning, Russian forces launched an airstrike against the eastern city of Sloviansk in the Donetsk region at approximately 9:45 a.m. local time, damaging two multi-story apartment buildings and injuring four people. In the northern Sumy region, a Russian loitering drone struck an emergency medical vehicle at approximately 5:00 a.m. while medical personnel were traveling through the Yampil territorial community toward an emergency call in Svesa. A 44-year-old driver and a 59-year-old paramedic sustained minor injuries and were evacuated by a follow-up medical crew. The strikes followed a late Saturday evening bombardment in the central city of Dnipro , where a Russian strike damaged the eighth and ninth floors of a residential high-rise, injuring four civilians, including two eight-year-old girls. snapshot.title: Hurricane Isaias kills at least four, leaves thousands without power in US
snapshot.evidenceText: A backyard is flooded in the aftermath of Hurricane Isaias in Destin, Florida, US. ( Reuters: Marco Bello ) Hurricane Isaias has killed at least four people, leaving hundreds of thousands without power across three US states. Florida, Alabama and Georgia have declared emergencies. Hazardous conditions remained and storm surges, flash flooding, damaging winds and a risk of tornadoes were expected across parts of the US, the National Hurricane Center said. At least four people have died and 800,000 Florida, Alabama and Georgia residents were without power after Hurricane Isaias made landfall. Authorities in Florida had received no search and rescue requests shortly after landfall in a sign of limited impact, Governor Ron DeSantis said. However, hazardous conditions remained and storm surges, flash flooding, damaging winds and a risk of tornadoes across parts of the US were expected, the National Hurricane Center said. The tornado threat is expected to continue today across parts of the Florida Panhandle, Georgia and the Carolinas, the NHC said. Florida, Alabama and Georgia have declared emergencies. The hurricane has left damage in multiple states. ( Reuters: Marco Bello ) In Florida, power restoration was marked as priority, authorities said, while highways, bridges and airports were reopening, and teams were assessing the damage. "They're going to make assessments this morning, and I think that'll give us a good sense about the future for the rapidity of the power restoration," Mr DeSantis said. He also warned that casualties might follow "in the days after". Some 16,000 utility linemen had prepared to respond to the storm, he said. More than 430,000 customers in Florida, over 280,000 in Alabama and some 100,000 in Georgia lost power as the storm hit shore, according to tracking firm PowerOutage.us. In Alabama and Florida, three people were killed by falling trees, according to local media and authorities. Sheriff Chip W Simmons of Escambia County, Florida has confirmed two "storm-related fatalities" via social media. "A tree fell on a house and unfortunately took the life of a lady," he said, and later confirmed that a man died from carbon monoxide poisoning. Alabama's emergency management agency said the downed trees and power lines made travel hazardous in Houston County, which is under a flash flood warning. "Due to the impacts of Hurricane Isaias, all Houston County roads are closed until further notice," it posted on X. Isaias rapidly lost wind speed after hitting the Florida coast as a Category 2 hurricane, the first of the 2026 Atlantic season. It is expected to produce gusty winds well inland before weakening below gale force later on Saturday, the NHC said. The clean up will begin in coming days across the affected states. ( Reuters: Marco Bello ) Oil and gas producer Shell has said it was beginning to redeploy personnel to its Mars, Olympus, Ursa, Vito, and Appomattox assets in the Gulf. President Donald Trump, asked about hurricane preparations on Friday, told reporters outside the White House that it was "under control." Earlier, emergency declarations were approved in Florida and Alabama to ensure federal resources would be available to respond to Isaias, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said on X. "There's also a lot of hazards post-storm that people should be careful of," DeSantis told FOX News. "But so far, we've had a lot of assets in place that have not been called on." A second hurricane has developed into a powerful category 4 system which is expected to make landfall "near or just inland" of Mexico's west-central coast on Sunday, local time. The National Hurricane Centre in Miami said Hurricane Simon's maximum sustained winds increased to 240km/h. A storm of that strength or greater is considered a major hurricane. The centre said the hurricane could bring as much as 25-50 centimetres of rain over parts of south-western Mexico, with some areas in the states of Michoacan, Colima and Jalisco receiving up to 76cm. "This rainfall will produce life-threatening flooding and mudslides, especially in areas of steep terrain," the centre warned in a bulletin that also urged residents to take immediate action to prepare as tropical-storm conditions were expected to arrive Saturday afternoon. representative.title: At least 2 deaths attributed to Isaias after hurricane bashes Florida and Alabama : NPR
representative.author: Bill Chappell

snapshot.title: At least 4 deaths attributed to Isaias after hurricane bashes Florida and Alabama
snapshot.evidenceText: A driver look at his overturned truck in a flooded parking lot on Saturday morning in Tiger Point, Fla., close to where Hurricane Isaias made landfall Friday night. Ronaldo Schemidt/AFP via Getty Images hide caption Emergency crews in Florida and Alabama are surveying damage and power outages wrought by Hurricane Isaias, after the storm bashed into the Gulf Coast as a Category 2 storm Friday night. At least four people have died from storm-related incidents, NPR has confirmed. Isaias brought 105 mph winds onshore, snapping trees and knocking out electricity. Officials warn that flash flood threats persist, but further inland. One death occurred in Escambia County, in the far west of the Florida Panhandle. Shortly before 9 p.m. local time Friday, a rescue team found a person pinned under a large tree, according to Sgt. Melony Peterson of the Escambia County Sheriff's Office. "The victim was inside the home when the tree collapsed," Peterson said via email. A person also died from carbon monoxide poisoning after running a generator in a room, according to Escambia County Sheriff Chip W. Simmons. Four others were hospitalized in the same incident. Many people use generators when they lose connection to the electricity grid. An uprooted tree is seen in Gulf Breeze, Fla., on Saturday. The southeastern U.S. faced a high risk of flooding as Isaias, weakened from a hurricane to a post-tropical cyclone, moved northward. Ronaldo Schemidt/AFP via Getty Images hide caption Another death was reported in Jefferson County, Ala., which includes Birmingham. "We did have a storm-related fatality overnight," Jefferson County Emergency Management Agency Director Jim Coker told NPR. "A tree did fall on the house," Coker added. "It was a single-family residence." A fourth death was confirmed by Alabama Gov. Kay Ivey's office, which told NPR that a person died in Barbour County, southeast of Montgomery. They did not provide details about the circumstances. More than 390,000 people across the state and Florida were without power as of Sunday morning. At least 95% of outages across the state are expected to be restored by midnight, Alabama Power said on Sunday. In Florida, the worst outages were in counties such as Santa Rosa; Holmes; Washington; and Walton – all of which had more than 80% of their residents without power, Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis said in a morning news conference. The governor said some 16,000 utility workers were busy trying to get power returned to homeowners. "Last night in the wee hours of the morning, those crews began working as early as 3 a.m.," DeSantis said. He added that teams were also working to remove trees blocking main roads -- and that both I-10 and Route 98 were open as of Saturday morning, along with all state bridges. Hurricane Isaias forced a Waffle House restaurant to shut down when it passed through Fort Walton Beach, Florida. Isaias made landfall as the season's first Atlantic hurricane. Joe Raedle/Getty Images hide caption Florida Power & Light Company said it hopes to have power restored to 95% of those impacted by Isaias by end of day Monday. Isaias made landfall near Destin, Fla., as a Category 2 hurricane around 8:30 p.m. local time Friday night, packing 105 mph winds, according to the National Hurricane Center . It brought a storm surge of some 5 feet -- short of the 6 to 9 feet forecasters had said was possible if landfall coincided with peak high tide. It arrived roughly two hours before high tide in Destin. Isaias was downgraded to a post-tropical storm hours after making landfall. By 5 a.m. local time on Saturday, its sustained winds had dropped to 35 mph, as the system sped its way through Alabama. "Multiple trees and power lines are down across the county," tweeted the emergency management agency in Jefferson County, Ala. It told residents to "avoid unnecessary travel if possible while crews clear roads and restore service." But the storm's effects extended for hundreds of miles. By around 9:30 a.m. Saturday, the system sent a long band of powerful thunder storms up the center of Georgia. And as the Florida Public Radio Emergency Network notes, forecasters warn that tornadoes could spin off of the system, causing further havoc far from the Gulf Coast. On Sunday, there were tornado warnings in North Carolina, as well as high risk of flooding. Other parts of the rest of the East Coast, including Virginia, also saw heavy rain. NPR's Chandelis Duster contributed to this report. NPR does not offer or accept money for coverage or interviews. Anyone who makes such an offer or request is not an NPR employee and does not represent NPR.

snapshot.title: What did Hurricane Isaias do to Florida? Take a look at the damage
snapshot.evidenceText: Hurricane Isaias made landfall in Destin as a Category 2 storm on Friday night, bringing wind gusts of more than 110 mph to the Florida Panhandle, downing trees, scattering debris and leaving at least two people dead. Hundreds of thousands of people remain without power as emergency response teams work to assess and clear damage, Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis said. “Although the center of the storm has moved out of the state, the threat of flooding remains,” Desantis said in a briefing on Saturday morning. He said there could be four to eight inches of rain across the Florida Panhandle and Big Bend this weekend. One person died in Escambia County when a tree fell on his home, DeSantis said at another briefing on Saturday afternoon. Another person was found dead inside his garage with a generator running, and DeSantis urged people to not run generators indoors. Much of the structural damage caused by the storm was the result of fallen trees, DeSantis said. By 7 a.m., about 448,000 households and businesses were without power, including 323,000 Florida Power & Light customers and 110,000 customers served by various cooperatives across Northwest Florida, DeSantis said. Several counties reported widespread outages, with more than 80% of customers without power in some areas. Santa Rosa County had the highest rate at 90%, followed by Holmes County at 89%, Washington County at 86%, Walton County at 85%, Escambia County at 75% and Okaloosa County at 53%. As of 11:30 a.m. Saturday, power has been restored to 43,000 customers, or more than 12% of those affected. Crews are working to restore power to the estimated 332,000 customers who remain without power, FPL said. A total of 430,000 households and businesses were without power by Saturday afternoon. All state-owned bridges have been reopened for travel, along with the Interstate 10 and U.S. 98. WESH 2 News in Orlando reported that a motel in Pensacola had its roof blown off. 🚨 EXTENSIVE STORM SURGE DAMAGE – PENSACOLA BEACH, FL! 🌊⚠️The aftermath of Hurricane Isaias is incredible across Pensacola Beach, Florida! Thick layers of sand cover many roads after powerful storm surge pushed water and debris inland. Damaged homes, missing roofs, partially collapsed structures, half-sunken boats, downed power lines, and scattered debris paint a devastating picture of the hurricane's impacts. snapshot.title: Mapping Hurricane Isaias' deadly path: How the violent Category 2 storm unfolded across Florida and Gulf Coast
snapshot.evidenceText: PENSACOLA, Florida – The most dangerous Gulf Coast impacts from Hurricane Isaias have passed, but the deadly storm continues to spread heavy rain, damaging winds and flooding inland after making landfall along Florida’s Gulf Coast Friday night. From the U.S. Gulf Coast to the East Coast, Isaias has already carved a destructive path with damaging winds, torrential rain, life-threatening storm surge and a tropical tornado threat, in total resulting in the deaths of least four people and injuring others. WHAT'S THE DIFFERENCE BETWEEN A HURRICANE MAKING A DIRECT HIT AND LANDFALL? Isaias is now a post-tropical cyclone after losing its tropical characteristics and is no longer fueled primarily by warm ocean waters as it moves inland toward Tennessee. TROPICAL STORM RACHEL FUELS MAJOR WEST COAST FLOOD THREAT WITH MONTHS OF RAIN POSSIBLE IN HOURS The storm continued to produce heavy rain across Alabama and Georgia, while a dangerous tornado threat lingered across parts of the Florida Panhandle, Georgia and South Carolina, spawning numerous confirmed tornadoes on Saturday. Hurricane Isaias made landfall near Destin, Florida, Friday night as a Category 2 hurricane with maximum sustained winds of 105 mph and a minimum pressure of 971 millibars, according to the FOX Forecast Center. Isaias made landfall at approximately 9:30 p.m. ET — just one hour shy of two years since Hurricane Milton’s Gulf Coast landfall near the same time on Oct. 9, 2024. HOW ARE HURRICANES RATED? Isaias marked the first Gulf Coast hurricane landfall since Milton, and the first hurricane of the Atlantic Basin season. The storm’s rapid evolution began Saturday night, when the National Hurricane Center identified an area to watch with a 20% chance of development. By Monday, the system had become Invest 92L, with development odds rising to 80%. Tropical Depression Nine formed Tuesday evening, followed by Tropical Storm Isaias early Wednesday. After Hurricane Hunter reconnaissance found 75 mph winds and a pressure of 982 millibars, Isaias strengthened into a hurricane late Wednesday night. By Thursday evening, it had become a Category 2 hurricane with winds of 105 mph. HURRICANE SEASON 2026: THESE ARE THE STORM NAMES YOU'LL SEE THIS SEASON Isaias briefly intensified into a Category 3 major hurricane Friday morning with winds of 120 mph, building upon the thousands of evacuations for Gulf Coast communities in Florida to Alabama ahead of the storm's arrival. The storm weakened back to Category 2 strength Friday evening while approaching the Florida coast before making landfall near Destin with winds of 105 mph. In the hours before landfall, Isaias unleashed a devastating barrage of hurricane-force winds, torrential rain, storm surge and tornadoes across the Gulf Coast, hammering communities across Florida and Alabama before moving inland, where dangerous threats still unfolding. WHAT IS STORM SURGE? Isaias turns deadly across the Southeast The powerful storm turned deadly across Florida and Alabama, where falling trees and a generator-related carbon monoxide incident claimed four lives as Isaias battered the Southeast Friday night into Saturday. A woman in Florida and another person in Birmingham, Alabama, were killed in separate incidents when trees fell onto their homes during the storm. In Florida, one man was found dead inside a garage following an incident involving a power generator, while four others inside the home were treated for carbon monoxide poisoning. The group had been running a generator indoors without proper ventilation, Escambia County Sheriff's Office said. 7 FACTS TO KNOW ABOUT HURRICANES A woman in Florida was killed when a large tree collapsed onto her home during the storm. In Birmingham, Alabama, one person was killed when a tree fell onto a home. Alabama officials also confirmed a second storm-related death in the state, though additional details were not immediately available. EL NIÑO SURGES TOWARD 'MONSTER' TERRITORY, SIGNALING AN ACTIVE WINTER FOR EAST AND WEST COASTS Panama City Beach records second-highest storm surge Panama City Beach recorded its second-highest storm surge on record, with water rising 5.60 feet above the average high tide, according to the FOX Forecast Center. The record was set during Hurricane Opal on Oct. 4, 1995. Hurricane Michael produced a 3.86-foot surge on Oct. 10, 2018, which ranked fifth. Power outages widespread across Gulf Coast impact zone Power outages continued across the Southeast as Isaias moved inland, with over one million Americans in the dark at the storm's peak. As of 10 p.m. ET Saturday, more than 450,000 customers were without power in the Southeast. Peak outages included: Top wind gusts The FOX Forecast Center reported wind gusts of more than 110 mph across parts of the Florida Panhandle, including: Top rain totals Rainfall totals topped a foot in parts of Alabama and Florida, according to the FOX Forecast Center.

snapshot.title: Isaias made hurricane history before hitting Southeast with 116-mph winds, tornadoes
snapshot.evidenceText: The first hurricane of the 2026 Atlantic season unleashed destructive winds, flooding and tornadoes across the Southeast after making landfall along the Florida Panhandle as a category 2 storm. Published Oct 11, 2026 11:41 AM EDT | Updated Oct 11, 2026 11:49 AM EDT Hurricane Isaias hit “like a freight train,” according to people there, but the recovery process is already underway. The first hurricane of the 2026 Atlantic season roared into the Southeast, where it unleashed flooding rain, destructive winds and tornadoes throughout the weekend. At least four storm-related deaths had been reported as of Sunday morning. As many as 930,000 customers were without electricity at one point late Saturday morning, but the number of outages has since fallen to around 427,000 nationwide, including 319,483 in Florida, according to PowerOutage.us. Isaias is now classified by AccuWeather as a Tropical Wind and Rainstorm, but rain and gusty winds continue to spread through parts of the eastern United States. Eight named storms formed in the Atlantic before Isaias , but none reached hurricane strength. When Isaias finally did, it broke a 121-year-old record for the latest date in the year that an Atlantic season produced its first hurricane. The storm intensified quickly in the Gulf, eventually peaking as a major Category 3 hurricane on Friday. By the time Isaias reached the coast, it was a Category 2 hurricane. The center made landfall near Destin , Florida, at 8:30 p.m. CDT Friday with destructive winds, torrential rain and storm surge hammering the western Florida Panhandle. Radar shows Hurricane Isaias moving onshore near Destin, Florida, on Oct. 9, 2026 after 8:30 p.m. CT. A wind gust of 116 mph was reported near Santa Rosa Sound, while storm surge reached 5.51 feet at Panama City Beach and 4.16 feet at Apalachicola. Rainfall totals topped 8 inches in parts of the panhandle, including 8.06 inches in Niceville. Daylight on Saturday revealed extensive damage across communities near landfall, with roofs torn from homes, businesses and other buildings in Pensacola Beach and Milton. Drone footage from Pensacola Beach showed overturned campers, damaged homes and businesses and significant damage to a high-rise building. Flooding also inundated parts of Fort Walton Beach, where cars were submerged and water entered homes and businesses. Farther west, downtown Pensacola was littered with fallen trees, shattered streetlights and debris. For Laura Dean and her family, the damage served as a reminder of how different the outcome could have been. Dean had planned to ride out Isaias with her 89-year-old father and son at their waterfront condo in Pensacola Beach. They decided at the last minute to evacuate after officials urged residents to leave. Hours later, Isaias ripped through the condo, tearing apart the wall of windows and heavily damaging the upper floor. "If they ever tell you to leave, leave, or we probably wouldn't be here today," Dean told AccuWeather. " Things can be replaced, your family cannot ." One Pensacola Beach woman says urgent pleas to evacuate pushed her to leave just in time. Hours later, Hurricane Isaias destroyed her home. Even people who rode out the storm with minimal damage are facing power outages that could last well into the start of the new week. For AccuWeather Storm Chaser Aaron Jayjack, who was in the Florida Panhandle for landfall, the extent of the blackout became clear when he started to make his way out of the hard-hit Florida Panhandle. "Widespread power outages across this area," Jayjack said. "We left the Destin area, got on I-10 and had to drive 30 miles east before we found power." The storm also spawned tornadoes as it moved inland. One tornado was caught on video crossing a highway near Newington, Georgia, while another long-lived tornado tracked through parts of Allendale and Barnwell counties in South Carolina. Preliminary reports from South Carolina included damage to a manufactured home and snapped power lines, with no injuries initially reported. Storm chaser Chris O’Neal captured these videos of a tornado spinning across at least two counties in South Carolina on Oct. 10. Recovery efforts were underway Sunday, but some communities were still dealing with extended outages and damaged infrastructure. Boil-water notices remained in effect for several Florida Panhandle water systems after the storm disrupted service, while crews continued clearing debris and making repairs. By Sunday morning, rain had spread across much of the mid-Atlantic as Isaias continued northward, accompanied by gusty winds. Rain and thunderstorms were also affecting parts of the Carolinas. A tornado watch had been issued for parts of North Carolina and South Carolina as storms fired on the southern side of Isaias. Additional rain and gusty winds will spread farther north through the East as Isaias continues its trek away from the Southeast. Isaias was just one of several major storms impacting North America over the weekend, with rare alerts issued in California from a different tropical threat. Rachel delivered tropical downpours to Southern California and other parts of the Southwest, with tropical storm watches issued for just the second time ever for Southern California, according to AccuWeather Vice President of Forecast Operations Dan DePodwin. The only other time was in 2023, leading up to Hurricane Hilary. Meanwhile, Hurricane Simon strengthened into a Category 4 storm in the eastern Pacific and headed toward Mexico. The weekend also featured a magnitude 7.7 earthquake in Panama , which triggered a tsunami threat. It was the third-strongest earthquake recorded worldwide so far in 2026. A satellite image from Friday, Oct. 9, 2026, showing Isaias nearing the Gulf Coast, Rachel churning southeast of California and Simon strengthening along Mexico's Pacific coast. (NASA Worldview) As recovery begins in the hardest-hit parts of the Southeast, hundreds of thousands of people remain without power and crews face days of cleanup following the first hurricane of the Atlantic season. snapshot.title: Isaias kills four, about 670,000 without power after landfall - Hawaii Tribune-Herald
snapshot.evidenceText: Damaged homes and buildings in Pensacola Beach, Fla., on Saturday, Oct. 10, 2026, after Isaias made landfall as a Category 2 hurricane in the Florida Panhandle on Friday night. A deluge of rain and heavy winds has battered the Gulf Coast as Isaias toppled trees and knocked out power for hundreds of thousands, leaving at least four people dead. (Zack Wittman/The New York Times) Four people died after Hurricane Isaias made landfall early on Saturday, and about 670,000 residents in Florida, Alabama, Georgia and Mississippi were still without power as the storm weakened to a post-tropical cyclone, according to local authorities and electricity monitoring services. Two of the deaths resulted from trees falling on homes, according to local media and authorities. Authorities in Florida had received no search and rescue requests shortly after landfall in a sign of limited impact, Governor Ron DeSantis said. But hazardous conditions remained and storm surges, flash flooding, damaging winds and a risk of tornadoes across parts of the U.S. Southeast were expected, the National Hurricane Center said. The tornado threat is expected to continue on Saturday across parts of the Florida Panhandle, Georgia and the Carolinas, the NHC said. In Florida, power restoration was marked as a priority, authorities said, while highways, bridges and airports were reopening, and teams were assessing the damage. “They’re going to make assessments this morning, and I think that’ll give us a good sense about the future for the rapidity of the power restoration,” DeSantis told a press conference in Tallahassee. Some 16,000 utility linemen had prepared to respond to the storm, he said. About 420,000 customers in Florida, 190,000 in Alabama, 43,000 in Georgia and 17,000 in Mississippi had no power as of midday Saturday, according to tracking firm PowerOutage.us. A separate storm on the Pacific Ocean, Rachel, was moving toward the coast of northern Baja California on Saturday, bringing wind gusts and increased tides, which left another 7,000 people without power in California. Alabama’s emergency management agency said the downed trees and power lines made travel hazardous in Houston County, which is under a flash flood warning. “Due to the impacts of Hurricane Isaias, all Houston County roads are closed until further notice,” it posted on X. A category 2 hurricane when it hit Florida’s coast and the first of the 2026 Atlantic season, Isaias is expected to produce gusty winds well inland before weakening below gale force later on Saturday, the NHC said. On Saturday, oil and gas producer Shell said it was beginning to redeploy personnel to its Mars, Olympus, Ursa, Vito and Appomattox assets in the Gulf, while Chevron was advancing efforts to redeploy staff to its platforms and seeking to restore full production. “Remobilization of crews will continue through Sunday,” it said. Despite the progress, about 69% of oil output and 57% of natural gas production in the U.S. Gulf of Mexico remained shut on Saturday, slightly down from Friday numbers, the Marine Minerals Administration said. Some 113 production platforms representing 30% of the total remained evacuated, according to the agency. President Donald Trump, asked about hurricane preparations on Friday, told reporters outside the White House that it was “under control.” The U.S. Energy Department said on Saturday it authorized an emergency exchange of up to 4 million barrels of crude oil from the Strategic Petroleum Reserve to address supply disruptions due to the hurricane. Emergency declarations were approved in Florida and Alabama to ensure federal resources would be available to respond to Isaias, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said on X. “There’s also a lot of hazards post-storm that people should be careful of, but so far, we’ve had a lot of assets in place that have not been called on,” DeSantis told FOX News early on Saturday. In the coastal city of Pensacola, a lack of drinking water is a problem, the mayor said. Pensacola airport, Florida’s 10th largest, was damaged by the storm and is closed to commercial flights until further notice. snapshot.title: Hurricane Isaias leaves 2 dead, widespread power outages across Southeast US
snapshot.evidenceText: At least two people were killed in storm-related incidents in Alabama and Florida as Hurricane Isaias weakened into a post-tropical cyclone Saturday, while officials warned of continued flooding and possible tornadoes. One person died in Birmingham, Alabama, early Saturday after a tree fell on a house, according to a Jefferson County emergency management official. Several other houses in the area were also damaged, according to NBC News. In Florida, a person was found dead after being pinned beneath a tree that collapsed onto a residential home in Pensacola on Friday evening, the Escambia County Sheriff's Office said. Alabama Gov. Kay Ivey warned residents of possible “spinoff tornadoes,” strong winds and heavy rainfall as the storm moved inland. “Hope for the best. Prepare for the worst,” she said, urging people to follow reliable information as weather conditions developed. Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis said the storm's center had moved out of the state, but the risk of flooding remained. Wind gusts reached 116 miles (187 kilometers) per hour near Santa Rosa Sound, while water levels rose about 5.5 feet (1.7 meters) above normal. The National Hurricane Center said Isaias had weakened to a post-tropical cyclone, with sustained winds of about 35 miles (55 km) per hour. The system was expected to move across Alabama and into the Tennessee Valley before dissipating Sunday. Forecasters warned of 4 to 8 inches (10 to 20 centimeters) of rain across parts of Alabama, Florida and Georgia, with localized totals reaching 15 inches (38 cm). Power outages affected about 872,000 customers nationwide, including more than 434,000 in Florida and around 317,000 in Alabama, according to PowerOutage.us.

snapshot.title: Isaias brought flooding, wind and tornadoes to the Southeast
snapshot.evidenceText: Hurricane Isaias made landfall in the late evening of Oct. 9 in the Florida Panhandle at Category 2 strength. Wind gusts over 110 mph were clocked in several panhandle locations, along with storm surge flooding. Over 700,000 customers are without power in its wake. Isaias made landfall near Destin, Florida, Friday evening with sustained winds of 105 mph, a Category 2 hurricane. That was the first hurricane to landfall in the mainland U.S. in exactly two years, since Milton slammed into western Florida on Oct. 9, 2024. A rarely-issued extreme wind warning was issued Friday evening for the western Florida Panhandle, including Pensacola and Destin, for the likelihood of wind gusts over 115 mph ahead of the eyewall of Isaias. The highest gust recorded was 116 mph in Santa Rosa Sound, Florida, where sustained winds of 91 mph were also measured. Set The Weather Company as a 'Preferred Source' to get quicker access to the news you value. Pensacola reported a 102-mph wind gust earlier Friday evening. Gulf Breeze, Florida, located across Pensacola Bay from Pensacola, reported a wind gust of 97 mph and sustained winds of 83 mph. Early observations show water levels surpassed 4.0 feet above normally dry ground in Destin and 5.6 feet in Panama City, Florida, and were likely higher in the western Panhandle. One caveat with these storm surge totals is they are measured relative to the Mean Higher High Water (MHHW) and this number includes tide influences so they should not be interpreted as storm surge heights alone. The highest wind gust reported was an impressive 117 mph three miles east-southeast of Oriole Beach. Two miles west southwest of Pensacola, at City Hall, a gust of 102 was reported. There was a roof blown off the Rest and Relax Inn on Plantation Road in Pensacola. Multiple collapsed gas station canopies were reported in Pensacola (Blue Angel Parkway and Mobile Highway) and also in Crestview. Trees were uprooted, one of which crushed a business on Fort Walton Beach. There were also multiple RVs blown over, including one onto US 98 between Gulf Breeze and Navarre. Less than 12 hours prior to landfall, an instrumented NOAA Saildrone measured a gust of 104 mph near the eyewall of Isaias, according to the National Hurricane Center. In Alabama, a gust of 75 mph was reported near Orange Beach while Birmingham saw a gust of 49 mph. Trees fell directly onto residences in Mountain Brook, Birmingham (Five Points & Ensley), Opelika (manufactured home), and Ladonia (tree through a house). All roads were impassable in Conecuh County due to debris and fallen trees. Georgia saw a 68 mph gust in Warner Robins while Hartsfield-Jackson Airport saw a gust to 45 mph. In terms of heavy rainfall, Bellwood, Alabama, saw over a foot of rain in just 13 hours. Caney Creek/FAWN Station, Florida, saw 12.06 inches in 24 hours, with 9.67 falling in 3 hours and 4.15 inches falling in 1 hour. Flash flooding reports were observed at Westland Apartments in Bellair, Florida, while flash flooding stranded a vehicle in floodwaters near Sale City, Georgia. In Florida, Bayside Subdivision and Destin saw 7.18 inches and 7.52 inches of rainfall, respectively. The Greater Atlanta area saw 1-3 inches of rainfall in a 6 hour period early Saturday. A flash flood warning was even in effect for part of Atlanta that morning. And on Saturday, multiple tornadoes were sighted by storm spotters in the Savannah River Valley including near Newington and Oliver, Georgia. There were also multiple tornado reports across South Carolina on Saturday. Near Appleton, South Carolina, four homes were severely damaged, as well as numerous trees and powerlines down. Barnwell County Aiken County, and Newberry County also had reports of tornadoes. On Oct. 11, remnants of Isaias moved into North Carolina, producing heavy rainfall, flash flooding and landslides. A few tornadoes were also reported in North Carolina, near Candor, Clarendon and Atkinson, North Carolina. Numerous flood watches and warnings were also issued across Virginia, West Virginia, Maryland and Pennsylvania on Oct. 11. Isaias replaced "Ike" on one of the Atlantic name lists after that name was retired following the destructive, deadly 2008 hurricane . It wasn't used during its first year of eligibility in 2014, since we only reached the eighth name, Hanna, that year. However, the name was used in 2020 for a storm that eventually tracked up the East Coast with destructive winds. The Weather Channel was found to be the world’s most accurate forecaster in ForecastWatch’s Global and Regional Weather Forecast Accuracy Overview, 2021-2024, commissioned by The Weather Company.

snapshot.title: Trump announces partial ceasefire in Ukraine war as Zelenskyy says deal is ‘news to me’
snapshot.evidenceText: Ukrainian president earlier rejected US call for Kyiv to stop bombing oil refineries, saying Moscow must first end attacks on energy infrastructure Ukrainian president earlier rejected US call for Kyiv to stop bombing oil refineries, saying Moscow must first end attacks on energy infrastructure Donald Trump has announced an energy ceasefire between Ukraine and Russia, apparently without consulting Volodymyr Zelenskyy , who said the deal to stop long-range attacks was “news to me”. In a social media post, the US president claimed the two sides had reached an agreement. “Effective immediately, there is an ENERGY CEASEFIRE in the War between Russia and Ukraine . Both parties have agreed. Do not break it!” he wrote on Truth Social. He offered no further details. Zelenskyy said he was surprised by the announcement but would agree to it if Vladimir Putin did the same. “If President Trump negotiated it with Putin – please tell us when the ceasefire begins. We are ready and we will accept it,” the Ukrainian president told the Axios website. Earlier, Zelenskyy rebuffed Trump’s demand made on Saturday that Kyiv stop bombing Russian oil refineries. Zelenskyy said Moscow had to first halt its own “brutal” attacks on his country’s energy infrastructure. Any deal to end long-range drone strikes by Ukraine on targets inside Russia would have to be “reciprocal”, he said. It should be backed by “real guarantees” – meaning punitive measures against Moscow from Ukraine’s allies, including the US. There was no sign that the Kremlin was observing Trump’s ceasefire. According to Zelenskyy, Russian drones took to the sky “throughout the day” on Sunday. There were also “unfortunately” several airstrikes, he said, including on energy infrastructure. The Ukrainian president said the Russians hit thermal power station No 5 in the eastern city of Kharkiv – the latest of more than 200 strikes this week against electricity generation and transmission facilities in Ukraine. There were another 17 hits on gas and oil facilities, he added. The fast-moving row between Washington and Kyiv began on Friday when Trump announced he was lifting sanctions on Russian diesel exports . He said the move would reduce global and domestic fuel prices before next month’s US midterm elections. A furious Zelenskyy called the decision “weak” and said it would generate “billions” in extra revenue for Putin, enabling him to wage war “even more intensely”. An equally irate Trump said Zelenskyy should “damn well stop” hitting Russian refineries. Ukraine needed a “new leader” , he said on Saturday. Responding to Trump, Zelenskyy said it was up to Ukrainians to choose “one or another leader”. He told ABC News he was willing to accept Trump’s demands and to organise elections, but only if Putin agreed to a “total” 60-day ceasefire. The bitter public feud is the most serious between the US and Ukraine since last year, when Trump berated Zelenskyy in the Oval Office . The Financial Times, citing officials in Europe , reported on Sunday that the US is ⁠threatening ⁠to stop ​the procurement ⁠system that provides ⁠Ukraine ​with ‌weapons to ‌press Kyiv to halt its ‌deep strikes on ​Russian energy infrastructure. The New York Times has reported that US officials have offered the Kremlin lucrative economic incentives in exchange for a ceasefire. They reportedly include releasing billions in Russian sovereign assets that are frozen. The Trump administration also revisited a plan to sell parts of Russia’s energy company, Lukoil. The multibillion deal would benefit Middle Eastern investors, the paper reported , some with “business ties” to US negotiators. On Saturday, Trump criticised Zelenskyy and said he had refused to make a deal to end the fighting. In response, Ukraine’s president laid the blame for Europe’s biggest war since 1945 on “Russia and Russia alone”. “It is possible to stop strikes on energy infrastructure as early as today, but Putin does not want to do so,” he said. Ukrainian officials point out that the White House is demanding Kyiv give up its most effective weapon, without demanding any corresponding concessions from Russia. In recent weeks, Kyiv has dealt a major blow to Russia’s economy, striking oil complexes, warehouses and datacentres. Russia’s own bombing campaign has been relentless. On Saturday it killed 23 people in the city of Zaporizhzhia, including four children, and hit a five-storey apartment block in the frontline town of Sloviansk. Zelenskyy said Moscow’s aerial campaign involved thousands of aerial bombs and jet-powered drones. It continued “unabated”, he said. A digest of the morning's main headlines from the Europe edition emailed direct to you every week day The head of Ukraine’s foreign affairs committee, Oleksandr Merezhko , said Trump’s “bullying” demand for Zelenskyy to quit had strengthened him at home “paradoxically”, after recent damaging corruption scandals. “Putin’s plan is to decapitate Zelenskyy and remove him as a wartime leader. Trump is siding with Putin,” Merezhko said. He added: “I’m afraid that behind this situation is Trump’s worldview. He wants to do business with Putin. For him, Ukraine seems like an obstacle to be removed. Both Trump and Putin wish to pressure us into capitulation.” Referring to the notorious 1939 agreement between Nazi Germany and the USSR, Merezhko said: “We are moving to a new Molotov-Ribbentrop pact and to a world of strongmen and spheres of influence.” Merezhko said Ukraine would continue to destroy enemy oil refineries, against US wishes, because they funded Russia’s war machine and acknowledged that a cutoff of US intelligence sharing with Kyiv – threatened by the Trump administration – would “blind” Ukraine’s air defence systems. “This would be an act of complicity with Putin’s genocide. It would mean more dead civilians and dead children,” he said. Ukrainian negotiators had been meeting in Florida with their American counterparts, Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, when Trump announced the US was lifting sanctions on Russian diesel. Blindsided, the Ukrainians went home early. “It felt like a trap,” one stunned Ukrainian official told the Kyiv Independent newspaper . On Sunday, Zelenskyy shored up support in a series of conversations with key allies including Canada’s prime minister, Mark Carney, the Polish leader, Donald Tusk, and the European Commission president, Ursula von der Leyen. Earlier Zelenskyy spoke with the UK prime minister, Andy Burnham, France’s president, Emmanuel Macron, and the Finnish president, Alexander Stubb. Downing Street said Burnham recognised the last 24 hours had been “difficult” for Ukraine and “reiterated his complete solidarity”. Downing Street said the two leaders agreed “to maintain pressure on Russia” and to strengthen the sanctions regime, despite Trump’s efforts to the contrary. “Russia should agree to an immediate energy ceasefire, ending its brutal strikes on Ukrainian infrastructure and its attacks on shipping in the Black Sea,” a statement added. Speaking over the weekend, Zelenskyy said Trump’s decision empowered Putin and gave him “extra money for the war”, running into millions and “perhaps billions”. “It is certainly not fair. It is certainly not how partners should act. And, in my view, it is a weak decision,” he said. Luke Harding’s Betrayal: Trump, Putin and the New Age of Conquest is published by Guardian Faber

snapshot.evidenceText: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy had pushed for a 60-day full ceasefire. US President Donald Trump has announced what he called an ‘energy ceasefire’ between Ukraine and Russia, after mutual attacks on energy infrastructure piled pressure on global energy prices. “Effective immediately, there is an ENERGY CEASEFIRE in the War between Russia and Ukraine. Both parties have agreed,” Trump wrote on social media on Sunday. “Do not break it! Thank you for your attention to this matter. President DONALD J. TRUMP.” Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy denied any knowledge of the agreement and said it was “news to him,” according to Axios. But he confirmed Ukraine would back the deal, saying in a post on Telegram: “Ukraine supports the ceasefire, and it is important that Russia support it as well. We are awaiting details from the American side.” Zelenskyy previously said on Sunday he would organise elections if Russian President Vladimir Putin agrees to a 60-day full ceasefire. On Saturday, Trump slammed the Ukrainian president for attacking Russian oil refineries, the day after the US temporarily lifted sanctions on Russian fuel that were originally imposed to sap Moscow’s war effort in Ukraine. “He better damn well stop,” Trump told reporters at the White House. “I think it’s time for Ukraine to get a new president,” he added. Earlier on Saturday, Zelenskyy said Trump’s announcement of the diesel deal with Putin had emboldened Moscow. Kyiv instead urged Washington to pressure Moscow for serious negotiations to end the four-and-a-half-year war. “Today, Russia said thank you for the lifting of sanctions on diesel exports by dropping five glide bombs on residential buildings in Zaporizhzhia,” Zelenskyy said. “Last night provided yet more confirmation that Russia perceives any easing of pressure as a signal that it can supposedly keep fighting, that it can supposedly keep dropping bombs on cities. Different signals are needed.” The southern Ukrainian city of Zaporizhzhia has been a regular target of Russian bombardment , with attacks intensifying in the past few months. On Saturday, a six-year-old girl was among those killed in Zaporizhzhia when one attack reduced part of an apartment block to rubble. Her grandfather, Anatoliy Chumniy, stood sobbing over her body, laid on the ground in a white bag, after rescuers pulled her from the wreckage. In response to Trump’s suggestion of a new leader, Zelenskyy said, “it’s up to Ukrainians” to choose their leader and noted that Putin would also like to change who is leading Ukraine. Earlier on Sunday, Zelenskyy said Ukraine was ready to halt attacks on Russian oil refineries if Moscow ceases its own attacks on Ukrainian energy infrastructure.

snapshot.title: Ukraine war latest: Russia pounds Kyiv's energy infrastructure as Trump’s energy ceasefire claim catches Ukraine off guard
snapshot.evidenceText: Help rescue animals from the front line — shop our Companion Collection 🐾 Kyiv's electricity and water grids came under renewed strain on Oct. 11, as Russia continued its attacks on civilian infrastructure despite U.S. President Donald Trump's call for an "energy ceasefire." "The enemy continues to attack energy infrastructure," warned Kyiv Mayor Vitalii Klitschko on the afternoon of Oct. 11, hours before Trump said an energy ceasefire was reached between Ukraine and Russia. A senior Ukrainian official told the Kyiv Independent Ukraine had no information about an energy ceasefire that Trump announced. Mayor Klitschko mentioned damage to a high-voltage power line. "Emergency crews are already working," he said. Large parts of the city have been without running water. Throughout the day, journalists from the Kyiv Independent heard explosions in both downtown Kyiv and further out. Ukrainian energy company DTEK also reported short power outages in different parts of the Ukrainian capital. The day before, Trump tried to pin the blame for the continuation of the war on President Volodymyr Zelensky, calling on him to stop attacking Russian oil refineries after he had signed a potentially illegal deal with Moscow to import diesel . But Zelensky made clear that these attacks, which have reduced Russian refining capacity by 45%, would only be called off once Moscow stops attacking Ukraine's energy infrastructure. Attacks on Kyiv already plunged the city into near-total darkness on Oct. 8, and the expectation is that Ukrainians will have to brace for more of the same over the winter months. Ukraine's defense ministry announced on Oct. 11 that it has ordered and received significantly more drones so far in 2026 than it had done for the whole of the previous year. A press release from the defense ministry notes that its procurement agency has contracted for 5.5 times as many drones as in the same period of 2025, and that the volume of deliveries has increased by almost 3.7 times. "The task of the Ministry of Defense is to give the army drones to work effectively at every level," said Defense Minister Yevhen Khmara in a press statement. "Technology and the availability of sufficient means increase combat effectiveness and at the same time reduce risks for our soldiers," Khmara said. "Such indicators became possible thanks to the direction of support from international partners and the scaling of the capabilities of the Ukrainian defense industry," reads the press statement. An increasing number of deals between Ukraine and other European countries are helping bolster drone procurement across the continent, whether it is the announcement of support packages from Germany , the U.K. signing a battlefield data deal with Kyiv to develop AI drone swarms, or the EU-Ukraine drone alliance beginning work in September. More EU money to help Ukraine procure drones is also expected to arrive by the end of 2026. The bloc disbursed 1.2 billion euros ($1.4 billion) on Oct. 7 and is expected to make another payment to Ukraine ahead of the Oct. 14 summit of EU leaders, two EU officials told the Kyiv Independent. Of the EU defense support available to Kyiv by the end of 2026 alone, 15.4 billion euros ($17.2 billion) remains unused. At least two people were killed and 25 others injured across Ukraine over the past day, as Russia continues to target residential buildings and energy infrastructure across the country. In Dnipropetrovsk Oblast , one child was killed and a further five people injured, of which two are children, said Serhii Lysak, head of the oblast's military administration. Following that announcement, Russia attacked a residential building, injuring at least four people, along which two eight-year-old girls, Lysak said , taking the total injured in the region to at least nine. One person was killed and four injured in Donetsk Oblast, reported Governor Vadym Filashkin. Kyiv Oblast 's military administration reports four people injured, with Russian drone strikes targeting "civilian facilities, housing, and energy infrastructure." While in Kharkiv Oblast, six people were injured, of which one child, Governor Oleh Syniehubov posted on Telegram. One person was also injured in Kherson Oblast , noted Oleksandr Prokudin, head of the Kherson regional military administration, while three people were evacuated from liberated communities in the region. Sumy Oblast military administration noted that two men were injured as a result of drone attacks. Chernihiv Oblast , Khmelnytskyi Oblast, Kirovohrad Oblast, Mykolaiv Oblast , Odesa Oblast, and Rivne Oblast were also attacked but no casualties or significant damage was reported. Russian technology giant Yandex's data center in Vladimir Oblast has been completely shut down following a reported drone attack, Russian state news agency TASS said on Oct. 11, citing the company. The reported strike marks the third near-consecutive day of attacks on Yandex data centers in Russia, following confirmed strikes in Ryazan and Kaluga oblasts on Oct. 8 and 9. Earlier on Oct. 11, Yandex Cloud reported power disruptions in an availability zone identified as being located at the company's data center in Vladimir. "There are power interruptions in the ru-central1-a availability zone. The team is working to resolve the issue," the company said in a statement published on its official Telegram channel. Yandex Go users across Russia reported being unable to order taxis on Oct. 11, with similar disruptions reported in Serbia, Kazakhstan, Belarus and Armenia, according to Russian independent media outlet Ostorozhno Novosti.. The outlet also reported that Yandex Pro, an application used by taxi drivers and couriers, was unavailable, while employees experienced problems accessing internal support systems. Users also reported disruptions to Yandex's smart home services. Russian independent media outlet ASTRA reported that Yandex Cloud experienced power disruptions at its Vladimir data center following warnings of a drone attack in the region. Ukrainian monitoring channels also circulated images purportedly showing a fire near the facility. The Kyiv Independent could not independently verify the images or the extent of damage at the facility or to any of the Yandex apps or services. The latest incident follows two drone strikes that Yandex has publicly acknowledged. On Oct. 8, a drone attack caused a fire at the company's data center in Sasovo , Ryazan Oblast, forcing it to suspend operations completely. Yandex said it could not yet determine when the facility's equipment could be restored. A second strike on Oct. 9 damaged the company's data center in Kaluga , disabling several modules and potentially disrupting services. President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Oct. 8 that Ukraine was responding to Russian strikes on Ukrainian data centers. "We always respond in kind," he told journalists, adding that Russia "has been and still is striking our data centers." In a statement on Oct. 9, Yandex described its data centers as critical infrastructure for its services and said employees were working around the clock to restore operations. On Oct. 10, Yandex updated its user agreement to include drone and missile attacks among circumstances of force majeure that could exempt the company from contractual obligations. Russian forces struck a residential neighborhood in Zaporizhzhia with guided aerial bombs early on Oct. 10, killing 20 people, including three children, and injuring 32, reported Zaporizhzhia Oblast's regional administration reported amid ongoing search-and-rescue operations. The injured victims also include three children, the State Emergency Service said . Russia attacked the neighborhood with five guided aerial bombs , nearly destroying parts of residential buildings and trapping civilians underneath the rubble, according to authorities. One strike partially destroyed a section of an apartment building, causing parts of the building to collapse to the second floor, according to Mykhailo Semikin , acting governor of Zaporizhzhia Oblast. A woman was pulled out from underneath the collapsed building after being trapped for eight hours. Rescue workers continue searching for people, as several individuals remain unreachable, Interior Minister Ivan Vyhivskyi said said in the afternoon. The State Emergency Service reported that three people had been rescued as of 6:15 p.m. local time. Ukraine's Air Force warned at around 5 a.m. that Russian tactical aircraft had launched guided aerial bombs toward Zaporizhzhia. Vyhivskyi said that despite the threat of a double-tap strike, Ukraine's first responders were trying to clear the rubble from the buildings as quickly as possible. The attack was "against ordinary homes, against families with children," Vyhivskyi noted. The attack came a day after Russian guided aerial bombs struck residential areas of Zaporizhzhia on Oct. 9, killing at least one person and injuring seven others, including a child, according to regional officials. Russian forces have repeatedly targeted Zaporizhzhia, a southeastern Ukrainian city near the front line, with guided aerial bombs, drones, and missiles. Russia has occupied parts of Zaporizhzhia Oblast since the beginning of its full-scale invasion in February 2022, while the regional capital of Zaporizhzhia remains under Ukrainian control. snapshot.title: Trump says Russia and Ukraine reach ‘energy ceasefire’ but gives no details
snapshot.evidenceText: President Trump said Sunday that Russia and Ukraine had agreed to an “energy ceasefire,” but offered no details. Trump’s brief social media post said only that the ceasefire took effect immediately, adding: “Do not break it!” Moscow did not immediately comment on the announcement, and the White House did not clarify the president’s post. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said on X: “We discussed the energy ceasefire announced by President Trump. Ukraine supports the ceasefire, and it is important that Russia support it as well. We are awaiting details from the American side.” Zelensky added that he had spoken with Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney, Finnish President Alexander Stubb and NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte. In an interview broadcast Sunday on ABC's "This Week," Zelensky said Ukraine was ready to stop striking Russian refineries if Moscow halted attacks on Ukraine’s energy system, and asked Trump to press the Kremlin to agree. “We are asking President Trump," he said, to give a signal not to "attack energy infrastructure of Ukraine." Trump said Saturday it was time for Ukraine to get a new president, suggesting Zelensky has not done enough to end the war and blaming him for high diesel prices in the U.S. Zelensky said in response to Trump's comments that Ukraine could hold elections if Russia agreed to a 60-day ceasefire. “Give us two months, 60 days off. Total ceasefire, 60 days, and we will organize elections,” he said, adding that Ukraine would be ready to accept whatever choice its people made. “With all respect to President Trump, it’s up to our society, up to our people to choose one or another leader,” he said. Zelensky added that holding a vote during the war would be unlawful and that Ukraine would need security guarantees to allow people to vote safely. Ukraine has been under martial law since Russian President Vladimir Putin launched the full-scale invasion in February 2022, and the Ukrainian Constitution bars elections while it remains in force. Beyond the legal barrier, a nationwide vote would be vulnerable to Russian attacks, and organizing one is widely seen as logistically impossible, with roughly a fifth of the country held by Russia, millions of Ukrainians displaced abroad and soldiers on the front line. Zelensky’s term formally expired in May 2024, but the constitution allows him to remain in office until a new president is sworn in. The exchange came as Kyiv pressed its campaign against infrastructure deep inside Russia, with a drone attack on Sunday shutting down a data center in the city of Vladimir, east of Moscow, run by technology giant Yandex. It was the third strike on the company’s facilities in four days. Russia and Ukraine have been locked in a long-range aerial war while their armies remain largely deadlocked on the front line. Trump, who on Friday struck a deal with Putin to buy diesel from Moscow in an attempt to address high fuel prices ahead of U.S. midterm elections, has been urging Zelensky for weeks to stop strikes on Russian energy infrastructure. He has sought to blame record U.S. diesel prices on Ukraine rather than the U.S.-led war in Iran, which has driven up world energy prices. Ukrainian and European officials reacted to the diesel deal with dismay, saying it will help pay for Russia’s war effort. The Ukrainian drone attack on the Yandex data center in Vladimir caused outages across the company's services, leaving users in dozens of Russian cities and in Kazakhstan, Belarus and Armenia unable to order taxis or access banking services, according to Russian independent news outlet Astra. “Operations at the data center have been completely halted. There were no injuries,” said the Yandex Cloud Telegram channel, which provides operational updates on service availability. Moscow residents described disruption to everyday tasks. Pavel Belyavskiy, a driver for Yandex Taxi, said it was unclear whether orders were coming through at all, and on several rides he had to cancel after waiting a long time because he could not reach the passenger. “I’d press the ‘call’ button to contact them, but nothing happens,” he said, “There’s nothing I can do, so I’m just forced to cancel.” Igor Mann said he went to check on an order on the Yandex Market shopping platform but the page was unavailable, and connecting through a virtual private network did not help. “Nothing worked,” he said. Another Muscovite, Eduard Malyavko, said the outages had “direct impact” and weren't just about “convenience.” “It’s also about work,” he said, adding that the outages also affected “healthcare, and everything else.” On Thursday, a drone attack took a Yandex data center offline in the Ryazan region, southeast of Moscow. The next day, Ukrainian drones hit the company’s major data center in the Kaluga region, southwest of Moscow, disabling part of the facilty, Yandex said. Yandex, often described as Russia’s Google, runs the country’s most popular search engine and a wide range of digital services, and is heavily involved in Russia’s artificial intelligence development. Elsewhere, search and rescue operations ended in the southern city of Zaporizhzhia after a Russian bombing on Saturday, according to Ivan Fedorov, former regional head and co-chair of the regional defense council. Zelensky said 23 people were killed in the attack, including four children. More than 30 people were wounded, Fedorov said, with eight still hospitalized. A man was killed and two women wounded in a Ukrainian drone strike on Russia's Bryansk border region, local officials said Sunday. Blann, Morton and Binkley write for the Associated Press. Blann reported from Kyiv and Morton from London.

snapshot.title: Trump announces Russia-Ukraine 'energy ceasefire,' which Zelenskyy says he hasn't seen but supports | CBC News
snapshot.evidenceText: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said he has discussed the possibility of an energy ceasefire with Russia with Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney, Finnish President Alexander Stubb and NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte but is waiting for more information from the United States. U.S. President Donald Trump had said in a social media post Sunday that Ukraine and Russia had agreed to what he described as an "energy ceasefire" without offering specifics on terms. In an interview with Axios, Zelenskyy said Trump's post was the first he had heard of the deal, though a senior Ukrainian official told Reuters that Ukraine was ready to agree to such a ceasefire, if Russia was. In a social media post of his own, the Ukrainian president said he had just spoken with Carney, Stubb and Rutte to discuss the alleged ceasefire announced by Trump. "Ukraine supports the ceasefire, and it is important that Russia support it as well. We are awaiting details from the American side," Zelenskyy wrote on X Sunday afternoon. "For our part, Ukraine always FULLY supports steps toward de-escalation, the protection of lives, and the decisions needed to end the war and guarantee lasting peace." The Prime Minister's Office said Carney reassured Zelenskyy that Canada will maintain its sanctions on Russia and support for Ukraine. "The Prime Minister was clear: this agreement is in direct opposition to the efforts of Ukraine, Canada, and our allies to create peace and stability in Europe," the statement read. "It will provide additional revenue for Russia and help finance its illegal, unjustifiable war against Ukraine." The announcement comes a day after Trump blamed Zelenskyy for attacking diesel facilities in Russia and contributing to a global shortage. Russia and Ukraine have repeatedly attacked each other's energy infrastructure during the war. Trump's brief post said only that the ceasefire takes effect immediately and that both sides had agreed to it. "Do not break it!" he said in his social media post. The White House did not immediately clarify the president's post or add detail. The Kremlin did not provide comment. Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskyy meets with U.S. President Donald Trump during the United Nations General Assembly, on Sept. 22 at the UN headquarters. (Julia Demaree Nikhinson/The Associated Press) Trump, whose war in Iran has been blamed for high diesel prices that are weighing on Republicans' prospects at next month's midterm elections, had previously announced an energy ceasefire in Ukraine in mid-September , though neither side ever confirmed such an agreement was reached. "Effective immediately, there is an ENERGY CEASEFIRE in the War between Russia and Ukraine. Both parties have agreed. Do not break it!" Trump wrote on Truth Social. Earlier on Sunday, Zelenskyy had repeated Ukraine's long-standing position that it was willing to halt attacks on Russian refineries, but only if Moscow ceased its own strikes on Ukrainian power infrastructure. Any such deal would need to come with "real guarantees," Zelenskyy said. "The real cause of the war in Europe is Russia and Russia alone," Zelenskyy said. "It's possible to stop strikes on energy infrastructure as early as today, but Putin does not want to do so." In a dramatic deterioration in their relations, Trump on Saturday had warned Zelenskyy that he had "better damn well stop" attacking Russian refineries, and he urged Ukrainians to replace Zelenskyy as their leader via new elections because he had missed several opportunities to strike a deal with Moscow. Appearing on ABC's This Week on Sunday, Zelenskyy responded that he would organize elections in Ukraine if Russian President Vladimir Putin agreed to a 60-day ceasefire. Zelenskyy said it was "up to Ukrainians" to choose their leader, but noted that there needed to be an end to the fighting first. Ukrainian law prohibits elections under martial law for security reasons. "Please tell Putin, give us two months, 60 days of total ceasefire, 60 days, and we will organize elections," Zelenskyy said. Trump says Ukraine should get a new president, blames Zelenskyy for U.S. diesel prices The Ukrainian leader rejected being blamed for energy price rises, adding that "everybody in the world" knew that the war in the Middle East was a bigger factor. The steep rise in global diesel prices, which followed the outbreak of the Iran war in February, has become a political liability for Trump's Republican Party ahead of the midterms, when opposition Democrats could gain control of one or both houses of Congress. On Saturday, Zelenskyy had responded angrily to Trump's announcement of a diesel supply deal with Russia, saying it would embolden Moscow's attacks on Ukraine and lead to a greater loss of civilian lives. Trump reverses course on Russian oil sanctions Analysts said Trump's diesel supply agreement with Moscow was unlikely to lead to sustained lower fuel prices as the volumes involved were too small. The diesel deal was also criticized by U.S. lawmakers, including one of Trump's fellow Republicans, Rep. Don Bacon, who said it was time to apply more sanctions, not lift them. On the streets of Kyiv, several residents expressed anger at Trump's suggestion that Ukraine should find a new leader willing to make a deal with Putin. "No one has the right to tell us what to do, especially since elections cannot be held during wartime," said Sabina, a 40-year-old primary school teacher. "In my view, it is a betrayal by our partners," she said, describing Trump's remarks. Zelenskyy said he would continue discussions with European leaders on Sunday, and there were daily conversations around additional air defence packages, including ammunition for combat aircraft that are used to down Russia's jet-powered drones. On Monday, Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha is due to participate in a European Union foreign affairs council meeting that is expected to discuss increasing sanctions pressure on Russia and advancing negotiations on Ukraine’s EU accession. A digest of the morning's main headlines from the Europe edition emailed direct to you every week day The head of Ukraine’s foreign affairs committee, Oleksandr Merezhko , said Trump’s “bullying” demand for Zelenskyy to quit had strengthened him at home “paradoxically”, after recent damaging corruption scandals. “Putin’s plan is to decapitate Zelenskyy and remove him as a wartime leader. Trump is siding with Putin,” Merezhko said. He added: “I’m afraid that behind this situation is Trump’s worldview. He wants to do business with Putin. For him, Ukraine seems like an obstacle to be removed. Both Trump and Putin wish to pressure us into capitulation.” Referring to the notorious 1939 agreement between Nazi Germany and the USSR, Merezhko said: “We are moving to a new Molotov-Ribbentrop pact and to a world of strongmen and spheres of influence.” Merezhko said Ukraine would continue to destroy enemy oil refineries, against US wishes, because they funded Russia’s war machine and acknowledged that a cutoff of US intelligence sharing with Kyiv – threatened by the Trump administration – would “blind” Ukraine’s air defence systems. “This would be an act of complicity with Putin’s genocide. It would mean more dead civilians and dead children,” he said. Ukrainian negotiators had been meeting in Florida with their American counterparts, Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, when Trump announced the US was lifting sanctions on Russian diesel. Blindsided, the Ukrainians went home early. “It felt like a trap,” one stunned Ukrainian official told the Kyiv Independent newspaper . On Sunday, Zelenskyy shored up support in a series of conversations with key allies including Canada’s prime minister, Mark Carney, the Polish leader, Donald Tusk, and the European Commission president, Ursula von der Leyen. Earlier Zelenskyy spoke with the UK prime minister, Andy Burnham, France’s president, Emmanuel Macron, and the Finnish president, Alexander Stubb. Downing Street said Burnham recognised the last 24 hours had been “difficult” for Ukraine and “reiterated his complete solidarity”. Downing Street said the two leaders agreed “to maintain pressure on Russia” and to strengthen the sanctions regime, despite Trump’s efforts to the contrary. “Russia should agree to an immediate energy ceasefire, ending its brutal strikes on Ukrainian infrastructure and its attacks on shipping in the Black Sea,” a statement added. Speaking over the weekend, Zelenskyy said Trump’s decision empowered Putin and gave him “extra money for the war”, running into millions and “perhaps billions”. “It is certainly not fair. It is certainly not how partners should act. And, in my view, it is a weak decision,” he said. Luke Harding’s Betrayal: Trump, Putin and the New Age of Conquest is published by Guardian Faber
