snapshot.title: Pakistan imposes emergency rule over Imran Khan's provincial government
snapshot.evidenceText: ISLAMABAD, Oct 11 (Reuters) - Pakistan's president declared a state of emergency and suspended a provincial government led by the party of jailed former Prime MinisterImran Khan on Sunday, which the federal government said had failed to tackle Islamist militancy in the province bordering Afghanistan. The state of emergency and imposition of a new governor in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa sharply escalates a standoff between Khan’s Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI) party and the government, and comes a week after PTI supporters gathered in theprovince intending to march on Islamabad to demand Khan's release. The party’s last large-scale protest two years ago ended in deadly clashes with security forces and Khan’s 2023 arrest sparked nationwide riots that threatened the military’s standing. Hundreds of activists and three of Khan’s sisters have been detained ahead of the planned march, in what the PTI called one of the strongest crackdowns in years. Pakistan's constitution allows the government to take over from provincial authorities during an emergency, and Law Minister Azam Nazeer Tarar said a provincial governor would take charge in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, which has suffered an increasing number of militant attacks in recent months. Tarar told a news conference in Islamabad that the governor will initially be in place for six months, but could stay for as long as needed.The interior ministry said it would be deploying troops in the province. The federal government and the military accuse PTI of failing to curb militants. The party rejects the charge and says Islamabad has not provided the funding and equipment it needs. Restrictions have been placed on the movements of Sohail Afridi, who had previously been in charge of the province, one of his close aides told Reuters. Khan's aide and PTI spokesperson Zulfikar Bukhari called the government's move "more of a coup disguised as emergency," adding that it risks leading to further bloodshed and instability and was intended to stop the protest. The government has expanded the military's powers and PTI accuses the army of dominating politics, which the military denies. Maulana Fazlur Rehman, leader of the JUI-F political party and engaged by the government to mediate with PTI, also condemned the move. "Imposition of emergency is an ambush on democracy," he told a news conference in Islamabad. The government has deployed tens of thousands of security forces in Islamabad and lined roads with containers ready to block roads, to bar protesters from reaching parliament. Candidates backed by Khan’s party won the most seats in the 2024 election but formed a government only in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa. Supporters of the 74-year-old former cricket star say the military rigged the vote against him, which the military denies. Cases against Khan range from concerns over state gifts to instigating violence and an accusation of an unlawful marriage. All but one conviction have been suspended or overturned, with appeals pending. He denies wrongdoing. President Asif Ali Zardari declared the emergency on the advice of Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif after a cabinet decision, the president’s office said. Sharif told the cabinet that security forces and citizens had been under attack for two years. “We can’t just act as a silent spectator.” Islamabad also accuses Afghanistan of harboring militants who launch attacks inside Pakistan, and says PTI has sympathized with the Taliban in Kabul and its domestic affiliates. Both deny the charge. (Reporting by Asif Shahzad and Ariba Shahid in Islamabad; Additional reporting by Mubasher Bukhari in Lahore; Editing by Jamie Freed, Elaine Hardcastle, Alexandra Hudson) Our correspondents are already on the next chapter. snapshot.title: Major earthquake hits Panama, injures at least 27
snapshot.evidenceText: A powerful 7.7-magnitude earthquake rocked Panama on Friday, collapsing buildings and roads in the center of the country and injuring at least 27 people, with no deaths reported. The shallow tremor was felt across the Central American nation of around 4.5 million people, according to the National Civil Protection System. The head of emergency operations Rene Garcia told AFP that there were no reports of fatalities so far. In Panama City, about 200 kilometers (120 miles) from the epicenter, there were scenes of panic as people rushed to evacuate from the city's emblematic skyscrapers. "I was scared because the shaking was very strong and prolonged," Salomon Andion, 46, told AFP after evacuating his 15-story building for the second time following aftershocks. "Heavy objects like dressers, the bed, and all the kitchen items were shaking." A video widely shared on social media showed water falling from the rooftop pool of a building more than 20 stories tall. Another showed a bridge over the Panama Canal shaking violently but remaining upright as vehicles traveled across it. "We are facing a major disaster," President Jose Raul Mulino said, adding that some roads had "completely collapsed." "It was horrible, like nothing we ever experienced. My daughter was trapped in school," Juana Alveo, a 38-year-old cashier at a store in the city of Penonome in central Cocle province, told AFP. There were 27 people with minor injuries across the country as a result of the quake, according to a statement from the National Civil Protection System. The US Geological Survey said the quake struck at 12:56 pm local time (1756 GMT) with an epicenter 10 kilometers (six miles) from the small town of Pitaloza Arriba in central Herrera province. The USGS initially estimated it to be a magnitude-8.0 quake before revising it down to 7.7. A tsunami warning was issued for the eastern Pacific but later lifted. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said on X on Friday that he was "closely monitoring" the situation, with his office "rapidly mobilizing resources and personnel to assist," at the Panamanian government's request. The Panama Canal Authority said shipping through the channel, which connects the Pacific and Atlantic oceans, was unaffected and operating "as normal." Mulino traveled to Penonome to coordinate the disaster response. Health Minister Fernando Boyd said the most affected areas were the provinces of Herrera and Cocle as well as Los Santos. He said the town of Tonosi in Los Santos was completely cut off. "We are trying to figure out how to get there by air, because it's impossible by land," Boyd said. Panama City's international airport, a major hub for the region, was temporarily closed. Several flights were diverted to other airports as a precaution, according to the Civil Aeronautics Authority. The leaders of Colombia, Ecuador and Guatemala all sent messages of solidarity and offers of aid. Benjamin Gonzalez, 52, said he was at a farm near the town of La Miel when the quake hit, and when he returned home he found "many houses devastated" and "everyone terrified" in the small town square, which was left without power. His neighbor, David Castillo, told AFP that residents were choosing not to return home because they are "afraid it will happen again." Earthquakes are rare in Panama and usually occur in western Chiriqui province, bordering Costa Rica. Former president Ricardo Martinelli posted pictures on Instagram of his house in the town of Sona in Veraguas province that collapsed. A church and a hotel in Penonome also suffered extensive damage, images shared on local media showed. More than 80 aftershocks, one above magnitude 6.0, were recorded by the local geosciences institute. "What happened should not be used to generate alarm and disorder," he wrote on X, adding that he had called for a report on the damage. The education ministry announced the suspension of classes in schools nationwide. The Panamanian quake is at least the fourth quake this year in Latin America surpassing 7.0 in magnitude, after devastating back-to-back earthquakes in Venezuela's Guaira in June and a powerful earthquake in western Colombia in August. snapshot.title: 2 powerful earthquakes and multiple aftershocks rock Panama
snapshot.evidenceText: People being evacuated from hospital after a severe 7.6 magnitude earthquake hit the country, in Panama City on Oct. 9, 2026. According to the U.S. Geological Survey (USGS), a magnitude 7.6 earthquake shook Panama sparking panic in the capital, though no casualties or damage have been reported so far. PANAMA CITY (AP) — Two powerful 7.7 and 6.6 magnitude earthquakes and a series of aftershocks roiled southern Panama Friday afternoon, collapsing buildings near the epicenter and prompting evacuations across the country. The earlier quake, felt as far away as neighboring Colombia , was centered about 6 miles southwest of the remote community of Pitaloza Arriba, in the central province of Herrera, the USGS said. It struck at a depth of 6 miles. The USGS initially reported the first quake as magnitude 8, then revised it to 7.6 and later to 7.7. (MORE: Hurricane Isaias is closing in on Gulf Coast landfall tonight ) Visibly shaken residents of Panama City, the capital, gathered outside as they waited for news of the quake’s impact on Friday. “We felt it very strongly. It knocked things over in the kitchen, but we’re okay, though we’re very scared," Rosendo Domínguez, 60, who is from Herrera province, where the earthquake struck, told The Associated Press by phone. “Everyone is outside, scared.” Set The Weather Company as a 'Preferred Source' to get quicker access to the news you value. Multiple aftershocks continued to rattle Panama, including several measuring magnitude 5.8, 5.5 and 5.2. Seismologists at the University of Panama recorded more than 45 aftershocks, though many were too weak to be felt. Despite the strength of the successive quakes, Panamanian President José Raúl Mulino said authorities had not documented anyone killed as of Friday evening, though he cautioned that could change in the coming hours or days. “Nobody was ready, and no one is ever ready for this type of disaster,” Mulino said, after calling for calm earlier in the day. People check their mobile phones outside the maternity ward of the Santo Tomas hospital, after a 7.6 magnitude earthquake hit the country, in Panama City on Oct. 9, 2026. A severe magnitude 7.6 earthquake shook Panama, according to the U.S. Geological Survey (USGS), sparking panic in the capital, though no casualties or damage have been reported so far. Images of crumbling buildings and deep fissures slicing through roads added to fears across a region battered by a series of devastating earthquakes in recent months. Two back-to-back 7.2 and 7.5 magnitude earthquakes roiled Venezuela’s La Guaira state in June , killing more than 6,500 people and leaving 17,000 homeless. In August, a 7.4 magnitude earthquake in Colombia killed at least 289 people . (Live updates: Tornado threat rises as Cat 3 Hurricane Isaias closes in ) The notably lesser toll in nearby Panama may have been due to the country's strict building codes, especially governing construction of skyscrapers in the capital, said Carlos Valdés, head of the Seismology Department at the National Autonomous University of Mexico. Omar Smith of the National Civil Protection Service said on the Telemetro Reporta news channel that damage was concentrated in the central provinces of Veraguas, Herrera and Los Santos and there were no reports of damages in Panama City. Smith said several injuries have been reported, including one person struck by debris from a partially collapsed structure in the city of Penonomé, around 93 miles from the capital. He confirmed a partial collapse and cracks at the cathedral in the district’s main square, as well as damage in the governor’s office building and the Dos Continentes hotel. Local news outlets also reported that the Church of San Atanasio, a colonial-style Catholic church in Panama’s Los Santos province, had collapsed. The church was declared a National Historic Heritage Site in 1938. Elsewhere, including in Veraguas province, large fissures ran along roadways. Tocumen International Airport in Panama City, one of the region’s busiest airports with more than 20 million passengers in 2025, temporarily suspended operations after the first quake but said Friday afternoon that it was reopening. The Panama Canal Authority said operations were continuing normally along the global trade route. It said its priority was the safety of employees, vessels and crews and that specialized technical teams were inspecting facilities for possible damage. The last major earthquake to cause widespread damage in Panama struck in 1991. A magnitude 7.4 quake, centered in nearby Costa Rica, killed 23 people, injured 559, and left thousands of people homeless in the border Bocas del Toro region. Earthquakes are common, especially along Panama's border with Costa Rica and its Pacific coast, because of the interaction of several tectonic plates, including the Cocos, Nazca and Caribbean plates. Panama lies along the “Ring of Fire,” a 25,000-mile arc of volcanoes and fault lines around the Pacific Basin, where most of the world’s earthquakes occur. The National Weather Service lifted a tsunami warning issued shortly after the quakes on Friday for the coasts of Panama, Colombia, Ecuador, Nicaragua and Guatemala. Alerts issued by El Salvador and Chile for Easter Island were also lifted. Néstor Luque, director of the Geosciences Institute at the University of Panama, said waves between 3 to 10 feet were expected around Isla Cañas and the southern coast of Los Santos province, but major waves weren't expected beyond that. Seawater had already reached homes near the coast on Isla Cañas, he said. Messages of support and offers of assistance flooded in from across the region on Friday afternoon. Mulino thanked fellow Latin American leaders for their support, saying he had spoken with the presidents of Chile, Uruguay and Guatemala, among others. U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said he was closely watching the situation in Panama and “rapidly mobilizing resources and personnel to assist” at the request of Panama's government. “The United States stands with the people of Panama,” Rubio wrote on X. Colombian President Abelardo de la Espriella , whose country was recently hit by earthquakes, expressed his solidarity with the Panamanian people and their government during what he called “difficult times.” Acting Venezuelan President Delcy Rodríguez, Costa Rican President Laura Fernández Delgado, Ecuadorian President Daniel Noboa and Peru's government also offered assistance. “Panama is not alone! You can count on Colombia’s support and our full willingness to provide whatever assistance is needed,” de la Espriella wrote on X. The USGS initially estimated it to be a magnitude-8.0 quake before revising it down to 7.7. A tsunami warning was issued for the eastern Pacific but later lifted. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said on X on Friday that he was "closely monitoring" the situation, with his office "rapidly mobilizing resources and personnel to assist," at the Panamanian government's request. The Panama Canal Authority said shipping through the channel, which connects the Pacific and Atlantic oceans, was unaffected and operating "as normal." Mulino traveled to Penonome to coordinate the disaster response. Health Minister Fernando Boyd said the most affected areas were the provinces of Herrera and Cocle as well as Los Santos. He said the town of Tonosi in Los Santos was completely cut off. "We are trying to figure out how to get there by air, because it's impossible by land," Boyd said. Panama City's international airport, a major hub for the region, was temporarily closed. Several flights were diverted to other airports as a precaution, according to the Civil Aeronautics Authority. The leaders of Colombia, Ecuador and Guatemala all sent messages of solidarity and offers of aid. Benjamin Gonzalez, 52, said he was at a farm near the town of La Miel when the quake hit, and when he returned home he found "many houses devastated" and "everyone terrified" in the small town square, which was left without power. His neighbor, David Castillo, told AFP that residents were choosing not to return home because they are "afraid it will happen again." Earthquakes are rare in Panama and usually occur in western Chiriqui province, bordering Costa Rica. Former president Ricardo Martinelli posted pictures on Instagram of his house in the town of Sona in Veraguas province that collapsed. A church and a hotel in Penonome also suffered extensive damage, images shared on local media showed. More than 80 aftershocks, one above magnitude 6.0, were recorded by the local geosciences institute. "What happened should not be used to generate alarm and disorder," he wrote on X, adding that he had called for a report on the damage. The education ministry announced the suspension of classes in schools nationwide. The Panamanian quake is at least the fourth quake this year in Latin America surpassing 7.0 in magnitude, after devastating back-to-back earthquakes in Venezuela's Guaira in June and a powerful earthquake in western Colombia in August. representative.title: US unveils sanctions on ICC in move court condemns as 'assault on rule of law'
representative.author: Tom Bateman

snapshot.title: US unveils sanctions on ICC in move court condemns as 'assault on rule of law'
snapshot.evidenceText: The Trump administration has unveiled sweeping sanctions on the International Criminal Court (ICC) in a significant acceleration of its attempt to "dismantle" what it sees as a "rogue" institution. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the measures - which include a ban on US entities making transactions with the ICC - were intended to "defend US sovereignty" and accused the court of seeking to prosecute Americans. The ICC said the measures were an assault on the rule of law and the foundations of the international legal order. The announcement came just hours after former ICC judge Navi Pillay was awarded the 2026 Nobel Peace Prize for her efforts to promote peace and international law. The US has already sanctioned 17 of the ICC's judges and officials, but this move sanctions the court itself as an institution and is intended to collapse its ability to operate financially. However, the US has provided a six month grace period before some of these latest sanctions kick in, meaning member states can keep paying for its operations - a move Washington says is to allow countries time to negotiate a "solution to address" US concerns. UN Secretary General Antonio Guterres called the US decision "a serious blow to our collective pursuit of international criminal justice, of which the ICC is a key pillar". The UK joined Canada, Denmark, Germany, France, Italy, Japan and the Netherlands in reaffirming their "continued and unwavering support" for the ICC and said they "regret and strongly disagree with" the sanctions. They also praised the court's staff for their work bringing "those accused of the most serious international crimes to justice", as well as supporting victims. The ICC was founded in 2002 to prosecute war crimes, crimes against humanity and genocide, and counts 125 countries as member states. Several major countries remain outside the ICC, including the US, Russia, China, India and Israel. The Trump administration argues the ICC is run by what it calls globalists who threaten American sovereignty. It is furious over a past investigation into actions of US soldiers in Afghanistan the court has since closed and by its arrest warrants for Israeli officials including Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. The new sanctions, however, do not say that those warrants must be withdrawn before the measures can be lifted. But Rubio said Trump would not allow the ICC to prosecute Americans, adding: "Either the ICC will end its threats, or we will end the ICC." The US sanctions will stop US companies from providing goods or services to the ICC, such as banking or software. Rubio said Washington had delayed imposing the sanctions in the hope that the ICC and its member countries would address US concerns. He said the measures had been structured to allow other countries to negotiate a possible solution. He also called on US allies that were ICC signatories, including the UK, to "rein in" the institution. The Netherlands, which hosts the court in The Hague and is also a Nato ally of the US, faces particular pressure. Dutch Foreign Minister Tom Berendsen has said the sanctions would seriously affect the court's ability to function. Netanyahu welcomed the sanctions, saying the ICC was "not a court" but a political body that threatened law-abiding democracies and "the very idea of national sovereignty". The ICC said that the sanctions were aimed at disrupting its work and intimidating those who co-operate with it - but that it "will not be deterred". It called the measures "an assault on the rule of law" and said no one should be punished for serving the cause of justice, adding: "History will judge this moment." This showdown potentially marks the gravest crisis in the court's 24-year history. Rather than targeting individual ICC judges and prosecutors, the US is now sanctioning the court itself. The sanctions could ultimately see the ICC unable to try cases, meaning detainees awaiting trial or judgment could have to be released, according to Professor Ryan Goodman from the New York University School of Law. Among those awaiting trial in The Hague is Rodrigo Duterte, the former president of the Philippines. The 81-year-old is accused of the extrajudicial killing of thousands during his deadly "war on drugs" between 2011 and 2019. Others awaiting trial or with pending appeals include former senior figures accused of war crimes in Libya, Sudan and the Central African Republic. Goodman says that as a senator, Rubio was "out front" highlighting Duterte's alleged crimes. He told the BBC such a release would be "enormously damaging to the global effort towards international justice [and] towards the Philippines". "[For] the victims, it just has to be incredibly traumatic because a lot of them participate in the ICC proceedings to put themselves on the line with a hope that justice will come around," adds Goodman, a former special counsel at the US Department of Defence. Among the carve-outs announced as part of today's sanctions are "licenses" allowing the ICC to continue "services for the operation of facilities used for the detention" of Duterte and others. However, Goodman says ultimately these detainees may have to be released "as a matter of law" if the financial sanctions mean the court cannot conduct fair trials or appeals. While the physical damage from Houthi attacks can be quickly repaired, the Saudi reputation for stability is taking a battering. Roofs were ripped off buildings after Isaias barrelled into the US on Friday evening, before it weakened to a post-tropical cyclone. All but one of those who died, including the gunman, were related, police say. A motive for the shooting is not yet known. The US president's said President Volodymyr Zelensky "wants to make problems for the world". Navi Pillay says the Trump administrations' sweeping penalties on the international tribunal were "unheard of".

snapshot.title: US sanctions International Criminal Court in major escalation
snapshot.evidenceText: Latest action seeks to stem resources to international tribunal Trump administration has vowed to dismantle. Washington, DC – United States Secretary of State Marco Rubio has announced a new set of sanctions against the International Criminal Court (ICC), this time targeting the entity itself, as opposed to the tribunal’s officials or groups that provide support. The announcement on Friday represented a major escalation from the administration of US President Donald Trump, which has vowed an “all of government” approach to dismantling the court. “We will ban transactions with this rogue court, cutting off their resources and crippling their ability to operate against us because our message is clear: the United States and the American people are not subject to the jurisdiction of this fake ICC,” Rubio said in a video posted on social media. “Either the ICC will end its threats, or we will end the ICC.” As justification for its actions, the administration has pointed to the court’s ongoing investigation into abuses committed in Afghanistan, which could ensnare US military and intelligence personnel, as well as the ICC’s arrest warrant for Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and former Defence Minister Yoav Gallant for war crimes committed in Gaza. Before Friday’s actions, the US had sanctioned ICC judges and prosecutors, a UN special rapporteur focusing on the occupied Palestinian territories and Palestinian rights groups that have provided evidence to the court. Several rights groups have challenged those sanctions in US federal court, saying restricting how US citizens interact with the court treads on their constitutional freedoms. Sanctioned ICC judges have also launched legal challenges in the US. Speaking to the Reuters news agency on Friday, deputy prosecutor Nazhat Shameem Khan said the sanctions “must be condemned”. “The sanctions are intended to undermine ⁠⁠⁠⁠the rule of ⁠⁠⁠⁠law internationally and the work that an ⁠⁠⁠⁠independent judicial institution ⁠⁠⁠⁠is doing,” ⁠⁠⁠⁠Khan said. “Our work will continue across all our ‌‌‌‌situations, our investigations and our ‌‌‌‌prosecutions.” In a statement, the ICC called on member states to redouble support. “History will judge this moment. Future generations, and above all the victims of mass atrocities, will ask how we responded when an institution created to protect them came under attack,” it said. The US and Israel are not parties to the Rome Statute, the founding treaty that establishes the court’s jurisdiction. However, the court has long ruled that abuses committed by US or Israeli citizens in the territories of countries that are ICC members can be prosecuted. Israel was among those cheering the Trump administration’s latest action. “Thank you for your leadership,” Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said in a statement posted on social media. To date, the court has not sought to prosecute any US citizens. A US law dating back to 2002, amid the so-called “Global War on Terror”, already prohibits extradition of US citizens to be tried by the ICC. It further authorises the use of military force in the event that a US citizen is held in detention while being prosecuted by the court, in what critics have dubbed the “Hague invasion clause”. Nevertheless, some US administrations, particularly those led by Democrats, have sought to provide support for the court and have espoused its founding principles. Rights observers have said that the US pressure campaign could have wide-ranging implications for the court’s investigations, particularly the network of local organisations and fact-finders upon which it relies to build cases. Mark Kersten, an international law expert and professor at the University of Fraser Valley in British Columbia, Canada, said ICC advocates have feared direct sanctions on the court itself since Trump took office for his second term in January last year. “This was the number one concern: the possibility not only that individuals would be sanctioned, but that the court itself would be sanctioned,” he told Al Jazeera. “That should give people a sense of the significance of this…the worst-case scenario has come about”. The US has also urged other countries to withdraw from the court, suggesting it would assess allies’ relationship with the court when determining foreign assistance. The appeal has dovetailed with wariness from some ICC members over what they have called the unequal application of international law, with offenders in the Global South more likely to face accountability. In July, Chad and Venezuela moved to withdraw from the court, following Burkina Faso, Mali and Niger. The years ahead, Kersten said, will be a test of support from ICC members, who will need to intervene to circumvent the US sanctions. Most of Europe, Latin America and large areas of Africa remain members of the tribunal, as do Canada and Australia. “Only with the support and concrete action of those states will the court really ultimately survive,” he said. The latest round of sanctions means that companies that provide services to the court could be penalised. Sanctioning the entire entity, which has about 900 staff, as opposed to individual officials, will make it more difficult for the court to insulate itself from such sanctions. The sanctions block “all property and interests in property” the court has in the US, while prohibiting “making of any contribution or provision of funds, goods, or services by, to, or for the benefit” of the court. The sanctions included several temporary exemptions, including for services providing maintenance, technology and pension plans. The State Department said the exemptions are meant to “provide time for States Parties to demonstrate meaningful progress on diplomatic and legal resolutions that address fundamental US concerns regarding the ICC”. William Schabas, a professor of international law at Middlesex University in London, said it was not immediately clear how impactful the sanctions would be. He said the court had been preparing for the eventuality for over a year. “They have been developing a plan B on how to get around this,” Schabas told Al Jazeera. That has included migrating some US-made software to European alternatives and recently ending its relationship with the French health and life insurance company Axa, which does business with the US. “How significant this will be remains to be seen,” he said. “Obviously for the institution it’s going to complicate things considerably.” Friday’s announcement came just hours after the Nobel Peace Prize was awarded to South African jurist and former ICC judge Navi Pillay. Pillay also oversaw the 2025 UN Human Rights report that found Israel’s actions in Gaza constituted a genocide. Schabas drew a connection to the timing of the State Department’s announcement and Trump’s ire towards the Nobel Committee, which he has maintained should award him the Peace Prize. “The prize is a recognition more generally of the international institutions with which Pillay was affiliated, in particular the International Criminal Court and also a kind of polite endorsement of the report that she wrote last year for the United Nations condemning Israel for genocide,” he said. “There’s often a political message lurking behind the award of the Nobel Peace Prize and I think this year is no exception,” he said. The Nobel judges said the prize comes at a time when “judges and institutions of international law are under political attack”. “An international legal system in which war ⁠⁠⁠⁠criminals are held to account, and the victims of abuse see justice served is a precondition for a peaceful world,” they said.

snapshot.title: Why is the US sanctioning the International Criminal Court?
snapshot.evidenceText: The sanctions targeting the ICC, which prosecutes humanitarian crimes, are the latest move by the US against the court. The United States has sanctioned the International Criminal Court (ICC), hours after one of its former judges was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize in what the Nobel committee said was, in part, a show of support for institutions under attack. South African judge Navanethem “Navi” Pillay, who is currently a judge at the International Court of Justice (ICJ), also in The Hague, was announced winner of the prize on Friday. Nobel Committee Chairman Jorgen Watne Frydnes said the system of international law was “under tremendous pressure” and its institutions were “under attack”. “In awarding this year’s Nobel Peace Prize, the Norwegian Nobel Committee wants to remind the world that the rule of law – national and international – underpins the system we have set up to ensure peace and resolve conflicts non-violently. Peace requires justice,” the committee said. The US move follows sanctions it has already imposed this year on judges and other personnel at the ICC. On Friday, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio announced the latest set of US sanctions targeting the ICC, this time focusing on the court itself, which was established in 2002 to prosecute war crimes, genocide and crimes against humanity. “We will ban transactions with this rogue court, cutting off their resources and crippling their ability to operate against us because our message is clear: the United States and the American people are not subject to the jurisdiction of this fake ICC,” he said in a video shared on social media. The Trump administration claims that the ICC has gone beyond its remit by pursuing non-member countries. In 2024, the Trump administration condemned the court when it issued arrest warrants for Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and former Defence Minister Yoav Gallant for suspected war crimes in Gaza. It also previously opened an investigation into the actions of US soldiers in Afghanistan. The US and Israel are not parties to the Rome Statute, the treaty that establishes the court’s jurisdiction. However, abuses committed by citizens of non-statute states in ICC territories or countries can still be prosecuted. “Either the ICC will end its threats, or we will end the ICC,” Rubio said in a statement, adding that if the US allies failed to “rein in the court”, the US would “continue its campaign to dismantle the ICC, brick by brick”. These sanctions are just the latest in the US’s campaign against the ICC. Previous measures have targeted dozens of ICC judges and prosecutors , the UN special rapporteur for Palestine, Francesca Albanese, and Palestinian rights groups which have provided evidence of war crimes committed by Israel to the court. In August, ICC President Tomoko Akane and senior lawyer Abdoulaye Sey were also sanctioned by the US, in what Rubio said was the US’s unwavering mission to protect Americans from this sham of a court”. Any assets they hold in the US are frozen, and US companies are limited in conducting transactions with them. The sanctions targeting the court could see companies that provide services to it penalised. They will also freeze any ICC assets held in US territories. However, they have given US companies a six-month grace period to wrap up any existing business with the court. There are also some other exemptions allowing for certain transactions. William Schabas, a professor of international law at Middlesex University in London, told Al Jazeera that the court has been “developing a plan B” to get around potential sanctions for more than a year. This includes migrating to European alternatives to US software, and ending its relationship with insurance company Axa, which does business with the US. “How significant this will be remains to be seen,” he said. “Obviously for the institution, it’s going to complicate things considerably.” “What Trump is trying to do is to make the world safe for American and Israeli war criminals,” Kenneth Roth, a senior fellow at Yale University and former executive director of Human Rights Watch, told Al Jazeera. The ICC itself released a statement condemning the US move, which it said was an attempt to “obstruct the course of justice” and intimidate those who work or cooperate with the court. “It is an assault on the rule of law and on the very foundations of the international legal order which strikes at the simple principle that no one stands above the law,” it said, calling on its 125 states parties to take action to ensure it can continue its work. “History will judge this moment. Future generations, and above all the victims of mass atrocities, will ask how we responded when an institution created to protect them came under attack,” it added. UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres said he was “deeply alarmed” by the decision, adding that it was “a serious blow to our collective pursuit of international criminal justice”. The foreign ministers of the UK, Denmark, France, Germany, Italy, the Netherlands, Canada and Japan all said they “strongly disagree” with the sanctions, and warned of the significant impact they would have on the court. Netanyahu thanked Trump for his leadership on social media, and accused the ICC of being a “political body that poses a mortal threat to law-abiding democracies worldwide”. The US targeting of the ICC threatens the rule of law, as international courts and tribunals must be able to operate without the threat of sanctions. The US itself has repeatedly ignored international law under President Trump. Its joint attack on Iran with Israel in February was criticised by observers as being in violation of both US law and Article 2(4) of the UN Charter , while the US military abduction of Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro from Caracas in January was also condemned as illegal. The Trump administration has also launched strikes against alleged drug smuggling boats in the Caribbean Sea and eastern Pacific, killing more than 200 people in what UN human rights experts warn are “ extrajudicial and unlawful “. Under Trump, the US has also pulled out of international organisations and agreements, from the Iran nuclear deal (the Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action) and the Paris Climate Agreement during Trump’s first term, to the World Health Organization and the UN Human Rights Council, more recently. “What Trump is doing is obstructing justice,” Roth said of the ICC sanctions. “If you look at Article 70 of the Rome Statute, it makes it a crime to intimidate or threaten court officials because of their official duties.” “But the court remains strong, it is very capable of doing its work,” he said, adding, “there’s important work for the court to do to protect victims in places like Ukraine, Sudan, Myanmar, Afghanistan, the Philippines. This is work that should continue, and it will.”

When major global news breaks, the Atlantic Council’s experts have you covered—delivering their sharpest rapid insight and forward-looking analysis direct to your inbox. Reports from the front lines of global policy—by the experts shaping it. A weekly column by Atlantic Council President and CEO Frederick Kempe, Inflection Points focuses on the global challenges facing the United States and how to best address them. UkraineAlert sources analysis and commentary from a wide-array of thought-leaders, politicians, experts, and activists from Ukraine and the global community. Adjust text size, contrast, link visibility, and motion from the same menu. Washington has issued its own verdict. On Friday, the Trump administration imposed sweeping sanctions on the International Criminal Court (ICC), extending a yearslong campaign beyond individual judges and prosecutors to the tribunal itself. The new sanctions threaten to disrupt the court’s access to essential banking, insurance, and technology services. What’s behind the US decision? And can the ICC continue to operate? Our experts weigh in below. Gissou Nia is the director of the Strategic Litigation Project at the Atlantic Council. A human rights lawyer, she started her career in The Hague, where she worked on war crimes and crimes against humanity trials at the International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia and the International Criminal Court. Today’s announcement from the US Department of State that the International Criminal Court has been sanctioned as an entity is a complete inversion of the intended use of sanctions. The sanctions designation places the ICC on the US Department of the Treasury’s financial blacklist and represents a measure normally used against global militant networks, drug cartels, and transnational gangs—not the lawyers, judges, and bureaucrats investigating and prosecuting them. The designation cuts the court off from the global financial system and, without aggressive countermeasures from supporting countries, will grind the court’s daily work to a halt. This risks depriving thousands of survivors and victims of the world’s most serious crimes—including murder, rape, torture, and mass starvation—of one of their last remaining paths to much-needed justice. The ICC is a court of last resort, meaning that it only steps in when a country is unwilling or unable to investigate or prosecute crimes committed within its borders or by its nationals. While US Secretary of State Marco Rubio claims that the sanctions are intended to prevent US service members from being charged by the court, the reality is that US personnel are not the subject of any current investigation, nor have they ever been a primary focus. In the past year alone, the court has convicted a Sudanese militia chief for crimes in Darfur, unsealed arrest warrants against top Taliban leaders in Afghanistan for crimes against humanity including gender persecution, confirmed charges against Ugandan warlord Joseph Kony, prepared for the trial of former Philippine President Rodrigo Duterte for widespread extrajudicial killings in a sweeping “war on drugs,” begun proceedings against a suspect accused of crimes against prison detainees in Libya, convicted a Central African Republic rebel leader for crimes against humanity, and more. This activity covers a range of global crimes—and none of these cases involves US perpetrators. A June 2026 statement from the ICC presidency described the body as “one of the most significant achievements of human civilisation.” The claim—coming from one of the court’s formal organs—could seem hyperbolic. But there is truth in those words. It is almost inconceivable in today’s polarized world that delegations from 120 countries could vote “yes” to establish an institution and voluntarily submit themselves to an accountability framework beyond their domestic justice systems for the greater good. The threatened destruction of what took decades to build should steel the determination of the court’s supporters to take the bold actions needed to save it. Matthew Kroenig is a senior fellow with the Atlantic Council’s Scowcroft Center for Strategy and Security, and a former US defense and intelligence official. The ICC has always been fraught strategically and geopolitically. The strategic vision was to deter and hold accountable tyrants engaged in grievous crimes. This is a noble goal. In practice, it may have had the opposite effect, incentivizing dictators engaged in civil wars, for example, to employ any means necessary to cling to power. A defeated Napoleon received an island exile; today’s defeated dictators are hauled off to The Hague. Geopolitically, the court has wrongly pursued powerful democracies engaged in legal wars consistent with the law of armed conflict, including US soldiers in Afghanistan and Israeli leaders in Gaza. Washington has never been a fan of and never signed the Rome Statute that established the ICC. Then-National Security Advisor John Bolton threatened sanctions in President Donald Trump’s first term, and Rubio is doubling down in the second. Multilateral institutions cannot survive without the backing of powerful states. The ICC may learn this lesson soon. Mark Klamberg is a nonresident senior fellow with the Atlantic Council’s Strategic Litigation Project. The latest US sanctions against the ICC are fundamentally more serious than previous measures. Until now, sanctions have targeted individual representatives; the new sanctions target the court as an entity. In concrete terms, this means it will become more difficult—or even impossible—for the court to pay its employees, settle bills, and rely on essential services. The court had already anticipated this risk and taken some precautionary measures. Last year, it decided to replace Microsoft Office with a European software alternative, amid mounting concerns about dependence on US technology. These sanctions appear to come in direct response to the ICC’s decision to issue arrest warrants against Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and former Israeli Defense Minister Yoav Gallant over alleged war crimes and crimes against humanity in Gaza. However, this case is just one among many that the court is currently pursuing. The ICC is simultaneously investigating the situation in Ukraine, where it has issued an arrest warrant against Russian President Vladimir Putin, as well as ongoing cases related to Sudan, Afghanistan, Myanmar, Venezuela, and the Philippines. This range of situations illustrates that the court’s mandate extends across vastly different geopolitical contexts, applying the same legal standards regardless of the power or alliances of the states involved—a fact that underscores, rather than undermines, its claim to impartiality. Supporters of the ICC, such as the European Union, the United Kingdom, and Canada, should consider using their blocking statutes to help companies withstand the risks of continuing to do business with the ICC. In short, blocking statutes contain provisions designed to counter the effects of foreign sanctions and trade restrictions. They not only prohibit persons and companies within their jurisdictions from complying with specified foreign sanctions, but also allow individuals and companies to recover damages through legal action for losses caused by the extraterritorial application of these foreign sanctions—as is the case under the EU blocking statute. More fundamentally, the US should reconsider its current adversarial stance toward the ICC. Since the Nuremberg trials, the US has played a key role in advancing international justice. There may be legitimate disagreement over individual decisions, but the court operates on core principles of judicial independence, complementarity, and fair-trial guarantees—principles the US itself has long championed. Lize de Kruijf is an assistant director within the GeoEconomics Center’s Economic Statecraft Initiative As the threat of US sanctions against the ICC has grown, the EU blocking statute has frequently been floated as a way to protect the court and allow it to continue its work. The statute essentially nullifies the effect of designated foreign sanctions within the EU. Adding the ICC sanctions to the blocking statute would mean that EU persons and entities would be prohibited from complying with them, and US court rulings enforcing them would be unenforceable in the EU. The Netherlands—which hosts the ICC in The Hague and is legally bound by its Headquarters Agreement to ensure the court’s continued operation—has so far prioritized working behind the scenes, seeking a resolution with Washington. However, in an interview during this year’s UN General Assembly, Dutch Foreign Minister Tom Berendsen stated that the Netherlands “will do everything it can to protect the court” and that it had asked the European Commission to prepare to activate a blocking statute in case sanctions were imposed on the entire ICC. Given the EU’s strong support for the court, activation of the blocking statute is a real possibility. However, even with the blocking statute, keeping the court operational may still prove challenging. Banks will risk losing access to the US financial system, a risk that large Dutch banks with international operations, in particular, may be unwilling to take. The statute also does not offer compensation for companies that lose US business as a result of complying with it. Their only recourse is to sue whoever caused the harm. The private sector’s tolerance for sanctions risk is typically very low. AXA, the France-based health insurance provider for the ICC, for example, recently cut ties with the ICC amid the growing threat of sanctions. As a result, there is a risk that companies may seek exemptions from the statute or quietly wind down their business with the court instead. Celeste Kmiotek is a senior staff lawyer for the Strategic Litigation Project at the Atlantic Council. The preamble of the ICC’s Rome Statute states that, in agreeing to establish the ICC, state parties were: “Mindful that during this century millions of children, women and men have been victims of unimaginable atrocities that deeply shock the conscience of humanity, Recognizing that such grave crimes threaten the peace, security and well-being of the world.” The ICC’s mandate is and always has been strictly tailored to address only these situations. Its jurisdiction is principally limited to four categories of crimes : war crimes, crimes against humanity, genocide, and aggression. There are preconditions for the ICC to exercise jurisdiction: Generally, either the state on whose territory the conduct occurred or the state of which the accused is a national must be a party to the Rome Statute or have otherwise accepted the ICC’s jurisdiction. The ICC’s authority narrows again through conditions governing the opening of investigations and the selection of cases. For example, it is a “ court of last resort ,” generally admitting cases only when a state is unable or unwilling to investigate and prosecute. The Office of the Prosecutor only prosecutes those alleged to be “ most responsible ” for a given crime. The system is then undergirded by procedural safeguards , such as the requirement that a Pre-Trial Chamber review the Office of the Prosecutor’s applications before issuing arrest warrants. In short, only an extremely select group of people have reason to fear ICC prosecution. In the twenty-four years since its establishment, there have been sixty-eight arrest warrants, twenty-three detentions, and fifteen convictions. In stark contrast, as of 2023 , 10,900 victims had participated in court proceedings, 2,500 had received court-ordered reparations, and over 130,000 survivors were supported by the ICC’s Trust Fund for Victims. In other words, a person is far more likely to interact with the ICC as a victim than as a defendant. The Trump administration’s apparent fear of the ICC is telling. These sanctions and the broader campaign against the ICC appeal to the legal concept of “sovereignty,” even as the US repeatedly carries out actions that seem to violate international law. representative.author: Mark Hallam

snapshot.title: US announces sanctions on the International Criminal Court
snapshot.evidenceText: The US has announced new sanctions on the International Criminal Court. It's the latest in a series of steps by the Donald Trump administration as it seeks to "dismantle" the intergovernmental organization. US President Donald Trump 's administration imposed sanctions on the International Criminal Court (ICC) on Friday, hours after one of its former judges won the Nobel Peace Prize. This comes as the US has in recent months made no bones about pursuing what Secretary of State Marco Rubio has called a "sweeping campaign to dismantle the threat posed by the International Criminal Court." The United States and Israel had both strongly opposed the court's arrest warrants for top Israeli officials, including Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu . Since 2020 and the back end of Trump's first term, the US had also opposed investigations into military actions in Afghanistan that "deprioritize" alleged US wrongdoings, focusing on the Taliban, but can nevertheless include them. To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video "President Trump will never allow the International Court to prosecute Americans," Rubio said in a statement . "That is why, today, the United States is sanctioning the International Criminal Court. We will ban transactions with this rogue court, cutting off their resources and crippling its ability to operate," he said. Rubio said that both US political parties had long agreed that the ICC should not have jurisdiction over US citizens, but said "only President Trump" resolved to take action. "Either the ICC will end its threats, or we will end the ICC. We expect our allies, many of whom are part of the ICC and that rely on American servicemembers for their defense, to rein in the court," Rubio said. "If they do not, the United States will continue its campaign to dismantle the ICC, brick by brick, until Americans are threatened no longer." The ICC said the US sanctions aimed to obstruct an independent international court supported by more than half of the UN's members. "The court will continue to fully discharge its mandate, with independence and impartiality, acting only on the basis of the law and the evidence, for the sake of the countless victims of grave crimes," said ICC President Tomoko Akane, who already faces US sanctions . The ICC called the Rome Statute, which underpins membership of the court, a "collective promise" that the most serious international crimes must not go unpunished. "That promise is only as strong as the resolve of those who made it," the court said. It appealed to members to take "concrete actions" to ensure the court would still have the necessary means to continue its work. "No one should be punished for serving the cause of justice," it said. "History will judge this moment. Future generations, and above all the victims of mass atrocities, will ask how we responded when an insitution created to protect them came under attack." A collection of US allies that are full members of the ICC including Germany issued a joint statement reaffirming their "continued and unwavering support for the independence, impartiality, and integrity of the ICC." "As committed supporters of the ICC we regret and strongly disagree with the announcement of sanctions to be imposed upon the Court by the United States," the governments of Canada, Denmark, Germany, France, Italy, Japan, the Netherlands and the UK said . They said that, despite the ICC's best efforts to prepare and mitigate their effect, the sanctions "will have a significant impact on the Court's work, its dedicated staff and their families." Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu thanked the US government for its "leadership" in issuing the sanctions. "The ICC is not a court. It is a political body that poses a mortal threat to law abiding democracies worldwide and to the very idea of national sovereignty," he said. The State Department released the announcement a few hours after the 2026 Nobel Peace Prize was awarded to Navi Pillay, who was an ICC judge from 2003 to 2012. Last year Trump repeatedly complained that he should have won the accolade for promoting world peace, prompting Venezuelan opposition leader Maria Corina Machado to present him with her trophy as a gift . Without naming names, the Nobel Committee clearly referenced US sanctions against the ICC when announcing Pillay as this year's laureate. "The Norwegian Nobel Committee wants to remind the world that the rule of law national and international — underpins the system we have set up to ensure peace and resolve conflicts non-violently," the Committee wrote. It said judges like Pillay "guard the thin red line between order and chaos," but lamented that "today ... these same judges are sanctioned, and their institutions are attacked." The International Criminal Court is an intergovernmental organization and international tribunal based in the Dutch city of The Hague. It's the only permanent international court with the theoretical jurisdiction to prosecute individuals for international crimes like genocide , crimes against humanity, war crimes and illegal aggression. The ICC was established in 2002 and is governed by the Rome Statute. More than half the countries in the world, 125 in total, are full parties to the Rome Statute, having signed and ratified it. Several of the world's most significant powers, including China, India, Israel, Russia and the United States, do not recognize the court's jurisdiction and are not parties to the statute. A grey area, however, remains since the court accepts challenges from ratified members against individuals from countries that do not recognize it. That is why high-profile arrest warrants against Russian officials, including President Vladimir Putin, and Israeli officials, including Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, have been issued in recent years — following respective complaints from Ukrainians and Palestinians. The US has been increasingly critical of the ICC during Trump's second term. Rubio has often led the charge. In July, he wrote an op-ed for the Wall Street Journal saying, "America never agreed to a world tribunal that can override our own courts and the Constitution." He argued it was possible for US "soldiers, police officers, Border Patrol agents and elected leaders" to be "dragged before an international court" and tried by judges "from random countries across the globe." Just over a week later, on July 25, Venezuela's new administration — transformed after the US abduction of Nicolas Maduro in January — announced that it planned to withdraw from the Rome Statute and the ICC. A few days later, the military junta in Chad announced that it was withdrawing from the ICC following a US request. The recent sexual misconduct scandal surrounding the ICC's chief prosecutor Karim Khan , who was dismissed in July, provided more ammunition the US could aim at the court. In August, the US imposed sanctions on the ICC's president, Japanese judge Tomoko Akane, and Abdoulaye Seye, a Senegalese trial lawyer at the court. representative.title: US unveils sanctions on ICC in move court condemns as 'assault on rule of law'
representative.author: Tom Bateman

snapshot.title: US unveils sanctions on ICC in move court condemns as 'assault on rule of law'
snapshot.evidenceText: The Trump administration has unveiled sweeping sanctions on the International Criminal Court (ICC) in a significant acceleration of its attempt to "dismantle" what it sees as a "rogue" institution. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the measures - which include a ban on US entities making transactions with the ICC - were intended to "defend US sovereignty" and accused the court of seeking to prosecute Americans. The ICC said the measures were an assault on the rule of law and the foundations of the international legal order. The announcement came just hours after former ICC judge Navi Pillay was awarded the 2026 Nobel Peace Prize for her efforts to promote peace and international law. The US has already sanctioned 17 of the ICC's judges and officials, but this move sanctions the court itself as an institution and is intended to collapse its ability to operate financially. However, the US has provided a six month grace period before some of these latest sanctions kick in, meaning member states can keep paying for its operations - a move Washington says is to allow countries time to negotiate a "solution to address" US concerns. UN Secretary General Antonio Guterres called the US decision "a serious blow to our collective pursuit of international criminal justice, of which the ICC is a key pillar". The UK joined Canada, Denmark, Germany, France, Italy, Japan and the Netherlands in reaffirming their "continued and unwavering support" for the ICC and said they "regret and strongly disagree with" the sanctions. They also praised the court's staff for their work bringing "those accused of the most serious international crimes to justice", as well as supporting victims. The ICC was founded in 2002 to prosecute war crimes, crimes against humanity and genocide, and counts 125 countries as member states. Several major countries remain outside the ICC, including the US, Russia, China, India and Israel. The Trump administration argues the ICC is run by what it calls globalists who threaten American sovereignty. It is furious over a past investigation into actions of US soldiers in Afghanistan the court has since closed and by its arrest warrants for Israeli officials including Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. The new sanctions, however, do not say that those warrants must be withdrawn before the measures can be lifted. But Rubio said Trump would not allow the ICC to prosecute Americans, adding: "Either the ICC will end its threats, or we will end the ICC." The US sanctions will stop US companies from providing goods or services to the ICC, such as banking or software. Rubio said Washington had delayed imposing the sanctions in the hope that the ICC and its member countries would address US concerns. He said the measures had been structured to allow other countries to negotiate a possible solution. He also called on US allies that were ICC signatories, including the UK, to "rein in" the institution. The Netherlands, which hosts the court in The Hague and is also a Nato ally of the US, faces particular pressure. Dutch Foreign Minister Tom Berendsen has said the sanctions would seriously affect the court's ability to function. Netanyahu welcomed the sanctions, saying the ICC was "not a court" but a political body that threatened law-abiding democracies and "the very idea of national sovereignty". The ICC said that the sanctions were aimed at disrupting its work and intimidating those who co-operate with it - but that it "will not be deterred". It called the measures "an assault on the rule of law" and said no one should be punished for serving the cause of justice, adding: "History will judge this moment." This showdown potentially marks the gravest crisis in the court's 24-year history. Rather than targeting individual ICC judges and prosecutors, the US is now sanctioning the court itself. The sanctions could ultimately see the ICC unable to try cases, meaning detainees awaiting trial or judgment could have to be released, according to Professor Ryan Goodman from the New York University School of Law. Among those awaiting trial in The Hague is Rodrigo Duterte, the former president of the Philippines. The 81-year-old is accused of the extrajudicial killing of thousands during his deadly "war on drugs" between 2011 and 2019. Others awaiting trial or with pending appeals include former senior figures accused of war crimes in Libya, Sudan and the Central African Republic. Goodman says that as a senator, Rubio was "out front" highlighting Duterte's alleged crimes. He told the BBC such a release would be "enormously damaging to the global effort towards international justice [and] towards the Philippines". "[For] the victims, it just has to be incredibly traumatic because a lot of them participate in the ICC proceedings to put themselves on the line with a hope that justice will come around," adds Goodman, a former special counsel at the US Department of Defence. Among the carve-outs announced as part of today's sanctions are "licenses" allowing the ICC to continue "services for the operation of facilities used for the detention" of Duterte and others. However, Goodman says ultimately these detainees may have to be released "as a matter of law" if the financial sanctions mean the court cannot conduct fair trials or appeals. While the physical damage from Houthi attacks can be quickly repaired, the Saudi reputation for stability is taking a battering. Roofs were ripped off buildings after Isaias barrelled into the US on Friday evening, before it weakened to a post-tropical cyclone. All but one of those who died, including the gunman, were related, police say. A motive for the shooting is not yet known. The US president's said President Volodymyr Zelensky "wants to make problems for the world". Navi Pillay says the Trump administrations' sweeping penalties on the international tribunal were "unheard of".

representative.title: Alberta Court of Appeal says Ottawa's impact assessment act is still unconstitutional | CBC News
representative.author: The Canadian Press

snapshot.title: Alberta Court of Appeal says Ottawa's Impact Assessment Act is still unconstitutional | CBC News
snapshot.evidenceText: The Alberta Court of Appeal has ruled the federal government's Impact Assessment Act is still unconstitutional. This was the second time the province of Alberta had challenged the act, which sets out a process to review the environmental, economic, health and social effects of proposed projects like ports, mines and pipelines. In a 4-1 decision issued Friday, the court said even though Ottawa modified the law after the Supreme Court struck down much of it in 2023, the new version still infringes on provincial jurisdiction. The Court of Appeal found that, among other things, the act still gives Ottawa the power to stop a project in provincial jurisdiction if it has even the smallest impact on federal jurisdiction. "While Parliament may have the power to create an impact assessment scheme that complements existing regulation in environmental matters, the [Impact Assessment Act] creates great uncertainty due to the potential for previously unpronounced standards to apply to designated projects," the court wrote. Canada's top court rules environmental impact law unconstitutional "This merely exacerbates the concern that a federal assessment scheme might enable the federal government, on the pretext of some narrow ground of federal jurisdiction, to conduct a far-ranging inquiry into matters that are exclusively within provincial jurisdiction." The court said while some of the changes Ottawa made to the previous version of the act weren't constitutionally problematic, the law still gave Ottawa overly broad powers in areas of provincial jurisdiction. "The decision maker may regulate the project causing the impacts through imposition of conditions and followup programs, or indefinite prohibitions on entire projects and matters within provincial jurisdiction rather than confining oversight to federal effects caused by the project," the court wrote. Alberta challenge to federal project review law being heard in court, again Ontario and Saskatchewan both backed Alberta in its legal challenge. The Impact Assessment Act — otherwise known as C-69 — has been staunchly opposed by oil and gas industry players and critics such as federal Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre. Former Alberta premier Jason Kenney dubbed it the "no more pipelines act." Alberta Premier Danielle Smith said on social media Friday that the ruling was "yet another big win for Alberta." "I'm calling on the federal government to accept this ruling, refrain from yet another appeal, and immediately work with Alberta and the other provinces to clean up this flawed Trudeau-era legislation once and for all so it no longer inhibits economic development in our country," she said. Friday's ruling comes as Ottawa and Alberta are partnering on a new oil pipeline to the West Coast. From left, Scott Burrows, CEO of the Pembina Pipeline Corp, Alberta Premier Danielle Smith and Prime Minister Mark Carney applaud on Oct 1 after Carney declared the Pacific Link pipeline project to be in the national interest. (Greg Halinda/The Canadian Press) Earlier this month, the Pacific Link pipeline project became the first to receive a national interest designation under Ottawa's new Building Canada Act. And while the Building Canada Act gives Ottawa the power to skirt a dozen federal laws to help move hand-picked projects forward, critics like Poilievre have long called for the Impact Assessment Act to be repealed. Why Danielle Smith has eased off the 'Kill Bill C-69' language in the Carney era Through the newly tabled Bill C-39, Ottawa is trying to transfer the assessment process for pipeline and energy transmission projects from the Impact Assessment Agency of Canada to the Canada Energy Regulator. The federal government has said it has been told by industry that the level of expertise on energy projects that existed at the Canada Energy Regulator couldn't be found at the Impact Assessment Agency. Ottawa has said the Canada Energy Regulator will still be bound by the provisions in the Impact Assessment Act — which the Alberta Court of Appeal now says is unconstitutional — when carrying out its reviews. In a statement, the office of federal Environment Minister Julie Dabrusin said the government is reviewing the decision and considering next steps. "To position Canada for long-term prosperity in a rapidly changing global economy, the Government of Canada is moving forward to build at a pace not seen in decades. The [Impact Assessment Act] is fundamental to the advancement of this work," wrote press secretary Amy Falkner. "The [Court of Appeal] opinion does not change our commitment to engage all provinces in the spirit of co-operative federalism." Audience Relations, CBC P.O. representative.title: Toronto approves 2026 budget with historic capital plan | The Canada Voice
representative.author: Toronto Voice Staff

snapshot.title: City Council approves Toronto's 2026 budget with $63.1-billion capital plan, frozen TTC fares
snapshot.evidenceText: The Canada Voice network · 13 local news sites across Ontario Toronto City Council has signed off on an $18.9-billion operating budget and the largest 10-year capital plan in the city's history, including frozen TTC fares and a property tax increase below inflation. October 10, 2026 at 6:18 p.m. · Updated October 11, 2026 at 2:10 p.m. · 2 min read Toronto City Council has approved the city's 2026 budget, signing off on an $18.9-billion operating plan and a 10-year capital budget that the city says is the largest in its history. The budget — Mayor Olivia Chow's third since her election in 2023 — was passed at a special meeting of council on Tuesday, according to a statement from Councillor Paula Fletcher , who represents Toronto-Danforth and published a budget breakdown on her website. The centrepiece of the plan is a $63.1-billion capital budget and plan covering 2026 to 2035, which Fletcher described as the biggest 10-year capital commitment the city has ever made. Fletcher said the budget's affordability measures — including frozen TTC fares and free meals for students — would save a working family with two children about $1,200 a year on groceries and transportation costs alone. The property tax increase for 2026 is set at 2.2 per cent, which Fletcher noted is below the rate of inflation. The budget also proposes what she called a fairer approach to funding city services, asking "empty home speculators and luxury property buyers" — the top 2 per cent of all buyers — to contribute more. The budget also includes $788 million in new savings and efficiencies, according to Fletcher, who said the city's financial position has improved over the past two years under Chow's leadership. Among the service investments, the budget funds seven-day-a-week library access and increases funding for tenant supports, home upgrade grants, flood protection, and programs that help seniors stay in their homes. On public safety, Fletcher said shootings, youth violence and 911 wait times have all significantly decreased. The budget builds on that trend, she said, by investing in more firefighters, paramedics, police officers and mental health workers, while boosting crime prevention programs. More than 25,000 residents took part in budget consultations held in October 2025, including telephone town halls and local events such as Fletcher's own budget town hall, ensuring the final plan reflected residents' priorities, her statement said. "I was pleased to support Mayor Chow's budget and her progressive vision of a more affordable, caring and safe Toronto," Fletcher wrote in her post. The budget vote came during a busy final stretch of the 2022-2026 council term. According to Fletcher's update, councillors also dealt with a maximum heat bylaw to protect tenants during extreme heat, a new funding deal to build more housing, and the provincial upload of the Gardiner Expressway and Don Valley Parkway. Other items on the agenda included Fletcher's motion about odours from the Ashbridges Bay sewage treatment plant, a redevelopment plan for Ookwemin Minising, and increased support from the mayor's office for vulnerable youth and low-income tenants. representative.title: Nobel Peace Prize for 2026 - Nobel Peace Prize
representative.author: Kristin Baann Asdal

snapshot.title: Nobel Peace Prize for 2026 - Nobel Peace Prize
snapshot.evidenceText: The Norwegian Nobel Committee has decided to award the Nobel Peace Prize for 2026 to Navanethem “Navi” Pillay for her efforts to promote peace and international law. The Nobel Peace Prize for 2026 goes to a person who with exceptional courage and integrity has led the way towards a more comprehensive global legal order. This year’s laureate has been instrumental in ensuring that war crimes, crimes against humanity and genocide are prosecuted. The Norwegian Nobel Committee has decided to award the Nobel Peace Prize for 2026 to Navanethem “Navi” Pillay for her efforts to promote peace and international law. Navi Pillay’s commitment to universal legal principles and her firm moral compass are constants in a long career. Born into a family of Indian Tamil origin under apartheid in Durban, South Africa, Pillay became a lawyer and legal pioneer, confronting deep structural discrimination, segregation and exclusion. A common thread runs from her early work defending Nelson Mandela and others who stood up against apartheid to her service as a judge in some of the key international court cases of our time This year’s laureate has significantly enlarged the scope and impact of international law. She has served as a judge on the High Court in South Africa, the International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda and the International Criminal Court. She was the United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights and, until recently, she chaired the UN Independent International Commission of Inquiry on the Occupied Palestinian Territory. Today Navi Pillay is a judge on the International Court of Justice in the case where Myanmar stands accused of genocide In historic international court cases, she has shown that legal measures can help prevent acts of war and violence. Navi Pillay has also contributed to strengthen the institutions of international law. Her independence, expertise and steadfastness have made her one of the most respected international jurists of our time. The first Nobel Peace Prize was awarded 125 years ago. Already then, the Norwegian Nobel Committee underscored the importance of resolving conflicts through international law – a theme that has remained prominent throughout the history of the Peace Prize. The reach of international law expanded after the Second World War, in particular with the creation of the UN institutions. The key insight was that lasting peace must be built on legal principles, not on the will of the strong or a fragile balance of power. Additional legal mechanisms were introduced in the post-war decades, and momentum picked up further after the end of the Cold War However, the rules-based international order has never been perfect. The greatest powers have often evaded responsibility. In practice, cases brought under international law have produced different results depending on who is the perpetrator and who is the victim. Nonetheless, we have seen that more and more conflicts are being addressed through diplomacy, treaties and legal mechanisms, rather than threats, violence and warfare. Leaders and populations alike have come to the same conclusion: international law is a foundation for a more peaceful world. At a time of existential challenges – including more wars and conflicts than the world has seen in a long time – international law is no longer just a supplement to peace and security. It is an absolute necessity. And yet, the system of international law is under tremendous pressure, and its institutions are under attack. We see a shift towards power politics at the expense of legal frameworks and global respect for law and justice. Whenever might overtakes right, it undermines stability, trust and peaceful co-existence. In awarding this year’s Nobel Peace Prize, the Norwegian Nobel Committee wants to remind the world that the rule of law – national and international – underpins the system we have set up to ensure peace and resolve conflicts non-violently. Peace requires justice History has shown that a world operating without the rule of law is unjust, unwise and inhumane. The judges – those who guard the thin red line between order and chaos – are therefore highly deserving of our praise. But today, as these same judges are sanctioned, and their institutions are attacked, we need people of courage, vision and determination – qualities that Navi Pillay demonstrates in her work on the bench Navi Pillay has held states and national leaders accountable and brought hope to victims of violence and conflict. In all the positions she has held, she has stressed the responsibility of individuals and states to comply with the rule of law. She has also helped define the relevant norms and legal principles. When the International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda established that rape and sexual violence could constitute a crime against humanity – as well as genocide – her influence was a significant factor. In the same case, Ms Pillay was instrumental in a separate legal breakthrough: for the first time, a defendant faced charges of incitement to commit genocide purely on the basis of spreading propaganda The Nobel Peace Prize for 2026 springs directly from Alfred Nobel’s will. Navi Pillay strengthens fraternity between nations and – by systematically advancing the use of tribunals for peace and justice – she provides substance, direction and motivation for peace conferences in their modern form. Navi Pillay is one of the great defenders of international legal principles in our time. Her distinguished career reminds us of the need to support, fortify and expand the global rule of law. Navi Pillay’s commitment to justice and human dignity is a source of hope and inspiration to all who seek to bring about a more peaceful world.
