snapshot.title: Navi Pillay, former UN human rights chief, wins Nobel Peace Prize
snapshot.evidenceText: Former UN human rights chief and International Court of Justice judge Navi Pillay has been awarded the 2026 Nobel Peace Prize. The South African judge was recognised "for her efforts to promote peace and international law", which paved the way for a "more comprehensive global legal order", the Nobel committee said. Pillay, 85, has taken part in high-profile work considering allegations of human rights violations during a decades-long career, including in Rwanda, Myanmar and Gaza. Her early work included defending anti-apartheid activists in South Africa, and on Friday she became the country's fifth Peace Prize winner - following in the footsteps of Nelson Mandela and Archbishop Desmond Tutu. Pillay's work had been "instrumental in ensuring that war crimes, crimes against humanity, and genocide are prosecuted", said the chair of the Norwegian Nobel Committee Jørgen Watne Frydnes. "Navi Pillay's commitment to universal legal principles and her firm moral compass are constants in a long career," he said. "At a time of existential challenges - including more wars and conflicts than the world has seen in a long time - international law is no longer just a supplement to peace and security. It is an absolute necessity." Frydnes said the committee had not been able to notify Pillay that she had won in advance, "so my message to her would be 'if you see a Norwegian number calling, please pick up'". Shortly afterwards, Pillay reacted to the news from Nuremberg's Palace of Justice by saying "it must be a joke" and thanked those who had gathered to applaud her. "If you clap a little bit more I may share this prize with Trump," she joked. Last year's winner, Venezuelan opposition leader María Corina Machado, gave her medal to the US president in January as "recognition for his unique commitment with our freedom" . Pillay dedicated her award to "all the survivors of international crimes" and the practitioners of international justice "whose compassion and courage continue to ensure that impunity will not be allowed to reign". Navanethem "Navi" Pillay grew up in South Africa during apartheid as a bus driver's daughter in a poor Indian section of Durban. She went on to become the first woman to establish a law practice in Natal Province in 1967, and later the first non-white woman to be appointed to the country's high court. Pillay served as a judge on the UN-backed International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda - focused on the 1994 genocide in which 800,000 people were killed - including four years as its president. She was elected to the International Criminal Court (ICC) in 2003. From 2021-25, she chaired the UN Independent International Commission of Inquiry on the Occupied Palestinian Territory - a fact-finding body established by the UN Human Rights Council to investigate alleged violations of international law. The commission concluded that Israel had committed genocidal acts in Gaza and that Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, and his former defence minister Yoav Gallant, had "incited the commission of genocide" in their speeches and statements. The three-member expert panel did not speak officially for the UN and had no legal authority. Israel rejected its findings and accused the three members of the commission of serving as "Hamas proxies". The panel had previously concluded that Hamas and other Palestinian armed groups committed war crimes and other grave violations of international law on 7 October 2023, in which about 1,200 people were killed and another 251 taken hostage. The same report also accused Israel of war crimes. Reacting to Pillay's award on Friday, Israel's Foreign Ministry said it represented a "grotesque weaponisation of an award to legitimise anti-Israel hatred and prejudice". It said in a statement: "Her role in the relentless, politically motivated demonisation of Israel and promotion of the genoLIE speaks volumes." US President Donald Trump, who has previously expressed a desire to receive the prize, reposted a statement on social media that said the Nobel committee had "demeaned" the award by giving it to someone it described as an "unabashed hater of America and Israel". The US later announced sweeping sanctions on the court , saying it wanted to restrict its resources and ability to operate. The ICC called the move an assault on the rule of law. Nobel committee chair Frydnes said the organisation was not taking a position on whether the Israeli offensive in Gaza amounted to genocide by handing Pillay the peace prize. Asked about Pillay's UN commission on the matter, he replied her award had been given "for her whole work". Pillay is currently a judge on the International Court of Justice (ICJ) in the case where Myanmar stands accused by The Gambia of genocide against the Rohingya people. Myanmar has denied deliberately trying to destroy the minority Muslim population, with a government representative telling the court in January that the allegation was "unsubstantiated" . UN human rights chief Volker Turk said Pillay's recognition was "a reaffirmation that human rights, the rule of law and justice, and accountability are fundamental to everything, to peace, to security, and prosperity". Meanwhile, UN Secretary General António Guterres said she had been "a steadfast, independent voice of justice amidst some of the most historic international legal cases of our time". South Africa's President Cyril Ramaphosa said she had been a "pioneering defence attorney for anti-apartheid activists" who had worked to "uphold human dignity and bring hope in South Africa and to peoples globally". Amnesty International secretary general Agnès Callamard said she was with Pillay when she learned she had won - and called her an "inspired choice" for the award. "At a time when both international law and justice are under attack, when too many states attempt to hollow them out, her Nobel Peace Prize could not come at a better time," she said. The fearsome pace quartet and Steve Smith's brilliance serves as a reminder of Australia's quality as the tourists take charge against South Africa. After nine years and 280 days, Matt Renshaw scores epic century to put Australia on top against South Africa and push his own case for a regular place. Navi Pillay says the Trump administrations' sweeping penalties on the international tribunal were "unheard of". The US president told a rally he had "never heard of" the winner, former International Criminal Court judge Navi Pillay. Several member states of the international tribunal, including the UK, say they "strongly disagree" with the sanctions.

snapshot.title: Former UN human rights chief Navi Pillay awarded Nobel Peace Prize
snapshot.evidenceText: South African jurist and former UN High Commissioner for Human Rights Navi Pillay was on Friday announced as the winner of the 2026 Nobel Peace Prize . She was honoured “for her efforts to promote peace and international law”, the Norwegian Nobel Committee said in a statement. The committee said the award was going “to a person who with exceptional courage and integrity has led the way towards a more comprehensive global legal order,” noting that she “has been instrumental in ensuring that war crimes, crimes against humanity and genocide are prosecuted .” Ms. Pillay served as the UN human rights chief from September 2008 through August 2014 , but her career has spanned more than 50 years - from fighting apartheid in her homeland to defending civilians in conflict zones. She is a former chair of the UN Independent International Commission of Inquiry on the Occupied Palestinian Territory and was appointed a judge at the International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda (ICTR) and the International Criminal Court (ICC) in the Hague, in addition to serving as an ad hoc judge with the International Court of Justice ( ICJ ), the UN's highest court. “ A common thread runs from her early work defending Nelson Mandela and others who stood up against apartheid to her service as a judge in some of the key international court cases of our time ,” the Nobel Committee said. In a statement congratulating the new Nobel laureate, UN Secretary-General António Guterres said Ms. Pillay has shown “that the force of law must prevail over the law of force and that defending human rights is the surest safeguard against injustice.” He hailed her as “a champion of international law and human rights, and a steadfast, independent voice of justice”, adding that “in its citation, the Nobel Committee reminded the world that peace must be built on lasting principles, not the will of the powerful." Navanethem “Navi” Pillay was born in South Africa in 1941 to a Tamil Indian family and was the first non-white woman to establish a legal practice in the country. As a lawyer, she acted as a defence attorney for anti-apartheid activists, exposing torture, and helping to establish key rights for prisoners on notorious Robben Island. In her role as chair of the Independent International Commission, which is appointed by the UN Human Rights Council , she oversaw its 2025 report that said Israel’s actions in the Gaza Strip constituted genocide. Listen back to our interview with Ms. Pillay on the commission's report: On receiving the news of Ms. Pillay's honour, the current UN human rights chief, Volker Türk, warmly congratulated the woman he described as a big sister. “ To say it is well deserved is a total understatement, and especially at a time when human rights are under attack on so many fronts , including from those who wield enormous power, this award is particularly poignant,” he said, speaking in Geneva. “It is an award to all those who around the world dedicate their lives to the defense of human rights, often at great risk to their security.” Moreover, it is “a recognition, a reaffirmation, that human rights, the rule of law and justice and accountability are fundamental to everything - to peace, to security and prosperity,” he added. In an October 2025 interview with UN News in Geneva, Ms. Pillay reflected on her lifetime of fighting for human rights, justice and equality. “I didn't think apartheid would end in my lifetime,” she recalled. “So, what happened? We had the collective support of people all over the world, even children. If we can achieve that, we can have a better human rights protection system.” Her experience in the anti-apartheid struggle shaped her belief in international solidarity, which she carried into her role as a judge and president of the ITCR, which prosecuted persons responsible for the 1994 genocide in Rwanda. During her eight years there, she helped establish groundbreaking legal precedents in the fight against genocide and gender-based violence. As UN human rights chief, Ms. Pillay continued to champion the participation of civil society and victims’ voices in shaping global human rights standards. “When the UN started, it was just a club for the States,” she told UN News . “Everything we have today for human rights protection didn’t happen just because the States woke up one day. It comes from the pressure of civil society. That’s why I value these institutions.”

snapshot.title: South African human rights lawyer Navi Pillay wins the Nobel Peace Prize
snapshot.evidenceText: South African lawyer Navanethem "Navi" Pillay sits at the Nuremberg Forum in Germany following the announcement that she will be awarded the 2026 Nobel Peace Prize. The Nobel Committee is honoring her for her efforts to promote peace and international law. Daniel Karmann/picture alliance via Getty Images hide caption Navanethem "Navi" Pillay, a leading South African jurist and former U.N. human rights chief, won the Nobel Peace Prize on Friday for her lifetime commitment to international law. At a ceremony in Oslo, Norwegian Nobel Committee Chair Jørgen Watne Frydnes called Pillay "one of the most courageous and important legal experts of our time." "There is a thread to her involvement in standing and supporting Nelson Mandela and the prisoners of Robben Island, to her being a key to all the major international court cases of our time," he said. The 85-year-old was attending a conference in Nuremberg, Germany, when she received the news. At a news conference, Pillay said she was deeply honored and dedicated the prize to "all of the survivors of international crimes" and "defenders of international justice." "We are living through an era when international law and human rights are under significant political attack," she added. Hours after her win, the United States issued new sanctions on the International Criminal Court, which the Trump administration has warned it is working to dismantle. Born in Durban in 1941, Pillay — who is a South African of Indian-Tamil descent — became the first woman of color to open a legal practice in her home province of Natal. She defended anti-apartheid activists, beginning a career studded with lasting achievements. In 1973, she successfully sued the government to establish that political prisoners on South Africa's infamous Robben Island , including Mandela, had the right to legal representation. A year after apartheid ended in 1994, Pillay became a high court judge in South Africa in 1995. She was shortly appointed to the International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda, where she presided over a landmark case that established that rape and sexual assault could constitute acts of genocide. Pillay later served as a judge at the International Criminal Court from 2003 to 2012, as well as the U.N. high commissioner for human rights from 2008 to 2014. Pillay was applauded by colleagues while in Nuremberg after receiving the news of her Nobel win. "If you clap a little bit more, I may share this prize with Trump," she joked in front of a small crowd of well-wishers. "Being a lawyer and a judge I still want to verify this information," she added, to laughter. The winner of last year's Nobel Peace Prize, Venezuelan opposition leader María Corina Machado, gifted Trump the physical gold medal she received in January. The Nobel Committee reacted to Machado's move by saying the prize cannot be transferred to others. Pillay referred to her recent work as chair of the Independent International Commission of Inquiry on the Occupied Palestinian Territory, which concluded in 2025 that Israel had committed genocide in Gaza . Israeli leaders strongly reject the accusation. In response to the Nobel prize decision, Israel's Foreign Ministry posted on X that it rewarded "anti-Israel hatred." It added: "Joseph Goebbels is certainly applauding from hell." Others, including South African President Cyril Ramaphosa , U.N. High Commissioner for Human Rights Volker Türk , as well as human rights advocates, praised the move to award Pillay the prize. "Congratulations to her, she's the fifth South African to achieve the Nobel Prize," South Africa's new ambassador to Washington, Roelf Meyer, told NPR. Pillay joins anti-apartheid luminaries Chief Albert Luthuli, Archbishop Desmond Tutu, President Nelson Mandela in winning the award, as well as former President F.W. de Klerk. But Meyer noted she is the first woman. "We as South Africans are very, very proud of her." Meyer also said she exemplified South Africa's constitutional legal system — which was established at the start of the nation's democracy, following the end of apartheid. But Pillay's award comes amid a diplomatic low-point between the U.S. and South Africa. President Trump has falsely accused the government of persecuting South Africa's white minority. The U.S. has also criticized South Africa's genocide case against Israel brought before the International Court of Justice. Although the Trump administration has not yet publicly commented on Pillay's win, its sweeping sanctions against the International Criminal Court (ICC) have sent a signal. "We will ban transactions with this rogue court, cutting off their resources and crippling its ability to operate," Rubio said in a statement announcing the sanctions. The move drew condemnation from human rights advocates as well as the court itself at the Hague, Netherlands. "The court firmly rejects these sanctions," ICC President Tomoko Akane said in a video statement . "As an ICC judge myself, I can assure you that the court is not politically motivated. We are an independent and impartial judicial institution, and our actions are guided only by the law and evidence." The U.S. had already sanctioned senior officials of the court, including half of its judges and its former chief prosecutor, piling significant pressure on the institution. The sanctions are connected to investigations into U.S. military personnel in Afghanistan, as well as arrest warrants issued for Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and former Defense Minister Yoav Gallant for alleged war crimes in Gaza. Nobel Peace Prize laureate Navi Pillay, then U.N. High Commissioner for Human Rights, visits a Palestinian family home near Ramallah in the Israeli-occupied West Bank on Feb. 7, 2011. Abbas Momani/AFP via Getty Images hide caption Neither the U.S. nor Israel is a member of the International Criminal Court, but the Trump administration has argued that the court threatens U.S. sovereignty. The Norwegian Nobel Committee said that continued attacks on the rule of law and its institutions had influenced its decisions. "This is a message that international law and its institutions are the cornerstone of a more peaceful world," Jørgen Watne Frydnes said. The news of Pillay's win will surely be seen as a blow to President Trump, who has long coveted the Nobel Peace Prize. He told reporters on Wednesday he believed he deserved it. "I settled eight wars," Trump said, while admitting that the Nobel Prize Committee had "a reputation for maybe not giving it to people like me." This year's Nobel Peace Prize attracted 287 nominations, including individuals and organizations. The award carries prize money of 12 million Swedish kronor, approximately $1.2 million. The 2026 prize marks the 125th anniversary of the Nobel Peace Prize, first awarded in 1901. Kate Bartlett contributed reporting from Johannesburg; Michele Kelemen contributed from Washington. snapshot.title: Nobel Peace Prize for 2026 - Nobel Peace Prize
snapshot.evidenceText: The Norwegian Nobel Committee has decided to award the Nobel Peace Prize for 2026 to Navanethem “Navi” Pillay for her efforts to promote peace and international law. The Nobel Peace Prize for 2026 goes to a person who with exceptional courage and integrity has led the way towards a more comprehensive global legal order. This year’s laureate has been instrumental in ensuring that war crimes, crimes against humanity and genocide are prosecuted. The Norwegian Nobel Committee has decided to award the Nobel Peace Prize for 2026 to Navanethem “Navi” Pillay for her efforts to promote peace and international law. Navi Pillay’s commitment to universal legal principles and her firm moral compass are constants in a long career. Born into a family of Indian Tamil origin under apartheid in Durban, South Africa, Pillay became a lawyer and legal pioneer, confronting deep structural discrimination, segregation and exclusion. A common thread runs from her early work defending Nelson Mandela and others who stood up against apartheid to her service as a judge in some of the key international court cases of our time This year’s laureate has significantly enlarged the scope and impact of international law. She has served as a judge on the High Court in South Africa, the International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda and the International Criminal Court. She was the United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights and, until recently, she chaired the UN Independent International Commission of Inquiry on the Occupied Palestinian Territory. Today Navi Pillay is a judge on the International Court of Justice in the case where Myanmar stands accused of genocide In historic international court cases, she has shown that legal measures can help prevent acts of war and violence. Navi Pillay has also contributed to strengthen the institutions of international law. Her independence, expertise and steadfastness have made her one of the most respected international jurists of our time. The first Nobel Peace Prize was awarded 125 years ago. Already then, the Norwegian Nobel Committee underscored the importance of resolving conflicts through international law – a theme that has remained prominent throughout the history of the Peace Prize. The reach of international law expanded after the Second World War, in particular with the creation of the UN institutions. The key insight was that lasting peace must be built on legal principles, not on the will of the strong or a fragile balance of power. Additional legal mechanisms were introduced in the post-war decades, and momentum picked up further after the end of the Cold War However, the rules-based international order has never been perfect. The greatest powers have often evaded responsibility. In practice, cases brought under international law have produced different results depending on who is the perpetrator and who is the victim. Nonetheless, we have seen that more and more conflicts are being addressed through diplomacy, treaties and legal mechanisms, rather than threats, violence and warfare. Leaders and populations alike have come to the same conclusion: international law is a foundation for a more peaceful world. At a time of existential challenges – including more wars and conflicts than the world has seen in a long time – international law is no longer just a supplement to peace and security. It is an absolute necessity. And yet, the system of international law is under tremendous pressure, and its institutions are under attack. We see a shift towards power politics at the expense of legal frameworks and global respect for law and justice. Whenever might overtakes right, it undermines stability, trust and peaceful co-existence. In awarding this year’s Nobel Peace Prize, the Norwegian Nobel Committee wants to remind the world that the rule of law – national and international – underpins the system we have set up to ensure peace and resolve conflicts non-violently. Peace requires justice History has shown that a world operating without the rule of law is unjust, unwise and inhumane. The judges – those who guard the thin red line between order and chaos – are therefore highly deserving of our praise. But today, as these same judges are sanctioned, and their institutions are attacked, we need people of courage, vision and determination – qualities that Navi Pillay demonstrates in her work on the bench Navi Pillay has held states and national leaders accountable and brought hope to victims of violence and conflict. In all the positions she has held, she has stressed the responsibility of individuals and states to comply with the rule of law. She has also helped define the relevant norms and legal principles. When the International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda established that rape and sexual violence could constitute a crime against humanity – as well as genocide – her influence was a significant factor. In the same case, Ms Pillay was instrumental in a separate legal breakthrough: for the first time, a defendant faced charges of incitement to commit genocide purely on the basis of spreading propaganda The Nobel Peace Prize for 2026 springs directly from Alfred Nobel’s will. Navi Pillay strengthens fraternity between nations and – by systematically advancing the use of tribunals for peace and justice – she provides substance, direction and motivation for peace conferences in their modern form. Navi Pillay is one of the great defenders of international legal principles in our time. Her distinguished career reminds us of the need to support, fortify and expand the global rule of law. Navi Pillay’s commitment to justice and human dignity is a source of hope and inspiration to all who seek to bring about a more peaceful world.

As a result, Canada's merchandise trade surplus with the world widened from $787 million in July to $4.2 billion in August. The total imports decrease during the month was the first decline since January. Despite the decrease, gains were observed in 6 of the 11 product sections. Predicted five-year net survival rates for those diagnosed from 2019 to 2021 were highest for thyroid (97%) and testicular (96%) cancers. representative.title: Canada loses all 2026 job gains. These sectors were hardest hit
representative.author: Reuters Staff

snapshot.title: Canada’s 2026 job gains have been erased. The hardest-hit area wasn’t the one facing U.S. tariffs
snapshot.evidenceText: OTTAWA — Canada’s economy shed a net 68,300 jobs in September and the unemployment rate edged up, data showed on Friday, erasing all the employment gains recorded earlier this year. The unexpected drop follows a decline of 41,700 jobs in August, Statistics Canada said. The unemployment level in September inched up to 6.5 per cent from 6.4 per cent in August. September was the first full month after a new round of U.S. tariffs took effect against Canada. However, the largest job losses were in the public sector, particularly health care, social assistance and education, as the government cut international student permits. Analysts polled by Reuters had forecast an increase of 9,200 jobs and an unemployment rate of 6.5 per cent. With September’s decline, Canada has lost a net 41,200 jobs so far this year, compared with a gain of 211,300 in the same period of 2025. Job losses were split almost evenly between full-time and part-time positions. Manufacturing, a sector partly exposed to U.S. tariffs, lost a net 12,700 jobs. Economists have said the latest U.S. tariffs are unlikely to have a major impact on employment data in the coming months. Money markets are no longer pricing in a rate increase from the Bank of Canada this month, although expectations of a 25 basis point hike had edged higher. Markets expect a 25-basis-point increase in December. “Given the recent deterioration in the labour market, Canadian central bankers will likely need to keep rates unchanged later this month,” Royce Mendes, head of macro strategy at Desjardins, said in a note. “That said, we expect that higher energy prices will begin feeding other categories of inflation this fall, and could force officials to tighten policy soon.” The labour force participation rate, which measures the share of the population either working or looking for work, fell 0.2 percentage points to 64.8 per cent in September, its lowest level in 29 years excluding the pandemic period. The decline was driven largely by an aging population leaving the workforce and slower immigration reducing the number of replacements. Employment among young people aged 15-24 fell by 48,000 in September after a smaller decline in August. Growth in average hourly wages for permanent employees, a closely watched measure of inflation pressures, accelerated to 2.3 per cent year on year in September from two per cent in August, Statistics Canada said. The Canadian dollar weakened after the report, falling 0.44 per cent to $1.4287 per US dollar, or 69.99 US cents. Yields on two-year Canadian government bonds were down 9.5 basis points at 2.410 per cent. --- Reporting by Promit Mukherjee. Editing by Dale Smith and Mark Potter

snapshot.title: Canadian economy lost 68,000 jobs in September, marking second straight month of surprise declines | CBC News
snapshot.evidenceText: Canada lost 68,000 jobs in September, according to Statistics Canada, marking a second straight month of losses. The unemployment rate ticked up by 0.1 percentage points to 6.5 per cent, which is where it stood at the start of 2026. The figures bucked economists' predictions for a gain of 9,200 positions in September. It comes after another surprise last month of 42,000 job losses for August , which snapped a hot streak for the labour market. Before the two monthly declines, Statistics Canada data showed employment trending upward, with 181,000 jobs added between April and July. Employment is still up compared to a year ago by 95,000 positions. BMO chief economist Doug Porter said job figures are often volatile, and have been especially so in recent years. Still, he noted it's rare to see two months in a row of job losses of this size. "There's no question, this is a disappointing result," Porter said. "It does suggest the economy was struggling in the early fall." By sector, educational services, health care and social assistance, and manufacturing led the declines. More workers in "other services," which includes things like repair and maintenance, offset the losses. Porter says the drop in education jobs, which was concentrated in Quebec, could be a bit of a blip, but says it could also point to weakness in the sector with fewer international students studying in the country. CIBC senior economist Andrew Grantham adds that while some data volatility is likely behind the poor report, losses in manufacturing could be a sign that new tariffs, which came into effect in August, are taking a toll. Statistics Canada says job losses were split between full- and part-time work and were concentrated in the public sector, which dropped 70,000 roles in the month. The number of public sector employees is down by 119,000 compared to the same time last year. The private sector added some jobs and held steady however — a silver lining, according to Porter. Deloitte Canada cuts GDP growth forecast by 20% as tariffs grip economy amid Trump's trade war The decline was concentrated in youth aged 15 to 24, who accounted for 48,000 job losses, according to the data agency. But the pool of young workers also shrank in September, leaving the unemployment rate for that group relatively unchanged at 13 per cent. Core-aged women, between 25 and 54 years old, also held 28,000 fewer positions, and the number of women in that age group looking for work increased. Quebec led the job losses by province, with 49,000 jobs lost in the month, while B.C. followed with 20,000 fewer jobs. Alberta, on the other hand, added 23,000 positions. Canada's economy still resilient, but U.S. trade war taking its toll The jobs data is the Bank of Canada's last look at the labour market before its next interest rate decision on Oct. 28. CIBC senior economist Andrew Grantham says despite volatility playing a factor, the drop in the number of jobs will likely keep the Bank of Canada from making any interest rate moves in the near future. "Overall, while the weakness in today's employment data is likely more a reflection of data volatility than the impact of new U.S. tariffs, it does support our call that the Bank of Canada will remain patient and keep interest rates on hold at the two remaining meetings this year," Grantham wrote in a note to investors. snapshot.title: September job losses pour cold water on Bank of Canada rate hike chatter
snapshot.evidenceText: Honda employees work along the vehicle assembly line in Alliston, Ont., on Thursday, April 25, 2024. THE CANADIAN PRESS/Nathan Denette Honda employees work along the vehicle assembly line in Alliston, Ont., on Thursday, April 25, 2024. THE CANADIAN PRESS/Nathan Denette OTTAWA - The labour market stalled for a second month in a row in September, pushing back on calls for interest rate hikes from the Bank of Canada. Statistics Canada said Friday the economy lost 68,000 positions in September, coming off a loss of 42,000 roles in August. Economists had expected a gain of 9,200 jobs in the month. StatCan said job losses were nearly evenly split between full- and part-time work and were concentrated in the public sector. The unemployment rate edged up a tenth of a point to 6.5 per cent last month, back to where it stood at the start of the year in January. September now marks the steepest single month of job losses since February. "There's no way to sugar coat it. It's a very bad jobs print for September and it follows up a bad print in August," said Robert Kavcic, senior economist at BMO Capital Markets. The only saving grace for the labour market, Kavcic noted, is that employers had been expanding their payrolls at a solid clip earlier in the year. Before recent weakness, employers had collectively added 181,000 positions from April through July. Employment was up 95,000 positions compared with last September. Smoothing out the often-volatile job figures over the past six months paints a picture of modest but steady gains, Kavcic said. "It's not a good sign going into the fourth quarter, but if you step back and ignore some of the month-to-month noise, it does look like the job market is holding in relatively well." Signs of stability in the private sector — despite four straight months of declines in public sector employment — were also reassuring to economists. The educational services sector led the declines with a loss of 35,000 positions last month, followed by the health care and manufacturing industries. September, meanwhile, recorded a gain of 17,000 jobs from a segment that includes repair, maintenance and other household and personal services. Young workers aged 15 to 24 bore the brunt of the losses last month with 48,000 fewer jobs, though women aged 25 to 54 also saw employment levels fall. Provincially, Quebec stood out with a loss of 49,000 jobs last month, while Ontario and British Columbia both shed 20,000 positions. Alberta added 23,000 roles. The September jobs report is one of the first major economic releases since the trade dispute between Canada and the United States ratcheted back up. Despite job losses in manufacturing, most economists weighing in Friday were not ascribing too much tariff weight to the data. "Most September losses came from non-trade-facing sectors and from educational services for Quebec in particular, so it would be premature to blame tariffs for the weakness," said Daniel Hyun, senior economist at KPMG Canada, in a note. Kavcic said pressure from tariffs will likely keep hiring at a subdued pace heading into the fourth quarter. The September jobs figures mark the Bank of Canada’s last look at the labour market before its next interest rate decision set for Oct. 28. The central bank's policy rate has been at 2.25 per cent for nearly a year. Most economists consider that rate to be slightly stimulative to the economy. TD Bank senior economist Andrew Hencic said in a note to clients that two months of weak labour market figures between Bank of Canada decisions will pour cold water on calls for interest rate hikes. While the central bank has been guarding against both tariff-induced economic weakness and price hikes from the war in the Middle East, Hencic said monetary policymakers have signalled lately they're more concerned about bubbling inflationary pressures. TD expects the Bank of Canada to remain on hold this month as new tariffs take some steam out of the economy and keep inflation in check. Financial market odds of a quarter-point hike from the Bank of Canada this month fell to roughly 25 per cent as of Friday afternoon, down from around 40 per cent before the latest jobs data, according to LSEG Data & Analytics. Hyun said the soft labour report casts a bit of doubt on KPMG Canada's call for a quarter-point hike in December. But for now the firm's economists still expect the central bank will push back against inflation risks by raising its policy rate to 2.5 per cent to end the year. Kavcic said that, zooming out, the broad weakness in the labour market does not call for higher rates. "These reports in August and September push back pretty hard against the Bank of Canada raising rates right now in the short term," he said. If the central bank does hike, he said, it will be on the back of trends in inflation data. Even then, it will take a few bad inflation reports in a row for the bank to move off its stand-pat stance and back into a tightening cycle, Kavcic argued. Also on Friday, the Canadian dollar fell to its lowest point against the U.S. greenback since early 2025. The loonie dipped briefly below 70 cents US before recovering somewhat. representative.title: The Weekly Review, October 5 to 9, 2026 - Statistics Canada
representative.author: Government of Canada, Statistics Canada

snapshot.title: The Weekly Review, October 5 to 9, 2026 - Statistics Canada
snapshot.evidenceText: Employment declined by 68,000 (-0.3%) in September, split between full-time work (-35,000; -0.2%) and part-time work (-33,000; -0.9%). Employment fell in educational services, health care and social assistance as well as manufacturing. Meanwhile, the employment rate fell 0.2 percentage points to 60.6%. In September, the unemployment rate increased 0.1 percentage points to 6.5%. In August, Canada's merchandise exports rose 2.5%, while imports were down 2.0%. As a result, Canada's merchandise trade surplus with the world widened from $787 million in July to $4.2 billion in August. The total imports decrease during the month was the first decline since January. Despite the decrease, gains were observed in 6 of the 11 product sections. Imports of motor vehicles and parts posted the largest decline in August. Source: Canadian international merchandise trade, August 2026 The operating revenue of the travel arrangement and reservation services industry group rose 8.8% to $18.3 billion in 2025. This follows an increase of 9.3% in 2024. Although operating revenues of these industries posted slower growth in 2025, they still topped the high of $16.8 billion recorded the previous year. In 2025, LGB+ (12%) and gender diverse (15%) people were over three times as likely to have experienced violent victimization (i.e., physical or sexual assault) in the previous 12 months compared with their heterosexual (3.6%) and cisgender (4.1%) counterparts. In addition, approximately half of LGB+ people had been sexually (49%) or physically (52%) assaulted since age 15, higher than their heterosexual counterparts (21% had been sexually assaulted and 31% had been physically assaulted). Source: Violent victimization and unwanted sexual behaviours experienced by 2SLGBTQ+ people in Canada, 2025 Critical mineral production contributed $26.3 billion to the total Canadian economy in 2024, representing roughly a 0.9% share, as measured by nominal gross domestic product (GDP). Measured by real GDP, critical mineral production, grew by 8.2% in 2024. Every aggregation of critical minerals experienced real GDP growth, with the most notable increases coming from platinum group metals (+16.7%) and unrefined prioritized critical minerals (+13.9%; including cobalt, copper and nickel). Source: Economic contribution of critical mineral production in Canada, 2024 The legacy of Terry Fox lives on, long after his death in 1981. Countless Canadians have taken part in the Terry Fox Run every year in September to raise awareness and funds for cancer research. Just over two in five people in Canada will be diagnosed with cancer in their lifetime , according to estimates based on data from the Canadian Cancer Registry. Cancer has been the leading cause of death in Canada since 2006 . Predicted five-year net survival rates for those diagnosed from 2019 to 2021 were highest for thyroid (97%) and testicular (96%) cancers. Source: Walking and running for the cure—remembering Terry Fox 45 years later For more information, contact the Statistical Information Service (toll-free 1-800-263-1136 ; 514-283-8300 ; infostats@statcan.gc.ca ) or Media Relations ( statcan.mediahotline-ligneinfomedias.statcan@statcan.gc.ca ).

representative.title: Dengue death toll nears 300 as 4 die, 1,631 hospitalised in 24 hours | The Business Standard
representative.author: TBS Report

snapshot.title: Dengue death toll nears 300 as 4 die, 1,631 hospitalised in 24 hours
snapshot.evidenceText: Four people died of dengue and 1,631 were admitted to hospitals across the country in the 24 hours until 8am today (10 October). The latest deaths have taken the country's dengue death toll to 299 this year, according to a press release issued by the Directorate General of Health Services (DGHS). Of the four deaths, one each was reported in Dhaka North City Corporation, Barishal, Chattogram and Khulna division. September recorded the highest monthly dengue death toll so far this year, with 148 deaths. Dengue claimed five lives in total from January to May, followed by 13 deaths in June, 36 in July and 43 in August. Meanwhile, 1,627 dengue patients were discharged from hospitals in the 24 hours, taking the total number of recoveries this year to 91,007. The cumulative number of dengue cases reported across the country has reached 97,082, according to the DGHS. representative.title: The FE - Major Dhaka hospitals face rising dengue patient load
representative.author: SM Najmus Sakib

snapshot.title: Major Dhaka hospitals face rising dengue patient load
snapshot.evidenceText: Published by Syed Nasim Manzur for International Publications Limited from Tropicana Tower (4th ﬂoor), 45, Topkhana Road, GPO Box : 2526 Dhaka- 1000 and printed by him from The Transcraft Limited, 229, Tejgaon Industrial Area, Dhaka-1208 PABX : 02223389780 (Hunting) | Mobile: 01917231083 | Fax : 880-2-02223387049 © 2026 - All Rights with The Financial Express About Us Contact Us Terms of Service Privacy Policy Pressure on major public hospitals dedicated to treating dengue patients is mounting as health authorities continue to record a rising number of cases across the country. Five more deaths reported on Thursday, taking this year's toll to 294 -- already well above the 220 deaths recorded during the corresponding period last year. The Directorate General of Health Services (DGHS) on Thursday reported 1,935 new hospitalisations due to the mosquito-borne viral disease, taking the total caseload to 94,151. Of the total hospitalisations, 88,208 patients have been discharged from hospitals after recovery. The number of cases has already doubled compared with the corresponding period in 2025. The DGHS registered 52,104 cases during the corresponding period last year. October has so far recorded 49 deaths, compared with 114 in September. The city's dedicated hospitals, mainly Dhaka Medical College Hospital (DMCH) and Mugda Medical College Hospital, have been receiving a major share of the total dengue patients. In the past 24 hours, DMCH admitted 69 new patients while treating a total of 236. Until Thursday, it had admitted a total of 3,063 patients this year. Mugda Hospital admitted 67 more patients, taking its total admissions this year to 2,552. Currently, 222 patients are receiving treatment at the hospital in Old Dhaka. Mugda Hospital is facing mounting pressure as 222 of its 300 beds dedicated to dengue patients are occupied, including beds arranged on the floor. DGHS Director (Hospital) Dr Md Nurul Islam told the FE that a daily average of 5,000-5,500 patients remain admitted this year, compared with about 3,500 last year. Therefore, there is pressure on hospitals. However, he claimed that the pressure remains manageable. The government is considering allocating the DMCH burn unit for dengue patients, which could add 50-100 beds, according to the official. However, there are more patients than the dedicated beds, with many patients being treated in medicine wards, he said. The health ministry has also increased the number of beds at Khulna Specialized Hospital by 50. Private hospitals have been asked to admit patients, said DGHS officials. However, there is no government support for admitting patients who cannot afford treatment at those facilities, as demanded by public health experts. "We don't have a plan right now to facilitate private hospitals with government funds to dedicate beds for patients who cannot afford private care. However, we have suggested that private hospitals consider the financial condition of dengue patients," the DGHS director added. Meanwhile, more worryingly, entomologists have forecast that the ongoing dengue outbreak could persist into November if favourable conditions continue, without any significant improvement in the number of cases. Prof Kabirul Bashar, a medical entomologist at Jahangirnagar University, told the FE that there was no sign of the dengue situation easing or any significant improvement in the number of patients throughout October and into November. "If rain, an increasing number of dengue patients, dengue manifestation and temperature all occur at once, then dengue cases rise geometrically in the model we forecast. And everything remains favourable for dengue to continue until November," he explained. The situation may improve in December, he anticipated. The health authorities only collect and register data from hospitals, including dedicated facilities. There are many public and private hospitals and clinics across the country that do not report their cases, while many patients do not seek hospital treatment. "The real situation may be up to 10 times higher than the reported cases. We don't have the exact data; we only report partial cases based on data provided by hospitals. The death rate in Bangladesh is the highest in the world. To take proper action and precautionary measures, exact data is crucial," he explained. Destroying breeding hotspots, applying larvicide and engaging communities are the major initiatives needed to deal with the dengue situation, said the expert. The mosquito-borne disease is transmitted to humans through infected mosquitoes, but there is no specific treatment for the infection. Bangladesh usually sees a dengue season between June and September. The country reported its highest-ever annual number of dengue deaths in 2022, when 281 people died.

representative.title: Teacher unions suspend two-week strike after meeting with Council of State - Graphic Online
representative.author: Emmanuel Bonney

snapshot.title: Teacher unions suspend two-week strike after meeting with Council of State
snapshot.evidenceText: The teacher unions have suspended their two-week old industrial action after a meeting with the Council of State on Friday. They have therefore directed their members to return to the classrooms from Monday, October 12, 2026. This follows a successful meeting with the Fair Wages and Salaries Commission and the Council of State on Friday. Council of State, Employment Ministry, FWSC meet pre-tertiary teachers over strike The government on Friday stepped up its discussions with the three teacher unions with a view to getting them to call off their nine-day industrial action. The move was to enable them to return to the classrooms on Monday, October 12, 2026, for the resumption of academic activities in first and second cycle institutions. In pursuit of that the unions held separate meetings at the Ministry of Labour, Jobs and Employment, Council of State and Fair Wages and Salaries Commission (FWSC). After the meeting with the sector minister at the Ministry of Labour, Jobs and Employment, Emmanuel Kwadwo Agyekum, he told journalists that the discussions had centered on the three issues that made them to declare a strike, reports Graphic Online's Emmanuel Bonney. "I would say that we have had a fantastic discussion with the teacher unions. The issues were to deal with their collective agreement, the other issue had to do with the deprived area allowance and the last one was to deal with promotions," he said. He said promotion was a bit problematic because "we had to come in from the front of the Ghana Education Service (GES) and that of the Controller and Accountant General." He said a team had been put together and for the past one week it had some very good results. "As of yesterday (Thursday), we had about 64,000 [teachers] that have been keyed in and confirmed by controller. "So I think definitely we would have a positive results today from the unions," he said. Education Ministry expresses appreciation to teacher unions for suspending strike Meanwhile the Ministry of Education has expressed appreciation to the three teacher unions, the Ghana National Association of Teachers (GNAT), the National Association of Graduate Teachers (NAGRAT), and the Pre-Tertiary Teachers Association of Ghana (PRETAG), for suspending their nationwide strike following constructive negotiations with the Government and the Fair Wages and Salaries Commission. It said the ministry acknowledged the unions’ decision as a positive step towards resolving outstanding concerns through dialogue, mutual understanding, and constructive engagement in the best interest of teachers and learners. "The ministry remains committed to working collaboratively with the unions, the Fair Wages and Salaries Commission, and other relevant stakeholders to address outstanding issues and promote teachers’ welfare, while ensuring stability and continuity in the delivery of quality education. "The Ministry appreciates the patience and resilience of teachers, parents, learners, and all stakeholders affected by the industrial action. We urge all parties to sustain the spirit of cooperation and good faith to ensure that the gains made through negotiations are consolidated," it said. The Ministry reaffirmrd its commitment to strengthening industrial harmony and creating an enabling environment in which teachers are valued, supported, and empowered to contribute meaningfully to Ghana’s education transformation agenda.

representative.title: NCPTA welcomes end of teachers’ strike, urges compliance  | Ghana News Agency
representative.author: GNA

snapshot.title: NCPTA welcomes end of teachers’ strike, urges compliance | Ghana News Agency
snapshot.evidenceText: Ghana's preferred news source: Accurate, Credible, Objective, Timely Kadjebi (O/R), Oct. 10, GNA – The National Council of Parent-Teacher Associations (NCPTA)-Ghana has welcomed the decision by teacher unions to call off their strike. The Council urged all parties to honour the timelines agreed upon to address outstanding concerns. The Council said the resumption of classroom activities would restore teaching and learning, protect the academic calendar and ease the burden on parents and guardians. The strike was called off following a communiqué signed on October 09, 2026, by the government, represented by the Fair Wages and Salaries Commission (FWSC) and the Ghana Education Service (GES), and teacher unions, including the Ghana National Association of Teachers (GNAT), the National Association of Graduate Teachers (NAGRAT) and the Pre-Tertiary Teachers Association of Ghana (PRETAG). In a press statement dated October 10 and signed by Mr Gapson Kofi Raphael, the General Secretary of NCPTA-Ghana, the Council expressed gratitude to President John Dramani Mahama and other stakeholders for their roles in resolving the impasse. It also commended the leadership and members of the teacher unions for returning to negotiations and agreeing to resume classroom work. The statement said the agreement outlined timelines for addressing key concerns, including the payment of salary arrears to 51,000 teachers by October 16, 2026, with the remaining payments expected by the end of October. It said modalities for the Deprived Area Allowance were expected to be addressed in January 2027, while the Digital Support Allowance and Continuing Professional Development (CPD) Allowance were scheduled for November and December 2026, respectively. The Council urged the FWSC, GES and teacher unions to work proactively to meet the agreed deadlines, particularly those concerning the expired Collective Agreement and the 20 per cent Deprived Area Allowance. It stressed the need for sustained dialogue and accountability to ensure that the commitments made during negotiations were fulfilled. The statement said the reopening of schools would benefit not only learners but also parents, businesses and the wider economy. It noted that the prolonged closure of schools had placed additional responsibilities on parents, many of whom had to supervise their children at home while working to provide for their families. It added that the disruption had affected school-related businesses, including food vendors, stationery shops, school transport operators, uniform suppliers and caterers under the Ghana School Feeding Programme. The Council said the return to school would help restore learning routines, improve preparations for the Basic Education Certificate Examination (BECE) and the West African Senior School Certificate Examination (WASSCE), and ensure continuity in government education programmes. It therefore urged parents and guardians of learners in public basic and secondary schools to prepare their wards for the resumption of classes. The Council also called on school-based PTA executives to collaborate with school management to develop strategies to recover the lost instructional hours. It reaffirmed the importance of cooperation among government, teachers, parents and other stakeholders in safeguarding the quality of pre-tertiary education in Ghana. Schools are expected to resume academic work on Monday is October 12, 2026. The three teacher unions – the Ghana National Association of Teachers (GNAT), the National Association of Graduate Teachers (NAGRAT) and the Pre-Tertiary Teachers Association of Ghana (PRETAG) – declared the industrial action on September 25, 2026. The unions are demanding payment of salary arrears for teachers who were promoted but had not received the corresponding salaries, payment of the 20 per cent Deprived-Area teacher Allowance and the renewal of their Collective Agreement. representative.title: GNAT directs teachers to resume work Monday after strike suspension - Adomonline.com
representative.author: Faridatu Seidu

snapshot.title: GNAT directs teachers to resume work Monday after strike suspension - Adomonline.com
snapshot.evidenceText: The Ghana National Association of Teachers (GNAT) has suspended its nationwide strike following a series of engagements with government and other stakeholders, including the Council of State. The Association has directed its members to resume normal duties on Monday, October 12, 2026, pending the fulfilment of commitments made during the negotiations. In a statement, GNAT said more than 51,000 members who had been promoted would be placed on their appropriate salary scales, with full payment of arrears and their October salaries, by October 16, 2026. It said the necessary inputs had been made and were awaiting validation. On the ongoing negotiations for a collective agreement, GNAT disclosed that the parties had agreed to increase the Cost of Professional Allowance (CPA) to GH¢3,100, tax-free, with payment expected in December 2026. The Complimentary Digital Support Allowance has also been increased to GH¢1,100, tax-free, and is expected to be paid by the end of November 2026. The Association said negotiations on the collective agreement remained inconclusive, adding that a procedural document outlining how teachers could access the benefits would be finalised with the Ghana Education Service (GES) once the agreement document was completed. GNAT further stated that an agreement had been reached in principle for budgetary provision to be made for the Deprived Area Allowance in the 2027 national budget, with payments expected to begin in January 2027. According to the statement, payments would initially cover teachers serving in island communities and hinterlands, with coverage expected to expand over time. The Association thanked its officers, executives, council members, staff and members for their solidarity and support throughout the industrial action. It assured members of its continued commitment to addressing outstanding concerns and improving conditions within the teaching profession. Ghana National Association of Teachers (GNAT)- Headquarters We wish to first of all thank each and every Officer, Executive, Council, Staff and Member for the love, solidarity and support during the period of this strike action. We are because you are. Today, after series of engagements of which at the apex of it was the Council of State, we wish to suspend our industrial action pending the fulfillment of promises, assurances given at the highest level as follows; Based on the aforementioned, we wish to humbly request our rank and file to resume normal duties by Monday, 12-10-2026. All other outstanding issues would be attended to and we assure our members of our commitment to making the profession better. representative.title: Bill C-39 advances to committee amid concerns over project approvals and labour rights | World Ports Organization
representative.author: Linh Nguyen

snapshot.title: Bill C-39 advances to committee amid concerns over project approvals and labour rights | World Ports Organization
snapshot.evidenceText: Bill C-39 has passed its first House of Commons vote, with Conservative support allowing the legislation to proceed to a special committee for further study. The bill proposes expanding Canada’s one-project, one-review approach, with a one-year federal review timeline, alongside broader reforms intended to strengthen trade infrastructure and reduce supply-chain disruptions. Conservatives plan to propose amendments to accelerate approvals further and protect workers’ rights, while the NDP, Greens, labour organizations and Indigenous leaders have raised concerns about consultation requirements, environmental protections and potential restrictions on strike action. The government maintains that the legislation will uphold Indigenous consultation obligations and workers’ rights while improving Canada’s economic competitiveness.

representative.author: David Baxter

snapshot.title: New Liberal major projects bill clears first vote, heads to special committee | CBC News
snapshot.evidenceText: A key piece of the Carney government's economic agenda, Bill C-39, passed its first vote in the House of Commons on Thursday, with Conservatives and the majority Liberals sending the bill for study by a special committee. The 243-page bill proposes to extend the government's approach to major infrastructure projects to other projects across the country. The government wants those projects to undergo one review instead of several reviews, and to have that single review completed within one year. The legislation is a core part of the Liberals' plans to pivot the economy away from reliance on the United States and present Canada as a reliable trading partner to overseas markets. Before the vote, Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre said his party would support sending the legislation to committee in order to propose amendments to what he called a "weak, watered-down, long-delayed" bill. Poilievre told reporters he wants the government to speed up the decision timeline on projects to between six months and a year, and to add measures to protect workers' rights. Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre says his party will be proposing amendments to Bill C-39. (Justin Tang/The Canadian Press) He also said Conservatives would seek to eliminate the industrial carbon price and create "shovel-ready zones" with pre-permitting for developments. Prime Minister Mark Carney's government will use a special committee formed to study the sweeping legislation. The 11-member committee includes MPs from the Liberals, Conservatives and Bloc Québécois, with the Liberals holding a majority of seats. It doesn't include representation from the NDP, which does not have official party status in the House of Commons, a requirement for automatic inclusion on standing committees. NDP House leader Don Davies said he asked the government to allow his party to participate in the committee but Government House leader Steven MacKinnon turned him down, a move Davies called "fundamentally undemocratic." Carney government to study new major projects bill with tool last used in Harper era Green Party Leader Elizabeth May said she also asked for committee standing but was denied. She said the bill is the "omnibus of omnibuses" and threatens to trample the environment in order to build things quickly. "What is currently happening, this Prime Minister's Office is more contemptuous of Parliament and less concerned about transparency and accountability than any previous PMO," May said, in a scrum with reporters before question period. Critics warn Bill C-39 puts environment at risk At a news conference Thursday with labour and First Nations leaders, Davies and NDP Leader Avi Lewis said the legislation must not pass as written because of what it does to labour and treaty rights. Lewis said the bill "must be scrapped" because of the massive changes it would unleash and because the government failed to consult adequately with Indigenous communities and other affected groups. He compared it to omnibus bills tabled during the Stephen Harper era. On Tuesday, B.C. Liberal MP Patrick Weiler took some shots at his own government's bill during debate in the House of Commons. Critics accuse Carney government of proposing 'sacrifice zones' for the environment Liberals table bill to speed up major project approvals, avert labour disruptions Weiler said while he agrees with the overall direction of the bill, he's not comfortable with C-39 giving cabinet the power to fast-track project timelines. He also warned the one-year project timelines under the bill could undermine the government's duty to consult with Indigenous communities. Lewis said Weiler took a "courageous stand" and he's heard similar concerns from Liberal voters. Carney faces climate, labour pushback over new nation-building bill "There are people in the progressive Liberal universe who are dismayed by this legislation and I encourage more of them to speak up before it's too late," Lewis said. Poilievre was asked how he would enforce the tight timelines he proposes while giving Indigenous communities and other stakeholders enough time to consider the proposals. He said Indigenous people have already given their consent to an aggressive infrastructure agenda. "Indigenous people want to build, and I believe that Indigenous Canadians can be the richest people anywhere on earth if we unblock our resources, get the government out of the way and get building," Poilievre said. Also on Thursday, Cold Lake First Nations filed in Federal Court for a judicial review of Ottawa's decision to designate the Pacific Link pipeline a project in the national interest. The First Nation accuses the government of failing to adequately consult with them on the project. Chief Shelly Moore-Frappier, of the Teme Augama Anishinabek nation, told Thursday's news conference with Lewis that her community is not anti-development but this legislation must not pass as written. She said she wants to see the bill amended to compel the government to obtain Indigenous consent for developments, eliminate the legislation's deadlines on consultation and require companies to clean up former industrial sites. "Last year I told the Senate that Bill C-5 was economic coercion. Ottawa used the threat of tariffs to push First Nations into line, and we got painted as the problem," Moore-Frappier said, referring to the Carney government's initial major projects law. "We were told the fast-track was temporary. C-39 takes it and makes it permanent." She said her community is home to deposits of copper, cobalt, platinum and other critical minerals — along with inactive mines that have been left unremediated. The government insists it will uphold its duty to consult with Indigenous groups on projects and argues the legislation does not threaten the right to strike. Bill C-39 proposes new rules on when the jobs minister can intervene in a labour dispute affecting a federally regulated sector. Any new restrictions on right to strike are 'unacceptable': Canadian Labour Congress Bea Bruske, president of the Canadian Labour Congress, called C-39 an attack on workers' rights at a news conference on Thursday. Bruske said changes to clarify a minister's power to scuttle a work stoppage when the "national interest" is at stake completely undermine unions' ability to use the threat of a strike to extract gains at the bargaining table. Jobs Minister Patty Hajdu has said the federal government will not compromise workers' rights to strike, but she did not answer directly when asked at the Senate earlier this week whether the bill could impose limits on that right. The Liberals argue changes proposed to the Canada Labour Code in the bill will put "guardrails" around the minister's ability to intervene in a labour dispute. Poilievre said the Conservatives will also introduce amendments at committee to protect workers' rights but offered no specifics. representative.author: Muriel Draaisma

snapshot.title: Ontario will officially begin removing Toronto bike lanes on Tuesday | CBC News
snapshot.evidenceText: Ontario to begin removing Toronto bike lanes. Here's what you need to know Ontario will begin removing bike lanes from a stretch on Bloor Street W. in Etobicoke on Tuesday, the Ministry of Transportation says. A notice of construction start, issued by the ministry, says the work will occur on a 1.2-kilometre section between Clissold Road and Royal York Road. Dakota Brasier, spokesperson for Ontario Transportation Minister Prabmeet Sarkaria, confirmed in an email on Thursday that bike lane removal will begin Oct. 13. "Following the ruling by the Ontario Court of Appeal, the province announced in September that it would immediately begin restoring motor vehicle lanes on Bloor Street West. That work begins Tuesday," Brasier said. T he Court of Appeal ruled in August that Premier Doug Ford’s government could rip out 19 kilometres of protected bike lanes in Toronto, reversing a lower-court decision made in July 2025. Toronto Mayor Olivia Chow said Thursday that the removal of the bike lanes is "completely unacceptable" and an affront to the city by Ontario Premier Doug Ford. "It is outrageous. He's overstepping," Chow said. "That is trampling on local democracy, the right of Torontonians through their municipal government to have a say over the municipal affairs of this city. Whether it is bike lanes, speed cameras, Island airport, every element we need to have our say. The city belong to all of us Torontonians through the municipal government," she said. "Cyclists needs to be protected, they need to be safe." The ministry-issued notice says existing pavement markings and pre-cast concrete curbs will be removed and new pavement markings and signs "to safely restore" an additional vehicle lane in each direction will be installed. Crews are expected to work primarily at night to reduce the impact on traffic, but may work during the day depending on weather, operational needs and staging requirements, the ministry-issued notice says. The notice says the work, which may lead to traffic delays, is expected to be finished in November. Toronto Mayor Olivia Chow says of the bike lane removal: 'That is trampling on local democracy, the right of Torontonians through their municipal government to have a say over the municipal affairs of this city.' (Mehrdad Nazarahari/CBC) Chow said, if re-elected mayor, she will mobilize efforts against the removal of bike lanes. "I will do everything I can. I will bring residents and citizens together. We will work together and we will fight back." Rival mayoral candidate Coun. Brad Bradford said bike lanes need to be removed if they are not working. "I ride more bikes than anyone who has ever been elected to Toronto City Council for sure. We've got the record for that. But I also am going to be pragmatic and recognize when some of the bike lanes aren't working like they should," Bradford said. "And that's why we're talking about the section on Etobicoke, part of Bloor from Resurrection Road to the South Kingsway, where you have 38,490 cars per day and 197 bikes. So you allocated 50 per cent of the space to half a percentage of road users and that doesn't work." Coun. Brad Bradford says: 'Big cities are going to have bike infrastructure and that's a positive thing. We're going to have it. But we also have to build trust with Torontonians to recognize if it's not working, we can fix it.' (Mehrdad Nazarahari/CBC) Bradford said some bike lanes, including those on Richmond Street W., Adelaide Street and Danforth Avenue, are working. "Big cities are going to have bike infrastructure and that's a positive thing. We're going to have it. But we also have to build trust with Torontonians to recognize if it's not working, we can fix it." Michael Longfield, executive director of local cycling advocacy group CycleTO, said the organization is "outraged but not surprised" that the government has rejected the mayor's "win-win offer" to restore car lanes but keep bike lanes in Etobicoke. "Ripping out these protected bike lanes against the will of Toronto city council is a colossal waste of $48 million. The province’s own experts know it will not ease traffic congestion, it will put people’s lives at risk, and there is no network of side streets that could replace these lanes." Ontario health-care coalition denounces province's plan to remove bike lanes across Toronto Ford government to begin ripping out, reconfiguring Toronto bike lanes after appeal court ruling In December 2025, the province completed work to restore a vehicle lane and maintain a bike lane on a 600-metre section of Bloor Street W. from Resurrection Road to Clissold Road. The work that begins Tuesday is east of that section. The notice says crews will attempt to minimize disruption, saying access to businesses and properties "will be maintained throughout construction," as well as sidewalk access and emergency access. Ontario Transportation Minister Prabmeet Sarkaria said in a Sept. 1 news release that the government is committed to tackling traffic congestion. “Our government was given a clear and direct mandate by the people of Ontario to fight gridlock, including by restoring motor vehicle lanes that are needed to keep drivers moving. We’re keeping our promise," Sarkaria said. Audience Relations, CBC P.O. snapshot.evidenceText: Bryan Passifiume began with the Calgary Sun in 2014 and has worked with the Toronto Sun since 2018. OTTAWA — Toronto cyclists will soon have fewer places to ride their bikes in the city. Last week, a statement issued to media confirmed a 1.2 km stretch of bicycle lanes along Bloor St. W. between Clissold Rd. and Royal York Rd. would be removed, with work commencing on the project on Tuesday, Oct. 13. “Our government was given a clear and direct mandate by the people of Ontario to fight gridlock, including by restoring motor vehicle lanes that are needed to keep drivers moving,” Transport Minister Prabmeet Sarkaria said in a statement. “We’re keeping our promise. Under Premier Ford’s leadership, we’re getting people and goods moving again and giving commuters back more of their time.” And this week, paper notices began appearing around Etobicoke informing residents of the impending removal, set to begin next Tuesday. “Construction involves removing existing pavement markings and pre-cast concrete curbs and installing new pavement markings and signage to safely restore an additional vehicle lane in each direction,” read a photo of one of the notices , posted Thursday to the /r/torontobiking subreddit. Your noon-hour look at what's happening in Toronto and beyond. A welcome email is on its way. If you don't see it, please check your junk folder. The next issue of Your Midday Sun will soon be in your inbox. We encountered an issue signing you up. Please try again Crews will begin work to return the lanes to vehicle traffic next Tuesday, continuing lane restoration work at Clissold Rd., where a 600-metre section of bike lanes was removed in December 2025 — and where restoration of vehicle lanes would involve a minimal amount of design work. Work is expected to be complete by next month. The province is also issuing a request for proposal (RFP) to facilitate removal of bike lanes in other parts of the city, including Bloor St., Yonge St., University Ave., Queen’s Park, Queen’s Park Cres. and Avenue Rd. In August, the Ontario Court of Appeal unanimously overturned a controversial Ontario Superior Court ruling that maintained removing the bicycle lanes would amount to a violation of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms. The case dates back to 2024, when cycling activists challenged a new law mandating removal of bike lanes as a means to relieve Toronto’s chronic gridlock problem. Cycling T.O. issued a statement to media blasting the province’s decision to remove the lanes. “Ripping out these protected bike lanes against the will of Toronto City Council is a colossal waste of $48 million,” the statement read, adding that side streets aren’t workable alternatives to bike lanes. “The province’s own experts know it will not ease traffic congestion — it will put people’s lives at risk.” bpassifiume@postmedia.com X: @bryanpassifiume Postmedia is committed to maintaining a lively but civil forum for discussion. representative.title: The Toronto bike lane removals just got real - Canadian Cycling Magazine
representative.author: Matt Hansen

snapshot.title: The Toronto bike lane removals just got real - Canadian Cycling Magazine
snapshot.evidenceText: Ontario’s plan to remove protected bike lanes across Toronto moves ahead Tuesday, with construction crews set to begin work on Bloor Street West in Etobicoke. The project covers a 1.2-km stretch between Clissold Road and Royal York Road. According to a Ministry of Transportation construction notice, crews will remove pavement markings and pre-cast concrete curbs before repainting the road and installing signs to reopen a vehicle lane in each direction, as reported by the CBC . The work is expected to be completed in November. Most construction will take place at night to limit disruption. Although daytime work is possible depending on weather and operational requirements. Access to businesses, properties, sidewalks and emergency services is expected to remain available throughout the project, according to the notice. This is just the latest development in a seemingly never-ending saga of the bike lanes saga, Ontario edition . The whole thing began in 2024 when Premier Doug Ford announced that the provincial government would be taking power away from municipalities when it comes to bike lane creation. Cycling advocates fought back, winning a Charter challenge. But alas, that didn’t stick. Of course there’s a car parked in the bike lane in Doug Ford’s video An August decision by the Ontario Court of Appeal allowed the provincial government to proceed with removing 19 km of protected bike lanes in Toronto. The ruling overturned a lower-court decision from July 2025 that had prevented the removals. The province has argued that restoring road space for motor vehicles is necessary to address congestion. Transportation Minister Prabmeet Sarkaria said in September that the government would move ahead with the work following the appeal court decision. The Bloor Street project is not the first change to the cycling infrastructure along this corridor. In December 2025, Ontario completed work on a 600-m section between Resurrection Road and Clissold Road, restoring a vehicle lane while retaining the bike lanes. Tuesday’s work will take place immediately east of that section. Cycling advocates have challenged the province’s approach, arguing that removing protected infrastructure will not deliver the promised traffic benefits and could increase risks for people riding bikes. As far as some of the other removals on main streets like Yonge, or University, that isn’t quite clear yet. The latest was the city putting in a request for proposals for external contracts. And there lies another wrinkle–it’s going to cost a lot. Michael Longfield, executive director of CycleTO, told the CBC that the group was “outraged but not surprised” by the government’s decision to proceed. He argued that the removals would waste $48 million, fail to ease congestion and put people’s lives at risk. The province’s construction notice warns that drivers may experience delays while crews work along the corridor. Which is, well, curious. If the government goes ahead with massive lane removals and reconstruction of intersections, gridlock could, and most likely will, be even worse for months and months. Those removals would be far more extensive than the Bloor Street project set to begin next week. So it will be interesting to see–if it does happen–how that all works. Cyclists are fighting back however, with lots of protest rides planning. Meanwhile, in other parts of Canada–notably Alberta, similar stuff is going down. There are plans by that government to try and emulate what’s happening in Ontario, and remove power from towns and cities’ abilities to plan or create bike lanes. snapshot.title: US seeks review of rejected $109m health deal with Ghana – Mahama
snapshot.evidenceText: President John Dramani Mahama has disclosed that the United States is seeking further discussions with Ghana to amend or remove some provisions in a proposed $109 million health funding agreement rejected by Cabinet. The compact was proposed as a replacement for health funding previously provided through the United States Agency for International Development (USAID). Ghana rejected the agreement after reviewing its provisions, raising concerns that some of the conditions were humiliating and could threaten the country’s sovereignty. Speaking at a citizens’ engagement in Goaso in the Ahafo Region, President Mahama said the United States had reached out to Ghana to review the deal, leaving room for further negotiations. “I have already spoken about the health funding deal sought by the U.S. The latest is that they have reached out to review the deal, and there is room for further discussions,” he said. The President maintained that Ghana remained firm in protecting its sovereign rights as discussions over the proposed health funding agreement continued.
