snapshot.title: US wants talks to amend or remove objectionable clauses in health compact - Mahama
snapshot.evidenceText: The US wants to revise its proposed $109 million health compact with Ghana, including clauses rejected by Cabinet, President Mahama has disclosed in Goaso. The United States is seeking to revise its proposed $109 million health compact with Ghana, including amending or removing clauses that led to its rejection by Cabinet, President John Mahama has disclosed. Speaking at a citizens’ engagement in Goaso in the Ahafo Region, the President said the US government has requested further discussions on the agreement. “The health compact the Americans brought to us, I have talked about it when I was in New York, so everyone knows about it. Later, they came back and said they wanted us to sit down and discuss the clauses we object to in the compact, with a view to either amending or removing them. We will sit down with them and discuss,” he said. The proposed compact was intended to provide approximately $109 million in US health assistance over five years, replacing some funding previously received through the United States Agency for International Development (USAID). Ghana rejected it after raising concerns about provisions relating to sensitive health information, national sovereignty, counterpart funding, and the regulatory authority of the Food and Drugs Authority (FDA). At a dialogue hosted by the Council on Foreign Relations in New York on 25 September 2026, President Mahama explained that Ghana had followed its established procedures. The Ministry of Health reviewed the document and submitted an information paper to Cabinet, which identified provisions the government considered problematic. One major concern was a requirement for Ghana to provide the US with its pathogen profile, which contains information about disease-causing organisms circulating in the country. “It states that we shall give the United States our pathogen profile. I’m sure there are medical experts who understand that better than me. And it also says we should give our medical records. I mean, who takes another country’s medical records?” he asked. He further said the agreement required Ghana to commit its own funds to the programme while restricting the FDA’s authority to inspect medicines and other medical products brought into the country under the arrangement. Describing the conditions, he said, “I mean, it was humiliating.” He added that Cabinet rejected the agreement, and the government decided not to proceed with it under the proposed terms. snapshot.title: China Unveils First Nationwide Labor Rules to Protect Gig Economy Workers
snapshot.evidenceText: China’s labor ministry on Thursday released draft rules that would set nationwide protections for workers in the fast-growing gig economy, including minimum-pay safeguards, limits on algorithmic decision-making and stronger obligations for internet platforms. The Ministry of Human Resources and Social Security is seeking public comment through Nov. 8 on the 54-article draft, which would be China’s first ministerial regulation specifically governing the rights of workers in new forms of employment, such as food-delivery riders, couriers, ride-hailing drivers and truck drivers. China Proposes Sweeping E-Commerce Overhaul to Protect Gig Workers, Counter Foreign Curbs Pioneering Injury Lawsuit Could Finally Hold China’s Gig Platforms Liable 1. China’s Ministry of Human Resources and Social Security has released a 54-article draft rule, open for public comment until Nov. 8, that would establish the country’s first ministerial regulation specifically protecting workers in the gig economy, including food-delivery riders, couriers, ride-hailing drivers, and truck drivers. The proposal reflects Beijing’s effort to extend labor protections to a workforce that has grown rapidly alongside internet platforms but often falls outside conventional labor-law definitions due to flexible and complex employment arrangements. [para. 1 ] [para. 2 ] [para. 3 ] 2. The draft determines employment relationships based on whether a platform exercises “controlling labor management” over workers. Workers subject to such control and meeting employment-relationship conditions must receive labor contracts; the same applies when a platform’s partner company recruits and manages workers in an employment relationship. If the relationship does not meet the formal threshold, platforms must sign a written work agreement—or a three-party agreement when both platform and partner jointly manage the worker. The rules do not apply to independent business operators or freelancers using platforms. Platforms must vet partners, bear employer responsibility for unqualified partners, and are prohibited from encouraging workers to register as sole proprietors or using multilayer subcontracting to evade obligations. In disputes, workers may name both platform and labor-service partner as joint parties. [para. 7 ] [para. 8 ] [para. 9 ] [para. 10 ] [para. 11 ] [para. 12 ] 3. The proposal sets detailed pay protections: minimum-wage calculations must subtract workers’ costs for providing their own equipment or tools, ensuring net earnings do not fall below local minimum wage. Workers can withdraw compensation on the agreed cycle without fees. The draft encourages positive incentives and prohibits abuse of fines and punitive measures, addressing complaints about arbitrary deductions. It also requires transparent rules and breaks to protect rest rights, as well as labor protections in severe weather, given the outdoor nature of much gig work. [para. 13 ] [para. 14 ] [para. 15 ] 4. The draft restricts platforms’ handling of worker data. Personal information may be processed only lawfully, properly, necessarily, in good faith, and only to the extent required for work management. Platforms must establish accurate work records that workers can conveniently view and download through apps or other channels, and companies must retain records for at least two years after a worker leaves. [para. 16 ] [para. 17 ] 5. A prominent section targets algorithmic management. Platforms must explain the basic principles and operating mechanisms of their algorithms to workers and are barred from algorithmic discrimination. Decisions with major consequences—such as suspending order assignments or banning accounts—cannot be made automatically by an algorithm and require human review. Wang Tianyu, deputy director of the social-law research division at the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences’ Institute of Law, said this provision addresses public concern that delivery riders and other platform workers have become trapped by algorithmically imposed targets. [para. 18 ] [para. 19 ] [para. 20 ] 6. The ministry noted existing labor laws do not always apply directly to platform work, but experience since a 2021 policy guideline on protecting gig workers allowed mature policies to be turned into binding institutional rules and address gaps. Wang said platform work has become an important part of China’s employment landscape, with complaints including withheld compensation, excessively long hours, inadequate safety protections, opaque algorithmic rules, and lack of occupational-injury coverage. Shen Jianfeng, a law professor at the Central University of Finance and Economics, said parts of the draft adapt traditional labor standards to platform conditions, while provisions on data protection and algorithm rules represent institutional innovations. Public comments can be submitted via the ministry’s website, mail, or email. representative.title: Arab News | Why returning to Syria is only the first step toward rebuilding lives shattered by war
representative.author: Lucas Chapman, Ali Ali

snapshot.title: Why returning to Syria is only the first step toward rebuilding lives shattered by war
snapshot.evidenceText: WASHINGTON D.C.: When Jihan Hamad Al-Khalaf and her extended family decided to leave Turkiye and return to Syria, there was little debate among them. Five of the seven related families had been away since 2013, while the other two left in 2018. Some of their children had only faint memories of Syria, while others had never seen it. Yet after the fall of Bashar Assad’s regime in December 2024, Al-Khalaf said their decision was “immediate and collective.” “Conditions and pressures in Turkiye helped accelerate the decision,” the Syrian journalist and humanitarian activist told Arab News. “But the main reason was that the country had been liberated and the war was over.” The children, raised on their parents’ memories of Syria, were among the most enthusiastic. “When they heard us saying that Syria had been liberated, they immediately began asking: ‘When are we going back? When will the car come to take us?’” Al-Khalaf said. The first family returned in January 2025. By the end of March, all seven were back. But they could not rebuild their old lives together. With too few habitable homes and limited work, the families divided themselves between Damascus, Deraa, and rural Deir Ezzor. Two families — around 20 people — shared a single house, while others settled according to surviving property, relatives, and job prospects. Their story is part of one of the largest recent return movements in the world. UNHCR, the UN refugee agency, estimated that about 1.82 million Syrians had returned from abroad between Dec. 8, 2024, and Oct. 1, 2026. Lebanon accounted for the largest number of returns in that estimate, at about 733,000, followed by Turkiye with about 713,000. About 299,000 had returned from Jordan. The estimates include registered and unregistered Syrians, as well as people in transit. Returns from Lebanon accelerated amid renewed hostilities and worsening economic conditions. A separate UNHCR crisis tally recorded about 1.08 million Syrian arrivals from Lebanon by Sept. 30, following the regional escalation that began in late February. About 226,000 reported intending to return permanently, and the agency cautions that some returns may be temporary. Many Syrians, however, are arriving in communities barely equipped to receive them. The International Rescue Committee’s July report, “Home, But Not Whole,” surveyed 425 returnees across seven governorates. Some 91 percent of respondents said essential services were missing in their communities, 71 percent were living in damaged housing, and only 18 percent said they had received adequate support during the return process. For Al-Khalaf’s family, the gap between the emotional idea of return and its reality on the ground became apparent almost immediately. One family home in Damascus had been stripped to little more than its walls, roof and floor. Another home had been struck by a projectile and used as a dumping ground for rubble and trash. “No organization, government agency, or anyone else helped us with the repairs,” Al-Khalaf said. During the first winter, two families lived together in one room. As relatives found work, they slowly installed windows, doors, and electricity. “Every month, we would put in one door or one window, or do some of the electrical work,” she said. Clearing rubble and waste from one house alone cost about 1 million Syrian pounds. The families had also spent much of their money simply getting to Syria. Al-Khalaf said the first family paid around $600 to reach Deraa. Some of the returnees sold their possessions in Turkiye to finance the journey. Available assistance often covers only a fraction of the need. Between January and August, UNHCR said 31,083 refugee-returnee households received return and reintegration cash assistance. Eligible households can receive a one-time $600 reintegration grant, while basic relief items reached 337,089 people, including returnees and other vulnerable households. Over the same period, UNHCR repaired 1,000 damaged homes and provided shelter cash assistance to 1,595 households. UNHCR’s regional Syria situation response, requiring $1.264 billion, was 34 percent funded as of Sept. 30. Funding shortfalls had forced six community centers in Syria to close in April and May. The World Bank estimated that rebuilding damaged physical assets will cost around $216 billion, nearly 10 times the country’s 2024 gross domestic product. For returning families, those figures translate into daily struggles over water, electricity, transportation, healthcare, and food. In Damascus, Al-Khalaf’s family initially paid 40,000 Syrian pounds for 10 barrels of non-potable water, and about 10,000 pounds for each 25-liter container of drinking water. Municipal supplies eventually improved, but the family still buys drinking water. Conditions were worse in rural Deir Ezzor, where damaged purification facilities meant that available water was often unsafe. “The children were constantly getting sick, especially in the beginning, because they weren’t used to the water,” Al-Khalaf said. More than 10 million people across Syria lack access to safe water, according to UNICEF’s August 2026 appeal. The IRC’s July report said some areas received only two to four hours of electricity per day. The difficulties, civil society workers say, do not end when water or electricity begin flowing or roofs or walls are repaired. Nadia Okasha, director of the Tastakel Center in Damascus, said the needs of returnees evolve as families move through different stages of rebuilding. The women-led nonprofit center focuses on civil peace, trust-building, and social cohesion rather than on distribution of humanitarian aid, but often directs returnees toward organizations and public bodies that can provide legal, humanitarian, or administrative services. “At first, inquiries concentrate on return procedures, documents, and access to basic services,” Okasha told Arab News. “Later, interest begins to shift toward more sustainable issues such as employment, education, and reintegration into society.” Many returnees understand that life will be difficult, Okasha said, but they often underestimate the time, effort, and patience required to reintegrate after years abroad and extensive changes inside the country. Some children born abroad or in displacement camps possess foreign records or temporary protection papers but lack documents recognized by Syrian institutions. Others were born during periods when civil registries were inaccessible, destroyed, or controlled by competing authorities. For Al-Khalaf’s orphaned nephew, the absence of paperwork could jeopardize his education. The boy’s father was killed before formally registering his marriage or obtaining a “family booklet.” More than a decade later, Syrian records still list the father as alive. Although the boy has Turkish temporary protection papers and his grandfather was granted legal guardianship by a Turkish court, those documents have not been accepted as sufficient in Syria. The family must now register the father’s death, prove the marriage, and establish the child’s parentage — processes requiring hundreds of dollars in legal fees which the family cannot afford. The local school allowed Al-Khalaf’s nephew to enroll provisionally after relatives signed pledges promising to produce his papers. But without them, the family fears he may be denied recognized certificates or progression through the education system. “Every time we go to one authority, they tell us we have to go to another,” she said. Children educated entirely in Turkish face an additional language barrier. Some of Al-Khalaf’s younger relatives required private tutors to catch up with Arabic-speaking classmates. Economic survival remains perhaps the greatest test. Some of Al-Khalaf’s relatives returned to jobs in public institutions, but others remained without work or income for more than a year. Relatives in rural Deir Ezzor began cultivating land beside their house, while even government employees in Damascus struggled with irregular salaries and high living costs. Al-Khalaf, who previously worked for Deraa’s education authority, has neither been reinstated nor found suitable work elsewhere. She depends heavily on monthly remittances from siblings in Europe. “Without them, we would not be able to buy what we need or cover our expenses,” she said. About 2.04 million internally displaced Syrians had also returned to their areas of origin since December 2024, according to UNHCR’s Oct. 1 figures — an even greater number than those arriving from abroad — adding another dimension to the challenge. Their problems often overlap with those of refugees returning from abroad, particularly in terms of housing, services, and livelihoods. But they can also face disputes over land and property, unresolved grievances, and the loss of social and economic ties built during displacement. Suleiman Jafer fled Afrin in March 2018. Before returning home in April 2026, he spent nearly six years in displacement camps in the Shahba area of northern Aleppo. The first thing he did after arriving, he told Arab News, was kiss the soil. But Afrin had changed so extensively that he nearly lost his way to his own house. When he entered, it was empty. “They did not leave me even a spoon or a fork,” Jafer said. “The doors were stolen — even the toilet, sinks, and bathroom fixtures were stolen.” Jafer said that repairing his village home cost about $10,000, while work on his house in Afrin city cost another $5,000. His car was missing, and a plot planted with olive trees, grapevines and almond trees had been cleared. Nevertheless, he described the current security situation as generally good and said he had not personally been harassed since returning. His greater concern is the destruction of Afrin’s agricultural economy. Many of Afrin’s families depended on olives and fruit. Jafer said damaged trees and orchards would need at least two years to recover. Wathiq Al-Hallaq, director of the Social Policies Directorate at Syria’s Ministry of Social Affairs and Labor, said the challenge facing institutions was multifaceted. “The matter is not primarily related to the scale or pace of return as much as it is related to the fragility of policies, the absence of databases, and outdated working mechanisms,” he told Arab News. Syria’s system of social services and protection programs needs to be redesigned in its structure, procedures, and objectives, he said, if it is to respond to returnees’ needs. The ministry is working to launch a national social protection program and has established a technical unit focused on returnees and internally displaced people, he said. The IRC has warned that donors and authorities must invest in water networks, roads, electricity, schools, healthcare, and livelihoods for returnees and established residents alike. Otherwise, shortages and unequal aid distribution may generate competition and undermine already fragile trust. Okasha said rebuilding social cohesion was inseparable from rebuilding homes and infrastructure. “Reintegration is not limited to meeting material needs,” she said. “It also requires a cohesive society in which everyone feels that they belong and are able to participate in building their future.” For Al-Khalaf, the question of whether Syria is ready for its people to return cannot be answered through statistics alone. When refugees in Turkiye ask her about conditions in Syria, she tells them that what they see will depend partly on what they expect. “If you put on rose-tinted glasses, you will see that returning is suitable and everything is good,” she said. “But if you wear black-and-white glasses, you will see everything in black and white.” Those expecting the same income, services and standard of living they had abroad are likely to struggle, she said. People with a job, trade, capital or relatives supporting them from overseas are in a far stronger position to endure the first months. Despite unemployment, damaged homes, and continuing dependence on remittances, Al-Khalaf said her family had never considered going back to Turkiye. “We are trying to arrange our lives here and adapt according to the income we have,” she said. “This is our country. This is our real place.” Stay on top of the issues that matter to you the most.

The women-led nonprofit center focuses on civil peace, trust-building, and social cohesion rather than on distribution of humanitarian aid, but often directs returnees toward organizations and public bodies that can provide legal, humanitarian, or administrative services. “At first, inquiries concentrate on return procedures, documents, and access to basic services,” Okasha told Arab News. “Later, interest begins to shift toward more sustainable issues such as employment, education, and reintegration into society.” Many returnees understand that life will be difficult, Okasha said, but they often underestimate the time, effort, and patience required to reintegrate after years abroad and extensive changes inside the country. Some children born abroad or in displacement camps possess foreign records or temporary protection papers but lack documents recognized by Syrian institutions. Others were born during periods when civil registries were inaccessible, destroyed, or controlled by competing authorities. For Al-Khalaf’s orphaned nephew, the absence of paperwork could jeopardize his education. The boy’s father was killed before formally registering his marriage or obtaining a “family booklet.” More than a decade later, Syrian records still list the father as alive. Although the boy has Turkish temporary protection papers and his grandfather was granted legal guardianship by a Turkish court, those documents have not been accepted as sufficient in Syria. The family must now register the father’s death, prove the marriage, and establish the child’s parentage — processes requiring hundreds of dollars in legal fees which the family cannot afford. The local school allowed Al-Khalaf’s nephew to enroll provisionally after relatives signed pledges promising to produce his papers. But without them, the family fears he may be denied recognized certificates or progression through the education system. “Every time we go to one authority, they tell us we have to go to another,” she said. Children educated entirely in Turkish face an additional language barrier. Some of Al-Khalaf’s younger relatives required private tutors to catch up with Arabic-speaking classmates. Economic survival remains perhaps the greatest test. Some of Al-Khalaf’s relatives returned to jobs in public institutions, but others remained without work or income for more than a year. Relatives in rural Deir Ezzor began cultivating land beside their house, while even government employees in Damascus struggled with irregular salaries and high living costs. Al-Khalaf, who previously worked for Deraa’s education authority, has neither been reinstated nor found suitable work elsewhere. She depends heavily on monthly remittances from siblings in Europe. “Without them, we would not be able to buy what we need or cover our expenses,” she said. About 2.04 million internally displaced Syrians had also returned to their areas of origin since December 2024, according to UNHCR’s Oct. 1 figures — an even greater number than those arriving from abroad — adding another dimension to the challenge. Their problems often overlap with those of refugees returning from abroad, particularly in terms of housing, services, and livelihoods. But they can also face disputes over land and property, unresolved grievances, and the loss of social and economic ties built during displacement. Suleiman Jafer fled Afrin in March 2018. Before returning home in April 2026, he spent nearly six years in displacement camps in the Shahba area of northern Aleppo. The first thing he did after arriving, he told Arab News, was kiss the soil. But Afrin had changed so extensively that he nearly lost his way to his own house. When he entered, it was empty. “They did not leave me even a spoon or a fork,” Jafer said. “The doors were stolen — even the toilet, sinks, and bathroom fixtures were stolen.” Jafer said that repairing his village home cost about $10,000, while work on his house in Afrin city cost another $5,000. His car was missing, and a plot planted with olive trees, grapevines and almond trees had been cleared. Nevertheless, he described the current security situation as generally good and said he had not personally been harassed since returning. His greater concern is the destruction of Afrin’s agricultural economy. Many of Afrin’s families depended on olives and fruit. Jafer said damaged trees and orchards would need at least two years to recover. Wathiq Al-Hallaq, director of the Social Policies Directorate at Syria’s Ministry of Social Affairs and Labor, said the challenge facing institutions was multifaceted. “The matter is not primarily related to the scale or pace of return as much as it is related to the fragility of policies, the absence of databases, and outdated working mechanisms,” he told Arab News. Syria’s system of social services and protection programs needs to be redesigned in its structure, procedures, and objectives, he said, if it is to respond to returnees’ needs. The ministry is working to launch a national social protection program and has established a technical unit focused on returnees and internally displaced people, he said. The IRC has warned that donors and authorities must invest in water networks, roads, electricity, schools, healthcare, and livelihoods for returnees and established residents alike. Otherwise, shortages and unequal aid distribution may generate competition and undermine already fragile trust. Okasha said rebuilding social cohesion was inseparable from rebuilding homes and infrastructure. “Reintegration is not limited to meeting material needs,” she said. “It also requires a cohesive society in which everyone feels that they belong and are able to participate in building their future.” For Al-Khalaf, the question of whether Syria is ready for its people to return cannot be answered through statistics alone. When refugees in Turkiye ask her about conditions in Syria, she tells them that what they see will depend partly on what they expect. “If you put on rose-tinted glasses, you will see that returning is suitable and everything is good,” she said. “But if you wear black-and-white glasses, you will see everything in black and white.” Those expecting the same income, services and standard of living they had abroad are likely to struggle, she said. People with a job, trade, capital or relatives supporting them from overseas are in a far stronger position to endure the first months. Despite unemployment, damaged homes, and continuing dependence on remittances, Al-Khalaf said her family had never considered going back to Turkiye. “We are trying to arrange our lives here and adapt according to the income we have,” she said. “This is our country. This is our real place.” Stay on top of the issues that matter to you the most.

selected.headline: Why returning to Syria is only the first step toward rebuilding lives shattered by war

editorial.headline: Why returning to Syria is only the first step toward rebuilding lives shattered by war
editorial.evidence: WASHINGTON D.C.: When Jihan Hamad Al-Khalaf and her extended family decided to leave Turkiye and return to Syria, there was little debate among them. Five of the seven related families had been away since 2013, while the other two left in 2018. Some of their children had only faint memories of Syria, while others had never seen it. Yet after the fall of Bashar Assad’s regime in December 2024, Al-Khalaf said their decision was “immediate and collective.” “Conditions and pressures in Turkiye helped accelerate the decision,” the Syrian journalist and humanitarian activist told Arab News. “But the main reason was that the country had been liberated and the war was over.” The children, raised on their parents’ memories of Syria, were among the most enthusiastic. The first family returned in January 2025. Their story is part of one of the largest recent return movements in the world. UNHCR, the UN refugee agency, estimated that about 1.82 million Syrians had returned from abroad between Dec. 8, 2024, and Oct. Lebanon accounted for the largest number of returns in that estimate, at about 733,000, followed by Turkiye with about 713,000. A separate UNHCR crisis tally recorded about 1.08 million Syrian arrivals from Lebanon by Sept. 30, following the regional escalation that began in late February. Some 91 percent of respondents said essential services were missing in their communities, 71 percent were living in damaged housing, and only 18 percent said they had received adequate support during the return process. During the first winter, two families lived together in one room. As relatives found work, they slowly installed windows, doors, and electricity. When refugees in Turkiye ask her about conditions in Syria, she tells them that what they see will depend partly on what they expect. “If you put on rose-tinted glasses, you will see that returning is suitable and everything is good,” she said.

snapshot.title: Treasury Imposes First Civil Penalty Under the Outbound Investment Rule
snapshot.evidenceText: Covington & Burling LLP operates as a limited liability partnership worldwide, with the practice in England and Wales conducted by an affiliated limited liability multinational partnership, Covington & Burling LLP, which is formed under the laws of the State of Delaware in the United States and authorized and regulated by the Solicitors Regulation Authority with registration number 77071.. On October 7, 2026, the U.S. Department of the Treasury (“Treasury”) announced its first enforcement action under the Outbound Investment Security Program (“OISP”), imposing a $200,000 civil penalty on Amidi, LLC (“Amidi”), a U.S. investor, for failing to submit a required notification for an investment by its controlled Chinese subsidiary in a Chinese artificial intelligence company. The penalty is notable not only because it is the first, but also because it suggests Treasury is prepared to bring enforcement actions that target investments undertaken by U.S. persons’ controlled foreign entities, even where the investments are relatively small and arguably may not implicate the core policy concerns that motivated the OISP. The importance of these early enforcement signals goes beyond compliance with the current OISP: they will carry increased importance in light of Treasury’s forthcoming regulations to strengthen and update the OISP under the Comprehensive Outbound Investment National Security (“COINS”) Act of 2025, especially given the National Security Science and Technology Strategy’s recent indication that the “Trump Administration will expand Outbound to encompass additional restrictions on U.S. investments in other areas implicated by China’s military-civil fusion strategy.” According to Treasury, on April 19, 2025, a Chinese investment fund controlled by Amidi invested approximately $92,478 in Shanghai Qiongche Intelligent Technology Company Limited (“Noematrix”), a private Chinese company that develops artificial intelligence systems for robotics applications. Treasury concluded that the investment was subject to the OISP’s notification requirements and imposed a $200,000 civil penalty after determining that Amidi did not submit the required post-closing notification. Treasury’s announcement emphasizes that the violation involved a transaction undertaken by a controlled foreign entity of a U.S. person. As discussed in our prior client alert , the OISP prohibits or requires notification for certain transactions by U.S. persons involving Chinese or Chinese-linked entities engaged in specified activities related to semiconductors, quantum information technologies, and artificial intelligence. The rule applies not only to direct U.S. person investments but also includes certain anti-circumvention provisions that carry extraterritorial effect. One of those provisions relates to controlled foreign entities: The OISP requires a U.S. person to submit a notification of any transaction undertaken by its controlled foreign entity if the transaction would have been notifiable had it been undertaken by the U.S. person directly. Treasury’s press release highlighted the OISP’s requirement that U.S. persons (here, Amidi) take “all reasonable steps to prohibit and prevent” transactions by their controlled foreign entities (Amidi’s Chinese fund subsidiary) that would constitute prohibited transactions if undertaken by the U.S. person itself. The OISP also requires U.S. persons to file notifications with Treasury for any transaction by a controlled foreign entity that would be a notifiable transaction if engaged in by a U.S. person. Treasury’s press release also notes that Amidi is the parent entity of the organization that does business as Plug and Play Tech Center. Publicly available announcements indicate that Plug and Play China participated in financing rounds involving Noematrix before the OISP took effect, meaning that the transaction underlying Treasury’s enforcement action was a follow-on investment in a company in which Amidi, through Plug and Play China, had previously invested. representative.title: Rooppur plant achieves first nuclear chain reaction in Unit 1 | The Business Standard
representative.author: TBS Report

snapshot.title: Rooppur Unit-1 achieves first nuclear chain reaction
snapshot.evidenceText: The first controlled nuclear chain reaction at Unit 1 of the Rooppur Nuclear Power Plant was achieved today (11 October), marking a major milestone in Bangladesh's first nuclear power project as the reactor entered its initial criticality stage ahead of electricity generation. The chain reaction marks the first of four stages before the plant can generate electricity. The subsequent stages involve thermal energy transfer, mechanical energy conversion, and finally electricity generation and supply to the national grid. Md Anwar Hossain, secretary of the Ministry of Science and Technology, confirmed the development to The Business Standard, saying the reaction was initiated after the required compliance procedures, technical parameters and external certifications had been completed. "Today at 3:34pm, we were able to achieve the chain reaction smoothly. By the grace of Allah, the parameters were within the desired ranges, and the reactor was very stable," he said. Inside a nuclear reactor, a controlled chain reaction splits uranium atoms through nuclear fission, releasing energy as heat. That heat is used to generate steam, which drives turbines to produce electricity. Russian specialists, Bangladeshi experts and other technical specialists were present to observe the process and assess the reactor's performance, Anwar added. He said nuclear fuel had already been loaded into the reactor and the fission process had now begun. Anwar said technical teams were working to complete the remaining processes as quickly as possible, while stressing that every stage must comply with the required procedures and safety standards. The Rooppur Nuclear Power Plant in Ishwardi, Pabna, is being built with two VVER-1200 pressurised water reactor units using Russian technology supplied by Rosatom. Each unit has a planned generation capacity of 1,200 megawatts, giving the plant a combined capacity of 2,400MW. energy / Rooppur Nuclear Power Plant / RNPP / neuclear energy While most comments will be posted if they are on-topic and not abusive, moderation decisions are subjective. representative.title: The FE - Rooppur Unit-1 crosses hurdle to get going in Dec
representative.author: M Azizur Rahman

snapshot.title: Rooppur Unit-1 crosses hurdle to get going in Dec
snapshot.evidenceText: Published by Syed Nasim Manzur for International Publications Limited from Tropicana Tower (4th ﬂoor), 45, Topkhana Road, GPO Box : 2526 Dhaka- 1000 and printed by him from The Transcraft Limited, 229, Tejgaon Industrial Area, Dhaka-1208 PABX : 02223389780 (Hunting) | Mobile: 01917231083 | Fax : 880-2-02223387049 © 2026 - All Rights with The Financial Express About Us Contact Us Terms of Service Privacy Policy Bangladesh has cleared a major regulatory hurdle for commissioning its first nuclear power plant, with the Bangladesh Atomic Energy Regulatory Authority (BAERA) approving the "first criticality" process for Unit-1 of the 2,400-MW Rooppur Nuclear Power Plant (RNPP). "We have issued the approval named B2 for Unit-1 to move forward in the second stage of rigorous scrutiny before initiation of its commercial operation," BAERA Chairman Mahmudul Hasan told The Financial Express on Thursday. The unit will require two more certifications, C and D, before commercial operation can begin, he said. The B2 approval clears the way for the reactor's physical start-up, during which it will achieve a self-sustaining nuclear chain reaction for the first time -- a key prerequisite for generating electricity. Project officials said the approval had been delayed due to technical complications involving the reactor's pilot-operated relief and safety valves, a critical component of the plant's safety systems. Russian experts were brought in to resolve the issue, following which the system passed a series of tests, paving the way for regulatory approval. Officials now expect Unit-1 to start supplying electricity to the national grid on a trial basis by the end of December. First criticality has long been regarded as one of the most challenging milestones for the Rooppur project. During the process, the reactor will transition from a static installation to an operating nuclear facility through the initiation of a stable and self-sustaining nuclear chain reaction. As part of the physical start-up, the reactor will initially operate at less than 1.0 per cent of its designed thermal capacity. Engineers and regulators will closely monitor reactor parameters, safety systems, control equipment and overall performance. The entire physical start-up process, including initial criticality, is expected to take between 30 and 40 days. If test results prove satisfactory, reactor power will be gradually increased in successive stages. Following completion of the physical start-up phase, the project will enter the power start-up stage, during which reactor output will be increased progressively, turbine synchronisation will be carried out and the generator will ultimately be connected to the national grid. Before entering this phase, the operating organisation will have to obtain a trial operational licence from BAERA. Electricity generation is expected to begin at around 3.0 per cent of capacity and gradually rise to 20-30 per cent, when power can be supplied to the national grid. Trial generation is expected to continue for seven to eight months after the reactor starts producing electricity. Project officials said the power start-up phase would involve significant technical and organisational challenges, requiring coordination among the reactor, turbine and safety systems, along with strict regulatory oversight and cooperation with external agencies. Once Rooppur starts supplying power to the grid, Bangladesh will become the world's 33rd nuclear power-producing nation, opening a new chapter in the country's energy security and technological advancement. The long-awaited achievement is also expected to strengthen Bangladesh's efforts to diversify its energy mix and ensure a more stable long-term electricity supply.

representative.title: The FE - Rooppur nuclear power plant moves closer to reactor start-up
representative.author: BSS

snapshot.title: Rooppur nuclear power plant moves closer to reactor start-up
snapshot.evidenceText: Published by Syed Nasim Manzur for International Publications Limited from Tropicana Tower (4th ﬂoor), 45, Topkhana Road, GPO Box : 2526 Dhaka- 1000 and printed by him from The Transcraft Limited, 229, Tejgaon Industrial Area, Dhaka-1208 PABX : 02223389780 (Hunting) | Mobile: 01917231083 | Fax : 880-2-02223387049 © 2026 - All Rights with The Financial Express About Us Contact Us Terms of Service Privacy Policy Bangladesh's first nuclear power plant, located at Rooppur in Pabna's Ishwardi, has made significant progress toward initiating nuclear fission in its first unit after regulators approved the results of safety valve tests, paving the way for the next phase of commissioning. If work proceeds according to the plan, the plant could begin supplying electricity to the national grid on a trial basis as early as next month, project officials said. The Rooppur Nuclear Power Plant has two units, each with a generation capacity of 1,200 megawatts (MW). Once both units are fully operational, they are expected to contribute a combined 2,400 MW to the national grid, diversify the country's energy mix and reduce dependence on fossil fuels. Officials concerned with the Bangladesh Atomic Energy Regulatory Authority (BAERA) said the initiation of heat production through nuclear fission in the first unit had initially been planned for September. However, technical defects identified during safety valve testing delayed the next stage of work. Following two rounds of high-pressure testing, the results were submitted to the regulatory authority, which approved them last Thursday, the project officials said. The tests assessed whether the control valves were functioning according to prescribed standards. Fire safety and radiation protection arrangements were also examined as part of the process. The approval allows the project to proceed with further reactor commissioning activities. However, the officials said that achieving first criticality, gradually increasing reactor power, starting the turbine and supplying electricity to the national grid are separate stages, each requiring the completion of relevant technical and safety checks. The next major milestone is 'first criticality', when a controlled, self-sustaining nuclear chain reaction is established inside the reactor. A series of tests and observations will follow - a process that could take around a month. Reactor power will then be increased gradually. Initially, the plant is expected to supply around 300 MW to the national grid on a trial basis. Further testing and technical assessments will be required before the facility reaches commercial operation. Built with technical assistance from Russia, Rooppur uses third-generation VVER-1200 reactor technology. Project estimates suggest that the plant could meet around 10 percent of Bangladesh's electricity demand when both units are operational at full capacity. Its actual contribution will depend on national demand, plant performance, maintenance schedules and grid conditions. Unlike coal-, oil- or gas-fired power plants, nuclear facilities generate heat through the fission of uranium atoms rather than by burning fossil fuels. The heat produces steam, which drives a turbine connected to an electricity-generating system. Rooppur is designed for an operational life of 60 years, potentially extendable by another 20 to 30 years, subject to technical upgrades, safety assessments and regulatory approval. Routine maintenance and fuel replacement will remain essential, with refuelling potentially required approximately every 18 months. Sheikh Mohammad Touhidul Islam, joint secretary (Nuclear Power Wing) of the Ministry of Science and Technology, told BSS that Rooppur was not merely an electricity generation project but also a major opportunity to strengthen Bangladesh's technological capabilities and develop skilled human resources. He said the first unit was in the final stages of preparation for generation, while uranium for the second unit had also arrived at the project site. He expressed hope that work could be completed ahead of schedule. Additional Secretary of the ministry Abul Khair Md Akkas Ali said the plant could reshape Bangladesh's electricity and economic landscape, supporting industrial production, attracting investment and creating employment opportunities. Science and Technology Secretary Md Anwar Hossain described Rooppur as a historic milestone for the country's energy security and economic progress, highlighting its potential to support reliable electricity supplies and peaceful applications of nuclear technology. The project has a long history, with feasibility studies and international cooperation initiatives dating back to the years following the independence. The arrival of nuclear fuel at the site in October 2023 marked a major step towards commissioning. The BNP's 2008 election manifesto also included a pledge to establish the Rooppur Nuclear Power Plant. Similarly, the party's 2026 election manifesto advocates for the continued peaceful use of nuclear energy in the power and energy sectors. As the first unit approaches its initial operational milestone, Rooppur is expected to play an increasingly important role in Bangladesh's long-term energy strategy, provided that all commissioning stages are completed in accordance with safety requirements and regulatory standards. The Ministry of Science and Technology's Nuclear Power Wing oversees and coordinates project progress on behalf of the government, while Russia's state nuclear corporation Rosatom provides technical assistance.

representative.author: Mohiuddin

snapshot.title: Rooppur nuclear power plant begins fission, moves closer to electricity generation
snapshot.evidenceText: <p>The first unit of the Rooppur Nuclear Power Plant has begun a nuclear fission reaction, bringing Bangladesh’s only nuclear power plant closer to starting electricity generation and supplying power to the national grid.</p><p>The reaction is the process through which nuclear energy is released and marks a crucial stage in the final preparations for electricity generation and supply. The plant is scheduled to supply 300 megawatts of electricity to the national grid in December.</p><p>According to sources at the Rooppur plant, the process of generating energy through nuclear fission was initially scheduled to begin in September. However, the schedule was delayed after defects were detected during tests of safety valves. The valves were tested under high pressure in two rounds last week. After reviewing the test results, the Bangladesh Atomic Energy Regulatory Authority (BAERA) approved the start of the reaction last Thursday. Nuclear fission began at 3:34pm on Sunday.</p><p>The Rooppur project in Pabna is the largest single project in Bangladesh’s history in terms of cost. The Bangladesh Atomic Energy Commission, under the Ministry of Science and Technology, is implementing the project. The state-owned Nuclear Power Plant Company Bangladesh Limited (NPCBL), under the commission, is responsible for operating the plant.</p><p>Russian contractor Atomstroyexport is constructing two units at Rooppur, each with a capacity of 1,200 megawatts.</p> .<p>NPCBL Managing Director Md Zahedul Hasan told Prothom Alo that the final process leading to the start of the nuclear reaction began on Saturday after three days of preparation. The controlled reaction successfully started on Sunday.</p><p>“This brings to an end the long wait following the beginning of Bangladesh’s journey towards the peaceful use of nuclear energy in 1961. This is a major milestone for the country’s science sector,” he said.</p><p>Sources at the plant said the reactor vessel of the first unit had achieved criticality for the first time. This is a significant milestone for Bangladesh’s nuclear power programme. Following criticality, all key reactor parameters have remained within the prescribed limits, and the process is being conducted under controlled conditions.</p><p>Officials involved in the project said the start of the nuclear reaction was a major step towards connecting the plant to the national grid. The next stages will involve reactor physics tests, verification of safety systems, a gradual increase in reactor power and the completion of tests and preparations required for grid connection, in accordance with the approved commissioning programme.</p><p>Each stage must comply with the highest safety standards, approved procedures and regulatory requirements.</p><p>According to plant officials, achieving reactor criticality is not merely a technical success but also a historic recognition of Bangladesh’s capabilities in science, engineering and nuclear technology. After years of effort, the country has reached a crucial stage in connecting its first nuclear power plant to the national grid.</p> .<p>Sources at the Rooppur plant said a series of tests would be conducted following the start of the nuclear reaction. The entire process could take 30 to 40 days.</p><p>The reactor’s power output will then be increased gradually. Nuclear fuel fission will generate heat, which will be used to produce steam and drive a turbine to generate electricity.</p><p>Once the reactor begins producing energy, electricity can be supplied to the national grid when its output reaches 30 per cent of capacity. At that stage, the plant is expected to supply 300 megawatts of electricity, potentially in December.</p><p>Plant officials said trial operations could continue for seven to eight months after the initial start-up. Once electricity is supplied to the grid, Bangladesh will become the world’s 33rd country to generate nuclear power.</p><p>Rooppur was recognised as a nuclear installation after nuclear fuel arrived at the project site in October 2023. With the receipt of the fuel, Bangladesh also joined the group of countries possessing nuclear energy capabilities.<br>According to plant sources, once operational, the nuclear power plant will be able to supply electricity continuously at a steady rate, 24 hours a day.</p><p>The reactor will require refuelling every 18 months. A unit may remain shut down for up to two months for the removal of spent fuel, loading of fresh fuel and maintenance.</p><p>The sources said that once one unit of Rooppur became operational, it could save USD 1 billion annually in fuel imports. However, the project has already been delayed by three and a half years.</p>.<p><br>The Rooppur project was originally scheduled to run until December 2025. Its deadline has been extended twice, with the latest completion date set for June 2028.</p><p>Although the deadline has been extended under the agreement with the contractor, there is no provision to increase the project cost under that agreement. However, the rise in the dollar exchange rate has increased the project's expenses by Tk 260 billion.</p><p>The total cost of the Rooppur Nuclear Power Plant is now expected to reach Tk 1.39 trillion.</p>

snapshot.title: Bangladesh enters nuclear era as fission starts at Rooppur unit-1
snapshot.evidenceText: Published by Syed Nasim Manzur for International Publications Limited from Tropicana Tower (4th ﬂoor), 45, Topkhana Road, GPO Box : 2526 Dhaka- 1000 and printed by him from The Transcraft Limited, 229, Tejgaon Industrial Area, Dhaka-1208 PABX : 02223389780 (Hunting) | Mobile: 01917231083 | Fax : 880-2-02223387049 © 2026 - All Rights with The Financial Express About Us Contact Us Terms of Service Privacy Policy The first controlled fission reaction started today (Sunday) at Unit-1 of the Rooppur Nuclear Power Plant, marking Bangladesh's entry into nuclear power generation. The reactor achieved first criticality — a self-sustaining nuclear chain reaction — after the Bangladesh Atomic Energy Regulatory Authority (BAERA) granted the B-2 licence on Thursday. BAERA Chairman Md Mahmudul Hasan confirmed that the regulator approved the unit to proceed to the criticality stage after resolving recent safety valve issues. The approval had been delayed due to failure of two automatic pressure relief valves (PORV/POSV) during commissioning. A Russian technical team spent the last month at the site to resolve the problem and all tests were successfully completed. Officials said two more licences — C and D — will be required before the 1,200 MW VVER-1200 reactor can be synchronized to the national grid. Heat generated through nuclear fission will turn water into high-pressure steam to drive turbines. “Simply put, we have now received approval to start the nuclear reaction needed to generate heat,” he said. Once first criticality is achieved, power will be raised gradually. When the reactor reaches about 37 percent thermal power, it can move toward power generation, initially supplying around 300 MW on a trial basis. If all stages are completed successfully, trial electricity supply to the national grid is expected by the end of December this year. Rooppur is Bangladesh’s first nuclear power plant, being built at a cost of $11 billion with Russian financial and technical assistance. Atomstroyexport, a subsidiary of Rosatom, is constructing two 1,200 MW units with a combined capacity of 2,400 MW, which could meet up to 10 percent of the country’s demand. Uranium loading or physical start-up at Unit-1 was inaugurated on April 28, while the first consignment of nuclear fuel for Unit-2 arrived on October 3.

snapshot.title: Rooppur Unit-1 achieves first nuclear chain reaction
snapshot.evidenceText: The first controlled nuclear chain reaction at Unit 1 of the Rooppur Nuclear Power Plant was achieved today (11 October), marking a major milestone in Bangladesh's first nuclear power project as the reactor entered its initial criticality stage ahead of electricity generation. The chain reaction marks the first of four stages before the plant can generate electricity. The subsequent stages involve thermal energy transfer, mechanical energy conversion, and finally electricity generation and supply to the national grid. Md Anwar Hossain, secretary of the Ministry of Science and Technology, confirmed the development to The Business Standard, saying the reaction was initiated after the required compliance procedures, technical parameters and external certifications had been completed. "Today at 3:34pm, we were able to achieve the chain reaction smoothly. By the grace of Allah, the parameters were within the desired ranges, and the reactor was very stable," he said. Inside a nuclear reactor, a controlled chain reaction splits uranium atoms through nuclear fission, releasing energy as heat. That heat is used to generate steam, which drives turbines to produce electricity. Russian specialists, Bangladeshi experts and other technical specialists were present to observe the process and assess the reactor's performance, Anwar added. He said nuclear fuel had already been loaded into the reactor and the fission process had now begun. Anwar said technical teams were working to complete the remaining processes as quickly as possible, while stressing that every stage must comply with the required procedures and safety standards. The Rooppur Nuclear Power Plant in Ishwardi, Pabna, is being built with two VVER-1200 pressurised water reactor units using Russian technology supplied by Rosatom. Each unit has a planned generation capacity of 1,200 megawatts, giving the plant a combined capacity of 2,400MW. energy / Rooppur Nuclear Power Plant / RNPP / neuclear energy While most comments will be posted if they are on-topic and not abusive, moderation decisions are subjective. snapshot.title: Inside Thailand’s cyanide murders and the search for its ‘most prolific serial killer’ in history
snapshot.evidenceText: When healthy people suddenly began dying, grieving families struggled to get answers. The series, Death Loans, retraces how a dogged investigator looking into a friend’s death helped police connect 15 cases to one woman eventually. BANGKOK: When her friend gave her some herbal medicine for her cough, Kantima “Pla” Paesaard did not think too much about it. She wasn’t to know it would turn out to be an alleged murder attempt. Less than 10 minutes after they went their separate ways, Pla started feeling short of breath. So she turned on the air-conditioner in her car and got a strong draught blowing at her face. “But no matter how I tried to breathe, I still couldn’t,” she recalled. After she called an ambulance, her hands started to stiffen. When the ambulance arrived a few minutes later, only her little finger could move a bit, she said. And once she was in the ambulance, “everything just went black”. Loading Hours went by before she started to awake. “After I regained consciousness, my husband told me, ‘Do you know that earlier, your heart had actually stopped beating?’” she recounted. “The doctor told me they did a brain scan. They checked my blood and examined my whole body, and there was nothing abnormal. So I thought it was an allergic reaction to the herbal medicine.” Her friend, Sararat “Aem” Rangsiwuthaporn, checked on her in hospital, seemingly worried for her health. Pla did not suspect anything. They had known each other for about 10 years. Their husbands — or ex-husband, in Aem’s case — were from the same police academy class. “I felt like Aem was part of the family. We’d always visit each other,” she said. Two months later, in November 2022, when the two friends went to a gathering together, Pla’s mum asked Aem (also spelt as Am) why she looked thinner. Weight-loss pills, she replied. “So my mum said, ‘If that’s the case, bring some for Pla to try so she can lose weight too,’” Pla recounted. After the gathering ended, Aem brought over the pills to their house in Thailand’s Kanchanaburi province. But Pla chose not to take them. She still did not have any suspicions of her friend, not until she heard the news about a woman who had been poisoned with cyanide months later, with Aem present at the scene. Pla, then 36, started googling the symptoms of cyanide poisoning and found that they included difficulty breathing and stiff hands. “At that moment, I was very shocked,” she said. She was the only survivor out of 15 victims identified by the police in what has become a historic set of cases, involving a pattern of deaths in different provinces starting as far back as 2015. Aem, now 39, is the “most prolific serial killer in Thai history”, according to Surachate Hakparn, the deputy police chief from 2022 to 2024. “She’s killed more people than Jack the Ripper, the Zodiac and BTK (did individually),” he charged. Only one of those three — BTK (Bind, Torture, Kill), the moniker for American killer Dennis Rader — was caught. And it took one of the largest investigations ever conducted in Thailand for the Royal Thai Police to catch their killer better known as Aem Cyanide. The series, Death Loans , tells how the country’s cyanide murders finally ended. WATCH PART 1: ‘She didn’t go alone’ — This CCTV footage helped expose Thai serial killer (46:57) Most of the victims were in their 30s and healthy. All died under mysterious circumstances. In Mukdahan province, Sawitree “Nim” Budsrirak, 40, had just given birth to a baby girl, “exactly as we’d hoped”, said her husband, Nitipon “Ta” Nuchit. A month later, in November 2020, he was back at work in Bangkok, 650km away. Nim was taking care of the children — their newborn and their five-year-old son — and cleaning the house. One day when he was on his break, he tried video-calling Nim. She did not answer. Then he sent her a message. It was left unread. So he video-called his son, Neo. “I asked him, ‘Who are you with? Where’s Mummy? I want to talk to Mummy.’ Neo turned the camera towards the mattress. I saw Nim lying face down, with her face resting on the edge of the mattress,” he recounted. Thinking that Nim was tired and had taken a nap, he decided to end the call. “After no more than 30 minutes, I tried video-calling again,” he continued. “Neo answered as before and turned the camera towards Nim, who was still lying in the same position. That’s when I realised something was wrong.” He immediately called a neighbour to check on Nim. Her lips had turned dark bluish, a trickle of blood was oozing from her mouth, and her body was covered in sweat. “Nim was found dead on the bed while our daughter was sleeping only a few feet away,” Ta said. “Nim was playing just fine with the children. It’s impossible that she’d then die. How could something like this happen?” At that time, he wasn’t to know the answer lay in Thailand’s money-sharing circles. These are rotating savings groups whose members save together. The money they contribute regularly is pooled, which members can borrow when needed. These loans are not free. Members pay a monthly interest — setting the rate themselves beforehand — on loans taken out from the group’s fund. They must also continue their regular contributions as they repay the loans. “It’s estimated that millions of Thais participate in share groups, with billions of baht estimated to be in circulation,” said Piriya Pholphirul, an economics professor at the National Institute of Development Administration. Nim was one of them, joining in as a way of earning additional income, said Ta. Sharing circles have existed for generations, built on friendship and trust. But the problem was that she joined an online sharing group with Aem. For another victim, Surat “Bee” Toraphap, 35, his friendship with Aem went back to childhood. They had been schoolmates. In January 2021, his brother “Koon” was at a temple when a neighbour in Kanchanaburi’s Tha Maka district called to say that Bee was in the bathroom and turning blue. Koon hurried over. “There were police all over the house. I saw my younger sibling sitting on the toilet in the bathroom, leaning to the right. I realised my sibling was no longer with me,” he said. “My younger brother was healthy, didn’t drink and didn’t smoke. His death was abnormal. I started getting suspicious and unlocked my brother’s phone and wondered why this friend named ‘Aem’ wasn’t responding to him.” It turned out that Bee had lent her money: 50,000 baht (US$1,500) at first and then another 10,000 baht. But for all of Koon’s suspicions, his brother’s death was classified as natural, as was the case for Nim and other victims. Aem’s victims could be categorised in a few groups, such as those in savings groups where she was the organiser, those whom she borrowed money from and those who loaned her money to lend out to others. One of the people she invited to lend money through her was her friend Siriporn “Koy” Khanwong, 32. On Apr 14, 2023, Koy told her mother she was going to run an errand. “She told me to wait,” recalled Thongpin Kiatchanasiri. “She said she’d come back in the evening and take me shopping. But she never came back.” Koy had two phones. “If one phone was off, the other one would still be on,” said her elder sister, Nipawan “Som” Khanwong. “But that day, both phones were off at the same time. I was so anxious, wondering why.” As Koy’s family tried to figure out where she was, a friend of hers, independent investigator Rapee Chamnanrua, received a photo of a person the police in Ratchaburi province were trying to identify. It was Koy. She had fainted and died by the Mae Klong River, 80km west of Bangkok. The police cited the official cause of death as a heart attack. But her mother “didn’t believe that her heart would fail”. “My daughter was only 32, healthy and strong,” said Thongpin, now 65. “I was shocked. I felt I was losing my sanity. … I kept asking where her bag went, where her phone went, because they were all gone.” Som also “felt something was wrong”, but the police “wouldn’t listen”, she recounted. The family’s request for a further probe into Koy’s death was turned down. Her body was returned to them the next day for Buddhist rites and cremation. The first person who listened to the family and thought her death was unnatural was Rapee. “How could someone so young just die so suddenly?” he questioned. “Because I knew her, this case was special (to me).” But at first, his investigation went down the wrong path. The family suspected a former boyfriend who had allegedly threatened her. This was a police officer named Navin — whose alibi ruled him out, according to the police. Doubting that the police would implicate one of their own, Rapee “asked people to go check on Navin”. He reasoned: “Navin had an intimate relationship with Koy.” Above all else, however, he wanted “someone in authority” to hear the family out before her cremation. So they met the police general Surachate, who is known in Thailand by his nickname, “Big Joke”. “I put all the evidence in front of him and asked him if he felt the local police had done their job,” recounted Rapee, who cited Koy’s missing belongings, among other things. “A heart attack doesn’t make belongings disappear.” Surachate gave credit to Rapee for getting him involved in the case. His own suspicions were aroused when Rapee showed him the autopsy report, which recorded that Koy was healthy. “This was unusual,” he said, adding that Navin’s alleged threats were also “concerning”. Things started moving “much faster” after Surachate got involved in the case, said Som. For example, the police called her in to watch the footage from the closed-circuit television cameras pointed towards the walkway along the river. Rapee said they were “very lucky” because the cameras had been recently repaired after being “broken for a long time”. Meanwhile, a second, more detailed autopsy was performed on Koy. When the toxicology results came out, forensic pathologist Smith Srisont, who ran the test, “was very shocked”. It was a cyanide poisoning case. His colleague at Ramathibodi Hospital, internal medicine doctor Sahaphume Srisuma, had “never seen this before” in his practice in Thailand. “Cyanide is one of the most lethal chemical compounds known to mankind. It’s virtually untraceable,” said Sahaphume. “The most dangerous thing is cyanide is lethal either by ingestion or inhalation. All it takes is a tiny dose, maybe smaller than a grain of rice.” That was not the only evidence that “changed the case immediately” as Surachate described. CCTV footage showed that when Koy went to release fish at the Mae Klong pier, she did not go alone. She was with Aem. It turned out Koy had transferred 300,000 baht to Aem for her to invest “because she was a friend and we trusted her”, said Som, who shared that she herself first met Aem at age 16. “Aem was very chatty, and she got along with people easily,” Som added. “But her personality changed when it came to money. She started getting involved with money matters, talking about it, pushing it, things like that.” Aem’s financial motives led the police to follow the money trail, which eventually led to gambling websites and gambling dens. “I’ll give one example. She was travelling from Kanchanaburi to Nakhon Pathom. She found a gambling den along the way. She goes straight in, plays and loses 10 million baht,” cited Surachate. “Whose money was that? Money she’d just borrowed from people.” Online savings groups and instant bank transfers — plus misplaced trust — allowed money to move with ease and feed her gambling addiction. “When asked to repay, if there’s no money to clear debts, what do you do?” remarked Surachate. Citing what he learnt from the Federal Bureau of Investigation, he added: “Serial killers, if they’re men, will commit crimes outside the city, and the motive is sexual in nature. But if it’s a woman, the motive must be money.” Prior to Aem, there was the case of serial killer Somkid Phumphuang, who raped and killed his victims — six of them — between 2005 and 2019. There are “many contributing factors”, however, in cases like Aem, according to Somdet Chaopraya Institute of Psychiatry deputy director Winyoo Chanakul, who has over 20 years’ experience in caring for psychiatric patients who have committed violent acts or even homicide. “Someone who has financial problems to the point of being able to kill others, and to do so repeatedly, can’t be explained by financial reasons alone. Otherwise, everyone in debt would be killing people,” he said. “The person must have certain personality traits that allow them to commit serious wrongdoing for their own benefit without feeling guilt. This includes a lack of empathy and a disregard for social rules.” Thinking back on Aem’s personality, Som remembered her once saying that if anyone were to fight with her or say something bad, “she wouldn’t let it go” and would “go as far as killing”. When the police arrested Aem, however, senior staff writer Pravit Rojanaphruk at news outlet Khaosod English remembers that “everyone was confused” by this woman from a middle-class background. “She looks just like anyone from an average neighbourhood,” he said. It became a major news story that many people have followed. “No one person has caused this much of an uproar before,” he added, citing the 14 murder charges. She has contested all the charges so far. One of her lawyers, Thannicha “Pat” Aeksuwannawat, said it was “impossible that Aem committed all 14 murders”. “The police want to dump the murder cases onto Aem so they don’t have to find the real perpetrator. It was clear that she was being targeted,” said Pat. “It’s media-driven momentum more than facts. “They said death was due to cyanide. … That cyanide mightn’t have come from Aem. This is the weakness of the case.” Buying cyanide in Thailand is not suspicious on its own. It is used in factories in metal-related industries, such as for metal plating and electroplating. It is used in gold shops and in research. And what the police found was that Aem “never used her own name to order cyanide”, said Surachate. “She had others order it, and then it reached her.” One of the cyanide bottles that the police seized had been sold by a company that called Grab to do the delivery. And the rider took a photo when delivering the cyanide to Aem in her Toyota Fortuner, recounted Rapee. “In that photo, a small pink Hello Kitty bag was visible beside the gear stick. Once the police … impounded the bag, we found this bottle,” he said, adding that the bottle had a registration number showing who the importer was. “Aem used her phone number to contact the company. All the evidence pointed directly to Aem. Game over.” Although Rapee said it was Aem’s “own mistakes that brought her down”, his involvement led to a breakthrough in the case in more ways than one. After he and Koy’s family appealed publicly for information once Aem was fingered as a suspect, his phone began ringing nonstop. Families across Thailand told of similar stories: sudden deaths, missing money and a connection to savings groups. One of those who came forward was Pla. She said Aem had asked for a loan to repay a fund, so she gave her 250,000 baht. “She was my friend. Why would I refuse?” said Pla. But she was lending the money only for a month. Then she asked Aem to return the entire amount as agreed because she had to pay for her car. “Reliving my ordeal wasn’t easy,” said Pla, who did it so that Aem “won’t be able to hurt anyone else again”. Pravit described her role as the “nail in the coffin” for Aem, who was sentenced to death in November 2024 for the murder of Koy. WATCH PART 2: ‘She tried to kill me twice’ — The witness who survived a serial killer (46:59) It is a penalty she deserves, said Thongpin, who was “very close” to Koy. “We’d travel together, perform Buddhist rituals together.” Koy and her sister were also close. Som called her the “pillar of the family” who took care of everyone. “Koy only had one child, so she doted on her. She loved her so much. Whatever the child wanted, she got,” said Som, referring to Koy’s daughter, now 13. “Everything she built, she built it for her daughter.” The murders of Nim and Bee, meanwhile, have not gone to trial yet. Koon said he thinks about his younger brother every day. “And whenever I do, my heart feels as if it’s going to break,” he lamented. As for Ta, if he had the chance, he would want to speak to Nim — whom he lovingly described as “good-hearted” and “always willing to help others” — one more time. “I’d want to thank her for coming into my life as my wife and as the mother of our children, for making my life better and helping me grow and become more mature,” he said. As of Sep 22, the criminal court has delivered three death sentences and two life imprisonments for Aem’s string of cyanide murders, plus acquittals in three cases where the court cited a lack of evidence in her favour. Since the end of 2009, Thailand has carried out only one execution, in 2018, even as several death sentences have been imposed. Aem’s next trial date is Nov 25, for the attempted murder of Pla.
