So they met the police general Surachate, who is known in Thailand by his nickname, “Big Joke”. “I put all the evidence in front of him and asked him if he felt the local police had done their job,” recounted Rapee, who cited Koy’s missing belongings, among other things. “A heart attack doesn’t make belongings disappear.” Surachate gave credit to Rapee for getting him involved in the case. His own suspicions were aroused when Rapee showed him the autopsy report, which recorded that Koy was healthy. “This was unusual,” he said, adding that Navin’s alleged threats were also “concerning”. Things started moving “much faster” after Surachate got involved in the case, said Som. For example, the police called her in to watch the footage from the closed-circuit television cameras pointed towards the walkway along the river. Rapee said they were “very lucky” because the cameras had been recently repaired after being “broken for a long time”. Meanwhile, a second, more detailed autopsy was performed on Koy. When the toxicology results came out, forensic pathologist Smith Srisont, who ran the test, “was very shocked”. It was a cyanide poisoning case. His colleague at Ramathibodi Hospital, internal medicine doctor Sahaphume Srisuma, had “never seen this before” in his practice in Thailand. “Cyanide is one of the most lethal chemical compounds known to mankind. It’s virtually untraceable,” said Sahaphume. “The most dangerous thing is cyanide is lethal either by ingestion or inhalation. All it takes is a tiny dose, maybe smaller than a grain of rice.” That was not the only evidence that “changed the case immediately” as Surachate described. CCTV footage showed that when Koy went to release fish at the Mae Klong pier, she did not go alone. She was with Aem. It turned out Koy had transferred 300,000 baht to Aem for her to invest “because she was a friend and we trusted her”, said Som, who shared that she herself first met Aem at age 16. “Aem was very chatty, and she got along with people easily,” Som added. “But her personality changed when it came to money. She started getting involved with money matters, talking about it, pushing it, things like that.” Aem’s financial motives led the police to follow the money trail, which eventually led to gambling websites and gambling dens. “I’ll give one example. She was travelling from Kanchanaburi to Nakhon Pathom. She found a gambling den along the way. She goes straight in, plays and loses 10 million baht,” cited Surachate. “Whose money was that? Money she’d just borrowed from people.” Online savings groups and instant bank transfers — plus misplaced trust — allowed money to move with ease and feed her gambling addiction. “When asked to repay, if there’s no money to clear debts, what do you do?” remarked Surachate. Citing what he learnt from the Federal Bureau of Investigation, he added: “Serial killers, if they’re men, will commit crimes outside the city, and the motive is sexual in nature. But if it’s a woman, the motive must be money.” Prior to Aem, there was the case of serial killer Somkid Phumphuang, who raped and killed his victims — six of them — between 2005 and 2019. There are “many contributing factors”, however, in cases like Aem, according to Somdet Chaopraya Institute of Psychiatry deputy director Winyoo Chanakul, who has over 20 years’ experience in caring for psychiatric patients who have committed violent acts or even homicide. “Someone who has financial problems to the point of being able to kill others, and to do so repeatedly, can’t be explained by financial reasons alone. Otherwise, everyone in debt would be killing people,” he said. “The person must have certain personality traits that allow them to commit serious wrongdoing for their own benefit without feeling guilt. This includes a lack of empathy and a disregard for social rules.” Thinking back on Aem’s personality, Som remembered her once saying that if anyone were to fight with her or say something bad, “she wouldn’t let it go” and would “go as far as killing”. When the police arrested Aem, however, senior staff writer Pravit Rojanaphruk at news outlet Khaosod English remembers that “everyone was confused” by this woman from a middle-class background. “She looks just like anyone from an average neighbourhood,” he said. It became a major news story that many people have followed. “No one person has caused this much of an uproar before,” he added, citing the 14 murder charges. She has contested all the charges so far. One of her lawyers, Thannicha “Pat” Aeksuwannawat, said it was “impossible that Aem committed all 14 murders”. “The police want to dump the murder cases onto Aem so they don’t have to find the real perpetrator. It was clear that she was being targeted,” said Pat. “It’s media-driven momentum more than facts. “They said death was due to cyanide. … That cyanide mightn’t have come from Aem. This is the weakness of the case.” Buying cyanide in Thailand is not suspicious on its own. It is used in factories in metal-related industries, such as for metal plating and electroplating. It is used in gold shops and in research. And what the police found was that Aem “never used her own name to order cyanide”, said Surachate. “She had others order it, and then it reached her.” One of the cyanide bottles that the police seized had been sold by a company that called Grab to do the delivery. And the rider took a photo when delivering the cyanide to Aem in her Toyota Fortuner, recounted Rapee. “In that photo, a small pink Hello Kitty bag was visible beside the gear stick. Once the police … impounded the bag, we found this bottle,” he said, adding that the bottle had a registration number showing who the importer was. “Aem used her phone number to contact the company. All the evidence pointed directly to Aem. Game over.” Although Rapee said it was Aem’s “own mistakes that brought her down”, his involvement led to a breakthrough in the case in more ways than one. After he and Koy’s family appealed publicly for information once Aem was fingered as a suspect, his phone began ringing nonstop. Families across Thailand told of similar stories: sudden deaths, missing money and a connection to savings groups. One of those who came forward was Pla. She said Aem had asked for a loan to repay a fund, so she gave her 250,000 baht. “She was my friend. Why would I refuse?” said Pla. But she was lending the money only for a month. Then she asked Aem to return the entire amount as agreed because she had to pay for her car. “Reliving my ordeal wasn’t easy,” said Pla, who did it so that Aem “won’t be able to hurt anyone else again”. Pravit described her role as the “nail in the coffin” for Aem, who was sentenced to death in November 2024 for the murder of Koy. WATCH PART 2: ‘She tried to kill me twice’ — The witness who survived a serial killer (46:59) It is a penalty she deserves, said Thongpin, who was “very close” to Koy. “We’d travel together, perform Buddhist rituals together.” Koy and her sister were also close. Som called her the “pillar of the family” who took care of everyone. “Koy only had one child, so she doted on her. She loved her so much. Whatever the child wanted, she got,” said Som, referring to Koy’s daughter, now 13. “Everything she built, she built it for her daughter.” The murders of Nim and Bee, meanwhile, have not gone to trial yet. Koon said he thinks about his younger brother every day. “And whenever I do, my heart feels as if it’s going to break,” he lamented. As for Ta, if he had the chance, he would want to speak to Nim — whom he lovingly described as “good-hearted” and “always willing to help others” — one more time. “I’d want to thank her for coming into my life as my wife and as the mother of our children, for making my life better and helping me grow and become more mature,” he said. As of Sep 22, the criminal court has delivered three death sentences and two life imprisonments for Aem’s string of cyanide murders, plus acquittals in three cases where the court cited a lack of evidence in her favour. Since the end of 2009, Thailand has carried out only one execution, in 2018, even as several death sentences have been imposed. Aem’s next trial date is Nov 25, for the attempted murder of Pla. editorial.headline: Inside Thailand’s cyanide murders and the search for its ‘most prolific serial killer’ in history
editorial.evidence: When healthy people suddenly began dying, grieving families struggled to get answers. The series, Death Loans, retraces how a dogged investigator looking into a friend’s death helped police connect 15 cases to one woman eventually. BANGKOK: When her friend gave her some herbal medicine for her cough, Kantima “Pla” Paesaard did not think too much about it. She wasn’t to know it would turn out to be an alleged murder attempt. Less than 10 minutes after they went their separate ways, Pla started feeling short of breath. So she turned on the air-conditioner in her car and got a strong draught blowing at her face. “But no matter how I tried to breathe, I still couldn’t,” she recalled. Pla, then 36, started googling the symptoms of cyanide poisoning and found that they included difficulty breathing and stiff hands. She was the only survivor out of 15 victims identified by the police in what has become a historic set of cases, involving a pattern of deaths in different provinces starting as far back as 2015. “She’s killed more people than Jack the Ripper, the Zodiac and BTK (did individually),” he charged. And it took one of the largest investigations ever conducted in Thailand for the Royal Thai Police to catch their killer better known as Aem Cyanide. The series, Death Loans , tells how the country’s cyanide murders finally ended. representative.title: Syria Begins Destroying Chemical Weapons Remnants

snapshot.title: Syria Begins Destroying Chemical Weapons Remnants
snapshot.evidenceText: Syria's Permanent Representative to the OPCW, Mohammad Katoub, announced that operations to destroy remnants of the Assad-era chemical program have begun, while warning that Israeli attacks hinder the process and that a timeframe for completion has not yet been set. Syria's Permanent Representative to the Organisation for the Prohibition of Chemical Weapons (OPCW), Mohammad Katoub, stated that his country continues full cooperation with the organisation's Technical Secretariat to completely eliminate remnants of the chemical weapons program from the Assad era. He confirmed that destruction operations have already begun, describing this as tangible progress in the capabilities of Syria's national teams working on this sensitive file. The announcement falls within an internationally monitored process overseen by the OPCW, the body responsible for verifying the elimination of banned weapons programs. Ongoing work includes verification, inspection, and destruction of remaining materials and facilities linked to the former program. Katoub pointed out that Israeli attacks constitute a real obstacle to the removal of the chemical program's remnants, imposing security challenges and operational complications on field teams. In practical terms, these obstacles tie the pace of work to security conditions at the affected sites, making movement, equipment handling, and field coordination more difficult. He explained that Syria is working with OPCW teams to develop a realistic timeframe for completing verification, inspection, and destruction operations, but this framework has not yet been announced, as work continues on shaping it in light of field and security conditions. The Syrian envoy stressed that pursuing and holding accountable those involved in developing and using chemical weapons is among Syria's top priorities at this stage. This judicial track runs parallel to the technical work of destroying the remnants, as part of an effort to close the file of the former chemical program from both ends: materially through destruction, and legally through accountability. The step marks a shift of the chemical file from declarations to actual destruction on the ground — a significant development for Syria's international standing and its relations with international organisations, which could gradually reflect in reduced pressures and isolation on the country. However, the absence of an announced timeframe means Syrians will not see a defined end to this file any time soon. The continued Israeli attacks as a disrupting factor also serve as a reminder that security conditions remain the key variable determining the pace of sensitive files like this one, directly affecting civilians in the affected areas. representative.title: ‘They searched my bag, and my Israeli passport was inside’: An extraordinary journey
representative.author: Assaf Kamar

snapshot.title: ‘They searched my bag, and my Israeli passport was inside’: An extraordinary journey through Saudi Arabia
snapshot.evidenceText: The religious police officers began rummaging through his bag. Hidden deep inside an inner pocket was the last thing he wanted anyone in Saudi Arabia to find: his Israeli passport. "They caught me in Medina, the city sacred to Muslims," adventurer Adam Jano, a resident of the northern Israeli community of Klil, told ynet. "They're not particularly pleasant people. They started searching through my things, and I was an idiot for bringing it with me," he recalled. "I had to move between hotels, so I thought, fine, I'll take it along. I hid it, and luckily they didn't see it." The encounter took place in the courtyard of the Prophet Muhammad's Mosque in Medina, one of Islam's holiest cities. "The religious police asked me, 'Are you Muslim?' I said, 'No, I'm not Muslim.' Then they started saying, 'Give us your bag.' They began searching, and my heart just sank." Fortunately for the Israeli traveler, whose identity could have landed him in serious trouble, the officers never opened the inner pocket, and his Israeli passport remained undiscovered. "It was a pretty frightening moment," Jano said. "Your heart starts racing, the adrenaline kicks in, and I have a wife and a child. Looking back, I think, wow, that was really stupid and dangerous. I should have handled things a little differently." It was Jano's second trip to Saudi Arabia, which he entered using a foreign passport. This time, he was determined to explore far beyond the modern capital, Riyadh. He embarked on long drives deep into the country's wild desert landscapes, reaching even the region bordering Yemen. One stretch of road that left a particularly strong impression followed the Red Sea coastline. "It's a beautiful road, and when you're driving north, the sea is always on your left, just like driving through Sinai, only from the other side." Most of the men Jano encountered wore the traditional white thobe, while the few women he saw were dressed in black. "They dressed me in a robe, and they were very proud of it," he laughed. "There are so many laundries on practically every corner. Because they constantly have to wash all those white clothes, it looks like the dry cleaners are making an absolute fortune." Ironically, it was the relative absence of tourists that made Jano's challenging journey so rewarding. "You meet people, you make friends," he said enthusiastically. "Suddenly, someone you met the day before calls you and says, 'I want to introduce you to my friend.' "Why did I meet so many people specifically in Saudi Arabia? If I went to Thailand, I'd just be another tourist, and the locals wouldn't find me particularly interesting. In Saudi Arabia, there aren't many tourists, so when you're a different face, you attract attention." One memorable encounter took place at a Western-style coffee shop in Riyadh, where several Saudi women approached him. "I'm standing in line, and these women wearing veils come up to me. You can only see their eyes. They ask, 'Where are you from?'" It was a perfectly ordinary question with an answer he could not afford to give. "I don't say Israel," he laughed. "Then they ask, 'Can we please pay for your coffee?' They were closed off for so many years, and now things are opening up. When unfamiliar faces start appearing, it sparks curiosity, and it's funny. "They take selfies with me while wearing their veils, and I'm thinking, wait a minute, what's going on here? You're taking a picture with someone whose face is covered, so what exactly can you see in the photo?" One of the highlights of Jano's journey was AlUla, one of Saudi Arabia's leading tourist destinations. Located in the country's northwest, the region is surrounded by dramatic sandstone cliffs, canyons and an ancient oasis. It was once an important stop along the Nabataean incense trade route connecting the Arabian Peninsula with the East and the Mediterranean. In recent years, AlUla has become a flagship project of Saudi Arabia's tourism ambitions, with luxury hotels, cultural attractions and extraordinary architecture emerging amid the desert landscape. Jano checked into one of the region's luxury resorts and discovered a swimming pool in the middle of the desert, gourmet restaurants, golf carts and impeccable five-star service. Almost everything was there, except the guests. "I was alone. There was nobody there," he laughed. "I was sitting alone in the restaurant, surrounded by waiters, and you're the only person there. They have golf carts to take you around because the hotel isn't just one building, it's an entire complex. "They ask you, 'Which restaurant would you like? There's a Thai restaurant or a Middle Eastern restaurant.' And whichever one you choose, you're the only guest. Everything is five-star. It's the top of the top." The hotel itself was designed to blend seamlessly into the surrounding desert. "The rooms are built into the mountain, and the swimming pool is there too. Even the stairs blend into the rocks. It's a very impressive, very special hotel, but being the only guest there feels strange." So where were all the tourists? "The employees tell me, 'Oh, they're coming.' They're coming. We want tourists." And what about the sightseeing bus? "I was the only passenger. Why would they even send out a bus? Can you imagine? An entire bus, and I'm riding in it alone." Beyond the luxurious hotels, the region is home to Nabataean archaeological sites and ancient tombs carved directly into the rock. "These are the same people who built what you see in Petra," Jano explained. "They carved straight into the rock, and it's incredibly impressive. Absolutely amazing." In AlUla, Jano also encountered a striking symbol of Saudi Arabia's ambitious transformation: Maraya, an enormous mirrored building that seems almost to disappear into the surrounding landscape, like a mirage reflecting the desert. "You can't see it," the veteran traveler said enthusiastically. "When you're walking through the desert and suddenly come across it, it tricks your eyes. It's like an optical illusion. It's a huge, square mirrored building, surrounded by mountains and desert, and the building reflects all the colors." Outside AlUla's lavish resorts, some of Jano's most memorable experiences took place around the dinner table. "Saudi food is very delicate and very good," he declared with the confidence of someone who has sampled plenty of it. "Think of Bedouin food, but imagine having a five-star chef prepare the meal and refine it," he laughed. "I particularly loved the lamb, slow-cooked with rice and spices." But the meal that stayed with him most was at the home of a Saudi friend he had met during his travels. "Arab hospitality is hospitality done properly," Jano said appreciatively. "When you're under someone's protection and they're responsible for you, you're treated like royalty." To protect his host's personal safety, we'll limit the description to the fact that he lives on a magnificent estate with a separate area designed specifically for entertaining guests. "He has this tent outside for visitors, and that's where they serve the food. He shows you photographs and things. He loves hunting, so he has stuffed animals and things from Africa. You sit on the carpet and eat with your hands." Yet beyond the hypnotic desert landscapes and luxury hotels, Jano had arrived in the mysterious kingdom with another, more discreet mission. "The Jewish story, wherever it exists, fascinates me," he said. "Everywhere I go, I try to put together another piece of the puzzle of Jewish history. And the very idea that there are 'hidden Jews' in Saudi Arabia made me curious to go looking for them and meet them." In a country where he himself had been forced to conceal his Israeli passport, the search for Jewish roots took on an entirely different level of significance. "You arrive there, you meet someone, and it's as if you're bringing them treasure," he said excitedly, recalling a discreet meeting with a person who identified as a secret Jew in Saudi Arabia. "You're bringing something into a place where it doesn't exist. And then they say, 'Wow, thank you for the siddur and the tefillin. How did you manage to bring those in?' It was incredibly moving." A siddur is a Jewish prayer book, while tefillin are small leather boxes containing biblical passages, traditionally worn during weekday morning prayers. The dusty city of Tabuk recently made headlines in Israel following the emergency landing of a flydubai aircraft carrying Israeli passengers. Jano, however, had traveled to the remote city for an entirely different reason: information about a Saudi citizen who secretly maintained a Jewish identity. After a four-hour drive to the edge of the desert, the man apparently got cold feet, and the much-anticipated meeting was called off. From there, the Israeli adventurer continued to an intriguing archaeological site near Al-Bad, known as the Split Rock of Horeb. The unusual natural formation is identified by proponents of the theory that Mount Sinai is located in Saudi Arabia as the rock from which Moses brought forth water for the Israelites, according to the biblical account. The identification is disputed and is not an established archaeological finding. "I felt, wow, if the Israelites really were here, and I've managed to make it all the way here, what now? What am I supposed to do?" Jano recalled. "So I said, let's do the Jewish thing. I put on tefillin in front of the rock, and I felt something incredibly powerful there. You're in a different desert, and you feel that you're different." Through connections he developed during his travels, the energetic Israeli also managed to meet Saudi citizens who introduced him to a contemporary Jewish story in the kingdom. One encounter was with a wealthy couple in Riyadh. "There are people living in Saudi Arabia who say they have Jewish connections," he said with a smile. "They say they're Jewish and that there's a Jewish community in Saudi Arabia. These are very wealthy people who lived in England and Europe and then returned to Saudi Arabia, but their Jewish identity is still hidden." Outwardly, he explained, they are part of mainstream Saudi society. "They live like modern people in Saudi Arabia," he said. "The man wears the traditional white clothing, and I didn't ask whether he goes to pray at the mosque. He looks like a modern person dressed in traditional clothes, but he's secretly Jewish." Then came the most emotional part of the encounter. "And then you bring him a gift, a Hebrew prayer book," Jano said, struggling to conceal his excitement. "It's as though you're unexpectedly bringing someone a treasure. 'Wow, thank you so much, a siddur.' The couple understood the value of the gift and what I had gone through to bring it to them. It was incredibly moving." Jano's search for Jewish roots in Saudi Arabia also brought him to an abandoned Jewish cemetery in the city of Al-Hofuf. "You imagine you're going to see gravestones, but all there was was this white sand that had been packed down by sandstorms," he recalled. "You're actually walking over the graves and can't see anything because the desert has covered everything. But the local Muslims still respect the place and don't build on it. It's still fenced off and recognized as a Jewish cemetery, a no-go zone." For Jano, visiting the cemetery was more than another stop on an extraordinary journey. "I'm not a religious person," he explained. "But if there's a hidden Jewish cemetery that really hasn't been visited in a very long time, then I feel that part of my responsibility is to go there and pay my respects."

In recent years, AlUla has become a flagship project of Saudi Arabia's tourism ambitions, with luxury hotels, cultural attractions and extraordinary architecture emerging amid the desert landscape. Jano checked into one of the region's luxury resorts and discovered a swimming pool in the middle of the desert, gourmet restaurants, golf carts and impeccable five-star service. Almost everything was there, except the guests. "I was alone. There was nobody there," he laughed. "I was sitting alone in the restaurant, surrounded by waiters, and you're the only person there. They have golf carts to take you around because the hotel isn't just one building, it's an entire complex. "They ask you, 'Which restaurant would you like? There's a Thai restaurant or a Middle Eastern restaurant.' And whichever one you choose, you're the only guest. Everything is five-star. It's the top of the top." The hotel itself was designed to blend seamlessly into the surrounding desert. "The rooms are built into the mountain, and the swimming pool is there too. Even the stairs blend into the rocks. It's a very impressive, very special hotel, but being the only guest there feels strange." So where were all the tourists? "The employees tell me, 'Oh, they're coming.' They're coming. We want tourists." And what about the sightseeing bus? "I was the only passenger. Why would they even send out a bus? Can you imagine? An entire bus, and I'm riding in it alone." Beyond the luxurious hotels, the region is home to Nabataean archaeological sites and ancient tombs carved directly into the rock. "These are the same people who built what you see in Petra," Jano explained. "They carved straight into the rock, and it's incredibly impressive. Absolutely amazing." In AlUla, Jano also encountered a striking symbol of Saudi Arabia's ambitious transformation: Maraya, an enormous mirrored building that seems almost to disappear into the surrounding landscape, like a mirage reflecting the desert. "You can't see it," the veteran traveler said enthusiastically. "When you're walking through the desert and suddenly come across it, it tricks your eyes. It's like an optical illusion. It's a huge, square mirrored building, surrounded by mountains and desert, and the building reflects all the colors." Outside AlUla's lavish resorts, some of Jano's most memorable experiences took place around the dinner table. "Saudi food is very delicate and very good," he declared with the confidence of someone who has sampled plenty of it. "Think of Bedouin food, but imagine having a five-star chef prepare the meal and refine it," he laughed. "I particularly loved the lamb, slow-cooked with rice and spices." But the meal that stayed with him most was at the home of a Saudi friend he had met during his travels. "Arab hospitality is hospitality done properly," Jano said appreciatively. "When you're under someone's protection and they're responsible for you, you're treated like royalty." To protect his host's personal safety, we'll limit the description to the fact that he lives on a magnificent estate with a separate area designed specifically for entertaining guests. "He has this tent outside for visitors, and that's where they serve the food. He shows you photographs and things. He loves hunting, so he has stuffed animals and things from Africa. You sit on the carpet and eat with your hands." Yet beyond the hypnotic desert landscapes and luxury hotels, Jano had arrived in the mysterious kingdom with another, more discreet mission. "The Jewish story, wherever it exists, fascinates me," he said. "Everywhere I go, I try to put together another piece of the puzzle of Jewish history. And the very idea that there are 'hidden Jews' in Saudi Arabia made me curious to go looking for them and meet them." In a country where he himself had been forced to conceal his Israeli passport, the search for Jewish roots took on an entirely different level of significance. "You arrive there, you meet someone, and it's as if you're bringing them treasure," he said excitedly, recalling a discreet meeting with a person who identified as a secret Jew in Saudi Arabia. "You're bringing something into a place where it doesn't exist. And then they say, 'Wow, thank you for the siddur and the tefillin. How did you manage to bring those in?' It was incredibly moving." A siddur is a Jewish prayer book, while tefillin are small leather boxes containing biblical passages, traditionally worn during weekday morning prayers. The dusty city of Tabuk recently made headlines in Israel following the emergency landing of a flydubai aircraft carrying Israeli passengers. Jano, however, had traveled to the remote city for an entirely different reason: information about a Saudi citizen who secretly maintained a Jewish identity. After a four-hour drive to the edge of the desert, the man apparently got cold feet, and the much-anticipated meeting was called off. From there, the Israeli adventurer continued to an intriguing archaeological site near Al-Bad, known as the Split Rock of Horeb. The unusual natural formation is identified by proponents of the theory that Mount Sinai is located in Saudi Arabia as the rock from which Moses brought forth water for the Israelites, according to the biblical account. The identification is disputed and is not an established archaeological finding. "I felt, wow, if the Israelites really were here, and I've managed to make it all the way here, what now? What am I supposed to do?" Jano recalled. "So I said, let's do the Jewish thing. I put on tefillin in front of the rock, and I felt something incredibly powerful there. You're in a different desert, and you feel that you're different." Through connections he developed during his travels, the energetic Israeli also managed to meet Saudi citizens who introduced him to a contemporary Jewish story in the kingdom. One encounter was with a wealthy couple in Riyadh. "There are people living in Saudi Arabia who say they have Jewish connections," he said with a smile. "They say they're Jewish and that there's a Jewish community in Saudi Arabia. These are very wealthy people who lived in England and Europe and then returned to Saudi Arabia, but their Jewish identity is still hidden." Outwardly, he explained, they are part of mainstream Saudi society. "They live like modern people in Saudi Arabia," he said. "The man wears the traditional white clothing, and I didn't ask whether he goes to pray at the mosque. He looks like a modern person dressed in traditional clothes, but he's secretly Jewish." Then came the most emotional part of the encounter. "And then you bring him a gift, a Hebrew prayer book," Jano said, struggling to conceal his excitement. "It's as though you're unexpectedly bringing someone a treasure. 'Wow, thank you so much, a siddur.' The couple understood the value of the gift and what I had gone through to bring it to them. It was incredibly moving." Jano's search for Jewish roots in Saudi Arabia also brought him to an abandoned Jewish cemetery in the city of Al-Hofuf. "You imagine you're going to see gravestones, but all there was was this white sand that had been packed down by sandstorms," he recalled. "You're actually walking over the graves and can't see anything because the desert has covered everything. But the local Muslims still respect the place and don't build on it. It's still fenced off and recognized as a Jewish cemetery, a no-go zone." For Jano, visiting the cemetery was more than another stop on an extraordinary journey. "I'm not a religious person," he explained. "But if there's a hidden Jewish cemetery that really hasn't been visited in a very long time, then I feel that part of my responsibility is to go there and pay my respects."

representative.title: How Tania stopped her own child marriage | Prothom Alo
representative.author: Zahin Jaimah Kabir

snapshot.title: How Tania stopped her own child marriage
snapshot.evidenceText: <p>While other students were preparing to enrol in college after completing secondary school, Tania of Satkhira was struggling to stop her own marriage. Meanwhile, the results of the Secondary School Certificate (SSC) examination were published. Astonishing everyone, she achieved not only a GPA of 5 but also A+ grades in every subject. She scored 100 out of 100 in chemistry and 99 in physics.</p><p>Yet she felt no joy at her remarkable achievement. Her mind was consumed by anxiety over her impending marriage and uncertainty about her future. Ultimately, thanks to the support of her teachers and her outstanding SSC results, the determined Tania managed to escape child marriage this time.</p><p>Today, Sunday, is the International Day of the Girl Child. This year’s theme is “End Child Marriage, Invest in Girls’ Rights”. The situation in Bangladesh, however, seems to tell a somewhat different story.</p>.<p>The latest Multiple Indicator Cluster Survey (MICS) 2025, conducted by the Bangladesh Bureau of Statistics (BBS) and UNICEF, shows that the rate of child marriage has fallen from 51.4 per cent in 2019 to 47.2 per cent. Nevertheless, among women aged 20–24, 47.2 per cent were married before turning 18, while 13.4 per cent were married before the age of 15.</p><p>The survey also found that the proportion of married women aged 15–19 rose from 32.9 per cent in 2019 to 38.9 per cent over the seven-year period. The adolescent birth rate has also increased. In 2019, there were 83 births a year for every 1,000 adolescent girls; by 2025, the figure had risen to 92.</p>.One in every two girls subjected to child marriage.<p>Tania Khatun is 17. Just before her SSC examinations, she learnt that a marriage proposal had come for her. Neither she nor her mother wanted the marriage, but other family members put considerable pressure on them. They cited the family’s financial hardship, concerns about girls’ safety in society and various other reasons.</p><p>Tania did not know what to do. Under pressure, she eventually said she might agree on one condition: she must be allowed to continue her education after marriage. But the prospective groom’s family refused to accept even that condition.</p><p>News of Tania’s proposed marriage spread through her school and the surrounding area. Her hopes began to fade. But the story took a turn when Tania and her mother visited Akleema Khatun, the school’s information and communication technology teacher, with sweets to celebrate Tania’s excellent results.</p><p>Tania recalled that the teacher told her mother, “She has achieved such good results. How can you marry her off like this? We have taught your daughter for five years. We also have a claim on her future.”</p>.<p>The teacher, along with fellow teacher Foyezul Haque and local human rights activist Sakibur Rahman, then began trying to persuade Tania’s family to abandon the marriage plan.</p><p>Eventually, they took Tania to the upazila nirbahi officer (UNO), or upazila executive officer. The UNO spoke to her family, and mounting pressure from the authorities ultimately led them to withdraw the marriage decision.</p><p>Sakibur Rahman told Prothom Alo that the greatest source of strength in Tania’s struggle was her mother, who holds a master’s degree. She had opposed the marriage from the outset. An educated mother, he said, can provide the greatest courage in such adverse circumstances.</p><p>Tania has enrolled in the first year of higher secondary education in the science stream at Satkhira Government College. Her excellent SSC results have also earned her the opportunity to receive private tuition free of charge.</p>.I was deprived of everything: Global report hears from over 250 girls who experienced child marriage.<p>Tania’s story is an inspiring one. But very different stories are also common. The main causes of child marriage are said to include school dropout, financial hardship within families, social customs and weak enforcement of the law. Inadequate birth registration is also seen as a major obstacle. A 2025 survey found that only 59.2 per cent of children under five had been registered at birth.</p><p>Under the Child Marriage Restraint Act 2017, the minimum legal age for marriage is 18 for women and 21 for men. However, exceptions are allowed in certain circumstances. If a marriage involving a minor takes place in the best interests of the minor, with a court order and parental consent and in accordance with the procedures prescribed by the rules, it is not considered an offence under the Child Marriage Restraint Act.</p>

representative.title: High silver prices threaten Lucknow’s famed bridal nagra craft | Longform | Al Jazeera
representative.author: Aatif Ammad

snapshot.title: High silver prices threaten Lucknow’s famed bridal nagra craft
snapshot.evidenceText: Lucknow brides can no longer afford traditional silver nagras In Lucknow, the capital of Uttar Pradesh and a city known for its Nawabi heritage and artisanship, 55-year-old Azhar Hussain sits at the bench where he has spent years making decorative footwear. His tools are still there, but the customers are not. Amid soaring silver prices over the past year, demand for his work has plummeted. The small workshop sits beside Chowk Bazaar, one of Old Lucknow’s oldest and busiest markets, a famed hub for wedding shopping full of silver jewellery and handcrafts. For three decades, Hussain has been one of the bazaar’s busiest craftsmen, making a distinctive form of silver slip-on shoes, known locally as nagras. He starts by cutting a thin silver sheet into the outline of a nagra, then sketches floral and leaf motifs onto the metal. Hussain then rests the sheet on heated lac, a soft natural resin that cushions the metal while he uses a hammer and engraving tool to tap intricate designs into place. Hussain then bends the silver around a foot-shaped furma, or mould, before fitting it over a base of cardboard, rubber and velvet, soldering the pieces together and polishing the pair. Craftsmen have used this process to make silver nagras since the 1600s. Originally, the decorative shoes were made for daily use by the Nawabi, Muslim rulers of the former kingdom of Awadh. “Silver nagras used to be the most important part of a nawab’s attire,” said 68-year-old Nawab Masud Abdullah, an eighth-generation descendant of Nawab Muhammad Ali Shah, the ninth Nawab of Awadh, who ruled from 1837 until he died in 1842. “They were not just footwear; they represented our culture and heritage,” he added. Once reserved exclusively for Nawabs, silver nagras have become a cherished wedding tradition over the last century, embraced by Lucknow’s middle and upper classes alike. “Our forefathers wore silver nagras every day. Later, they became reserved for celebrations and eventually only for special occasions,” Abdullah explained. “The good thing was that the tradition spread beyond the Nawabs. People, particularly brides across Lucknow, embrace it as their own and now a bride is considered incomplete without a nagra.” Hussain and his family of craftsmen have seen this transformation firsthand. “In the past, only Nawabs could afford these shoes because they symbolised wealth, power and status,” he said. “But over the last seven or eight decades, they became popular among middle-class and wealthy families too, especially for weddings and special occasions.” There are two types of silver nagras — open-toed chappals and closed-toed jutis, and customers can choose different patterns, ornamentation and designs. Hussain’s family has been making nagras since the early 1900s and the trade has provided a comfortable living. Before each wedding season, he has typically made about 10 pairs a month, he says, with each priced between $105 and $230 (10,000 and 22,000 rupees). “We lived with dignity,” he said quietly. “We earned enough to feed our family, educate our children and save a little every month. We never imagined that one day we would struggle even to run our household.” Over the past year, however, the orders have vanished with the rise in silver prices. The metal was already costing a bit more before the U.S.-Iran war launched in February, owing to tight supplies and growing investor demand. But the conflict added another jolt, as uncertainty in global markets drove investors towards silver and put the metal — and the nagras — out of reach for many Lucknow shoppers. Prices for precious metals actually began rising with Russia’s invasion of Ukraine back in early 2022, but economists say prices surged significantly with the US and Israeli attacks on Iran. In 2023, silver prices in India largely fluctuated between $725 (70,000 rupees) and $830 (80,000 rupees) per kilogramme, rising to around $985 (98,000 rupees) in 2024. But this year, amid the conflict with Iran, silver prices briefly soared as high as $4,670 (450,000 rupees) per kg before easing after the ceasefire. Even now, after some decline, prices are hovering around $2,600 (250,000 rupees) per kg, more than three times their levels just a few years ago. Dr. Salahuddin Ayyub, an economist and international trade expert with India’s Ministry of Commerce and Industry, said geopolitical conflicts have triggered unprecedented volatility in global commodity markets. “When stock markets become volatile, investors move their money into safer assets, such as gold and silver,” Ayyub explained. “This sudden surge in demand pushes the prices of precious metals sharply upwards.” The consequences have been particularly severe in India, he said, because gold and silver remain deeply intertwined with weddings, other cultural traditions and family savings. As prices continue to rise, many households are increasingly opting for lower-cost alternatives, such as artificial jewellery. He warned that while consumers may find substitutes, those whose livelihoods depend on the precious metals industry, including artisans, silversmiths, jewellery shopkeepers and traditional craftsmen, have far fewer options. “The impact extends well beyond consumers,” Ayyub said. “Entire communities whose incomes depend on these metals are now facing shrinking demand and growing economic uncertainty.” The surge in silver prices has had another consequence that is often overlooked by the government and policymakers. According to Ayyub, when a country witnesses a sharp rise in demand for imported precious metals, governments often intervene to curb imports and protect their foreign exchange reserves. “India depends heavily on imported silver. A sudden spike in imports puts pressure on the country’s foreign exchange reserves, so the government tries to discourage excessive imports through tariffs and other restrictions,” Ayyub said. These import duties are eventually passed on to consumers. “As tariffs increase, the landed cost of silver rises. That is one of the reasons why silver prices in India are currently trading above global prices,” he said. Globally, silver currently costs $2,100 (201,000 rupees) per kg, but in India, it’s more than 20 percent higher because of heavy government import taxes and strict licensing that chokes off supply. India depends on imports to meet more than 80% of its domestic silver demand and its purchases account for over 20 percent of the global trade in refined silver. India more than doubled its effective import taxes on gold and silver in May. That saw silver imports plunge by 87 percent to just $75.6 million that month, down from $566.2 million the previous year, the country’s lowest level in over three years. High silver prices are now forcing Lucknow’s brides to make tough, sometimes devastating, decisions. For 28-year-old Lucknow resident Uzma Siddique, who is set to marry in December, owning and wearing a pair of silver nagras on her big day has always topped her wedding wishlist. “My mother wore silver nagras at her wedding in 1992. So did my grandmother and so did my great-grandmother,” Siddique said. “I always imagined myself wearing them and taking my wedding photographs in them and posting them on Instagram. It was never just footwear; it was an emotion and a family tradition.” But when she visited the market with plans to order a pair, the prices stunned her. “A pair that cost around $156 to $208 (15,000 to 20,000 rupees) just a few years ago is now selling for nearly $673 (65,000 rupees),” she said. Determined to have a pair, she decided to give up on other wedding luxuries instead. “I had to cut back on many other wedding expenses. I bought a lighter lehenga (long skirt), reduced the number of suits I planned to purchase, and trimmed my budget in several places, just so I could afford these nagras.” Despite the financial strain, she says giving up the footwear tradition was never an option. “They have become incredibly expensive, but our emotions are attached to them. That’s why I still bought them,” she said. But many of her friends have had to go without. “Some had dreamed of wearing silver nagras on their wedding day, but they had to let go of that dream because they simply couldn’t afford them. They are deeply hurt by it,” she said. Not far from Siddique’s home lives her friend, 25-year-old Safiya Khan, who is also getting married in December. Unlike Siddique, Safiya has not been able to buy silver nagras for her wedding. From a lower middle-class family, she says soaring prices put upholding that tradition out of reach. “My entire wedding shopping budget is around $1,250 (120,000 rupees). I simply cannot spend more than half of it on a pair of shoes,” Khan said, noting that she was sad to end the family tradition. “I think this tradition will end with my generation,” she said. “My mother had a pair of silver nagras, but she had to sell them last year because of financial difficulties. We always believed we would buy another pair for my wedding. Had we known silver prices would rise so dramatically, we would never have sold them.” She has been shocked by how a distant war has so negatively affected this beloved local tradition. “I know the recent conflicts have pushed silver prices higher, but I never imagined that a war thousands of km away could take away a tradition so close to my heart,” she said. “I had always dreamed of taking my wedding photographs in silver nagras. Now that dream will never come true.” Naseem Jahan, a Lucknow resident in her late seventies, still treasures the pair of silver chappals her mother gave her for her wedding in 1972. “I remember my mother paid around $2.50 (250 rupees) for this pair,” Jahan recalled. “We had to wait nearly seven months after placing the order before it was finally ready. Those were beautiful days.” More than five decades later, the silver slippers remain one of her most cherished possessions. She has them polished every three years and proudly wears them to weddings and other important family gatherings, as do many of the older women in Lucknow. “Every time I wear them, people come to admire them and praise their beauty. That makes me so happy,” she said with a smile. But Jahan fears the tradition may not continue into the next generation. “Today, very few people can afford such footwear,” she said. When she recently visited the market to buy a similar pair for her granddaughter, the soaring price of silver made it unaffordable. Still, she wants her granddaughter to have traditional bridal footwear, so she has made a tough decision. “I have decided to gift her my own pair,” she said. “Let these slippers adorn her feet now. I want them to continue their journey.” As the only precious keepsake she has preserved from her wedding, Jahan knows how connected brides feel to the shoes. “I have developed an emotional bond with them. They remind me of my mother, my wedding day and the Lucknow I grew up in. I only wish silver prices would come down again so that more people could experience this tradition.” Jahan’s decision to part with her silver nagras will keep a pair in her family, but it will not bring new work to the craftsmen who once made the footwear for Lucknow’s brides. In Chowk Bazaar, dwindling demand has left many artisans facing the prospect of a trade that may not survive long enough to serve the next generation. Jabbar Hussain, 48, a fourth-generation craftsman and shopkeeper who makes nagras and sells them in his shop, sits in his empty store in Lucknow’s Chowk Bazaar, struggling to understand what has happened to a business that once flourished. Between June and September, Hussain’s shop would normally be crowded with customers placing orders for nagras. But over the past three months, Hussain says, he has not sold a single pair. He blames the unprecedented rise in silver prices for making the handmade footwear a luxury few can now afford. “A pair that once sold for around $125 (12,000 rupees) now costs between $622 and $778 (60,000 and 75,000 rupees) because silver has become so expensive,” he said. “People still walk into the shop, admire the craftsmanship and ask about the price. But the moment they hear it, they quietly leave. snapshot.title: High silver prices threaten Lucknow’s famed bridal nagra craft

His tools are still there, but the customers are not. Amid soaring silver prices over the past year, demand for his work has plummeted. The small workshop sits beside Chowk Bazaar, one of Old Lucknow’s oldest and busiest markets, a famed hub for wedding shopping full of silver jewellery and handcrafts. For three decades, Hussain has been one of the bazaar’s busiest craftsmen, making a distinctive form of silver slip-on shoes, known locally as nagras. He starts by cutting a thin silver sheet into the outline of a nagra, then sketches floral and leaf motifs onto the metal. Hussain then rests the sheet on heated lac, a soft natural resin that cushions the metal while he uses a hammer and engraving tool to tap intricate designs into place. Hussain then bends the silver around a foot-shaped furma, or mould, before fitting it over a base of cardboard, rubber and velvet, soldering the pieces together and polishing the pair. Craftsmen have used this process to make silver nagras since the 1600s. Originally, the decorative shoes were made for daily use by the Nawabi, Muslim rulers of the former kingdom of Awadh. “Silver nagras used to be the most important part of a nawab’s attire,” said 68-year-old Nawab Masud Abdullah, an eighth-generation descendant of Nawab Muhammad Ali Shah, the ninth Nawab of Awadh, who ruled from 1837 until he died in 1842. “They were not just footwear; they represented our culture and heritage,” he added. Once reserved exclusively for Nawabs, silver nagras have become a cherished wedding tradition over the last century, embraced by Lucknow’s middle and upper classes alike. “Our forefathers wore silver nagras every day. Later, they became reserved for celebrations and eventually only for special occasions,” Abdullah explained. “The good thing was that the tradition spread beyond the Nawabs. People, particularly brides across Lucknow, embrace it as their own and now a bride is considered incomplete without a nagra.” Hussain and his family of craftsmen have seen this transformation firsthand. “In the past, only Nawabs could afford these shoes because they symbolised wealth, power and status,” he said. “But over the last seven or eight decades, they became popular among middle-class and wealthy families too, especially for weddings and special occasions.” There are two types of silver nagras — open-toed chappals and closed-toed jutis, and customers can choose different patterns, ornamentation and designs. Hussain’s family has been making nagras since the early 1900s and the trade has provided a comfortable living. Before each wedding season, he has typically made about 10 pairs a month, he says, with each priced between $105 and $230 (10,000 and 22,000 rupees). “We lived with dignity,” he said quietly. “We earned enough to feed our family, educate our children and save a little every month. The metal was already costing a bit more before the U.S.-Iran war launched in February, owing to tight supplies and growing investor demand. But the conflict added another jolt, as uncertainty in global markets drove investors towards silver and put the metal — and the nagras — out of reach for many Lucknow shoppers. Prices for precious metals actually began rising with Russia’s invasion of Ukraine back in early 2022, but economists say prices surged significantly with the US and Israeli attacks on Iran. In 2023, silver prices in India largely fluctuated between $725 (70,000 rupees) and $830 (80,000 rupees) per kilogramme, rising to around $985 (98,000 rupees) in 2024. Dr. Salahuddin Ayyub, an economist and international trade expert with India’s Ministry of Commerce and Industry, said geopolitical conflicts have triggered unprecedented volatility in global commodity markets. “When stock markets become volatile, investors move their money into safer assets, such as gold and silver,” Ayyub explained. “This sudden surge in demand pushes the prices of precious metals sharply upwards.” The consequences have been particularly severe in India, he said, because gold and silver remain deeply intertwined with weddings, other cultural traditions and family savings. As prices continue to rise, many households are increasingly opting for lower-cost alternatives, such as artificial jewellery. He warned that while consumers may find substitutes, those whose livelihoods depend on the precious metals industry, including artisans, silversmiths, jewellery shopkeepers and traditional craftsmen, have far fewer options. “The impact extends well beyond consumers,” Ayyub said. “Entire communities whose incomes depend on these metals are now facing shrinking demand and growing economic uncertainty.” The surge in silver prices has had another consequence that is often overlooked by the government and policymakers. According to Ayyub, when a country witnesses a sharp rise in demand for imported precious metals, governments often intervene to curb imports and protect their foreign exchange reserves. “India depends heavily on imported silver. A sudden spike in imports puts pressure on the country’s foreign exchange reserves, so the government tries to discourage excessive imports through tariffs and other restrictions,” Ayyub said. These import duties are eventually passed on to consumers. “As tariffs increase, the landed cost of silver rises. That is one of the reasons why silver prices in India are currently trading above global prices,” he said. Globally, silver currently costs $2,100 (201,000 rupees) per kg, but in India, it’s more than 20 percent higher because of heavy government import taxes and strict licensing that chokes off supply. It was never just footwear; it was an emotion and a family tradition.” But when she visited the market with plans to order a pair, the prices stunned her. “A pair that cost around $156 to $208 (15,000 to 20,000 rupees) just a few years ago is now selling for nearly $673 (65,000 rupees),” she said. Determined to have a pair, she decided to give up on other wedding luxuries instead. “I had to cut back on many other wedding expenses. I bought a lighter lehenga (long skirt), reduced the number of suits I planned to purchase, and trimmed my budget in several places, just so I could afford these nagras.” Despite the financial strain, she says giving up the footwear tradition was never an option. “They have become incredibly expensive, but our emotions are attached to them. That’s why I still bought them,” she said. They are deeply hurt by it,” she said. Not far from Siddique’s home lives her friend, 25-year-old Safiya Khan, who is also getting married in December. That makes me so happy,” she said with a smile. But Jahan fears the tradition may not continue into the next generation. “Today, very few people can afford such footwear,” she said. When she recently visited the market to buy a similar pair for her granddaughter, the soaring price of silver made it unaffordable. Still, she wants her granddaughter to have traditional bridal footwear, so she has made a tough decision. “I have decided to gift her my own pair,” she said. “Let these slippers adorn her feet now. representative.title: Eskasoni, efuel company create joint venture to make jet fuel from seawater | CBC News
representative.author: Tom Ayers

snapshot.title: Eskasoni, efuel company create joint venture to make jet fuel from seawater | CBC News
snapshot.evidenceText: A Mi'kmaw community in Cape Breton is placing a big bet on new technology that it says can turn seawater into environmentally friendly jet fuel. Eskasoni First Nation has invested $1.5 million and is the majority owner in a joint venture called eFuels Mi'kmaq Limited that plans to build a pilot project on band-owned land in Cape Breton Regional Municipality's industrial park in Sydney harbour. Bertram Bernard, a band councillor and chair of Eskasoni Corporate Services, said the investment will create local jobs for band members and is an important step in taking a meaningful role in a growing industry. "For us, this is about creating long-term economic opportunities, while continuing to be responsible stewards of our land and waters," he said during an announcement Thursday at the Sarah Denny Cultural Centre in Eskasoni. The newly formed eFuels Mi'kmaq plans to extract hydrogen from seawater and draw carbon dioxide from the air to create what is known as drop-in fuel, meaning it can be burned like any other fuel without any engine modifications. The process is expected to be powered by wind energy from onshore and offshore sources as they become available. Eskasoni band councillor Bertram Bernard says the joint venture will create lasting economic benefits while ensuring stewardship of resources. (Tom Ayers/CBC) The joint venture is with Aeon Blue, a company that started in the United States but moved to Sydney to take advantage of federal government incentives and the research facilities at the Verschuren Centre on Cape Breton University's campus. Lark Meadow, a co-founder and CEO of Aeon Blue, said it was important to her and her brother, co-founder Deois Ua Cearnaigh, to have Indigenous participation. "We are partnering all the way from piloting to commercialization, so we are going to grow our partnership and the facilities together," she said. Ua Cearnaigh, who is an electrochemist, said the technology to separate hydrogen from seawater and combine it with carbon dioxide to make all kinds of fuels has been around for decades. Aeon Blue CEO Lark Meadow says although the process can produce a wide range of fuel types, jet fuel was chosen because of growing demand. (Tom Ayers/CBC) But he said his patented process improves on the technology and makes it economical on a commercial scale. "It's kind of like saying the cart, four-wheeled vehicles, are thousands of years old, but the car only came around in the 1910s," he said. It also draws more carbon from the air than it uses, with the excess carbon dioxide being sequestered. Meadow said that may be in the ground or in other ways that have yet to be decided. Although the process can produce a wide range of fuel types, Meadow said jet fuel was chosen because there's a growing demand for green fuel in air travel. Officials say the joint venture is expected to produce 12 jobs next year and up to 80 when the efuel process reaches full commercialization. (Tom Ayers/CBC) Ua Cearnaigh said the move from their home in Texas not only made sense because of the government's financial incentives, but he said the Verschuren Centre's laboratories are superior to others and the geography means all of the components needed for the process are readily available. "Cape Breton has sort of this magical location where it is as close to the southern extent of winter sea ice as you can go and still have ice-free ports in the winter, and yet also the wind howls like nobody's business," he said. "It really is an X marks the spot. If you were going to do an efuels project, doesn't matter who you are, you would pick this island." Meadow said a pilot project will be located on Eskasoni's land in Sydport and is expected to start making fuel next year. It is expected to scale up the following year, with full commercialization to follow by 2030. eFuels Mi'kmaq Ltd. plans to build a pilot project on Eskasoni land in Sydport industrial park to make jet fuel from seawater. (Tom Ayers/CBC) Meadow said large-scale commercialization will require more land, but the manufacturing site will still be located along the coast of Cape Breton. The joint venture is expected to start training up to 12 Eskasoni band members in engineering, operations and management next year, and could create up to 80 full-time jobs when full commercialization is achieved. Steve Parsons, CEO of Eskasoni's corporate division, said the deal has been in the works for about 18 months. "We're very excited," he said. "This is a great opportunity for the community." representative.title: Burkina Faso to Kasoa on Foot: Man completes 22-day anti-galamsey march

snapshot.title: Burkina Faso to Kasoa on Foot: Man completes 22-day anti-galamsey march
snapshot.evidenceText: Marathon walker, King Klottey, has successfully completed his remarkable 22-day cross-border trek from Burkina Faso to Kasoa, aimed at raising public consciousness over the destruction and pollution of Ghana's major water bodies. In viral footage circulating online, and sighted by GhanaWeb on October 11, 2026, Klottey was seen arriving in Kasoa, flanked by supporters waving flags and security personnel, to mark the end of his grueling journey. The activist undertook the multi-week walk to draw urgent attention to environmental degradation, illegal mining (galamsey), and toxic contamination threatening river systems and drinking water sources across West Africa. Throughout his trek from the Burkinabe border through several Ghanaian towns, King Klottey engaged local residents and climate conscious youth on the imperative need to protect aquatic ecosystems and hold environmental polluters accountable. Illegal small-scale mining (galamsey) remains one of Ghana's most pressing socio-ecological challenges, leading to widespread heavy metal pollution in key river basins such as the Pra, Ankobra, Birim, and Densu. Watch the video below: Marathon walker King Klottey completes his 22-day walk from Burkina Faso to Kasoa, undertaken to raise awareness about the widespread pollution and destruction of Ghana’s water bodies. https://t.co/2OYXb3aX9B
