snapshot.title: The girls in the Gaza school photograph
snapshot.evidenceText: Just before the genocide, 15 Gaza schoolgirls posed for a photograph. Three years on, Al Jazeera went looking for them. Nuseirat, Gaza Strip — Maha Taha fills the old blackboard with equations and sets her students to work. For the next few minutes, the classroom settles into the scratch of pens and the low murmur of girls working through the problems. Maha, 43, has taught mathematics for 20 years. Dressed in an olive-green jalabeya and beige hijab, she steps quietly to her desk at the side of the room, as her students work through the maths problems. She has watched generations of girls pass through her classroom, preparing for exams and applying to universities. Asked about the girls she taught before the October 7 genocide began, Maha pauses before reaching for her phone. While scrolling back to find a photograph taken in June 2023, she speaks softly, so as not to disturb the girls in the classroom. “I was proud of them," she says. "I could see that they had bright futures ahead of them. They were very special in their personalities, even before it came to their studies. But October 7 changed the course of their lives.” In the photo, 15 teenage girls in navy school robes and white scarves crowd around Maha in the schoolyard. Some have their arms around one another; others lean towards the camera. All are smiling. They had just finished their mock exams and wanted a photograph together. Sara Rayan took it, holding out the phone so everyone fit in the frame. The girls were 17 and 18. Like many teenagers their age, they worried about exams and university places, talked about what they wanted to become, and imagined the lives that lay ahead. Four months later, Israel's war on Gaza began. Three years on, one of the girls in the photograph has been killed in an Israeli air strike. Four have left Gaza. Others have been displaced - their education interrupted and their plans for the future upended. Al Jazeera set out to find the 15 girls, to discover what had happened to them and the futures they once imagined, and to see whether they could be brought together again for a photograph in the same schoolyard. Muscat Secondary School is still standing, although it was struck by artillery in February 2024 and became a shelter for displaced families. Some classrooms still bear the marks of the war: holes left by quadcopter gunfire, windows damaged by shelling and soot stains where families cooked over open fires. On the walls, children have drawn kites, flowers and a Palestinian flag. Some have written their names: Haya, Marah, Mohammed and Khaled. Displaced families still shelter in parts of the school, while a tent at the edge of the yard serves as a makeshift classroom for younger pupils whose own school can no longer accommodate them. It's just past 10am on a Thursday in late September when Yasmin Abu Zaid arrives. Then Aya Adnan arrives, quickening her pace when she sees Yasmin and pulling her into an embrace. “I haven’t seen you for three years,” she says. “Where have you been? You never show up.” Lina Yunis Abd al-Qader arrives a few minutes later, carrying a plastic bag of books for Aya’s younger sister, who is preparing for the Tawjihi, Gaza’s national secondary school graduation exams. Aya and Lina have seen each other since leaving school. Their families have been friends for years, and they still live in the same neighbourhood of Nuseirat. But Yasmin, who once lived nearby, was displaced early in the war. With the fighting making it difficult to meet, neither has seen her for three years. The three have also kept in touch with Ghaida Zaqout, who now lives in Egypt. Together, they have a private WhatsApp group where they chat regularly and check on one another. When Maha finishes teaching, she greets "my girls" with arms wide open. They erupt into chatter, talking over one another and trying to catch up. In time, Maha pulls up the old photograph on her phone. The girls huddle around her, then point at the tree behind them, recognising it from the photograph. Now, they begin recalling the school days they shared. There were the ordinary intimacies of teenage friendship: who would lend you a pen, who would explain homework you didn't understand, who whispered through lessons and who worried for days about an exam. Ghaida was the girl whose laughter could be heard before she entered the classroom, and who rarely stopped talking, even when teachers moved her to another desk. Sara and her twin sister Fatima were forever taking selfies, while Lina al-Hour was quieter, often bringing novels to read during breaks. The girls talked about clothes, television programmes and football. They bought food together during breaks and wondered aloud about university and what they might become. Some dreamed of studying medicine; another wanted to design buildings. Their futures still seemed to turn on exams, marks, university places and what their families could afford. Maha remembers Sara Rayan laughing, and Ghaida, she says, is in Egypt now, studying dentistry. Here, she pauses, enlarges Lina’s face on the screen and falls silent. Her smile has disappeared. When she speaks again, her voice is quieter and catches slightly. “This is my well-mannered student, Lina,” she says softly. “She is a martyr.” On November 17, 2023, Lina was killed in an Israeli air strike. She was 18. For a moment, the girls wrap their arms even tighter around one another in silence. Standing in the same schoolyard three years later, they tell one another they wish they could return to those days. But most of the girls in the photograph are missing at this reunion. Aya takes out her phone and holds it at arm's length, trying to recreate the selfie Sara took three years earlier. “Sara should have been here to take it,” she says. But Sara cannot come. She now works for an NGO, using her wages to help pay her university fees and contribute to her family's income. Aya Adnan stands with the three in the new photograph, tall, with a dimple in her chin and her hijab falling behind her shoulders. Three years earlier, she had been looking forward to university. She wanted to become a doctor, preferably a neurosurgeon. Aya enjoyed studying. She arrived early for extra physics lessons and worked through difficult material until she understood it. She had also noticed how few female surgeons there were in Gaza and disliked hearing that surgery was too demanding a profession for women. Her interest in neurology had become personal in the 11th grade, when she suffered a severe headache and dizziness that lasted 24 hours. “It felt like my head was heavier than my body,” she recalls, “as if it might fall off.” After undergoing scans and seeing a neurologist, she was told pressure from the vertebrae in her neck was affecting her spinal cord. The experience only made her more determined to study neurology. When her final school results came, she had scored 96 percent. But studying medicine was expensive, and the family - her father was an UNRWA social worker - could not comfortably afford the fees. Seventeen years her senior, Yasser was a lawyer with his own practice, a wife and three children: Adnan, nine, Ahmad, seven, and three-year-old Ilaf. He helped support their parents and hoped one day to teach law at university. “I used to always tell him, ‘You're a second father to me,’ because he was so kind to me, just like my father,” Aya says. Aya remembers a summer's day in August 2023. Yasser, still dressed in his smart work clothes, came to take her from Nuseirat to the Islamic University of Gaza. "Together, we went from department to department, trying to find a course that was affordable and that I would enjoy," she says. Professors suggested engineering. But when they came out, Aya told Yasser she couldn't imagine herself studying computers or becoming an engineer. “I could picture myself wearing a white coat, that's all,” she told him. “Maybe I could study something in the medical field,” Aya suggested. “I really liked medical laboratory sciences.” Yasser knew that his sister was giving up the version of university she had imagined. But he refused to let her see the decision as the end of something. "Perhaps it's for the best," he told her. "Maybe one day you'll become a doctor in the field you choose to specialise in. You don't have to be a medical doctor; you could become a university professor with a PhD." Then, he offered her a thought that has stayed with her. "He told me, 'Sometimes what is withheld from us can be better for us than what is given to us,' and I believe him." Afterwards, he took her to Al-Taboun restaurant for lunch, while they kept talking about university and the choices available. Aya enrolled in medical laboratory sciences, and Yasser bought her books and supplies. University had barely completed its first week when the war began. A strike on a neighbouring two-storey house badly damaged the family home in Nuseirat, where they had lived for more than 35 years. They moved into an aunt's house. The new university timetable that had occupied Aya only weeks earlier disappeared. Instead of laboratories and lectures, her days revolved around finding water, helping prepare food, and learning how to cook without the things the family had once taken for granted. She didn't know how to build a fire; she hadn't needed to. Yasser would continue to return to the family's damaged home, partly to check on what they had left behind and partly because he feared their possessions would be stolen. Sometimes, he stayed there. On one of those visits, he asked Aya to come with him. There were dishes to wash, floors to sweep, rooms to tidy. She said she couldn't. She was helping their mother prepare food. On December 12, as the family gathered for afternoon prayers at her aunt's house, they heard a missile strike. Several minutes later, one of Aya's friends called. She wanted to know where the family was. Then she asked about Yasser, who had returned to their damaged home alone. The strike had hit the house, killing him. He was 32. Aya would return again and again to Yasser asking her to come with him, and her reply that she couldn't. It was an ordinary exchange between siblings, insignificant enough that Aya might never have remembered it, except it was also their last conversation. When she returned to the house about a week later, she found what remained of the plastic shopping bags that held the university supplies Yasser had bought for her only months earlier. Shaking off dust and ash, she opened them one by one. “I was surprised I found them at all; they reminded me of Yasser,” she says. Some books had survived, but others were almost entirely burned; only three pages remained from one set of lecture notes. Ballpoint pens, markers, and coloured pencils lay among the notes. Aya gathered, and still has, what remained. After 18 months, when universities started offering remote learning, Aya logged on whenever electricity and an internet connection allowed. Medical laboratory sciences was supposed to be hands-on: equipment, experiments, laboratories. Aya was trying to learn it without any of those things. "My major is very practical, and most of its courses are practical," she says. "It was difficult for me to study them online when I wasn't even at the university, and there were no laboratories or equipment in front of me." She kept going, and so did another girl in the photograph who once imagined herself in a white coat. Lina Yunis Abd al-Qader, known as “the tall one”, had also imagined becoming a surgeon. At school, she had loved Turkish dramas and anime and had a habit of doodling on her desk, much to the annoyance of her biology teacher. Those interests have since fallen away. She graduated with 98.3 percent and enrolled in medicine at the Islamic University of Gaza on September 10, 2023. Less than a month later, the war brought her studies to a halt. Her father, Yunis Abd al-Qader, works as a paramedic with the Palestinian Red Crescent. During the war, he worked 24-hour shifts and returned home only for brief rest. “I would wonder if he would come back the next day," she says. "I wished I could be there with him, to help him through the difficult things he was seeing.” Usually quiet and reserved, her father tried to spare the family the details of what he encountered. But sometimes, he came home exhausted, and the strain showed. One account he shared stayed with Lina. After an Israeli strike, he had been recovering human remains. Initially, he believed they belonged to seven people. As he continued working, he realised there was an eighth. Having witnessed the scale of amputations, fractures and other injuries, she wants to specialise in orthopaedic surgery. As she continued her medical studies, Lina became close to another student, Shams Majdi. Their friendship was still new when Lina struggled with a physiology problem and messaged Shams on WhatsApp for help. Shams lived in northern Gaza, where internet access was unreliable. With Israeli quadcopters overhead, she travelled several kilometres to find a connection so she could help solve the problem with Lina over the phone. Lina remembers the trouble her new friend took to help her. Later, the two sat the same exam remotely, from different parts of Gaza. Shams had again travelled away from home to find an internet connection. After finishing the exam, Lina opened WhatsApp. Lina says Shams was usually quick to respond, when she could. So she waited. About 45 minutes later, a message appeared in their medical college group announcing that Shams Majdi had been killed. For about 10 minutes, she says that she struggled to comprehend that it was the same Shams whose reply she had been waiting for. She kept sending messages throughout the day. None was answered. Shams had been killed in an Israeli strike on her home, alongside members of her family. For the following week, Lina says, she cried whenever she opened her medical books. There had been another Lina in Maha's classroom. Lina al-Hour, the quieter girl who loved novels and wrote letters to her friends, had also enrolled in medicine. She had attended her first week of university before the war began. On November 17, 2023, an Israeli air strike hit her family's home. Lina was killed alongside her parents, siblings and other relatives. With no surviving parent or sibling for Al Jazeera to interview, her former classmates and teacher helped piece together memories of her life. Maha remembers the way she listened in class. The girls remember how easily they could make her laugh. Lina Abd al-Qader remembers the strangeness of sharing a name with a friend who is now gone. “I and my friend who was killed had the same name,” she says. “But my friend was killed, and I still cannot get over it.” Ghaida Zaqout is now in Egypt, more than 300km (186 miles) from the schoolyard where she once posed with her classmates. Speaking to Al Jazeera by phone, she recalls how she used to fill her schoolbooks with drawings of the wooden houses she admired in Japanese anime, and dreamed of becoming an architect. By then, her sister Asmaa, her husband and their two children had moved in after losing their home in an Israeli air strike. Her maternal uncle's family was staying with them, too. About 15 people were living under one roof. Ghaida decided to make herself a small birthday cake. She found eggs, flour and baking powder and began arranging the ingredients in the kitchen, joking with her sister's children as she worked. Then, her aunt called with news that her cousin Majdi, 33, had been killed. He had always made Ghaida laugh. At family birthdays, he liked to scoop cream from the cake and smear it across her face. A natural storyteller, he could turn even the simplest anecdote into something funny. They had last seen each other on October 5, when the family went to Roots Cafe on Gaza's seafront. Ghaida left the ingredients on the kitchen counter and went to check on her mother. She doesn't remember who eventually cleared away the eggs and flour. Her mother had previously undergone surgery for breast cancer and was receiving follow-up treatment at Nasser Hospital in Khan Younis, including medication and radiotherapy. As her mother's treatment became harder to continue inside Gaza, because of the genocide, the family decided Ghaida would accompany her out. Leaving presented a problem she had never imagined having to solve. "I thought, how can I fit 17 years of my life into one bag?" she says. Ghaida began with paper. She gathered every certificate she could find, going all the way back to kindergarten: school results, awards, certificates from courses she had taken. She packed photographs of friends and family and the little gifts her friends had given her, keeping the messages and notes that came with them. There were practical things too, like her charger, Lyon potato chips and Al Awda’s crackers, and her pair of white wool pyjamas, speckled with red cherries, that she particularly loved. They had an old camera that had been used to document their lives since before Ghaida was born, along with CDs and a box of photographs accumulated over generations. There were pictures of her grandparents, her mother as a student, her parents before they married, their wedding and the announcement of their marriage. Ghaida wanted to take the box, but there wasn’t enough room for it. What she remembers most clearly about packing was deciding what she could bear to leave. "I wished I could carry the whole house with me," she says, "not the material things, but the things that had meaning for us. You know what I mean? The things that touched our hearts." The photographs were among the things that stayed behind. Later, certain they would not be able to return, the family asked a relative to go back to the house. There were too many photographs for him to carry away, and they did not want their family pictures falling into other hands. She crossed through Rafah with her mother and 16-year-old brother Abdul Rahman and eventually settled in Madinaty, in the east of Cairo. That first day, they ate fried chicken. For the first time in months, the things that had become difficult in Gaza were suddenly easy. Food was available. There was electricity. She could sleep without hearing shelling or drones overhead. Her friends were still in Gaza. Ghaida would call and hear about the difficulty of finding food and water. Then, she would look at what was available around her in Egypt. She lost her appetite and her weight plummeted by more than 10kg (22 pounds). It was not until September 2025 that Ghaida finally began university. She was 19, a month short of 20, sitting among students two years younger. And she was no longer studying architecture. She chose dentistry to help people in Gaza when she returns. "If the crossings open permanently," she says, "I will return immediately." Yasmin Abu Zaid had grown up as "the pampered one", in the words of her older sisters, and something she admits to herself. She is the youngest of three sisters and remained the family's youngest child for 10 years, until her brother was born. She had few household responsibilities. If she asked for something, her family usually found a way to get it for her. Her grandfather was particularly indulgent. Whenever he went to the market, he would return with something for Yasmin, food, sweets, whatever had caught his eye and made him think of her. Within days of the war beginning, Yasmin's life changed. Her family lived on the third floor of the Ain Jalut towers in Nuseirat, in an apartment along Salah al-Din Street. When a nearby mosque was bombed that October, their home was badly damaged. The family temporarily moved into her grandmother's nearby flat. A strike on a neighbouring two-storey house badly damaged the family home in Nuseirat, where they had lived for more than 35 years. They moved into an aunt's house. The new university timetable that had occupied Aya only weeks earlier disappeared. Instead of laboratories and lectures, her days revolved around finding water, helping prepare food, and learning how to cook without the things the family had once taken for granted. She didn't know how to build a fire; she hadn't needed to. Yasser would continue to return to the family's damaged home, partly to check on what they had left behind and partly because he feared their possessions would be stolen. Sometimes, he stayed there. On one of those visits, he asked Aya to come with him. There were dishes to wash, floors to sweep, rooms to tidy. She said she couldn't. She was helping their mother prepare food. On December 12, as the family gathered for afternoon prayers at her aunt's house, they heard a missile strike. Several minutes later, one of Aya's friends called. She wanted to know where the family was. Then she asked about Yasser, who had returned to their damaged home alone. The strike had hit the house, killing him. He was 32. Aya would return again and again to Yasser asking her to come with him, and her reply that she couldn't. It was an ordinary exchange between siblings, insignificant enough that Aya might never have remembered it, except it was also their last conversation. When she returned to the house about a week later, she found what remained of the plastic shopping bags that held the university supplies Yasser had bought for her only months earlier. Shaking off dust and ash, she opened them one by one. “I was surprised I found them at all; they reminded me of Yasser,” she says. Some books had survived, but others were almost entirely burned; only three pages remained from one set of lecture notes. Ballpoint pens, markers, and coloured pencils lay among the notes. Aya gathered, and still has, what remained. After 18 months, when universities started offering remote learning, Aya logged on whenever electricity and an internet connection allowed. Medical laboratory sciences was supposed to be hands-on: equipment, experiments, laboratories. Aya was trying to learn it without any of those things. "My major is very practical, and most of its courses are practical," she says. "It was difficult for me to study them online when I wasn't even at the university, and there were no laboratories or equipment in front of me." She kept going, and so did another girl in the photograph who once imagined herself in a white coat. Lina Yunis Abd al-Qader, known as “the tall one”, had also imagined becoming a surgeon. At school, she had loved Turkish dramas and anime and had a habit of doodling on her desk, much to the annoyance of her biology teacher. Those interests have since fallen away. She graduated with 98.3 percent and enrolled in medicine at the Islamic University of Gaza on September 10, 2023. Less than a month later, the war brought her studies to a halt. Her father, Yunis Abd al-Qader, works as a paramedic with the Palestinian Red Crescent. During the war, he worked 24-hour shifts and returned home only for brief rest. “I would wonder if he would come back the next day," she says. "I wished I could be there with him, to help him through the difficult things he was seeing.” Usually quiet and reserved, her father tried to spare the family the details of what he encountered. But sometimes, he came home exhausted, and the strain showed. One account he shared stayed with Lina. After an Israeli strike, he had been recovering human remains. Initially, he believed they belonged to seven people. As he continued working, he realised there was an eighth. Having witnessed the scale of amputations, fractures and other injuries, she wants to specialise in orthopaedic surgery. Their friendship was still new when Lina struggled with a physiology problem and messaged Shams on WhatsApp for help. Shams lived in northern Gaza, where internet access was unreliable. By then, her sister Asmaa, her husband and their two children had moved in after losing their home in an Israeli air strike. Her maternal uncle's family was staying with them, too. About 15 people were living under one roof. Ghaida decided to make herself a small birthday cake. She gathered every certificate she could find, going all the way back to kindergarten: school results, awards, certificates from courses she had taken. editorial.headline: The girls in the Gaza school photograph
editorial.evidence: Just before the genocide, 15 Gaza schoolgirls posed for a photograph. Three years on, Al Jazeera went looking for them. Nuseirat, Gaza Strip — Maha Taha fills the old blackboard with equations and sets her students to work. For the next few minutes, the classroom settles into the scratch of pens and the low murmur of girls working through the problems. Maha, 43, has taught mathematics for 20 years. Dressed in an olive-green jalabeya and beige hijab, she steps quietly to her desk at the side of the room, as her students work through the maths problems. She has watched generations of girls pass through her classroom, preparing for exams and applying to universities. Three years on, one of the girls in the photograph has been killed in an Israeli air strike. Others have been displaced - their education interrupted and their plans for the future upended. Muscat Secondary School is still standing, although it was struck by artillery in February 2024 and became a shelter for displaced families. Displaced families still shelter in parts of the school, while a tent at the edge of the yard serves as a makeshift classroom for younger pupils whose own school can no longer accommodate them. But Yasmin, who once lived nearby, was displaced early in the war. On November 17, 2023, Lina was killed in an Israeli air strike. But most of the girls in the photograph are missing at this reunion. The experience only made her more determined to study neurology. She didn't know how to build a fire; she hadn't needed to. Yasser would continue to return to the family's damaged home, partly to check on what they had left behind and partly because he feared their possessions would be stolen.

evaluation.strongest_fact: One of the girls in a specific school photograph was killed in an Israeli air strike, while others were displaced.

representative.title: Why this Canadian farmer is letting his land grow wild - North Bay News
representative.author: Danielle Tocker Photo/Be Giant

snapshot.title: Why this Canadian farmer is letting his land grow wild
snapshot.evidenceText: Lorne Scott calls his farm an island. Given that it’s in the prairie pothole region of southern Saskatchewan – a sweep of shallow wetlands left by glaciers – this is a metaphor, but it works: in all directions from where we stand, on a sunny day in June, are cultivated croplands. They’ve been planted to within an inch of their lives with canola, wheat, lentils. Except for a few shelterbelts, there are no trees from here to the horizon. Then there’s Scott’s land, thick with trees, shrubs and grasses. Parts of his farm grow wild, or “never broke,” as he puts it, with aspen, snowberry, starflower, Solomon’s seal and northern bedstraw, from which the Cree, who were here before settlement, made red dye. The bedstraw seeds, when roasted, work as a coffee substitute. Scott doesn’t drink coffee. Nor does he harvest any of the Indigenous plants on his land, which sits about nine kilometres south of Indian Head and about 75 kilometres southeast of Regina. They’re just here, left to grow any which way. His land is wild on purpose. It’s fair to call Scott a conservationist, one of the most respected in the province, still active in the community at 79. Soft-spoken and gentle, he is still a farmer: he grows wheat and oats, albeit on a small patch – 32 hectares planted this year. His grandfather was a farmer too, on a property two kilometres east, where Scott grew up. Letting more than a quarter of his farm grow wild is a radical act. Scott wouldn’t say so. He does it “for nature,” he says, to protect the life that’s disappearing, from insects to owls to moose. The day before we met, he saw two yearling moose, as well as a whitetail doe with a fawn and a mule deer. There are bluebird nesting boxes all over the property. What makes all of this radical is the context. Modern agriculture is a high-tech, data-driven industry that uses autonomous field equipment that relies on AI, drones and satellite imagery to maximize resources – land – for profit. “Only a wild man could be so reckless as to let a valuable thing like land go free,” says Andrea Olive, a political science professor at the University of Toronto, a friend of Scott’s and the author of Protecting the Prairies: Lorne Scott and the Politics of Conservation . “It must bother his neighbours, who only see cash crops where Lorne sees true growth.” It does, and some have asked, politely, to rent those perfectly good hectares of his, to plow them under, get things going as God and the commodities markets intended. He tells them no, that their equipment is too big, “and they shake their heads and walk away.” There’s a sign at the entrance to his farm that says, “This Property Is Forever Protected.” That means there’s a conservation easement on part of the property to preserve its natural state. Scott still owns the land and can pass it to his children or whoever he wants, but the restrictions on development are permanent. Scott knows about easements: he served as Saskatchewan’s minister of environment and resource management for four years in the late ‘90s, in Roy Romanow’s NDP government, and was responsible for the Conservation Easements Act, aimed at restricting development of wild land on private property. Under the act, the farmer still owns the land but enters into an agreement with a non-profit, like Ducks Unlimited, to keep it wild, as, say, wetland or grassland. There are thousands of hectares under easement in Saskatchewan. Some ranchers find them useful for protecting natural grasslands for grazing. Grazing is good for grasslands. It disturbs the plants (as does wildfire) in ways that help them grow. A conservative estimate is that 80 per cent of the grassland in Saskatchewan has been lost since commercial agriculture began, most recently through the sale of Crown lands after Ottawa dismantled the 74-year-old Prairie Farm Rehabilitation program in 2009. In the first 20 years of the 21st century, the average farm size increased by about 20 per cent, while the number of farms shrank by 23 per cent. Farms are getting bigger, land prices are rising, and while most farms are owned by the families that work them, one to two per cent are owned by investors and 2.4 per cent by large-scale private landowners. From Manitoba to the Cypress Hills, southern Saskatchewan was once grassland where bison grazed and First Nations hunted. It’s now mostly agricultural, and many farms are dotted with oil wells and pumpjacks, sometimes called “nodding donkeys.” To Scott and groups like the Saskatchewan Wildlife Federation, a non-profit he used to head, the mixed grasslands and fescue prairie are home to more than 30 species at risk, including the greater sage-grouse, and are valuable for that fact alone. Ottawa and the private sector (including Mosaic, a potash mining company, and the Weston family, which backs Be Giant ) have donated millions of dollars to prairie habitat preservation. “Everything gets bigger and better, supposedly,” says Scott, a man of few words until he gets wound up. “The biggest impact I see is on the natural environment. The wetlands, the bush are being cleared, and with equipment and technology, everything is workable these days for growing canola or wheat, whatever, and it's really made a big impact on the natural environment, and consequently some bird species have declined by 90 per cent or more, and largely due to agriculture, intensive farming.” According to Environment and Climate Change Canada, burrowing owl numbers declined 90 per cent from 1990 to 2000, then another 64 per cent between 2005 and 2015. They are small, oddball birds with long legs for running that live underground in tunnels dug by badgers. There are now fewer than 800 pairs left in Saskatchewan and Alberta. “Out in the country and the wild west, I call it, anything goes as long as it benefits you,” Scott says. Scott is not a born politician. He’s not an ideologue. He ran for office as a New Democrat, but in the 1980s, he joined the Progressive Conservative Party. As a boy on the farm, he was more interested in birds than politics, particularly the bluebirds that nested near sloughs and aspen bluffs, in grain bins and any natural cavity, including tractor wheel wells. On a farm, bluebirds bring good luck. But as early as the 1920s, they lost habitat to industrial agriculture and urban spread, and Scott took to building simple wood houses and tacking them up on farm fences to give them a place to nest. In 1969, he got a licence to band bluebirds and tree swallows, and in the first year banded nearly 1,000. Since then, he has banded tens of thousands of birds. With other volunteers, he built a “bluebird trail” of nesting boxes, from Brandon, Manitoba, to Raymore, Saskatchewan, north of Regina. He would drive 800 kilometres four times a year to check on the nests. It was, he says, the longest bluebird trail in the world. Then everything changed: the climate, and the business of agriculture. Large grain farms replaced natural aspen bluffs, wetlands and grasslands. Extreme weather in the bluebirds’ Texas breeding grounds changed migration patterns. By 2014, only six came back to nest near Indian Head, and the next year, none. Scott hasn’t seen bluebirds on his property since. To get to the wild acreage on Scott’s farm, we drive there in a Dodge Caravan (licence plate: BLUEB1RD), not by road but over the hummocky farmland itself . He points to an eastern kingbird on the fence. “From central South America,” he says. The place is home to bees and other insect pollinators, owls, hawks, moose and songbirds. Tree swallows have taken to nesting in the old bluebird houses, and we pull up next to one on a fencepost. He opens the top to show me five white eggs in a nest. Past the fence is a new project: a tree and shrub sanctuary with dozens of species, planted on four hectares when the federal sanctuary in Indian Head was shut down in 2012 following cuts by the Stephen Harper government. Scott is growing sea buckthorn, snowberry, high bush cranberry, apples, crabapples, buffalo berry, chokecherry and poplar – 80 different species – to serve as a seed bank. There is an easement on this land, too. Meanwhile, researchers and neighbours are welcome to take cuttings from the trees. His house is cluttered with school pictures of grandchildren and paintings of ducks and birdhouses. Below a picture of a meadowlark is a small, framed photo of Scott in a suit and Canada-flag tie, receiving the Order of Canada in 2008 from Governor General Michaëlle Jean. The Governor General’s website cites his volunteer work, his political life and his reputation “throughout Western Canada as a staunch defender of wildlife and natural habitats.” I ask him why he practises what he preaches on his own farm, whether this kind of “rewilding,” as it’s called, is more than a gesture. After all, a few hectares of aspen and bedstraw won’t save the planet. “That's the way the land was when I grew up on my dad's farm, you know,” he says. “Back then, people lived more in harmony with nature. They didn't feel it necessary to cultivate every acre, and they relied on the sloughs [for water] and the grass for pasture for hay, the aspen bluffs for wood and [the shrubs for] berry picking.” That’s not radical. He’s talking about an idea of land use that accommodates wildlife alongside a less destructive form of agriculture, not either-or. He’s a farmer. But he paraphrases Teddy Roosevelt: wildlife in its habitat can’t speak, so we must and we will. “Somebody has to,” Scott says. Tom Jokinen is a Winnipeg writer and broadcaster. He writes for The Walrus, Literary Review of Canada and is a regular contributor to CBC Radio Ideas. He's won a National Magazine Award, a New York Festivals Gold Award for audio documentary, and his book Curtains , about the funeral industry, was a Canadian bestseller. The bedstraw seeds, when roasted, work as a coffee substitute. In the first 20 years of the 21st century, the average farm size increased by about 20 per cent, while the number of farms shrank by 23 per cent. From Manitoba to the Cypress Hills, southern Saskatchewan was once grassland where bison grazed and First Nations hunted. In 1969, he got a licence to band bluebirds and tree swallows, and in the first year banded nearly 1,000. Meanwhile, researchers and neighbours are welcome to take cuttings from the trees. He follows cycling and Italian football closely. If you would like to apply to become a Verified Commenter , please fill out this form .

representative.title: China shock: EU says trade deal could cut up to 50% of Chinese EV and plug-in hybrid imports | Fortune
representative.author: Sam McNeil, Kanis Leung, Elaine Kurtenbach, The Associated Press

snapshot.title: EU says trade deal could cut up to 50% of Chinese EV and plug-in hybrid imports and lower tariffs for some European exports to China | Fortune
snapshot.evidenceText: The top trade envoys for China and the European Union agreed Friday on a broad initial deal following two days of talks aimed at calming escalating tensions over trade imbalances, the EU trade commissioner said. Neither side provided clear details on the preliminary deal, but European Commissioner for Trade Maros Sefcovic said it includes lower tariffs for some European goods to China as well as measures to stabilize rare earth supply chains. The EU trade envoy said the deal could cut up to 50% of Chinese electric and plug-in hybrid vehicle imports to the EU and could lower tariffs on products benefiting “almost every” EU nation. The deal would require approval from leaders across the 27-nation EU. He said that “by this step we are actually preventing several millions of car exports from China to the European Union.” The two sides were seeking to resolve key factors behind China’s growing trade surplus, which hit 360 billion euros ($403 billion) last year. China’s Commerce Ministry posted online that Chinese Commerce Minister Wang Wentao expressed concerns about the EU’s recent restrictive measures. He said that China is not the root of the EU’s problems but a partner in solving them. The head of the European Automobile Manufacturers’ Association, Sigrid de Vries, said that the deal appears to avert further instability in the EU and “can help facilitate the transition to a new era of Chinese presence in the European market in an orderly way and this is in the long-term interests of all parties.” Sefcovic said he will brief EU leaders meeting in Brussels next week and seek their approval. “They would have to see that this is convincing enough to take the other steps,” he said. “We are in a situation that they (China) could put under the threat whole sectors in the European industry, literally thousands of jobs and the public opinion and the leaders clearly expect very fast action from our side.” Sefcovic also said both sides reached understandings to further facilitate China’s export licensing for rare earths and permanent magnets, as well as to improve access to the Chinese market for various EU products through lower most-favored-nation tariffs, including car parts, olive oil and footwear, totaling almost 4 billion euros (about $4.5 billion) in current export value. The two sides will meet next by video in January and then in person in March. China has been pushing for the EU to stop blocking Chinese imports of advanced computer chipmaking machines, restrictions imposed on national security grounds at Washington’s behest. Earlier, Sefcovic had said the talks this week were the culmination of three months of intensive work. He had set an October deadline for meaningful results on trade rebalancing. Earlier in the week, the Chinese Commerce Ministry issued a statement urging the EU to avoid protectionist measures, warning that such moves could backfire. Trade tensions have grown in recent months, with both sides imposing or considering curbs on each other’s imports. The EU has moved to limit imports of Chinese-made electric vehicles and EV batteries and enacted measures to protect the European steel industry. It also is limiting duty-free imports of e-commerce small parcels, essentially targeting Chinese fast fashion firms. Last week, China launched an anti-dumping investigation into imports from the EU of p-nitrotoluene, a chemical compound used in dyes and pharmaceuticals. Chinese officials and businesses have raised concerns over reports some EU members are pushing for new measures to protect local industries. Worries over surging Chinese exports to Europe and other parts of the world in what some are calling a China shock 2.0 have deepened as the U.S., especially since U.S. President Donald Trump returned to the White House, has raised tariffs and enacted other measures to try to reduce its own huge trade deficit with Beijing. Despite the backlash from some of its trading partners, China’s global trade surplus hit $1.2 trillion in 2025 and is forecast to surpass $1 trillion again this year. The EU’s trade deficit with China widened to 103.3 billion euros (about $116 billion) in the second quarter, as imports rose to 153.6 billion euros ($172 billion), while European exports to China climbed to 50.3 billion euros ($56 billion), according to EU statistics. And on Wednesday, Germany blocked the sale of a major logistics firm in the port of Hamburg to the state-owned Chinese shipping behemoth Cosco over security concerns. “As Europe’s largest economy, Germany welcomes foreign investment. At the same time, some investments can endanger the country’s security,” the German economic ministry said in a statement. “The acquisition would have deepened dependencies and jeopardized the resilience of supply chains in Germany and the EU.”
snapshot.imageAlt: Chinese Vice Premier He Lifeng, also a member of the Political Bureau of the Communist Party of China Central Committee, meets with European Commissioner for Trade and Economic Security Maros Sefcovic in Beijing, capital of China, Oct. 9, 2026.

representative.title: This 345-Million-Year-Old Fossil Fooled Scientists for Decades
representative.author: American Museum of Natural History

snapshot.title: This 345-Million-Year-Old Fossil Fooled Scientists for Decades
snapshot.evidenceText: A famous Scottish fossil is forcing scientists to rethink what claw-like feet really reveal about the move onto land. Pressed flat inside two slabs of Scottish rock, a 345-million-year-old skeleton seemed to carry some unmistakable signs of life on land. Its four limbs ended in five-digit feet, and the tips of its fingers and toes looked strikingly like claws. For decades, those features helped make Westlothiana lizziae , better known as “Lizzie,” a landmark in the story of how vertebrates moved away from water and gave rise to reptiles, birds, and mammals. Yet the fossil had been crushed so badly that much of its anatomy remained hidden inside the stone. Peering through that rock with X-rays has now exposed a very different animal. Researchers from the American Museum of Natural History and the University of Oxford, working with the European Synchrotron Radiation Facility in Grenoble, France, reconstructed structures that could not be seen from the fossil’s surface. Their results, published in Nature , revealed a primitive skull, ossified internal gills, and a fish-like mouth packed with thousands of tiny teeth. “Lizzie has been an icon for the early evolution of amniotes for decades,” said Xavier Jenkins, a postdoctoral fellow in the Museum’s Division of Paleontology and co-lead author of the study. “But when we were finally able to see inside the fossil, we found an animal that looked very different from what we expected.” Discovered in Scotland in 1984 and formally described in 1990, Westlothiana had initially been interpreted largely from the anatomy exposed on the surfaces of its two slabs. Its nearly complete skeleton stood apart from many animals living around the same time because its limbs looked more suited to supporting a body than the more fin-like appendages seen in some early tetrapod relatives. Those visible feet helped secure Lizzie’s reputation as an early amniote, the branch of vertebrates that eventually produced reptiles, birds, and mammals. Researchers repeatedly used the fossil as an important reference point when estimating when animals with fully land-adapted lifestyles began appearing. Inside Lizzie’s skull, however, the synchrotron scans uncovered features that do not fit that interpretation. The internal gills and tooth-filled, fish-like mouth instead place the animal on a much older branch of the tetrapod family tree and indicate that it was aquatic or amphibious rather than a fully terrestrial reptile ancestor. “The surprisingly primitive features of the skull show us that Lizzie was not only not a reptile but belonged to a much more ancient lineage. It turns out looks can be deceiving, and Lizzie lived a completely different lifestyle than we previously thought,” said Ben Igielman, co-lead author of the study, who started this research during his graduate work at the University of Oxford. Keeping those reptile-like feet creates another surprise. Five toes, claw-like tips, and limb structures once treated as hallmarks of land-adapted amniotes were apparently already present in more ancient members of the stem lineage leading toward tetrapods. In other words, some pieces of the body plan associated with later land animals evolved before the animals carrying them had fully left the water behind. “This is a big surprise,” said study co-author Roger Benson, the Museum’s Macaulay Curator of Paleontology. “It shows that, although we think of amphibians as being more ‘primitive’ than reptiles today, some of the traits of reptiles were already there in the ancestor of both amphibians and reptiles.” Claw-shaped impressions preserved in still older fossil trackways may now need the same kind of caution. Some tracks dating to the Devonian Period, more than 359 million years ago, have been interpreted as evidence that amniotes had already evolved because they record four-limbed animals walking on claw-like digits. If creatures as primitive as Westlothiana could also possess claw-like structures, those tracks no longer provide a simple fingerprint of an amniote. Some may instead have been left by amphibious tetrapod relatives that carried land-like anatomical features while still dividing their lives between water and shore. “The broader lesson is that terrestrial-looking traits, such as a reptile-like foot, a weight-bearing forelimb, and claw-like phalanges were not unique features of tetrapods, but rather accumulated piecemeal in their close relatives, in animals that were still living in and out of the water,” Jenkins said. Reference: “Evolution of terrestrial anatomy revealed by a derived stem tetrapod” by Ben Igielman, Xavier Jenkins, Jason Head, Vincent Fernandez, Lucy Roberts, Timothy Smithson and Roger Benson, 30 September 2026, Nature . DOI: 10.1038/s41586-026-11090-6 Support for this study was provided by the National Science Foundation (grant number EAR-PF 2518154), the National Environment Research Council (grant numbers NE/S000739/1, NE/W007576/1, and NE/L002507/1), and the Biotechnology and Biological Sciences Research Council (grant number BB/X014819/1). representative.title: Codebreaker, 103, kept his WW2 heroics a secret for decades - BBC News
representative.author: Isaac Ashe, Simon Ward

snapshot.title: Codebreaker, 103, kept his WW2 heroics a secret for decades
snapshot.evidenceText: Fred Vanke was sworn to secrecy but his work as a codebreaker has finally been recognised "My wife died and didn't know. I never told anybody. In fact, she always complained - all your friends, when they come visit, they all have stories to tell and you never tell anything." From fleeing the Nazi invasion of his native Poland, to training as an operative to work behind enemy lines, to helping to crack the codes which turned the tide of the conflict, Fred Vanke had an eventful World War Two. Sworn to secrecy however, his family and friends almost never learned of the true role the 103-year-old played in the Allied war effort. But research into the life story of Vanke, now living in Breaston, Derbyshire, has written a new chapter on the history of Bletchley Park's famed codebreakers. About 100 Poles based in the UK carried out work on behalf of Bletchley Park between 1940 and 1945. After Fred shared his story, research has added the names of 27 Polish codebreakers and signals intelligence (sigint) to the Bletchley Park Roll of Honour, and more could follow. The additions represent one of the most significant expansions of the documented Polish contribution to Britain's wartime codebreaking effort in recent years, helping historians better understand the scale of the intelligence partnership between Britain and the Polish government-in-exile. Fred fled Poland after a happy childhood in Krakow Believed to be the last surviving member of these Polish codebreakers, Ferdynand Stanislaw Vanke grew up in Krakow, but fled at the age of 16 when war arrived on his doorstep in 1939. He said: "I did wake up in the morning hearing the planes. I ran to the window and I could see Germans coming over but I thought it was Polish Air Force training. "People were screaming and falling to the ground and we could hear machine gun fire. My father burst in and said 'in to the cellar, the Germans are coming'. That's how my war started." Fred, his sister and a friend travelled east in a Polish Army Hospital van, to his grandparents' home, avoiding Nazi gunfire on the roads. "I could see people coming from all over the place, masses of people," he said. "When Germans would come, my sister said to me 'under the van, under the van'. That's the first time I've seen people being injured to that extent." Fred and his father served together in the Middle East After his initial destination Syria was lost with the invasion of France, he instead made his way to British-controlled Palestine where he joined the newly-formed Polish brigade, the Carpathian Rifle Brigade alongside his father. "I'm going to be a soldier at last," Fred remembers thinking. He proved his worth and after officer training in Tel Aviv he was sent to Glasgow to join the Cichociemni, a Polish special forces unit trained for occupied Poland. "Cichociemni in Polish means dark and quiet," he said. "I've gone right through the courses, how to use the poison, how to kill people quietly, and all that sort of thing. "One day my commanding officer, Colonel Mayer, called me and explained 'you're young, I've got a son like you, you volunteer to be dropped in Poland you will last four or five months on average and that's the end of you. I've got something better'. Fred served in the Middle East before his service took an unexpected turn Instead, a captain visited from Bletchley Park, the then-secret headquarters of the Government Code and Cypher School, the forerunner of GCHQ, and the base for Allied codebreaking. "He gave us all a lecture and a little puzzle," said Fred. After cracking the first, he was given a second which he also deciphered. "He said, 'you've got a gift which very few people have'," Fred recalled. So despite being in his early 20s, several years younger than anyone else on the unit, Fred was recruited to work at The Arches in Boxmoor, a Polish sigint station near Hemel Hempstead which supported Bletchley Park. The Arches was from the street a large but unassuming house but inside the building featured more than a dozen rooms turned into offices for codebreakers, and its garden was filled with huts housing radio operators. One of dozens of Polish codebreakers based there, Fred would work in a team listening to German signals and attempting to decode them. Poles like Fred worked in secret under the guidance of Bletchley Park Fred said: "You start with the simple things. You've got to learn the language, how it is built, and what is the quirk in that language, and you base your guessing on that. "When I arrived there first, I never knew anybody there, it was a little strange, but very very soon it was like a holiday." However outside of The Arches, life was tougher for Fred. He said: "The people in Hemel Hempstead, because we had uniforms with Poland, they spat on you and called 'why don't you eff off to fight Germans instead'. "You couldn't say what you're doing, so that was a little bit upsetting." But what Fred and his Polish compatriots were doing, both before the war and during it, was pivotal in the Allied war effort. Bletchley Park was the secret headquarters of the Government Code and Cypher School Among those identified during the research were Marian Rejewski and Henryk Zygalski, two of the three Polish mathematicians who alongside Jerzy Różycki first broke the German military Enigma cipher before the war, and who continued codebreaking work in Britain after escaping occupied Europe. At the Pyry Conference near Warsaw in 1939, Polish cryptologists invited French and British counterparts, including Alastair Denniston and Dilly Knox, to share their pioneering success in breaking the German Enigma machine cipher. Dr David Kenyon, the research historian at Bletchley Park Trust who investigated Fred's story, said: "This meeting was important because it laid the groundwork for partnership between the British and the Polish and significantly helped the subsequent British attack on Enigma." Fred said: "I was very pleased when I received a letter from the British government for what I've done. But I was very proud of Zygalski, Rejewski and Różycki - that's our three real codebreakers." Fred and Patricia met in Nottingham after the war After the war, Fred moved to Nottingham where he started a photography firm with a fellow Polish ex-paratrooper. "I met my wife in Jessops in one of the shops," he said. "She was a model there, once I saw her, I said 'this is my wife'." The couple raised three children, and were together until her death in 1996 - but Fred never told her about his wartime role. "My wife died and she still didn't know what I was doing. I never told anybody," he said. "In fact, she always complained - 'all your friends, when they come visit, they all have stories to tell, you never tell anything'. "You were sworn not to tell, so I kept that." Having reached the age of 103, Fred puts his long life down to luck, whiskey and stopping smoking in 1963, and believes he must now be the last surviving Polish codebreaker. "I'm bound to be, I am 103-and-a-half, and I was the youngest by two years," he said. Fred and 26 other Poles who served under Bletchley Park have been added to its Roll of Honour Kenyon said: "Due to the secrecy of the work at Bletchley Park, so much of this work remained classified for decades - the full scale of Polish involvement in Britain's WW2 codebreaking effort is still being pieced together. "Adding these Polish names to our Roll of Honour pays tribute to the contribution made by Polish citizens in the wider Allied effort in WW2, not only on the fighting fronts, but also at Bletchley Park, and in other secret intelligence work, a contribution which may have been overlooked in the past." Rafał Wiśniewski, Chargé d'Affaires a.i. at the Embassy of the Republic of Poland in London, said: "The work of Polish cryptologists, well before and during WW2, was instrumental in cracking the Enigma cypher and, ultimately, in the Allied victory, which helped save countless lives. "The evidence proving direct links to Bletchley Park and other secret intelligence work is truly important and shows the depth of our co-operation, which needs to be recognised." Caroline Whelan said her father's story showed the importance of intelligence and the role it can play in bringing about peace Fred's daughter Caroline Whelan, 60, said: "We've had a very happy, normal life, considering dad had a really traumatic start to his. "It is unbelievably fantastic that he is able to witness the acknowledgement that so many people haven't been able to," she said. "He's one of the people that you never get bored of talking to, and he's always got a story to tell now." snapshot.title: Codebreaker, 103, kept his WW2 heroics a secret for decades
snapshot.evidenceText: Fred Vanke was sworn to secrecy but his work as a codebreaker has finally been recognised "My wife died and didn't know. I never told anybody. In fact, she always complained - all your friends, when they come visit, they all have stories to tell and you never tell anything." From fleeing the Nazi invasion of his native Poland, to training as an operative to work behind enemy lines, to helping to crack the codes which turned the tide of the conflict, Fred Vanke had an eventful World War Two. Sworn to secrecy however, his family and friends almost never learned of the true role the 103-year-old played in the Allied war effort. But research into the life story of Vanke, now living in Breaston, Derbyshire, has written a new chapter on the history of Bletchley Park's famed codebreakers. About 100 Poles based in the UK carried out work on behalf of Bletchley Park between 1940 and 1945. After Fred shared his story, research has added the names of 27 Polish codebreakers and signals intelligence (sigint) to the Bletchley Park Roll of Honour, and more could follow. The additions represent one of the most significant expansions of the documented Polish contribution to Britain's wartime codebreaking effort in recent years, helping historians better understand the scale of the intelligence partnership between Britain and the Polish government-in-exile. Fred fled Poland after a happy childhood in Krakow Believed to be the last surviving member of these Polish codebreakers, Ferdynand Stanislaw Vanke grew up in Krakow, but fled at the age of 16 when war arrived on his doorstep in 1939. He said: "I did wake up in the morning hearing the planes. I ran to the window and I could see Germans coming over but I thought it was Polish Air Force training. "People were screaming and falling to the ground and we could hear machine gun fire. My father burst in and said 'in to the cellar, the Germans are coming'. That's how my war started." Fred, his sister and a friend travelled east in a Polish Army Hospital van, to his grandparents' home, avoiding Nazi gunfire on the roads. "I could see people coming from all over the place, masses of people," he said. "When Germans would come, my sister said to me 'under the van, under the van'. That's the first time I've seen people being injured to that extent." Fred and his father served together in the Middle East After his initial destination Syria was lost with the invasion of France, he instead made his way to British-controlled Palestine where he joined the newly-formed Polish brigade, the Carpathian Rifle Brigade alongside his father. "I'm going to be a soldier at last," Fred remembers thinking. He proved his worth and after officer training in Tel Aviv he was sent to Glasgow to join the Cichociemni, a Polish special forces unit trained for occupied Poland. "Cichociemni in Polish means dark and quiet," he said. "I've gone right through the courses, how to use the poison, how to kill people quietly, and all that sort of thing. "One day my commanding officer, Colonel Mayer, called me and explained 'you're young, I've got a son like you, you volunteer to be dropped in Poland you will last four or five months on average and that's the end of you. I've got something better'. Fred served in the Middle East before his service took an unexpected turn Instead, a captain visited from Bletchley Park, the then-secret headquarters of the Government Code and Cypher School, the forerunner of GCHQ, and the base for Allied codebreaking. "He gave us all a lecture and a little puzzle," said Fred. After cracking the first, he was given a second which he also deciphered. "He said, 'you've got a gift which very few people have'," Fred recalled. So despite being in his early 20s, several years younger than anyone else on the unit, Fred was recruited to work at The Arches in Boxmoor, a Polish sigint station near Hemel Hempstead which supported Bletchley Park. The Arches was from the street a large but unassuming house but inside the building featured more than a dozen rooms turned into offices for codebreakers, and its garden was filled with huts housing radio operators. One of dozens of Polish codebreakers based there, Fred would work in a team listening to German signals and attempting to decode them. Poles like Fred worked in secret under the guidance of Bletchley Park Fred said: "You start with the simple things. You've got to learn the language, how it is built, and what is the quirk in that language, and you base your guessing on that. "When I arrived there first, I never knew anybody there, it was a little strange, but very very soon it was like a holiday." However outside of The Arches, life was tougher for Fred. He said: "The people in Hemel Hempstead, because we had uniforms with Poland, they spat on you and called 'why don't you eff off to fight Germans instead'. "You couldn't say what you're doing, so that was a little bit upsetting." But what Fred and his Polish compatriots were doing, both before the war and during it, was pivotal in the Allied war effort. Bletchley Park was the secret headquarters of the Government Code and Cypher School Among those identified during the research were Marian Rejewski and Henryk Zygalski, two of the three Polish mathematicians who alongside Jerzy Różycki first broke the German military Enigma cipher before the war, and who continued codebreaking work in Britain after escaping occupied Europe. At the Pyry Conference near Warsaw in 1939, Polish cryptologists invited French and British counterparts, including Alastair Denniston and Dilly Knox, to share their pioneering success in breaking the German Enigma machine cipher. Dr David Kenyon, the research historian at Bletchley Park Trust who investigated Fred's story, said: "This meeting was important because it laid the groundwork for partnership between the British and the Polish and significantly helped the subsequent British attack on Enigma." Fred said: "I was very pleased when I received a letter from the British government for what I've done. But I was very proud of Zygalski, Rejewski and Różycki - that's our three real codebreakers." Fred and Patricia met in Nottingham after the war After the war, Fred moved to Nottingham where he started a photography firm with a fellow Polish ex-paratrooper. "I met my wife in Jessops in one of the shops," he said. "She was a model there, once I saw her, I said 'this is my wife'." The couple raised three children, and were together until her death in 1996 - but Fred never told her about his wartime role. "My wife died and she still didn't know what I was doing. I never told anybody," he said. "In fact, she always complained - 'all your friends, when they come visit, they all have stories to tell, you never tell anything'. "You were sworn not to tell, so I kept that." Having reached the age of 103, Fred puts his long life down to luck, whiskey and stopping smoking in 1963, and believes he must now be the last surviving Polish codebreaker. "I'm bound to be, I am 103-and-a-half, and I was the youngest by two years," he said. Fred and 26 other Poles who served under Bletchley Park have been added to its Roll of Honour Kenyon said: "Due to the secrecy of the work at Bletchley Park, so much of this work remained classified for decades - the full scale of Polish involvement in Britain's WW2 codebreaking effort is still being pieced together. "Adding these Polish names to our Roll of Honour pays tribute to the contribution made by Polish citizens in the wider Allied effort in WW2, not only on the fighting fronts, but also at Bletchley Park, and in other secret intelligence work, a contribution which may have been overlooked in the past." Rafał Wiśniewski, Chargé d'Affaires a.i. at the Embassy of the Republic of Poland in London, said: "The work of Polish cryptologists, well before and during WW2, was instrumental in cracking the Enigma cypher and, ultimately, in the Allied victory, which helped save countless lives. "The evidence proving direct links to Bletchley Park and other secret intelligence work is truly important and shows the depth of our co-operation, which needs to be recognised." Caroline Whelan said her father's story showed the importance of intelligence and the role it can play in bringing about peace Fred's daughter Caroline Whelan, 60, said: "We've had a very happy, normal life, considering dad had a really traumatic start to his. "It is unbelievably fantastic that he is able to witness the acknowledgement that so many people haven't been able to," she said. "He's one of the people that you never get bored of talking to, and he's always got a story to tell now." snapshot.title: Meet “Noo-Noo”: A 99-Million-Year-Old Insect with a Surprising Secret
snapshot.evidenceText: TAU researchers discover a new insect species from the age of the dinosaurs, revealing an unusual feeding mechanism that has disappeared from the insect world today. • Tel Aviv University researchers identified a previously unknown insect species preserved in 99-million-year-old amber from the age of the dinosaurs. • The new species, Cretodorus noonoo, nicknamed “Noo-Noo,” had exceptionally long, flexible mouthparts reaching nearly twice its body length. • Researchers believe these mouthparts helped the insect reach sugar-rich fluids deep inside cracks in tree bark. • The discovery reveals an ancient evolutionary adaptation with almost no modern equivalent and offers new insights into the ecosystems of Cretaceous forests. Some 99 million years ago, during the age of the dinosaurs, a tiny insect belonging to a species previously unknown to science became trapped in tree resin. The resin hardened and turned into amber, and the fossil preserved within it has now enabled a team of researchers from the School of Zoology and The Steinhardt Museum of Natural History to identify and describea new species: Cretodorus noonoo, or “Noo-Noo.” Alongside the description of the new species, the study reveals an extraordinary biological adaptation that characterized Noo-Noo and its close relatives: exceptionally long and flexible mouthparts, which in Noo-Noo reached nearly twice the length of its body. The researchers believe that this unusual structure enabled the insects to reach food sources that were inaccessible to insects with more rigid mouthparts, deep inside cracks and crevices in tree bark. The study, published in the journal Insects, was conducted by Dolev Fabrikant and Dr Leonidas-Romanos Davranoglou of the School of Zoology, Wise Faculty of Life Sciences, The Steinhardt Museum of Natural History and New Environmental School at Tel Aviv University, in collaboration with Dr Yanzhe Fu of the Nanjing Institute of Geology and Palaeontology of the Chinese Academy of Sciences. The newly described species - Cretoduros noonoo, Photo credit: Dolev Fabrikant The researchers examined insect fossils belonging to Neazoniidae, an ancient family of planthoppers, including 13 specimens preserved in Kachin amber from Myanmar. In their modern relatives, the mouthparts are structured like a simple needle, allowing them to pierce plant tissues and suck fluids from them. The ancient insects examined in the study, however, were found to possess extremely elongated mouthparts, the surface of which was densely covered with transverse folds. Using high-resolution micro-computed tomography, the researchers were able to reconstruct their internal structure. The scans showed that the folds were not merely external ornamentation, but part of the structure itself. They likely gave the mouthparts flexibility while preventing them from kinking or collapsing — much like a bendy drinking straw or a corrugated flexible hose. Further evidence comes from the fossils themselves: in several specimens, the mouthparts were preserved in a bent position. Because the amber froze the insects in place when they became trapped in the resin, the researchers view this as further evidence that the mouthparts were also flexible during the insect’s lifetime. Such a structure is unknown among their living relatives today, pointing to an ancient evolutionary solution that has since disappeared. The new species’ unusual appearance also inspired by its name: Cretodorus noonoo. The epithet “Noo-Noo” was chosen after the friendly vacuum cleaner from the children’s television series Teletubbies, whose long, flexible hose resembles the mouthpart of the ancient insect. But why would an insect need such long mouthparts? Butterflies might immediately come to mind, as they use a flexible proboscis to drink nectar, but the researchers believe that the resemblance is only superficial. The mouthparts of “Noo-Noo” pointed backward and functioned as a piercing-and-sucking system, which like those of their modern relatives are less suitable for feeding on nectar. Moreover, despite examining numerous fossils, the researchers found no convincing evidence of pollen accumulating on their bodies — a sign that would have indicated a role as pollinators. The explanation proposed by the researchers is that these insects were specialists in sucking sap from trees. Their long, flexible mouthparts could have snaked through narrow cracks in the bark and guided the piercing organs toward the deep vascular tissues. At the tip was another unusual feature: a structure with two grooved lobes that likely opened during feeding, helping to anchor the mouthpart to the walls of the crack — much like a wall plug expanding inside a drilled hole. The researchers’ discovery may also have broader significance for our understanding of Cretaceous forests. Long or corrugated feeding structures appeared in several unrelated insect groups during this period, raising the possibility that forests rich in thick-barked trees provided an advantage for insects capable of reaching deeper tissues. The study notes that resin-producing forests of the Cretaceous period were also associated with evidence of recurrent fires, and that trees in fire-prone environments often develop thicker bark. The researchers cautiously suggest that such conditions may have created ecological opportunities for unique feeding strategies — strategies that are almost entirely absent among planthoppers today. Dr. Leonidas-Romanos Davranoglou stated: “The discovery of ‘Noo-Noo,’ a new species that lived approximately 99 million years ago, gives us an extraordinary glimpse into the insect world of the age of the dinosaurs. This is not merely an insect previously unknown to science, but an animal that developed an evolutionary solution with almost no modern equivalent: a long, flexible, and durable feeding organ that likely enabled it to reach food deep within tree bark. The fact that similar structures appeared in several insect groups during the Cretaceous period suggests that ancient forests created ecological conditions and opportunities very different from those we know today. The discovery of a new species like this is therefore not simply the addition of another name to the tree of life, but another piece of the puzzle that enables us to reconstruct what ecosystems looked like and how they functioned tens of millions of years ago.” Lead Authors of the study. Dolev Fabrikant (right), Dr. Leonidas Romanos Davranoglau (left), Photo credit: Dolev Fabrikant

snapshot.title: Scientists found a 9-million-year-old capybara relative's tooth in Chile's Atacama Desert, one of Earth's driest places; the water-loving animal adds evidence that the region once supported wetlands and a much wetter climate
snapshot.evidenceText: The Atacama Desert is a landscape where water is measured in millimetres, not rivers. Today, parts of this vast Chilean desert receive almost no rain, making the discovery of an animal that depended on plentiful freshwater all the more surprising. Buried in an ancient deposit, a single tooth has now offered scientists another glimpse of a very different Atacama, one with wetlands, vegetation and enough water to support a large, semi-aquatic rodent.According to a report by Live Science, researchers identified the roughly 9-million-year-old tooth as belonging to an extinct relative of today's capybaras, adding to growing evidence that the Atacama was not continuously hyperarid throughout its long geological history.A surprising fossil in the desertThe Atacama occupies northern Chile and is considered one of the oldest and driest deserts on Earth. Its hyperarid core receives less than 2 millimetres of rainfall per month in some areas. The region's extreme dryness is partly linked to its geography. The Chilean Coast Range blocks moisture arriving from the Pacific, while the Andes restrict moisture from the Atlantic. However, geological research suggests that the desert's aridity began taking shape millions of years before the Andes reached their present heights, adds the online report by Live Science.The newly discovered tooth provides another reason to reconsider how the region looked in the distant past, the report claims.As per Live Science, the fossil belonged to a large capybara relative identified as Hydrochoerus and Cardiatherium, which lived during the late Miocene. Modern capybaras are the world's largest rodents and depend heavily on stable freshwater environments. They feed on vegetation that also requires sufficient water to grow. Finding one in today's Atacama therefore points towards an environment dramatically different from the barren landscape visible now.Evidence of an ancient wetlandThe tooth was discovered in a geological layer containing evidence of a shallow marine environment that existed between about 7 million and 10 million years ago, claims the report. It was not an isolated clue. Researchers have also found microscopic plant remains known as phytoliths, indicating that palms, grasses, gingers and other flowering plants once grew in the region. Together, these discoveries paint a picture of a landscape that periodically supported far more water and vegetation than the Atacama does today.Other fossil evidence from the region has pointed to freshwater fish and crocodiles, strengthening the possibility that wetlands and waterways periodically spread across parts of the desert. The capybara relative adds another piece to that ecological puzzle because its semi-aquatic lifestyle would have required access to dependable water.How did capybaras get there?According to Live Science, the discovery also raises a geographical mystery. The Andes presented a formidable barrier between the animal's likely habitats farther east and the fossil site in northern Chile, with elevations reaching around 5,500 metres. Researchers suggest the animals may have travelled instead along South America's western coast, moving between wetlands, rivers and other freshwater habitats. The tooth itself also makes long-distance transport an unlikely explanation. Its size makes it difficult to imagine being carried hundreds of kilometres by wind, while a waterway capable of transporting such material would itself point towards a wetter environment.A changing picture of the AtacamaThe fossil does not mean the entire Atacama was once a lush landscape. Rather, it strengthens the case that the region experienced periods of significantly wetter conditions during the late Miocene. For a desert famous for its extreme dryness, the tiny fossil offers a surprisingly big lesson: landscapes that appear permanently hostile today can have remarkably different histories. The capybara tooth is another fragment of that history, revealing a time when water-loving mammals could survive in a place that now seems almost entirely defined by its absence.Images Courtesy: istock and Science Alert
