snapshot.title: New large docodont fossil sheds light on Jurassic mammaliaform diversity
snapshot.evidenceText: SHENYANG, Oct. 11 (Xinhua) -- An international team led by Chinese scientists has discovered a new docodont mammaliaform species, the largest known of its kind, in Jurassic strata dating back about 160 million years, enriching scientific understanding of Jurassic mammaliaform diversity. The new species has been named Megacauda sungei. Its fossil specimen, discovered in Ningcheng, north China's Inner Mongolia Autonomous Region, measures roughly 52 centimeters in length and is estimated to have weighed around 2 kilograms, making it the largest known docodont mammaliaform. Its skull is clearly preserved, its trunk is robust, and its most striking feature is an unusually long, coiled tail. The specimen also retains well-preserved pelvic bones, hind limbs and tail vertebrae, suggesting it was adapted for swimming. Based on its distinctive teeth, researchers believe it could have hunted small animals living in the same environment, with a lifestyle possibly similar to that of the modern platypus. The study also sheds light on the animal's throat structure. The bones in its throat are similar to those of modern mammals, suggesting that behaviors such as swallowing, lapping and suckling may have already existed in the early ancestors of mammals, long before modern mammal groups appeared. "Mammaliaforms from the Mesozoic are often imagined as tiny creatures under dinosaur feet, but Megacauda sungei clearly raises the size limit of this group," said Li Yikun, an associate professor at Shenyang Normal University in northeast China. The study was published online in the journal Nature on Oct. 7. ■

representative.title: Jurassic fossil reveals ancient origins of how mammals drink milk
representative.author: Ohio University

snapshot.title: Jurassic fossil reveals ancient origins of how mammals drink milk
snapshot.evidenceText: edited by Sadie Harley , reviewed by Robert Egan This article has been reviewed according to Science X's editorial process and policies . Editors have highlighted the following attributes while ensuring the content's credibility: An international team of researchers has uncovered new evidence illuminating the evolutionary origins of one of the defining features of mammals: the ability to suckle and consume milk during infancy. Their findings, published in Nature , suggest that key anatomical structures required for mammalian suckling, swallowing and breastfeeding behaviors evolved nearly 165 million years ago, long before the appearance of modern mammals. The findings describe a newly discovered species called Megacauda sungei, a large mammaliaform that lived during the Middle Jurassic Period in what is now Inner Mongolia, China. The research was led by scientists from the University of Chicago, Shenyang Normal University, Shandong University of Science and Technology, the University of Bonn and Ohio University. Using high-resolution microCT imaging, the team reconstructed the skull and skeletal anatomy of the fossil. They discovered an unexpected combination of traits. Megacauda had specialized blade-like cheek teeth resembling those of modern seals, a platypus-like pelvis and an otter-like tail, indicating it was likely a semiaquatic predator that hunted small vertebrates and invertebrates in freshwater environments. More significantly, the researchers identified a pair of small bony projections on the roof of the mouth that closely resemble features found in living therian mammals, a group that includes marsupials (such as kangaroos and opossums) and placental mammals (such as elephants and humans). In modern mammals, these structures help support the soft palate and muscles involved in suckling, swallowing and protecting the airway. Because soft tissues are rarely preserved in fossils, scientists have long struggled to determine when these important feeding structures first evolved. "The anatomy of Megacauda suggests that structures involved in coordinating swallowing and sucking had already begun to evolve by the Middle Jurassic. This discovery helps us better understand the biological foundations of one of the defining characteristics of mammals: feeding young with milk," said Zhe-Xi Luo, Ph.D., professor of organismal biology and anatomy at the University of Chicago and senior author of the study. The researchers also found highly specialized hyoid bones in the throat region. In living mammals, these bones help anchor muscles for swallowing. Together, the evidence suggests that Megacauda likely possessed an early version of the coordinated muscular system used by modern mammals to move milk and food safely from the mouth to the esophagus. The discovery challenges a longstanding assumption about how these structures evolved. Researchers found that the newly identified therian-like bony hooks existed alongside more primitive bony ridges known from earlier mammaliaforms and mammalian ancestors. Their coexistence in the same animal suggests the modern structures did not evolve directly from the primitive ridges as previously believed. "This fossil captures an important stage in mammalian evolution," said Luo. "For decades, scientists have wanted to know when the soft-tissue structures necessary for suckling and complex swallowing first appeared. Megacauda provides some of the clearest evidence yet that many of these innovations emerged well before the rise of modern mammals." The research also has important implications for understanding living mammals. While therian mammals use a sophisticated suckling mechanism supported by the soft palate and constrictor muscles, monotremes such as platypuses and echidnas use a different method for obtaining milk and lack some of these anatomical features. The new evidence suggests that monotremes likely lost elements of the ancestral suckling apparatus during their evolutionary history and developed an alternative method of milk intake. Beyond feeding biology, Megacauda highlights the remarkable ecological diversity of mammaliaforms living alongside dinosaurs. At approximately the size of a modern otter, it is among the largest known Jurassic mammaliaforms and represents one of the earliest examples of adaptation to a semiaquatic lifestyle. "These discoveries continue to reveal that the age of dinosaurs was also a time of extraordinary evolutionary innovation among early mammals," said Peishu Li, Ph.D., assistant professor in the Department of Biomedical Sciences at the Ohio University Heritage College of Osteopathic Medicine and a co-author of the study. representative.title: Mississauga election 2026: Mayoral candidates talk redeveloping Living Arts Centre, platform policy planks
representative.author: Nick Westoll

snapshot.title: Mississauga mayoral candidates talk redeveloping Living Arts Centre, platform policy planks
snapshot.evidenceText: With two-and-a-half weeks to go until Mississauga election day, talk about potentially redeveloping a notable chunk of the city’s downtown entered into the campaign on Thursday as mayoral candidates put forward various policy ideas and focuses. While unveiling the remaining parts of her campaign platform, Bonnie Crombie said she wants to put a stop to studying the potential demolition of the Living Arts Centre as part of a massive redevelopment project. “I will cancel Carolyn Parrish’s proposed redevelopment of the Living Arts Centre and surrounding civic lands, a $2.5-billion vanity project at a time when residents are struggling with everyday bills; this is the wrong priority,” she told reporters, arguing any potential municipal funding should be redirected to other priorities and initiatives. The Living Arts Centre, located just north of Mississauga city hall and west of Square One, opened in 1997. It has a 1,300-seat main auditorium along with various meeting rooms and exhibition spaces. Earlier in 2026, Mississauga city council voted to begin a study and consultation process that could ultimately result in a downtown transformation. The major part of the planning centres around potentially replacing the Living Arts Centre and a nearby park, which totals around 12 acres, with a new convention centre, hotel, music hub, offices, apartments and retail spaces. It is not clear when a possible vote on whether or not to proceed with that vision could be held. While making an announcement on providing additional infrastructure and supports for Ridgeway Plaza as part of a broader small business plan, Alvin Tedjo rejected the idea of proceeding with the potential massive redevelopment. “The mayor’s plan to build a $2.5-billion convention centre is a terrible idea; no one is asking for this. They’re also going to be taking out the parkland and the parking in the area. That green space is so valued for the residents who live in that area,” he said, adding he wants residents to help determine the future for the area and is open to potentially renovating the Living Arts Centre. Dipika Damerla also rejected the idea, saying she wants to proceed with a vision for downtown Mississauga that is focused on a health care innovation district. “[It] will bring young talent and make Mississauga the Silicon Valley of commercializing health care innovation,” she said, pointing to existing and upcoming hospital and education infrastructure in the city and region. Speaking with CityNews ahead of an apartment groundbreaking in Port Credit Thursday afternoon, Parrish said she backs the proposed redevelopment concept. She said a majority of the required funding would come from the private sector and noted there would be an elevated park for residents to use. “I think it’s a fabulous job creator. I think it’s a wonderful way to increase our income and taxes at the City and to enliven our city centre, it’s perfect,” she said. “We’re a modern city and we’re looking at modern ideas.” Parrish said if the plan proceeded, the Living Arts Centre would not be torn down until a new building gets erected. She also said the convention centre could be as big as 300,000 square feet and added she would like to see a five-star hotel opened to support the redevelopment. As advance voting continues in Mississauga until the end of Sunday , the leading Mississauga mayoral candidates continue to put forward policy ideas and focuses. During her announcement Thursday afternoon, Crombie touted various policy proposals on a variety of areas. “I will put the priorities of Mississaugans first and they’re clear: To bring taxes under control, protect jobs, attract investment, get Mississauga moving again and make our neighbourhoods safer,” she said. Damerla told CityNews she plans to keep campaigning and promoting the key themes of her campaign. “Here [are] the highlights of my plan: Freeze property taxes in 2027 and thereafter keep them at or below inflation, stop the waste at city hall (and) hire an independent auditor general, stop the $100 million that we’re bleeding every year to Brampton by fixing the unfair policing formula, (and) allowing ‘six-plexes’ as of right on certain arterial roads to make housing more affordable and realistic for young families,” she said Thursday afternoon. When asked what she wanted to accomplish if she gets elected for a full term, Parrish said she was focused on two areas. “Housing, I want to keep that up. I was at a topping-off ceremony yesterday for three towers on the other side of Port Credit. This is a ground-breaker, and it’s all because of the incentive that we brought in as a council,” she said Thursday afternoon, adding the changes have resulted in support from developers. “We’ve got to work on the taxes, that’s a big one. Step one was getting the road maintenance moved down from the region so we don’t have to subsidize Caledon $30 million next year, another $18 million or so on waste that we’ve moved down from the region. “Of course I’m working on the police budget, which is a 38 (per cent)-62 (per cent) split (with Brampton) and I do have a commitment from the premier that he is going to do it (addressing the funding disparity between the two cities).” Tedjo, speaking outside of Ridgeway Plaza Thursday morning, talked about his small business policy plank, which is part of his broader overall campaign platform. He said initiatives include a new 100-day guarantee for “qualified small-business permits,” small business hubs with “more affordable commercial space,” and expanded youth opportunities. He also said he would pursue bringing a Peel Regional Police substation to the plaza, which has seen crackdowns by officers amid concerns over nuisance gatherings , and extra parking at a nearby site to support the plaza. “Local entrepreneurs are spending too much time navigating city hall, small businesses are struggling to stay afloat and younger people are having a harder time getting a foot in the door. My plan will transform the City of Mississauga from a barrier into a partner,” Tedjo said. Click here for a list of all 14 candidates running for mayor. Election day in Mississauga and all of Ontario’s municipalities is on Oct. 26. representative.title: The animal kingdom may be 800 million years old: Mongolia removes a ceiling from the molecular clock
representative.author: Guido Donati

snapshot.title: The animal kingdom may be 800 million years old: Mongolia removes a ceiling from the molecular clock
snapshot.evidenceText: A team from Oxford, Berkeley, Zurich and Yale places the origin of animals between 800 and 700 million years ago, 126 to 226 million years before the oldest animal fossils. The argument rests on an absence in a Mongolian rock, not on a new fossil. The study appeared in Science Advances on 2 October 2026. The dates in play for the origin of animals, in millions of years ago: the molecular-clock estimate of Lole Durbin et al., the deposits proposed as a maximum limit, the Kheseen Biota, the biomarkers, the Weng’an Biota and the earliest animal fossils. Ages and localities marked with an asterisk come from the University of Oxford press release. Chart produced by ScienceOnline from data in Lole Durbin O.M. et al., Science Advances 2026, doi 10.1126/sciadv.aeg6289.Image file: 2026-10-08_02_grafico_en.png In Mongolia there is a rock that preserves microfossils exceptionally well. It is called the Kheseen Biota and it formed between 550 and 526 million years ago, when animals certainly existed. It holds no definite animal.That absence is the starting point of a study by Orin Lole Durbin, Eliel Anttila, Derek Briggs, Francis Macdonald and Ross Anderson, published in Science Advances on 2 October 2026. Lole Durbin is first author. Anderson, of the Museum of Natural History at the University of Oxford, leads the work. The team includes researchers from Berkeley, ETH Zurich and Yale.The problem is one of dates. Lipid biomarkers, fossil molecules left by cell membranes, point to animals before 635 million years ago. Body fossils go back no further than 574 million. Between the two lies a gap of about sixty million years with no visible animal. Molecular clocks are meant to bridge it. Differences in the DNA of living species build up over time, and counting them dates the split between two lineages. The clock has to be calibrated with fossils. A fossil fixes a group’s minimum age, because the group existed when that organism died. A maximum age is harder to set. It needs a deposit where animals would have been preserved had they been there, and where they are missing.For years that role went to the Weng’an Biota in China, dated by the University of Oxford press release to about 590 million years. Weng’an preserves microfossils in fine detail and contains no definite animals. Many analyses took it as a ceiling, with no animals before Weng’an. The team compared Weng’an with Kheseen. The two sites share similar preservation and similar microfossils, and neither shows a definite animal. representative.title: Concerns as Residents Eat Fish From Fuel-hit River Nyando Following Leak | Dawan Africa | Dawan Africa
representative.author: Hassan Wekesa

snapshot.title: Concerns as Residents Eat Fish From Fuel-hit River Nyando Following Leak
snapshot.evidenceText: Kenya, 11 October 2026 - Some residents of the villages neighbouring the riverbanks of the River Nyando in Kisumu County are eating fish caught after fuel leaked into the water from a Kenya Pipeline Company (KPC) line. Health concerns are mounting, while Kisumu Governor Prof Anyang’ Nyong’o on Friday demanded an impartial investigation into the fuel leak. The leak, reported on 8 October 2026, occurred on the Sinendet-Kisumu petroleum pipeline, which runs beside the river near Muhoroni, Kibigori and Ahero. Some locals risked their lives trying to collect fuel floating on the water. Others have since been catching and eating fish from the affected stretch. In their initial response, KPC officials suspected that the leak was caused by intentional interference with the line. They have since alerted detectives from the Directorate of Criminal Investigations (DCI) and the Energy and Petroleum Regulatory Authority (EPRA) to investigate and arrest any culprits. Accounts of what exactly happened differ. It was first reported that the pipeline was damaged while workers dug to build gabions on the riverbank to curb erosion ahead of the El Niño rains. However, on Friday last week, other residents near the affected section claimed that Kenya Railways workers maintaining the railway line struck the pipe with an excavator, exposing it to leakage. Detectives will be able to establish what exactly happened, whether it was the result of gabion construction, accidental breakage by railway workers or intentional tampering with the line. On 9 October 2026, Governor Nyong’o called for impartial investigations and fair compensation for residents around Kibigori and Muhoroni. He said the reported spill from KPC infrastructure poses serious risks to public health, the environment, livelihoods and critical national infrastructure. He urged the agencies to establish the facts quickly and professionally, without prejudging the outcome, and to ensure accountability where wrongdoing is proved. He insisted that containment, clean-up, environmental assessments and remediation proceed without delay. The extent of contamination and the risks to water sources, ecosystems, public health and livelihoods must be established, he said, with clear public guidance on precautions. All affected individuals, households, farmers and businesses should receive fair compensation for verified losses, in a process that is transparent, accessible and sensitive to vulnerable households, the governor added. He commended KPC’s initial response but said the company and relevant agencies must strengthen safeguards through better surveillance, routine integrity inspections, detection of unauthorised interference, prompt reporting and coordinated emergency response. He urged residents to remain calm, cooperate with authorities and share credible information with investigators. One thing is clear: the residents are facing a chemical incident, which the World Health Organization (WHO) describes as an uncontrolled release of a toxic substance, potentially resulting in harm to public health and the environment. WHO further explains that chemical incidents can occur as a result of natural events or as a result of accidental or intentional events. “These incidents can be sudden and acute or have a slow onset when there is a ‘silent’ release of a chemical. They can also range from small releases to full-scale major emergencies,” WHO states. These chemical incidents can be caused by anthropogenic or technological events. Besides oil spills and leaks from storage units during transportation, other chemical incidents include explosions at factories that store or use chemicals, contamination of the food or water supply with a chemical, deliberate release of chemicals in conflict or terrorism, and outbreaks of disease associated with chemical exposure. Between 2009 and 2018 alone, about 65,000 people died as a result of technological events. A fuel leak poses a major health risk because crude oil contains polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs), and these carry over into refined products such as diesel, super petrol and jet fuel, which the Sinendet-Kisumu line transports. Several PAHs are genotoxic and carcinogenic. Fuels also contain benzene, for which Kenya’s Onshore National Contingency Plan sets a worker exposure limit of 1 part per million over eight hours. The plan also notes that light products such as diesel and jet fuel are more acutely toxic than heavier oils. River Nyando is a freshwater, non-navigable water body, and most of the fish there are teleosts, or bony fish. According to scientific researchers, teleost fish can metabolise PAHs efficiently, breaking them down and excreting them. This typically leaves lower residues in their edible flesh than in shellfish and, in principle, reduces the risk to people who eat them. That does not make fish from fuel-affected water safe. Metabolism may not keep pace with heavy or continuing exposure, and oil can taint flesh and...

representative.title: River swallows char beside Padma Bridge, 4 villages under water | The Daily Star
representative.author: Jahid Hasan

snapshot.title: River swallows char beside Padma Bridge, 4 villages under water
snapshot.evidenceText: Copyright: Any unauthorized use or reproduction of The Daily Star content for commercial purposes is strictly prohibited and constitutes copyright infringement liable to legal action. The clang of hammers and crowbars echoed across Alam-Khankandi village yesterday morning as families dismantled their own homes, racing against a river that has already devoured four char villages and is eating into a fifth. In two years, 1,803 families in five villages have lost their homes to erosion of char land beside the Padma Bridge. Of them, 303 families in Alam-Khankandi have been displaced since August, according to the Shariatpur Water Development Board (WDB) and Purba Naodoba Union Parishad. About 150 families still living in the village are at imminent risk. The char emerged about three decades ago in Painpara mouza on the northern bank of the Padma. According to WDB sources, the char formed Naodoba Union Parishad, which includes six villages and constitutes wards 2 and 3. During a visit yesterday, this correspondent found families preparing to leave. Those already homeless lived beside roads or in tin-sheet shelters on rented land, while others planned to cross the Padma by engine-run trawlers to rent land in Zajira or Munshiganj. Duluna Begum, 60, travelled from Digholi in Bikrampur, Munshiganj, after her daughter called her at night on her phone to tell her that her in-laws’ house was being devoured by the river. “I came here early in the morning with other people to help them dismantle the house before the river swallowed it whole,” she told The Daily Star. “Five days ago, nine bighas of cultivated land were lost in river erosion. Now where will my daughter go with her four children?” Maksuda Begum, 55, of Farazi Kandi in Zajira also came with helpers to dismantle her daughter’s in-laws’ house. For Md Shahid Fakir, 38, erosion destroyed both his livelihood and his house. He once owned 25 bighas, where he grew ginger, garlic, and vegetables, and a trawler to carry the produce across the river. “Having lost everything to river erosion, I am now destitute. I have no place to call my own anymore,” he said. He is now building a shack on land lent to him by someone. “If the government gave a little space to live on khas (government) land, then I could somehow spend my life raising a house there,” he said. Last year, erosion destroyed four villages in ward 2 of the union. They are Ahammad Majhikandi, Mongol Majhikandi, Alim Uddin Beparikandi, and Majhikandi, leaving around 1,500 families homeless. Painpara Government Primary School No 52 was washed away in August 2024, and about a year later Rezia Amin Government Primary School and a community clinic followed, said Altaf Hossain Khan, chairman of Purba Naodoba Union Parishad. At least 5,000 acres of cropland in Painpara mouza have been lost over the past year, and No 122 Altaf Khan Government Primary School is now under threat, he added. A 4.5-kilometre paved road built in 2021 has lost four kilometres to the river. Electricity reached 1,200 consumers across the six villages through a 30-kilometre transmission line, including submarine cables along the riverbed, at a cost of Tk 4.5 crore. Nazmul Hasan, deputy general manager (technical) of Shariatpur Palli Bidyut Samity, said 22 kilometres of the line had been dismantled as villages disappeared. Another 3.5 kilometres were removed from the Alam-Khankandi area in the past three months to keep the line from falling into the river, though supply continued. Residents now living in the open without power can apply for reconnection under existing rules if they relocate near electricity poles, he said. The chairman of Purba Naodoba Union Parishad said residents had informed the WDB repeatedly about the erosion for the last 3-4 years, but saw no effective action from their part. He said some displaced families had moved to Louhajang in Munshiganj, while others rented homes or leased land in Shariatpur. At least 250 families who cannot afford either have taken shelter at a construction yard near the Padma Bridge’s southern end, living in fear as the Bangladesh Bridge Authority occasionally serves eviction notices. Appeals to the UNO and DC have yielded little, he said. With few jobs remaining nearby, many families struggle to eat adequately, he added. “The way the WDB treats us makes us feel like as though we are criminals. They do not answer our calls, nor do they want to speak to us even when they visit,” he said. MP Sayeed Ahmed distributed rice, lentils and dry food among 273 affected families about a month ago, the chairman said. WDB Executive Engineer Md Milton Hossain said the board was aware of the erosion and had informed higher authorities. “Protecting the mainland is our priority in cases of river erosion. That is why it is often not possible to take measures in char areas,” he said, adding that the Ministry of Water Resources was not currently taking emergency measures there. He said he would inspect the area and take necessary steps, subject to approval from higher authorities. editorial.evidence: Copyright: Any unauthorized use or reproduction of The Daily Star content for commercial purposes is strictly prohibited and constitutes copyright infringement liable to legal action. The clang of hammers and crowbars echoed across Alam-Khankandi village yesterday morning as families dismantled their own homes, racing against a river that has already devoured four char villages and is eating into a fifth. In two years, 1,803 families in five villages have lost their homes to erosion of char land beside the Padma Bridge. Of them, 303 families in Alam-Khankandi have been displaced since August, according to the Shariatpur Water Development Board (WDB) and Purba Naodoba Union Parishad. About 150 families still living in the village are at imminent risk. The char emerged about three decades ago in Painpara mouza on the northern bank of the Padma. According to WDB sources, the char formed Naodoba Union Parishad, which includes six villages and constitutes wards 2 and 3. During a visit yesterday, this correspondent found families preparing to leave. “Five days ago, nine bighas of cultivated land were lost in river erosion. Now where will my daughter go with her four children?” For Md Shahid Fakir, 38, erosion destroyed both his livelihood and his house. “Having lost everything to river erosion, I am now destitute. I have no place to call my own anymore,” he said. Last year, erosion destroyed four villages in ward 2 of the union. The chairman of Purba Naodoba Union Parishad said residents had informed the WDB repeatedly about the erosion for the last 3-4 years, but saw no effective action from their part. He said he would inspect the area and take necessary steps, subject to approval from higher authorities.

evaluation.reason: A concrete, tragic example of land erosion in Bangladesh affecting specific villages and families.
evaluation.strongest_fact: In two years, 1,803 families in five villages near the Padma Bridge have lost their homes to river erosion.

representative.title: Kauai’s Hawaiian salt makers seek help restoring harvest area | Hawaii News Now
representative.author: Dillon Ancheta

snapshot.title: Kauai’s Hawaiian salt makers seek help restoring harvest area
snapshot.evidenceText: HANAPEPE (HawaiiNewsNow) - The 22 Kauai families keeping traditional Hawaiian salt making alive in Hanapepe are seeking the community’s help to restore their harvest site. Storm surge from Hurricane Lowell drastically changed the area. “The sand dunes were depleted. It was gone. It was a new landscape. I didn’t recognize it,” said Malia Nobrega-Olivera. Nobrega-Olivera and her ‘ohana have been Hawaiian salt makers for decades. She said the storm damage was the worst she’s seen. “It is different from all of my 55 years growing up in Hanapepe. It was a new space,” she said. Lowell pushed incredible amounts of sand into the beach park and salt beds, changing the composition of the land, making the clay more porous. “We are using this clay to seal the aina so that it can evaporate over time. But with the mixture of the sand, the practice doesn’t exist,” she said. Nobrega-Olivera is also the president of Hui Hana Pa’akai O Hanapepe, the group established for the salt makers. Together, they’re hosting a community work day on Saturday to restore the area. “Bring your tools. If you don’t have, just show up and your hands will be a good enough tools to be with us,” she said. They’ve also been getting assistance from the county and other partners to move sand as they prepare for the work day. There have been floods in recent years, and the group was already working on a dune restoration project. “Our practice is dictated by the weather, so you know, we wait until everything dries up and then we’re ready to go back in,” Nobrega-Olivera said. “And once the place is flooded, our salt-making time gets shorter and shorter.” She added the best harvest she’s had yielded 55 large buckets worth of salt. But if conditions aren’t right, that number is drastically less. Steeped in tradition, Hawaiian Salt is crucial to the culture. “Salt is not only used for our food, salt is used for medicinal purposes, for healing in all different ways,” she said. The workday runs from 8 a.m. to 2 p.m., and more will be scheduled in the future. To stay connected with the group, contact them online at ProtectPaakai.org .

representative.title: L.A. homeless agency meeting canceled after voter turnout surge - Los Angeles Times
representative.author: Doug Smith

snapshot.title: Bass-led turnout surge crashes meeting to replace L.A. homeless outreach agency
snapshot.evidenceText: It's not unusual for a public meeting to be canceled for lack of a quorum. But there isn't even a word for what happened Friday when a once-obscure board canceled a meeting to decide the future of homeless services in Los Angeles because too many people came to vote. More than 1,500 potential voters signed up for a meeting of the Los Angeles Continuum of Care board to pick a replacement for the core duties of the beleaguered Los Angeles Homeless Services Authority. Under the board's unusual charter, they all were eligible to vote merely because of their interest in homelessness. The onslaught was organized by Los Angeles Mayor Karen Bass, who sent out a blast message through her communications networks urging people to join the meeting via Zoom to vote down the board's recommendation that Los Angeles County assume those duties. The response was overwhelming, but it didn't work. Over cries of foul from those who came in person, the board's attorney Shayla Myers announced the meeting was canceled because the Zoom channel had a capacity of only 1,000. Later, the board issued a formal statement saying, "The vote had to be continued today to ensure that all LA CoC members would be able to participate, given an unexpectedly high number of individuals who joined the online meeting." Bass and four City Council members then put out a statement lambasting the board for a failure that disenfranchised members. "Without collaboration and transparency, management of this complex issue will continue to falter, and worse, our unhoused neighbors will continue to suffer," the statement said. The cancellation deepens a crisis over the region's federally mandated homelessness functions. At stake is control over the annual homelessness count, the database that tracks every interaction with homeless people, the matching system that determines who receives housing and the responsibility for submitting applications for federal funding on behalf of dozens of local agencies. The Trump administration touched off the crisis in June when it suspended LAHSA as the agency performing those functions, citing a history of mismanagement and possible fraud. The U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development said local homeless service providers would have to apply directly to it for funding. LAHSA contested the move in federal court. U.S. District Judge David O. Carter temporarily stayed the suspension, keeping LAHSA in place for now but allowing 60 days to choose a replacement to assume its duties. That decision, upheld on appeal, put the onus on the Continuum of Care, an amorphous entity with a board and open membership that had long functioned as an appendage of LAHSA but actually had the statutory power to hire or fire the agency. Carter ordered the CoC, as it is commonly called, to report on its recommendations Tuesday and set Oct. 27 as the date to name the new agency. The CoC board, which includes representatives of homeless services contractors, hired outside consultants to set up an emergency bidding process and score the applicants. The City of Los Angeles applied for two of LAHSA's functions, the homeless database and the matching system, but scored below Los Angeles County in both. The county applied for all four functions and won the recommendation. The final step was a vote of the membership on Friday. The meltdown was foreseeable. A member of LAHSA's governing commission predicted it in an August LinkedIn post. Noting that membership “consists of persons and entities interested in collaborative, solution-oriented planning to address homelessness in LA County,” Justin Szlasa concluded, "that could arguably include tens or even hundreds of thousands of people. No comprehensive list of general members currently exists," and it would be almost impossible to compile one. "As the LA CoC takes on more authority and moves out of the orbit of LAHSA, effort should be made to broaden and deepen engagement with stakeholders in our homeless response system ... who are all, by definition, members of the LA CoC," Szlasa wrote. Bass turned that advice into a crash course. As enrollment in Friday's Zoom passed the 1,000 mark, Myers, the CoC attorney, told those present in the downtown meeting room that "because we have reached capacity on Zoom and CoC members are not able to participate, we have to continue this." The board is now working to upgrade its Zoom account and has yet to set a new date. Bass and the council members blamed the CoC for not planning adequately for a large audience. "Angelenos want a voice in the future of homelessness services, and they were silenced today. The current proposal for County-only administration, recommended by the LA CoC Board, leaves no room for those voices to be heard," the statement said. Ben Kay, chair of the CoC board, countered that it could not have anticipated the mayor and City Council using their "immense communications infrastructure to push public turnout" to defeat the recommendation. "Suggesting the board was unprepared for the city's unprecedented actions plays directly into the hands of HUD, which started all of this by saying the L.A. region shouldn't be allowed to make its own decisions about homeless services," Kay said. In a statement Saturday, Supervisor Lindsey Horvath said that, "failing to hold yesterday’s meeting is unacceptable and erodes public trust." Horvath said the county is prepared to partner with every city in the county to "listen to their concerns, and work toward solutions that address them." The county has committed that the City of Los Angeles would "at a minimum" maintain its access to the database and matching system, Horvath said. Times staff writer David Zahniser contributed to this report.
snapshot.imageAlt: Los Angeles, CA - June 02, 2026: LA Mayor Karen Bass speaks at the Mayor Bass' election party for the California 2026 Primaries at the LINE Hotel on Tuesday, June 2, 2026 in Los Angeles, CA. (Carlin Stiehl/For The Times)

snapshot.title: OrbitalHub » CHIME detects cosmic hydrogen on its own
snapshot.evidenceText: Domain is for sale. $50,000,000.00 USD. Direct any inquiries to contact@orbitalhub.com. The Canadian Hydrogen Intensity Mapping Experiment, run out of a low-slung cluster of wire-mesh cylinders near Penticton, British Columbia, has just done something the rest of cosmology has been waiting on for the better part of two decades. In a paper published in The Astrophysical Journal on 28 September 2026 and posted to arXiv as 2511.19620, the CHIME Collaboration reports the first standalone detection of the cosmological 21-centimeter signal, the faint radio glow of neutral hydrogen from an era when the universe was roughly five billion years old. The result reached a signal-to-noise ratio of 12.5 across 94 nights of observing, a clean confirmation that intensity mapping can carry cosmological information without leaning on any other telescope. The detection matters because it removes a crutch that earlier 21cm cosmology work could not do without. To pick a faint hydrogen signal out of the radio sky, every previous CHIME result had to be cross-correlated with an external galaxy or quasar catalog, so that any structure showing up in both maps could be trusted. That technique works, but it ties a hydrogen experiment to the schedule and depth of someone else’s survey. The new measurement is an auto-correlation, meaning the team trusted only CHIME’s own data and still recovered a statistically unambiguous clustering signal. Splitting the 608.2 to 707.8 megahertz frequency window in two yields independent detections at 8.7 and 9.2 sigma. Two independent confirmations in a single dataset is the kind of robustness that turns a hint into a measurement. The reason this is exciting rather than merely incremental comes down to what intensity mapping is meant to do. Galaxy surveys like DESI, Euclid, and the Vera Rubin Observatory’s LSST build their maps by detecting and counting individual galaxies, a process that consumes enormous telescope time and tends to miss the dim, hydrogen-rich galaxies where most of the universe’s atoms actually live. CHIME does something different. Its four 100-metre cylindrical reflectors look at the whole northern sky every day, with no moving parts, and instead of resolving individual galaxies they sum the faint 21cm emission from millions of unresolved sources inside each patch of sky. The result is a low-resolution three-dimensional map of where the neutral hydrogen is, calibrated by redshift because cosmic expansion has stretched the original 21cm line into longer and longer wavelengths the further back in time one looks. CHIME’s full operating band runs from 400 to 800 megahertz, which corresponds to redshifts between roughly 2.5 and 0.8, an epoch the collaboration describes as substantially younger than the one surrounding Earth today but old enough to capture the period when dark energy began to dominate the cosmic energy budget. The new paper uses only the cleaner half of that window, between 608.2 and 707.8 megahertz, which corresponds to redshifts of 1.34 down to 1.01, with a mean redshift of 1.16. That is exactly the slice where the universe had finished its early formative fireworks but had not yet been completely taken over by the accelerating expansion driven by dark energy. Why this matters comes down to what the team can now attempt to do with the rest of the CHIME archive. The instrument has been collecting data continuously since first light in 2017 and the collaboration says it now has nearly seven years of observations in hand, most of which has not yet been analyzed. The Sept 28 paper uses 94 nights from 2019 only. If the new processing pipeline can keep extracting the auto-power spectrum cleanly from older data, CHIME should be able to push the measurement to higher redshifts, into the period when the universe was only about three billion years old, and to lower redshifts, where the dark-energy signal is strongest. That spans almost the entire window during which dark energy transitioned from negligible to dominant. Tracing the universe’s expansion history across that span, with a single instrument and a single tracer, is the prize the collaboration has been working toward since construction finished in 2017. The first detection was a 2023 paper that cross-correlated CHIME’s hydrogen maps with optical galaxy and quasar catalogs from eBOSS. That cross-correlation approach was scientifically productive but also exposed. The hydrogen experiment needed a second, much larger optical survey to confirm any signal. The new result flips that around: CHIME is now the primary instrument, and any cross-correlation with another survey becomes an optional consistency check rather than a requirement. Co-author Dr. Mark Halpern, a University of British Columbia physicist and CHIME principal investigator, called the result a fundamentally new way of probing the cosmos, built on an instrument conceived, paid for, and operated entirely by Canadian institutions. The technical work that made this possible is what most readers will not see and what most of the team spent the most time on. The 21cm cosmological signal at these frequencies is buried under several layers of brighter noise. Galactic synchrotron emission from our own Milky Way dominates by orders of magnitude. Distant radio galaxies and active galactic nuclei add another, structured layer on top. Human radio-frequency interference from satellites, radar, and cell towers adds a moving, partly unpredictable foreground. And small imperfections in CHIME’s receivers and correlator can mix otherwise smooth foreground signals into patterns that look like cosmological structure. Pulling the hydrogen out required the team to develop new radio-frequency interference detection algorithms, achromatic beamforming techniques that keep the telescope’s synthesized beam stable across frequency, and a foreground-filtering step that runs before time-averaging so that spectral leakage does not smear bright foregrounds into faint cosmological modes. Independent sub-band splits, null tests on the data, and many alternative processing choices were all checked before the team trusted the result, a process Chakraborty described as working very hard to convince ourselves that this was not a false alarm. The team’s analysis goes one step beyond the headline detection. In a companion paper they take the auto-power spectrum at face value as a measurement of how strongly neutral hydrogen clusters at redshift 1.16, and they compare it with predictions from the IllustrisTNG cosmological simulations. The observed hydrogen clustering disagrees with the simulated clustering by about 3.1 standard deviations for the TNG100 simulation volume and 4.0 standard deviations for the larger TNG300. That is not a crisis. The team reads the gap between observation and simulation as a clue about how tightly hydrogen is packed at the small, non-linear scales the new measurement is most sensitive to, not as evidence that the total hydrogen inventory is wrong. It shows that CHIME’s standalone data can test models of how gas actually populates galaxies and dark-matter halos, not just deliver a number for dark-energy cosmology. The long-term target is still baryon acoustic oscillations, the imprint of pressure waves from the hot early universe that act as a cosmic standard ruler. Tracking how that ruler stretches at different redshifts is one of the cleanest ways to measure how the universe’s expansion rate has changed over time, and therefore to test competing models for what dark energy is doing. The current measurement does not yet deliver BAO. Foreground-removal eliminates some of the largest-scale modes the BAO analysis needs, and the detected power spectrum occupies smaller non-linear scales where gravitational clustering has already scrambled the clean linear signal. What the Sept 28 paper establishes is the prerequisite: a telescope designed to map the universe through hydrogen can isolate that hydrogen without another survey pointing out where to look. The next step is to apply that capability across more of the CHIME archive and across the wider redshift range the telescope was built for. For a community that has spent more than a decade waiting for a 21cm cosmology result that does not need a galaxy survey attached, the message from the Okanagan Valley this week is that the wait is over, and the next decade of dark-energy measurements just got a new instrument. Co-author Dr. Mark Halpern, a University of British Columbia physicist and CHIME principal investigator, called the result a fundamentally new way of probing the cosmos, built on an instrument conceived, paid for, and operated entirely by Canadian institutions. The technical work that made this possible is what most readers will not see and what most of the team spent the most time on. The 21cm cosmological signal at these frequencies is buried under several layers of brighter noise. Galactic synchrotron emission from our own Milky Way dominates by orders of magnitude. Distant radio galaxies and active galactic nuclei add another, structured layer on top. Human radio-frequency interference from satellites, radar, and cell towers adds a moving, partly unpredictable foreground. And small imperfections in CHIME’s receivers and correlator can mix otherwise smooth foreground signals into patterns that look like cosmological structure. Pulling the hydrogen out required the team to develop new radio-frequency interference detection algorithms, achromatic beamforming techniques that keep the telescope’s synthesized beam stable across frequency, and a foreground-filtering step that runs before time-averaging so that spectral leakage does not smear bright foregrounds into faint cosmological modes. Independent sub-band splits, null tests on the data, and many alternative processing choices were all checked before the team trusted the result, a process Chakraborty described as working very hard to convince ourselves that this was not a false alarm. The team’s analysis goes one step beyond the headline detection. In a companion paper they take the auto-power spectrum at face value as a measurement of how strongly neutral hydrogen clusters at redshift 1.16, and they compare it with predictions from the IllustrisTNG cosmological simulations. The observed hydrogen clustering disagrees with the simulated clustering by about 3.1 standard deviations for the TNG100 simulation volume and 4.0 standard deviations for the larger TNG300. That is not a crisis. The team reads the gap between observation and simulation as a clue about how tightly hydrogen is packed at the small, non-linear scales the new measurement is most sensitive to, not as evidence that the total hydrogen inventory is wrong. The current measurement does not yet deliver BAO. Foreground-removal eliminates some of the largest-scale modes the BAO analysis needs, and the detected power spectrum occupies smaller non-linear scales where gravitational clustering has already scrambled the clean linear signal. What the Sept 28 paper establishes is the prerequisite: a telescope designed to map the universe through hydrogen can isolate that hydrogen without another survey pointing out where to look. editorial.evidence: Direct any inquiries to contact@orbitalhub.com. representative.title: Phantom land, false signature: How agents allegedly duped migrant worker quota system | Malaysiakini
representative.author: B Nantha Kumar

snapshot.title: Phantom land, false signature: How agents allegedly duped migrant worker quota system | Malaysiakini
snapshot.evidenceText: In a small office near Jalan Makbar Darat, Kuantan, Nazlan Mokhtar, 57, sits in his chair as usual. The secretary of Koperasi Kijang Mas Negeri Pahang Berhad has spent years managing the affairs of the cooperative’s thousands of members. However, for the past few months, that chair has felt much heavier to sit in. This is no ordinary tale of a village cooperative. This is the story of how a quota of 1,125 migrant workers, allegedly worth millions of ringgit on the black market of labour trading, was approved under the name of an Orang Asli cooperative - without the full knowledge of those who were supposed to sign off on it, through questionable methods, and with the possibility that the quota was misused. A Malaysiakini investigation revealed application documents built upon non-existent land acreage, agreements with an unlicensed company, the cooperative chairperson's signature allegedly being forged, and conflicting marriage records for a company director between two government agencies. In a small office near Jalan Makbar Darat, Kuantan, Nazlan Mokhtar, 57, sits in his chair as usual. The secretary of Koperasi Kijang Mas Negeri Pahang Berhad has spent years managing the affairs of the cooperative’s thousands of members. However, for the past few months, that chair has felt much heavier to sit in. This is no ordinary tale of a village cooperative. This is the story of how a quota of 1,125 migrant workers, allegedly worth millions of ringgit on the black market of labour trading, was approved under the name of an Orang Asli cooperative - without the full knowledge of those who were supposed to sign off on it, through questionable methods, and with the possibility that the quota was misused. A Malaysiakini investigation revealed application documents built upon non-existent land acreage, agreements with an unlicensed company, the cooperative chairperson's signature allegedly being forged, and conflicting marriage records for a company director between two government agencies. Meanwhile, the approved quota never brought a single worker to the cooperative’s land. "I’m stressed out," Nazlan said, half-joking, half-serious, during an interview with Malaysiakini . This story begins not with success, but with failure. The roots of Koperasi Kijang Mas can be traced back to the late 1980s, when it was known as Korporasi Orang Asli Maju Rompin. It was subsequently administered under the Orang Asli Affairs Department (JHEOA) and later the Orang Asli Development Department (Jakoa). According to Nazlan ( above ), in 2023, the cooperative applied for a migrant worker quota on its own through its committee member, but the application failed. For a cooperative already struggling with financial difficulties while its membership continued to shrink, any opportunity for an injection of manpower and new income looked like a way out. It was during that critical situation, according to Nazlan, that two individuals emerged in the cooperative's affairs. They were an Indian national man and a Malaysian woman. In the interview, Nazlan referred to the man as “Mr G” as the main agent, and the woman as "Ms K", stressing that these were not their real names. According to Nazlan, after the two came into the picture, the quota matters slipped out of the cooperative’s full control. "First, we applied for a migrant worker quota but were rejected. Then, they came in as agents to assist us. They handled everything, including preparing the application documents until more than 1,100 quotas were approved," he said. According to Nazlan, Mr G handled the second application entirely. As a result, a quota of 1,125 migrant workers was approved under the name of Koperasi Kijang Mas. However, there were several suspicious matters in the process. A document Malaysiakini sighted showed that an "Agreement Deed" was signed on Aug 1, 2024, between the cooperative and Agensi Pekerjaan Uni Jobs Sdn Bhd - a company with an address at Plaza Prima, Jalan Klang Lama, Kuala Lumpur. In the document, Uni Jobs was named the "contractor" while the cooperative was named the "landowner". The agreement appeared to give Uni Jobs the right to bring in migrant workers, manage them, and fulfil all rules, requirements, and welfare of the migrant workers, including all government regulations and wages. In return, the contractor was required to harvest rubber from the cooperative’s land. However, a check with the Human Resources Ministry revealed that Uni Jobs did not possess a valid Private Employment Agency (APS) Licence. This licence is a mandatory requirement under the law for any entity wishing to operate as an employment agency. Meanwhile, Nazlan claimed that the signature appearing above the cooperative chairperson’s name on the document was not his. In a police report lodged by Nazlan on behalf of the cooperative, he accused Mr G and Ms K, among other things, of forging the signature. Malaysiakini could not independently verify the signature forgery allegations. Additionally, Nazlan said the cooperative chairperson had never attended any interview session with the authorities for the migrant worker quota application. Another anomaly in the agreement document was the land size claimed to be owned by the cooperative. The document stated that the cooperative owned 4,500ha of land. The same figure is believed to have been used in the application handled by Uni Jobs to obtain the quota. However, that land size does not exist. Instead, Nazlan said, the actual size of the land cultivated by the cooperative for vegetable crops was only around 300 to 400 acres (121.4 to 161.9ha) - as seen by Malaysiakini when visiting the area. Besides the migrant worker quota issue, there were other anomalies surrounding the case. A search with the Companies Commission of Malaysia (SSM) found that Uni Jobs has two directors, both Malaysian citizens. Based on official documents from the Immigration Department, one of them is Mr G’s wife. However, a check by Malaysiakini with the National Registration Department (NRD) showed that the Malaysian woman was also married to a man of another nationality, and that marriage remained valid as they were not divorced. Malaysiakini has submitted official queries to the Home Ministry to clarify this discrepancy in records. Malaysiakini had also contacted Mr G, Ms K, both directors of Uni Jobs (including the woman alleged to be Mr G’s wife), and her lawful husband on Sept 1, 2026, to seek comments regarding the allegations against them, but has yet to receive a response. According to Nazlan, the real trouble began after the cooperative received approval for the quota. The cooperative waited for the workforce to arrive to develop their land, but days passed without certainty. When the cooperative tried to get the latest status on the workers, Ms K allegedly offered various excuses, including claiming that there were issues on the immigration side. As time went on without a single worker setting foot on the cooperative’s land, suspicions grew stronger. The cooperative eventually suspected that the two agents had illegally sold the quota to third parties and abused the cooperative’s name and status without any authorisation or legal power. "The quota of 1,125 migrant workers that was supposed to be used to develop the cooperative's land was issued and sold to third parties as a standalone commodity. "While the cooperative was merely a name on paper to validate the approval of the quota," he said. The real shock came when the Home Ministry itself contacted the cooperative. According to Nazlan, Home Ministry officers, together with Immigration Department officers, first came to Kuantan, and later requested cooperative representatives to attend a detailed interrogation session in Putrajaya. "When Home Ministry came to the office, they asked me, 'Do you know that these migrant workers have already entered the country?'" Nazlan asked, recalling the moment that changed everything. In Putrajaya, officers showed documents and interrogated the cooperative representatives. After determining that the cooperative had likely been duped, Home Ministry officers advised the cooperative to lodge a police report as a step to protect its own standing. On Jan 19, Nazlan lodged a report at the Travers police station in Brickfields, Kuala Lumpur. In the report, he denied the cooperative’s link to any involvement in the fraudulent activities, while also reporting the misuse and forgery of the cooperative's documents. He emphasised that the cooperative was not involved, did not sign any agreement, and received no payment or profit from the management or sale of the quota linked to the cooperative's name. Nazlan also requested the police to conduct a thorough investigation into Mr G, Ms K, and any other parties involved, as well as take legal action for offences of cheating, document forgery, breach of trust, and abetment. According to him, the actions caused reputational damage and legal risks to the cooperative. In response to Malaysiakini’s queries on the matter, the Home Ministry, together with the Peninsula Labour Department and the Malaysian Palm Oil Board, are taking action against the parties involved, particularly regarding document forgery offences, immigration offences, and alleged elements of human trafficking linked to the case. "The ministry has also conducted oversight inspections and further investigations, and found that there were parties involved in document forgery as well as elements of human trafficking. "This case also serves as another proof of how important it is for the Home Ministry to conduct transparent and comprehensive oversight inspection processes to ensure any misuse of migrant worker quotas can be detected and contained at an early stage," they added. At the end of the interview, when asked what his actual demands to the government were, Nazlan did not ask for compensation or drastic action. His request was much simpler. "I ask the government to pay attention to the relevant departments, whether regarding migrant labour or other matters, and take good care of them. "The Orang Asli, if no one guides them, they don't know about these things," he said. "We didn't even know we were walking into a trap and getting scammed. "We hope Home Ministry returns our quota so that we can bring in migrant workers to cultivate our land," Nazlan added. snapshot.title: A Distant Planet Emitted a Burst of Radio Waves. Why? - Nautilus
snapshot.evidenceText: Astronomers pinpoint the origin of a 10 billion‑year‑old millisecond signal from space More than 10 billion years ago, something in a distant galaxy gave off an incredibly bright burst of radio waves which lasted just a few milliseconds. In new research published today in Science , our team tracked it back to its origin in a small galaxy filled with many young stars, when the universe was only one-fifth of its current age. Fast radio bursts like this one are a mystery scientists have been trying to unravel for almost 20 years since they were first discovered. Our discovery is the most distant such burst whose host galaxy has yet been identified. Finding a Radio Signal from 10 Billion Years Ago We detected the burst, dubbed FRB 20240304B, with the MeerKAT radio telescope in South Africa, using a system called MeerTRAP which is designed to catch fast-changing transient radio signals from space in real time. The different frequencies of the radio burst arrived at slightly different times. We call this effect “dispersion”, and it happens because the signal has travelled through a lot of electrically charged material in space on its journey to Earth. By measuring the amount of dispersion, we can tell how much of this material the signal has passed through – which in turn lets us calculate how far the signal has travelled and how far away from us it was created. The FRB 20240304B burst showed a large amount of dispersion, which suggested it was probably coming from a great distance. We were also able to pinpoint its position on the sky. But when we looked at that position with large ground-based telescopes like the Keck Telescopes , we couldn’t see a host galaxy. The galaxy was simply too faint. So we turned to the James Webb Space Telescope ( JWST ). The space telescope’s infrared camera revealed a tiny galaxy very close to the position of the fast radio burst. We then broke down light from the galaxy into the spectrum of different frequencies that made it up. We know what part of this spectrum “should” look like, and seeing how those frequencies have changed lets us calculate how fast the galaxy is moving away from us due to the expansion of the universe – which in turn lets us figure out how old it is. These calculations confirmed that we were looking at a galaxy 10.6 billion years ago. It contains only about 10 million times the mass of our Sun, which is a tiny fraction of the mass of our own Milky Way galaxy. The host galaxy appears to be a young galaxy still forming many stars, with a very low amount of metal content, and very different from many of the larger galaxies in which most other fast radio bursts have been found. This is consistent with one theory about the source of at least some fast radio bursts – that they are produced by young, highly magnetised neutron stars called magnetars . At the same time, fast radio bursts come in different shapes and sizes, we don’t think all of them necessarily have the same kind of origin. However, observations like ours give us another piece of the puzzle. By studying the host galaxies and the environments of fast radio bursts across cosmic time, we can start to understand which types of galaxies and stellar environments produce them. The most exciting thing about this discovery, however, may not be the distance itself. As the radio signal made its way to Earth, it picked up the imprint of everything it passed through, bearing a record of the magnetic fields, changes in the space environment, and turbulence that it encountered. This makes it a gold mine of information about the cosmos that is otherwise difficult to access. This includes how electrons are distributed through the cosmic web, as well as information on magnetic fields that pervade the universe. As the signal encounters magnetic fields along the way they subtly twist the orientation of its radio waves. By measuring this twist, we learn about the magnetic field complexities across many billions of light years. FRB 20240304B does more than tell us about one distant galaxy. It gives us a new data point for studying how electrically charged matter has been distributed through the universe over cosmic time, and also how magnetised the cosmos is. Our discovery has shown for the first time that fast radio bursts were being produced all the way back to around 3 billion years after the Big Bang, during the period when the universe was most actively forming stars and galaxies. This lets us probe electrically charged matter across about 80% of cosmic history. Finding fast radio bursts at such large distances is difficult because of the combination of detecting increasingly faint bursts and identifying galaxies that are themselves extremely faint. With larger samples of distant fast radio bursts, we can use these brief flashes as cosmic signposts, revealing how matter is spread through the universe, how galaxies grow, and how the space between them changes over time. representative.title: How a rebel force held the world to ransom in a single night of chaos and panic
representative.author: Vivian Nereim, Saeed Al-Batati, Shuaib Almosawa

snapshot.title: How a rebel force held the world to ransom in a single night of chaos and panic
snapshot.evidenceText: In a matter of hours, an Iran-allied militia trounced Saudi-backed forces to take control of Yemen’s Red Sea coast. No one was able – or willing – to stop them. You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Riyadh, Saudi Arabia: In the weeks before the Iran-backed Houthi militia fanned out along Yemen’s Red Sea coast, sending their foes into a frenzied retreat, a Yemeni government commander called for help. It was obvious to the commander, Lieutenant General Tariq Saleh, that the Houthis wanted to seize his territory to reach the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, one of the most important waterways in the world. According to three Yemeni officials, he tried to warn his powerful allies in Saudi Arabia and the United States. About 10 per cent of global trade goes through the strait. Amid the US-Israeli war with Iran, both countries had an interest in preventing an Iran-linked militia from winning a perch beside it. Yet last month – when the Houthis did just that – no one was able, or willing, to stop them. The militia’s stunning triumph over the Bab el-Mandeb, which unfolded in a single night of chaos and panic, set off a cascade of events that plunged Yemen back into a war with global reverberations. This month, Saudi Arabia began a bombing campaign to help the Yemeni government reclaim the territory it lost , with intelligence and targeting assistance from the US military. Government-allied forces claimed to have since made significant gains, besieging the Houthi fighters who held the strait. It is unclear whether the Houthis’ advance will hold, or where they will stop if it does. The Saudi government has pledged to help the Yemeni government “eliminate” the Houthis. The last time they took up that mantle, a decade ago, it devolved into a bloody quagmire. This is the inside story of the battle that reignited Yemen’s war and the dark lessons it imparts for the next phase of fighting. The Houthi victory on September 10 showed how a ragtag militia transformed itself into a formidable force with advanced technology. It was a major defeat for the Yemeni government and its Saudi patrons, demonstrating that they were plagued by internal strife and unable to fight cohesively. This article is based on interviews with more than 15 people who participated in the fighting or were briefed on what happened, including soldiers, Yemeni military officers, officials with Yemen’s internationally recognised government, US officials and Houthi officials. Almost all of them spoke on condition of anonymity, either because they feared retribution from the Houthis or Saudi Arabia, or because they were not authorised to discuss what happened. Their accounts make it clear that while the Houthis’ victory last month surprised many, it was foreseeable. For months, the US military and intelligence agencies had warned Saudi Arabia about a resurgent threat from the Houthis and urged Saudi officials to unify the fractious forces of the Yemeni government, according to two senior US officials and one former senior US official. In the lead-up to his defeat, Saleh had reached out to Saudi and US officials, seeking greater support in holding back the Houthis, according to a Yemeni government official and two senior Yemeni military officers. The officers said he had asked the Saudis for air cover and the Americans for electronic jamming of Houthi communications. Saleh received little from either country, the three officials said. Even some in his own government seemed disinclined to intervene. US officials offered assistance with planning and intelligence – including on Houthi troop movements – but emphasised that their aid was limited and would not include airstrikes, the current and former US officials said. It is unclear why Saudi Arabia, equipped with US fighter jets and bombs, did not step in more intensively on its own. The Saudi government did not respond to a request for comment, nor did the White House. The Houthis, who survived a US bombing campaign last year, gained international attention during the war in the Gaza Strip by launching missiles and drones at Israel and vessels in the Red Sea. Holding territory along the Red Sea would make it even easier for the group to disrupt shipping, analysts say. Whether any foreign military campaign could have held back the militia remains an open question. Mohammed al-Bukhaiti, a Houthi political official, attributed their victory to progress they had made in developing their military capabilities throughout years of war. The Houthis are fighting “to liberate Yemen from occupation”, he said, dismissing their foes as Saudi “mercenaries”. Two Yemeni government soldiers interviewed by The New York Times said they ultimately blamed their own feckless leaders for their defeat. It was just after sundown on September 9 when everything crumbled, according to one of their comrades, who spoke on condition of anonymity, fearing retribution. He recalled how he had been stationed with other soldiers outside Mokha, a historic port city near the Bab el-Mandeb, when they received reports of Houthi fighters advancing from multiple directions. Suddenly, their communications went dark, he said, severing contact with other units. They heard shouting. “Retreat! Retreat! Retreat!” he remembered his comrades yelling. “The Houthis are already here!” The Houthis’ recent conquest belies their simpler origins. The group began in the 1990s as a religious movement focused on Zaydism, an offshoot of Shiite Islam. Its leaders later mounted an armed rebellion against Yemen’s government, saying that they were battling corruption and foreign influence. Scholars debate when Iran began supporting them, but the Houthis eventually became a key Iranian ally. In 2014, they took over Yemen’s capital, Sanaa, routing the government and starting a civil war. Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates began a disastrous military campaign to restore the government. Hundreds of thousands of people died from violence, hunger and disease. The Houthis survived, cementing their rule over northern Yemen. After a truce in 2022, the Houthis used the lull in fighting to become stronger and more self-sufficient, expanding their arsenal, analysts say. The Yemeni government did not. During the war, it had become increasingly fragmented and weak, beholden to its Saudi and UAE patrons – which were often at odds with each other. “The Yemeni government is basically a fiction at this point,” said Gregory Johnsen, a non-resident fellow at the Arab Gulf States Institute in Washington. “They spend more time fighting one another than they do the Houthis.” One of the key players in this government was Saleh. The nephew of Yemen’s former authoritarian leader, he had made plentiful enemies over the years as he seesawed from one alliance to another – siding with the Houthis, then joining the government. In Mokha, with UAE backing, he formed his own armed faction. His soldiers, numbering about 50,000, served as a bulwark against the Houthis pushing south towards the Bab el-Mandeb. Then, in January, the UAE withdrew from Yemen amid a feud with Saudi Arabia. Saudi officials consolidated their control over the government’s many factions. Once again, Saleh found himself with a new sponsor: Saudi Arabia. When the US and Israel attacked Iran in February , the Houthis appeared willing at first to sit out the war. But behind the scenes, Yemen’s truce had become a brittle stalemate. Talks aimed at a long-term peace deal – from which the Houthis hoped to gain greater authority and access to oil revenue – had stalled. Poverty in Houthi territory was dire, putting pressure on the group. They blamed Saudi Arabia and bristled at Saudi restrictions on Yemeni airspace. The tensions came to a head in July. The Houthis accused Saudi Arabia of bombing Sanaa’s airport to prevent an Iranian aircraft from landing. They declared a blockade on Saudi shipping in the Red Sea, now a crucial route for oil exports during the Iran war. They launched missiles and drones into Saudi Arabia, and the kingdom launched airstrikes on Yemen. This escalation dovetailed with the interests of Iran, where officials were pushing to widen the war with the US, raising its costs for President Donald Trump. As the Houthis put pressure on oil markets, some Yemeni government officials sensed an opportunity to solicit foreign support to fight the Houthis. Clashes reignited inside Yemen, and Houthi officials accused Saudi Arabia and their Yemeni allies of preparing a new offensive against them. Quietly, the militia readied its own plans. On August 9, the Houthis began to shower Mokha with missiles and drones, damaging the port and seeking to cut off the city’s supply line from the sea, according to two Yemeni military officers. Then, on September 3, the Houthis began a huge ground offensive. A 39-minute video released by the Houthis, which they said was filmed during fighting for control of the Red Sea coast, shows their militiamen scaling rugged mountains on foot and waving guns in jubilation. The video, which the Times was unable to independently verify, also shows the bodies of what appear to be Yemeni government fighters slumped inside vehicles. At the end, a toothless Houthi fighter vows to “pursue the enemy into their very lairs”. For more than five days, the government force held off the militia, battling in the mountains above Mokha. Eventually, the Houthis were able to push forward, with an onslaught of missiles, drones and shelling. Saudi Arabia carried out only minimal airstrikes to assist its Yemeni allies, according to the two Yemeni military officers. On the evening of September 9 and into the next morning, the government forces collapsed. In a flurry of confusion, they beat a rapid and disorganised retreat. The Houthis seized a major military camp in the foothills east of Mokha – leaving their enemies on the coastal plain exposed and vulnerable. Instead of reorganising, the government’s soldiers withdrew all the way to the southern city of Aden, handing the entire Red Sea coast, including an island inside the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, to the Houthis. Overnight, Yemen’s government had lost more than 4500 square kilometres of territory. At least 500 of Saleh’s fighters were killed and more than 1500 wounded, according to a statement by his group. The Houthi death toll is unknown. Soon after Mokha fell, Saleh and several of his comrades flew to the Saudi capital of Riyadh, according to one of the Yemeni government officials and two of the military officers. There, they decamped to a five-star hotel, where easy listening music echoed through a cavernous lobby and servers brought tea with madeleines. One of the military officers, who is close to Saleh, told a Times reporter that he was now focused on regrouping his forces and treating the wounded. Eventually, there will be an investigation into what went wrong, he said. In Yemen, Saleh’s soldiers have scattered. Some were left stranded outside Aden after fighters from other factions – ostensibly their allies – barred them from the city, according to the officer close to Saleh and another soldier. Speaking by phone from their makeshift encampment, that soldier said that they had gone days without food. In public statements, the Houthis sought to reassure the international community that they posed no threat to maritime security – only to Saudi Arabia, one of the world’s largest exporters of oil. As oil prices surged above $US100 a barrel, the Houthis began pushing to expand their territory further, promising to “liberate” all of Yemen. Last weekend, the Yemeni government’s leader, Rashad al-Alimi, declared a full-blown war against the militia. The government’s goal, he said, was to reclaim all the territory lost to the Houthis over the past 12 years. For Yemeni civilians, already facing dire poverty and hunger, the war’s return portends deeper suffering. More than 180,000 people have been displaced in recent weeks, often piling onto pick-up trucks and motorcycles as they rushed to escape. “The moment felt like doomsday, with everyone looking out for themselves,” said Hassan Sughair, a civilian who fled from a town near Mokha. “We did not even say goodbye to our neighbours, and we do not know what happened to them.” This article originally appeared in The New York Times .
