Talks aimed at a long-term peace deal – from which the Houthis hoped to gain greater authority and access to oil revenue – had stalled. Poverty in Houthi territory was dire, putting pressure on the group. They blamed Saudi Arabia and bristled at Saudi restrictions on Yemeni airspace. The tensions came to a head in July. The Houthis accused Saudi Arabia of bombing Sanaa’s airport to prevent an Iranian aircraft from landing. They declared a blockade on Saudi shipping in the Red Sea, now a crucial route for oil exports during the Iran war. They launched missiles and drones into Saudi Arabia, and the kingdom launched airstrikes on Yemen. This escalation dovetailed with the interests of Iran, where officials were pushing to widen the war with the US, raising its costs for President Donald Trump. As the Houthis put pressure on oil markets, some Yemeni government officials sensed an opportunity to solicit foreign support to fight the Houthis. Clashes reignited inside Yemen, and Houthi officials accused Saudi Arabia and their Yemeni allies of preparing a new offensive against them. Quietly, the militia readied its own plans. On August 9, the Houthis began to shower Mokha with missiles and drones, damaging the port and seeking to cut off the city’s supply line from the sea, according to two Yemeni military officers. Then, on September 3, the Houthis began a huge ground offensive. A 39-minute video released by the Houthis, which they said was filmed during fighting for control of the Red Sea coast, shows their militiamen scaling rugged mountains on foot and waving guns in jubilation. The video, which the Times was unable to independently verify, also shows the bodies of what appear to be Yemeni government fighters slumped inside vehicles. At the end, a toothless Houthi fighter vows to “pursue the enemy into their very lairs”. For more than five days, the government force held off the militia, battling in the mountains above Mokha. Eventually, the Houthis were able to push forward, with an onslaught of missiles, drones and shelling. Saudi Arabia carried out only minimal airstrikes to assist its Yemeni allies, according to the two Yemeni military officers. On the evening of September 9 and into the next morning, the government forces collapsed. In a flurry of confusion, they beat a rapid and disorganised retreat. The Houthis seized a major military camp in the foothills east of Mokha – leaving their enemies on the coastal plain exposed and vulnerable. Instead of reorganising, the government’s soldiers withdrew all the way to the southern city of Aden, handing the entire Red Sea coast, including an island inside the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, to the Houthis. Overnight, Yemen’s government had lost more than 4500 square kilometres of territory. At least 500 of Saleh’s fighters were killed and more than 1500 wounded, according to a statement by his group. The Houthi death toll is unknown. Soon after Mokha fell, Saleh and several of his comrades flew to the Saudi capital of Riyadh, according to one of the Yemeni government officials and two of the military officers. There, they decamped to a five-star hotel, where easy listening music echoed through a cavernous lobby and servers brought tea with madeleines. One of the military officers, who is close to Saleh, told a Times reporter that he was now focused on regrouping his forces and treating the wounded. Eventually, there will be an investigation into what went wrong, he said. In Yemen, Saleh’s soldiers have scattered. Some were left stranded outside Aden after fighters from other factions – ostensibly their allies – barred them from the city, according to the officer close to Saleh and another soldier. Speaking by phone from their makeshift encampment, that soldier said that they had gone days without food. In public statements, the Houthis sought to reassure the international community that they posed no threat to maritime security – only to Saudi Arabia, one of the world’s largest exporters of oil. As oil prices surged above $US100 a barrel, the Houthis began pushing to expand their territory further, promising to “liberate” all of Yemen. Last weekend, the Yemeni government’s leader, Rashad al-Alimi, declared a full-blown war against the militia. The government’s goal, he said, was to reclaim all the territory lost to the Houthis over the past 12 years. For Yemeni civilians, already facing dire poverty and hunger, the war’s return portends deeper suffering. More than 180,000 people have been displaced in recent weeks, often piling onto pick-up trucks and motorcycles as they rushed to escape. “The moment felt like doomsday, with everyone looking out for themselves,” said Hassan Sughair, a civilian who fled from a town near Mokha. “We did not even say goodbye to our neighbours, and we do not know what happened to them.” This article originally appeared in The New York Times . representative.title: FoN Campaign Defends Ghana's Expanded Fishing Zone
representative.author: Kwame Darko

snapshot.title: FoN Campaign Defends Ghana's Expanded Fishing Zone
snapshot.evidenceText: Government has doubled Ghana's Inshore Exclusive Zone from six to 12 nautical miles for artisanal fishers — now Friends of the Nation is training coastal communities in Ahanta West to stop trawlers from crossing the new line. Barely days after a canoe fisherman in Butre spoke of his fears that marine protection rules could push small-scale operators further out to sea, an environmental NGO has launched a campaign aimed at making sure the opposite happens — that industrial trawlers, not artisanal canoes, are kept out of protected waters. Friends of the Nation (FoN) launched its "Protecting Our Zone, Securing Our Future" campaign at a day-long workshop held in Upper and Lower Dixcove in the Ahanta West Municipality of the Western Region on 11 October 2026, according to the Ghana News Agency (GNA). The workshop brought together fishers, fishmongers and other industry stakeholders to explain recent regulatory changes and the boundaries of Ghana's newly expanded Inshore Exclusive Zone (IEZ). The IEZ is a stretch of sea reserved exclusively for canoe fishers and other small-scale, artisanal operators, where larger industrial vessels are barred from casting nets. According to FoN, government has extended this protected zone from six nautical miles to 12 nautical miles offshore, effectively doubling the area set aside for Ghana's coastal fishing communities. Mevuta Donkris, FoN's Executive Director, thanked government for the extension but cautioned that the new boundary would only mean something if fishers themselves remained alert, GNA reports. He warned that pair trawlers — heavy industrial vessels that fish in coordinated pairs — could still attempt to encroach on the IEZ and deplete stocks of small pelagic fish, the smaller species such as sardinella that artisanal fishers depend on for their livelihoods. Kenneth Arthur, Secretary-General of the Canoe and Fishing Gear Owners Association of Ghana (CaFGOAG), welcomed the extension and said any Chinese-owned pair trawlers fishing within the IEZ would be committing an unlawful by-catch. He noted that such encroachment had already been a problem when the protected zone was only six nautical miles, and urged fishers to stay united and vigilant now that the boundary has been pushed further out, according to GNA. Frank Eshun, an official of the Fisheries Commission in Takoradi representing the Western Regional Director, told the workshop that heavy vessels are permitted to pass through the 12-nautical-mile zone but are prohibited from fishing within it. He compared pair trawling to galamsey, describing both as ecologically destructive practices that disrupt natural ecosystems — in this case, marine life. Eshun said the Commission would continue sensitising artisanal fishers to protect their boundaries and to report any trawlers caught fishing inside the IEZ to the authorities for action, GNA reports. The campaign comes amid an ongoing crisis around declining fish catches along Ghana's coast, which has repeatedly strained the incomes of canoe fishers and fishmongers in towns like Dixcove and Butre. As Chale News reported earlier this month , some fishers worry that new marine protection measures could complicate their own access to fishing grounds even as the rules are meant to shield them from industrial competition. FoN's campaign appears designed to address that tension by ensuring the expanded zone works in fishers' favour rather than becoming another source of confusion or conflict at sea. None of the sources indicate a specific timeline for further workshops or enforcement actions beyond the Fisheries Commission's stated intention to continue sensitisation efforts and to act on reports of encroachment. It also remains unclear from available information how boundary violations will be monitored or policed in practice along the 12-nautical-mile line. representative.author: Sam Lee

snapshot.title: These women are bringing Darwin’s rheas back to Chilean Patagonia
snapshot.evidenceText: If you liked this story, share it with other people. PATAGONIA NATIONAL PARK — Chile. Mongabay traveled to Chile’s Patagonia National Park to follow a women-led team on a mission to bring 13 Darwin’s rheas back to the wild in April 2026. Working with Rewilding Chile Foundation , these dedicated rangers care for the birds around the clock, facing harsh weather, predators like pumas, illegal livestock grazing, and other threats to the park’s fragile ecosystem. For more than a century, the Chacabuco Valley, where the park is located, was dominated by sheep and cattle ranching. Fences fragmented the vast Patagonian steppes and rheas (Rhea pennata) nearly disappeared. But one of South America’s most ambitious rewilding efforts is helping to turn the tide. Tompkins Conservation, the organization behind Rewilding Chile, acquired former ranchlands and began removing thousands of kilometers of fencing, allowing native wildlife to reclaim the landscape. Now, the team is preparing for another milestone: Releasing 13 Darwin’s rheas into the wild. Mongabay followed the rangers in the days leading up to the release, documenting their preparations, the challenges they faced, and their determination to give these birds the best possible chance of survival. representative.title: Retracing the steps of Mark Dennis, the 'brilliant' barrister with a dark side - ABC News
representative.author: Charlotte Grieve, Kyle Taylor, Daryna Zadvirna

snapshot.title: Mark Dennis went from top silk and charity 'big boss' to accused predator
snapshot.evidenceText: Mark Dennis built a reputation defending accused criminals before he himself became the accused. ( ABC News: Sharon Gordon ) Warning: This article contains references to child sexual abuse and suicide. There is a small terrace house in Sydney's inner west that always gave builder Chad Loxsom an uneasy feeling. "I've been in thousands and thousands of people's houses," he said, but this one "was a little bit strange". The Leichhardt property belonged to Mark Dennis SC, a criminal defence barrister, who Loxsom said had a "weird demeanour" and was "just odd". But what he saw inside is what gnawed at him for years. "All over the walls of his house, he had dozens upon dozens upon dozens of pictures of him with little kids," he said. In some photos, Loxsom said Dennis was hugging shirtless children. Loxsom shared his suspicions with an electrician. "His gut was this guy was doing something bad with kids as well," he said. The electrician first noticed the "come back with a warrant" doormat, and then the large mirror fixed to the ceiling above Dennis's bed. But, like Loxsom, what really alarmed him was the sheer volume of photographs in almost every room, even the kitchen. "It was just disturbing. Like, these kids weren't happy," he said. Dennis was found dead in his home in Sydney's inner west in February. ( ABC News: Sissy Reyes ) Eventually, Loxsom decided to make a report with the child protection hotline. "I didn't do it straight away, which now I regret," he said. In January, Dennis came onto the police's radar again when he was searched at Sydney Airport as he returned from a trip to Cambodia. What was found on his devices led to his arrest, a raid of his house, and child abuse material charges from evidence prosecutors described as "disturbing". Dennis was released on bail, and soon after, was found dead in his home . Last week, Background Briefing and ABC Investigations revealed his death did not bring the police investigation to an end . Codenamed Operation Queenstown, Cambodian and Australian national police have been quietly probing Dennis's network and links to famous children's charity Sunrise Cambodia all year. The ABC travelled to Cambodia in June to retrace Dennis's steps to reveal the inside story of how an accused predator accumulated power within a high-profile charity and gained access to vulnerable children. In an investigation that combines a tranche of internal documents with dozens of interviews, the ABC can reveal allegations that Dennis sexually harassed a former Sunrise staff member and made teenage girls feel uncomfortable by excessive touching. Listen to Dark Menace , a new three-part investigative podcast from Background Briefing and ABC Investigations, via the ABC Listen app or wherever you get your podcasts. The claims raise important questions for all children's charities that must balance the need to fundraise with child safety, as multiple former Sunrise staff say they saw Dennis's bad behaviour but felt they could not report it. "They saw this," one former staff member told the ABC through a translator. "But they could not do anything because he's a big sponsor." A spokesperson for Sunrise said they were never aware of any complaints about Dennis and police had told them no current or former Sunrise child had been identified as one of his victims. The charity defended its child protection policies, saying the children always came first. Dennis grew up in a large family on Sydney's northern beaches, and by 2001, was a criminal defence barrister with a room at the prestigious Forbes Chambers. "You don't get to go to Forbes unless you are absolutely brilliant," says one solicitor who briefed Dennis. "He was one of those people who was married to the profession." His nickname was "Dark Menace" — a play on words that several acquaintances said reflected his personality and black sense of humour, exemplified by his "WASNTME" personalised number plate. Across his career, Dennis was known to have mentored junior lawyers and published papers under provocative titles and on topics like defending accused paedophiles and cross-examining child witnesses. Some of the legal papers authored by Dennis. ( ABC News / supplied ) "You need to watch the child witness carefully and assess matters such as intelligence, level of vocabulary and articulation, degree of self-confidence, general demeanour," he wrote in 2017. One lawyer who knew Dennis for more than a decade said he was "not shocked" by the charges because he had a reputation for sexual harassment and aggression towards women. "It's one of those situations where, and I know I'm not the only person who's thought about this, I think a lot of us in retrospect are like, 'This was actually f***ing obvious,'" he said. Three lawyers told the ABC about an incident where Dennis was intoxicated at the 2012 Aboriginal Legal Service (ALS) Christmas party in Sydney, when he lunged at a woman with an open fist. He was then banned from ALS Christmas parties. Barrister Charles Waterstreet, who worked at Forbes alongside Dennis for more than a decade until facing his own sexual misconduct allegations, described his former colleague as "very ambitious" but "an oddball". "He loved a drink, especially on Friday nights," he said. "He sort of became another personality." Forbes Chambers is on the 11th floor of a building overlooking Sydney's Hyde Park. ( ABC News: Sissy Reyes ) In 2011, Dennis began hosting legal conferences to raise funds for his charity, Reasonable Cause, that pledged to help "disadvantaged young Cambodians to further their education". Tickets cost $450, and the guest list included magistrates, silks and politicians, according to the 2024 invitation. In interviews with more than 20 sitting Forbes barristers, some were quick to defend their late colleague — insinuating the evidence was thin, based on industry rumours, and one said they did not think his charity work should be "smeared". "It did such good work. I don't think it was connected … to some sexual interest," they said. However, despite some celebrating his work and attending his legal conferences, many could not name the charity the money went to. The largest recipient of Dennis's fundraising was Sunrise Cambodia — a high-profile children's charity founded by Adelaide-born Geraldine Cox. Cox has spent decades crisscrossing the globe, and according to her 2011 report, delivering speeches to company executives in the United Arab Emirates, government officials in Australia, private schools, and lawyers like Dennis. "I flew to Sydney to address a group of lawyers at an event arranged by sponsor Mark Dennis, where over $14,000 was raised. Who said lawyers do not have hearts!" Cox wrote. Her work has been celebrated internationally. She has won awards, been praised by Australian media and rubbed shoulders with Hollywood celebrities and Australian prime ministers. Geraldine Cox's work has brought her into contact with the likes of Angelina Jolie, Brad Pitt and Anthony Albanese. ( ABC News / supplied ) Starting in 2008, Dennis personally sponsored a handful of children at Sunrise whom he visited in the orphanages each year. Over time, he backed the whole organisation — raising at least $340,000 in seven years through the legal conferences. In 2010, he also began funding and attending Sunrise's annual beach holidays to Sihanoukville, a once-sleepy Cambodian coastal town now filled with scam compounds and casinos. Itineraries for these trips obtained by the ABC show the children played football, shared meals, performed concerts and socialised with sponsors, including Dennis. Photographs from these trips show Dennis on the beach, and hugging and playing with young children at the hotel. There is no suggestion the photographs are sexual. Dennis playing with children during one of the Sunrise trips to Sihanoukville. ( ABC News / supplied ) A spokesperson for Sunrise said sponsors were not permitted to initiate contact with children. representative.title: Last call? Not for this 103-year-old bartender. | The Seattle Times

snapshot.title: Last call? Not for this 103-year-old bartender.
snapshot.evidenceText: Irvin E. Koch, at 103, has been perfecting his one-liners for decades. He deals them out quickly, with a half smile that reveals the four remaining teeth on his top gums and a flash of mischief in his clear blue eyes. After 63 years tending bar, he has his setup-pause-punch line down to a science. When a patron on a recent evening asks him whether he is the oldest bartender in the world, he doesn’t miss a beat. “Don’t ask me,” he says. “I haven’t been around the world yet.” By many unofficial accounts, Irv (as he is widely known) is indeed the world’s oldest bartender. And since 1963, he has been bartending at Club Sunset Knoll, a dive in a Baltimore suburb that is better known as Irv’s Basement Bar because, well, it’s in Irv’s basement. The waterfront house that Irv bought when John F. Kennedy was president sits at the end of a gravel driveway in Pasadena, Maryland. It has plastic-wrapped windows and a sliver of red above the gray exterior siding, as if the painter went off to fetch a ladder and never came back. When we, two Post reporters, pull into a small, otherwise empty lot on a September afternoon, Irv’s stepgrandson Jason Cook walks outside and ushers us down a concrete staircase. We step through a nondescript door. Irv’s Basement Bar looks today as it has for decades: a retro redoubt from the rest of the world above. The drinks are cheap, the lights are dim, and the jukebox is playing. Scrawled messages cover every surface at Irv’s, from its cracked bathroom walls to its tiled ceilings to its leathery chairs. (“Raise Hell, Praise Irv” reads one note not far from a haphazardly inked phallus. But mostly, people just write their names.) The bar’s round card tables are scuffed. Underneath one, a stray cheetah-print slipper lies forgotten. There are nude Polaroid photos hung next to police department patches from across the country. The pool table takes quarters, and the Smith Corona cash register is about as old as Irv himself. A large banner with his smiling face on it lords above his subterranean kingdom: “Drinking where the sun don’t shine,” it reads. The bar’s most notable feature, however, is the ever-growing collection of bras — padded, underwire, lace — that hang from the ceiling tiles like a tree canopy. They’re mostly graffitied, too, with the names of the women who left them there. The first of them, decades ago, was named Amy. “She did it, I didn’t do it,” Irv says. “Most of the girls want to do it. You probably want to do it yourself.” Cook, who is sitting nearby, has come to expect these sorts of comments. “He don’t hold back anything,” Cook, 43, says later. “That’s for sure.” Nothing here is formal, and the bar only operates on Irv time. “The hours are very simple,” he tells us later. “When the first one gets here, that’s when it opens up.” He closes whenever patrons leave, or when he gets tired. Over a few hours at Irv’s, we learn about many of his dislikes: tattoos, bar covers, the church, babies, naps (“wasting your life away”), cities (“too many people”) and credit cards (“the government can trace everything you do”). He hasn’t had a dog since he was a kid and never bought a cellphone. Irv’s penchant for “telling everybody what he thinks,” Cook says, is one of two qualities that generations of regulars appreciate most about him. The other, according to Cook, is that Irv is a genuinely kind man. When Cook was a toddler, he says, his mother became unable to care for him, and Irv and his wife took him in. Cook recently moved back to the house (with his wife and four children) to care for Irv. Born in 1923, Irv grew up poor in a south Baltimore neighborhood, largely during the Great Depression. As a teenager, he joined the Navy and served in the Philippines during World War II. His younger brother Harry followed him into the armed forces. After the war, Irv worked as a builder for Sears and as a plumber with Harry. Going into the bar business just sort of happened. The house he now lives in was built in 1912 as a summer home for a prominent Baltimore meatpacking family, and later became an inn before Irv bought it in 1963. “This was up for sale,” Irv says unsentimentally. “We needed a house, so we bought the house — and guess what? snapshot.title: Last call? Not for this 103-year-old bartender.
snapshot.evidenceText: Irvin E. Koch, at 103, has been perfecting his one-liners for decades. He deals them out quickly, with a half smile that reveals the four remaining teeth on his top gums and a flash of mischief in his clear blue eyes. After 63 years tending bar, he has his setup-pause-punch line down to a science. When a patron on a recent evening asks him whether he is the oldest bartender in the world, he doesn’t miss a beat. “Don’t ask me,” he says. “I haven’t been around the world yet.” By many unofficial accounts, Irv (as he is widely known) is indeed the world’s oldest bartender. And since 1963, he has been bartending at Club Sunset Knoll, a dive in a Baltimore suburb that is better known as Irv’s Basement Bar because, well, it’s in Irv’s basement. The waterfront house that Irv bought when John F. Kennedy was president sits at the end of a gravel driveway in Pasadena, Maryland. It has plastic-wrapped windows and a sliver of red above the gray exterior siding, as if the painter went off to fetch a ladder and never came back. We step through a nondescript door. Irv’s Basement Bar looks today as it has for decades: a retro redoubt from the rest of the world above. The drinks are cheap, the lights are dim, and the jukebox is playing. Scrawled messages cover every surface at Irv’s, from its cracked bathroom walls to its tiled ceilings to its leathery chairs. Underneath one, a stray cheetah-print slipper lies forgotten. There are nude Polaroid photos hung next to police department patches from across the country. The pool table takes quarters, and the Smith Corona cash register is about as old as Irv himself. They’re mostly graffitied, too, with the names of the women who left them there.
